children.translated_text: One, immortal, unborn, consciousness, imperishable, bliss—
Not-all [yet] all, fearless—we bow to <s>Prajāpati</s>. (MBs 1.1)

children.text:
vedānteṣu vipratipadyante vipaścitaḥ ---
kecidaprāmāṇyaṃ manyante, ātmanaḥ pramāṇāntarasiddhatve teṣāmanuvādakatvam, asiddhatve saṃbandhāgrahaṇāt, apadārthatve vākyasyāviṣayatvāt, pravṛttinivṛttyanupadeśe cāpuruṣārthatvāt /
anye tu pratipattikartavyatāprāmāṇyavyājenāprāmāṇyamevāhuḥ /
anye tu karmavidhivirodhātpratyakṣādivirodhācca śrutārthaparigrahe upacaritārthānmanyante /
tannirāsārthamucyate --- ānandamiti /
parāṃ ca devatāṃ guṇābhidhānalakṣaṇayā stutyā kāyavāṅmanaḥprahvatālakṣaṇayā ca praṇatyā pūjayati /
prakaraṇārthaṃ copakṣipati ---
vipratipattinirākaraṇamukhena vedāntānāmevaṃbhūte 'rthe prāmāṇyapratipādanādyato bhavatyeṣo 'pi prakaraṇārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Regarding the <s>Vedānta</s> [texts], the learned disagree: Some consider them non-authoritative—[arguing that] if the self is already established by other means of knowledge, [the <s>Vedānta</s> texts] are mere restatements; if [the self is] not established, then due to non-apprehension of the relation [between word and referent]; or if [the self] is not an object [of words], then the sentence has no object; and [being] without instruction on activity or cessation, they serve no human purpose. Others, under the pretext of [granting] authoritativeness for [determining] what is to be done in practice, effectively assert non-authoritativeness. Yet others, due to contradiction with injunctive ritual texts and contradiction with perception and the rest, consider them to have a figurative meaning when their literal meaning is adopted. To refute those [positions], it is said: '<s>Ānanda</s>' (Bliss). And [the author] praises the supreme deity through a eulogy characterized by the description of [its] qualities, and through prostration characterized by the humility of body, speech, and mind

children.text:
atra kecit ---
ānandātmakatve brahmaṇaḥ, ānandarāgānmumukṣupravṛttiḥ syāt /
rāganibandhanā ca pravṛttiḥ saṃsārabījamiti na muktaye syāt /
śāntasya dāntasya cātmani darśanamucyate /
na cānandānurāgātpravartamānaḥ śānto bhavati /
tasmātsakaladuḥkhātige brahmatattve duḥkhebhya udvignaḥ sukhebhyaśca vītarāgaḥ pravartamāno mucyate /
ānandaśrutayaśca sakaladuḥkhātikramamevāhuḥ /
dṛṣṭo hi kṣudduḥkhādinivṛttau sukhaśabdaḥ /
saiva ca sukhamityanye /
na cāśmādau prasaṅgaḥ, pratyagvṛtterupalabhyamānāyāḥ sukhatvāt, tadviśiṣṭātmopalabdhervā /
tān pratyāha --- ānandamiti /
na tāvadduḥkhanivṛttireva sukham, yugapatsukhaduḥkhayordarśanātsaṃtāpavataḥ śītahrade nimagnārdhakāyasya /
atha

children.translated_text: KKS 2

children.text:
satyapyanimagnārdhakāyaduḥkhe itarasyābhāvātsukhamiti, kumbhīpāke pacyamānasya narakāntaraduḥkhābhāvātsukhitvaprasaṅgaḥ /
ekendriyadvāraduḥkhasya ca indriyāntardvāraduḥkhābhāvāt /
itaśca, aduḥkhasyāpi viṣayaviśeṣasaṃparkātsaṃvedyāhlādotpatteḥ /
yatrāpi duḥkhavigamaḥ, tatrāpi na tanmātrameva sukham, annapānaviśeṣopādānāt /
duḥkhavigamo hi yaistairannapānaiḥ sidhyati /
na ca sa viśeṣavān, yena tadviśeṣāya tatsādhanaviśeṣo 'pekṣyeta /
sukhe tvatiśayavattvādyuktā tatsādhanātiśayāpekṣā /
children.translated_text: Even granting that when half the body is not submerged [in boiling water], pleasure [exists] due to the absence of the other [half's suffering]—there would be the absurd consequence that one being cooked in the <s>Kumbhīpāka</s> hell is happy due to the absence of the suffering of other hells. Likewise [there would be happiness] due to the absence of suffering through one sense-door when suffering exists through another. Furthermore, even for one who is not suffering, from contact with a particular object, a perceptible delight arises. And even where there is the cessation of suffering, that cessation alone is not pleasure, because of the adoption of specific food and drink. For the cessation of suffering is accomplished by those very foods and drinks. And that [cessation] is not differentiated, such that a differentiation of its means would be required. But since pleasure has degrees of intensity, it is fitting that a corresponding differentiation of its means be expected.

Here, some [object]: If <s>Brahman</s> has the nature of bliss (<s>ānanda</s>), then the seeker of liberation would engage [toward it] out of desire for bliss. And engagement rooted in desire (<s>rāga</s>) is the seed of <s>saṃsāra</s>, and thus would not lead to liberation. For [the <s>śruti</s>] states that one who is tranquil and self-controlled sees [<s>Brahman</s>] in the self. And one who engages out of attachment to bliss is not tranquil. Therefore, the one who is distressed by sufferings and free from attachment even to pleasures, engaging toward the reality of <s>Brahman</s> that has transcended all suffering—that one is liberated. And the <s>śruti</s> passages on bliss also speak only of the transcendence of all suffering. For the word 'pleasure' (<s>sukha</s>) is seen [used] in the cessation of the suffering of hunger and the like. And that very [cessation] is pleasure, according to others. Nor is there the consequence [of attributing pleasure] to a stone, since the inward-turned [consciousness] is observed

children.text:
yadapi manyante ---
yadāpi nānyadduḥkhaṃ nivartyam, tadāpi kāmasya duḥkhātmakatvāttannibarhaṇarūpaṃ sukham /
tatrāpyakāmasya viṣayaviśeṣopabhoge na sukhitā syāt /
bhavati ca madhyastho 'pi ramaṇīyaviṣayasaṃparke hlādavān /
syādetat ---
yatraiva kāmaḥ sa eva sukhayati viṣayaḥ, netaraḥ /
tasmātkāmanivṛttyaiva viṣayāḥ sukhayitāraḥ /
anyathā ya ekasya sukhaḥ sa sarvasya syāt /
kāmanivṛttyā tu sukhatve yatra yasya kāmo 'bhiruciḥ sa eva tasya sukha iti yujyate /
tatrākāmasyāpi viṣayaviśeṣopabhogātkāmābhivyaktau tannivṛttau tatsukhitvamiti /
tadapyasāram, yato viṣayopabhogā nāvaśyaṃ kāmanibarhaṇāḥ /
uktaṃ hi ‘na jātu kāmaḥ kāmānāmupabhogena śāmyati'; iti /
tathā ‘bhogābhyāsamanu vivardhante rāgāḥ, kauśalāni cendriyāṇām'; iti /
viṣayadoṣadarśanādapi ca kāmanivṛttiḥ, tatropabhogatulya āhlādaḥ syāt /
samāne ca prārthitārthalābhe pramodabhedo na syāt, kāmanivṛtteraviśeṣāt /
syādetat ---
kāmātireke tannivṛttau sukhātiśayābhimānaḥ, itaratrānyatheti /
tacca na /
kāmātirekātprayasyantamavāpto 'rtho na tathā prīṇayati, yathāprārthito vinā prayāsādupanataḥ /
tathāhi ---
kleśādavāpto 'yamiti na tena tathā prīyate, yathānāśaṃsitopanatena /
kāmābhāvamātre ca sukhe 'kāmitaviṣayopabhoge na bhogāvasthāyāḥ pūrvāpare avasthe bhidyeyātām /
kāmapradhvaṃse vā parāvasthā na bhidyeta /
bhogāvasthāyāṃ prabuddhādhvastakāma eveti cetpūrvā

children.translated_text: KKS 3

children.text:
parayorapi dvayoravasthayostarhi sukhī itaratra duḥkhītyanubhavaviruddhamāpadyeta /
aprāptaśca smaraṇaviparivartī viṣayaḥ kāmasyodbodhakaḥ, prāpto nivartakaḥ /
prāptasyodbodhatve na tato nivṛttiḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: Then, in those two other states as well, the absurd consequence would arise, contradicting experience, that one who is happy [in one state] would be unhappy in another. And an object that is unattained, [merely] recollected in memory, arouses desire; [but when] attained, it removes [desire]. If the attained [object] were to arouse [desire], there would be no cessation [of desire] from it.

As for what [they] think: 'Even when there is no other suffering to be removed, since desire (<s>kāma</s>) itself is of the nature of suffering, pleasure consists in its eradication'—in that case too, for one without desire, there would be no happiness in the enjoyment of particular objects. Yet even one who is indifferent experiences delight in contact with an attractive object. [One might say]: Only that object toward which there is desire brings pleasure, not another. Therefore, objects bring pleasure only through the cessation of desire. Otherwise, what is pleasurable for one would be so for all. But if pleasure consists in the cessation of desire, then [it is fitting that] that toward which one has desire and inclination—that alone is pleasurable for that person. [But] even for one without desire, from the enjoyment of particular objects, desires arise

children.text:
na ca yatra kāmastatra sukham, manorathaśatārthitasyāpyupabhogena kasyacidduḥkhitvadarśanāt /
sukhapūrvakastu kāmaḥ, anubhūtatadbhāve taddarśanāt /
yāpi kācidananubhūte 'pi jātiviśeṣabhājāṃ kāmapravṛttiḥ sāpi prāgbhavīyānubhavanibandhanā /
yathā ca kasyacitkvacitkāmo jātibhedādinimittaḥ, tathā kiñcitkasyacitsukhamiti nāvyavasthā /
api ca kāmanivṛttyāpi keciddūyante, tadabhāve viṣayopabhogasāmarthyābhāvāt /
na tarhi nivṛttikāmāḥ /
nivṛttikāmā viṣayaṃ prati, tasya kutaścinnimittādanupabhogyatvāt /
kimiti tarhi dūyante? anubhūtacarasya tajjanmanaḥ sukhasyāprāpteḥ /
yathā pittādyupahatendriyā viśiṣṭebhyo 'nnapānebhyo nivṛttikāmāḥ, tathaiva kāmanivṛttyā tapyante /
tatrānubhūtacaratajjanmāhlādavicchedānnānyo hetuḥ /
tasmātpratyātmavedanīyasukhapratyākhyānamayuktam /
sukhasaṅgijanopacchandanāya tu tatrabhavadbhirvarṇitamiti paśyāmaḥ /
tadevaṃ duḥkhanivṛtteranyatsukham /
sa cānandaśabdasya mukhyo 'rthaḥ /
śabdapramāṇake ca yathāśabdaṃ pratipattiryuktā /
children.translated_text: Nor is there pleasure wherever there is desire, since it is observed that someone, even though desired a hundred times in imagination, is still unhappy upon [actual] enjoyment. Rather, desire is preceded by pleasure, since desire is observed when the experience of that [pleasure] has been had. And whatever engagement of desire arises in those belonging to a particular birth-class even toward what has not been experienced—that too is rooted in experience in a previous life. And just as someone's desire for something is due to causes such as difference of birth, so too something is pleasurable for someone—thus there is no indeterminacy. Moreover, some suffer even from the cessation of desire, because in its absence there is no capacity for the enjoyment of objects. Then [one objects]: they are not those whose desire has ceased. [Reply]: Their desire has ceased with respect to the object, because, for some reason, it has become unenjoyable for them.

children.text:
na ca rāganibandhanā tatra pravṛttiḥ /
na hīcchāmātraṃ rāgaḥ /
avidyākṣiptamabhūtaguṇābhiniveśaṃ rāgamācakṣate /
tattvadarśanavaimalyāttu tattve cetasaḥ prasādo 'bhirucirabhīcchā na rāgapakṣe vyavasthāpyate, yathā saṃsārāsāratātattvadarśananiṣpanno nodvegastato dveṣapakṣe /
anyathā sarvaduḥkhātige 'pi tattve taddveṣanibandhanā pravṛttiriti saṃsārānubandhaḥ syāt /
api ca dṛṣṭaparotkarṣarāgibhyo 'pīndriyajaya upadiśyate sādhanatvena kāmādityāgātmakaḥ, tathehāpi bhaviṣyati /
kathaṃ ca tatra samīhitetaraviṣayābhiṣvaṅganiṣedhaḥ? sarvaniṣedhe 'pravṛttidarśanāt /
tathottamasukharāgāditarasmādupanatādapi nivṛttiḥ /
tathā coktam ---
‘kāmātmatā na praśastā na caivehāstyakāmatā'; iti /
children.translated_text: And the engagement there is not rooted in attachment (<s>rāga</s>). For mere desire (<s>icchā</s>) is not <s>rāga</s>. They define <s>rāga</s> as fixation on unreal qualities, impelled by ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). But the clarity of mind toward reality (<s>tattva</s>), the delight, the favorable inclination, arising from the purity of the vision of truth—these are not classified under the category of <s>rāga</s>; just as the disenchantment born from the vision of the truth of <s>saṃsāra</s>'s worthlessness is not [classified] under the category of aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>). Otherwise, even in the case of a reality that has transcended all suffering, engagement rooted in aversion toward that [reality] would result in bondage to <s>saṃsāra</s>. Moreover, even for those who are seen to have attachment to the excellence of others, the conquest of the senses is prescribed as a means, consisting of the renunciation of desires and the like; the same will apply here as well. And how could the desired [goal] there

children.text:
syādetat ---
ānandaścedbrahmaṇi saṃvedyaḥ, karturanyatkarmeti dvaitaprasaṅgaḥ /
kartṛkarmabhāvaśca na kriyāṃ karaṇaṃ cāntareṇa yataḥ /
tataḥ ‘ānandaṃ brahma';

children.translated_text: KKS 4

children.text:
iti ca na syāt /
tadvattayā vyapadeśe advitīyamiti na yujyate /
asaṃvedane sannapyasatkalpa iti vyarthaṃ tatsaṃkīrtanam /
puruṣārthatvāya hi tatsaṃkīrtanam, asaṃvedyaśca kathaṃ puruṣārthaḥ? ucyate ---
phalavatkartṛvaccedaṃ draṣṭavyam /
tathā hi ---
pramāṇasya phalamarthāntaramanarthāntaraṃ vā sarvaparīkṣakaiḥ pratijñāyate prajñāyate ca /
na ca tadasaṃvedyam, tadasaṃvedyatve sarvāsaṃvedyatvaprasaṅgāt, tatkṛtatvātsaṃvedyabhāvasya bhāvānām /
na ca saṃvedyam, phalāntarānupalabdheranavasthāprasaṅgācca /
tasmātsaṃvedyam, ātmaprakāśatvāt /
asaṃvedyaṃ ca, viṣayavatkarmabhāvābhāvāt /
yathā ca kartaryātmanyasaṃvedye saṃvideva na syāt /
na hi tadaivaṃ bhavati ---
mayedaṃ viditam ---
iti /
na hyātmāsaṃvedyaḥ phale viṣaye cānusaṃdhātuṃ śakyaḥ /
ananusaṃdhāne ca svaparasaṃvedyayoḥ ko 'tiśayaḥ? na ca saṃvedyaḥ, karmatve karturvyatirekaprasaṅgāt anātmatvaprasaṅgācca /
tasmādātmaprakāśataiva tasya saṃvedyatā /
tathā brahmaṇaḥ svātmaprakāśasyānandasvabhāvo na saṃvedyaḥ, karmatvābhāvāt /
na cāsaṃvedyaḥ, svaprakāśatvāt /
‘tatkena kaṃ paśyet?'ityapi niṣedhaḥ karmaviṣayaḥ /
tathā hi sarvakarmapratyastamayahetuka eva sa ucyate ‘yadāsya sarvamātmaivābhūt'; iti /
children.translated_text: would not be [correct]. And if [<s>Brahman</s>] is designated through such [a designation of bliss], then 'without a second' would not be fitting. If [bliss is] not experienced, even though existing, it would be like what does not exist—so the proclamation of it would be pointless. For the proclamation of it is for the sake of [establishing] the goal of human life (<s>puruṣārtha</s>), and how can what cannot be experienced be a goal of human life? [Reply]: This should be viewed like the fruit [of knowledge] in relation to the agent. For: The fruit of a means of knowledge is acknowledged and recognized by all examiners as being either something different [from the cognition] or not something different. And it is not unexperienced, because if it were unexperienced, there would be the consequence that everything would be unexperienced, since the experienceable nature of things is produced by that [cognition]. And it is not [something separately] experienced either, because of the non-apprehension of another fruit and the consequence of infinite regress

[One might object]: If bliss in <s>Brahman</s> is something to be experienced, then there would be the absurd consequence of duality, since the object of action is different from the agent. And the agent-object relation does not [hold] without an action and an instrument. Therefore, '<s>Ānandaṃ Brahma</s>' (Bliss is <s>Brahman</s>)

children.text:
anye manyante ---
dvividhā dharmāḥ ---
bhāvarūpā abhāvarūpāśceti /
tatrābhāvarūpā nādvaitaṃ vighnanti, yathā ---
‘ekamamṛtamajam'; iti /
na hi bhedodayavyayānāṃ nivṛttiḥ kiñcidvastu, yena dvaitamāvahet /
ānandaśca yadi bhāvaḥ, tasya dharmitve vijñānaṃ dharmaḥ syāt /
atha vijñānaṃ dharmirūpam, ānando dharmaḥ /
na hyekasya dve rūpe yujyete, virodhāt /
tatra ‘vijñānamānandaṃ brahma'; iti bhāvarūpayorānandabrahmaṇordharmadharmiṇorbhedādadvaitavighātaḥ /
syādetat ---
dharmo 'pi dharmiṇo na bhinnaḥ, bhede gavāśvavaddharmadharmibhāvānupapatteḥ /
tadasat, abhede 'pi dharmirūpavattadanupapatteḥ /
tasmātkathañcidbhinno dharmaḥ /
tathā cātyantikabhedābhāvaśrutiḥ ‘ekamevādvitīyam'; iti na yujyate /
evaṃ yo 'pyekasya rūpadvayaṃ pratipadyate /
tasmādvijñānātmano brahmaṇo duḥkhābhāvopādhirevānandaśabdaḥ,

children.translated_text: KKS 5

children.text:
yathā ---
sthūlābhāvādyupādhayaḥ ‘asthūlamanaṇvahrasvam'ityādayaḥ śabdāḥ /
na ca vijñānānandayorekatvameva, śabdadvayaprayogavaiyarthyāt /
kathaṃ cāparyāyaśabdābhidheya ekatvam? tasmādduḥkhoparama evānandaśabdasya brahmaṇyartha iti /
children.translated_text: [different from] the property-bearer. For example, limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhis</s>) such as non-grossness are [expressed by] words such as 'not gross, not fine, not short' and the rest. Nor is there absolute identity between consciousness and bliss, since the use of two words would be pointless. And how can oneness be the meaning of non-synonymous words? Therefore, the word 'bliss' in relation to <s>Brahman</s> means only the cessation of suffering.

Others think: <s>Dharmas</s> (properties) are twofold—those having the nature of a positive entity (<s>bhāva</s>) and those having the nature of an absence (<s>abhāva</s>). Among these, those having the nature of absence do not violate non-duality, as [stated]: 'One, immortal, unborn.' For the cessation of division, origination, and destruction is not some [positive] entity that would introduce duality. And if bliss is a positive entity, then if it is a property, consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) would be the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>). If consciousness is the property-bearer, then bliss is the property. For it is not fitting for one [entity] to have two forms, due to contradiction. Therefore, in '<s>vijñānamānandaṃ brahma</s>' ('consciousness-bliss is <s>Brahman</s>'), since bliss and <s>Brahman</s>, both being positive entities, are different as property and property-bearer, non-duality is violated. [One might say]: A property too is not

children.text:
atrocyate ---
viśiṣṭasyāhlādātmanaḥ prakāśasya cāndramasasyeva śabdadvayena pratipādanānna doṣaḥ /
yathā ca ---
prakṛṣṭaḥ prakāśaḥ savitā ---
iti /
na ca prakṛṣṭaprakāśaśabdayoḥ paryāyatvam /
atha ca eka evābhyāmarthaviśeṣaḥ pratipādyate prakāśaviśeṣaḥ /
na hi prakarṣo 'nyaḥ prakāśarūpātsavitari, na prakāśarūpo vā prakarṣāt, api tu prakāśabhedaḥ śabdadvayopāyaḥ pratīyate /
tathā ‘vijñānamānandaṃ brahma'; ityānandabhedo vijñānabhedo vā brahmarūpamiti śabdadvayenāvagamyate /
paramatāmapyasya kecitsādhanapāratantryalakṣaṇāyāḥ kṣayitālakṣaṇāyāśca duḥkhatāyā abhāvānmanyante /
tadapi yathāśabdaṃ pratipatteḥ śabdapramāṇake 'rthe nānumanyante /
na hi svarūpataḥ paramatāsaṃbhave virodhyasaṃsargādupacaritā sā yuktā bhavitum /
tasmādātmaprakāśaprakṛṣṭātmasvabhāvameva brahmeti yuktam /
evaṃ ca laukikānanda etasya mātreti yujyate, avacchedāt /
duḥkhanivṛttau tu duryojametat /
itaścānandasvabhāva ātmā, parapremāspadatvāt /
śrūyate hi parapremāspadatvam- ‘tadetatpreyaḥ putrāt'; iti /
pratīyate ca /
tathā hi ---
sarvasyeyamātmāśīḥ kṛmerapi ‘mā na bhūvam, bhūyāsam'; iti /
sā ca priye 'vakalpate /
premā ca sukhātmani /
na duḥkhe, nobhayarūparahite, dveṣādupekṣaṇācca /
anye tu suṣupte ‘sukhamahamasvāpsam'; iti parāmarśādātmani sukhānubhavamāhuḥ /
na hyananubhave parāmarśa evaṃ syāt, suṣuptābhyupagamaśca /

children.translated_text: KKS 6

children.text:
na cānyathānubhave sukhamiti parāmarśaḥ /
na ca tatrātmano 'nyadanubhavanīyamasti /
tathā cāharaharbrahmalokāvāptiḥ śrūyate /
tatrānya āhuḥ ---
duḥkhoparamādapi tathā parāmarśasiddhernaikāntataḥ sukhitvasiddhiḥ /
tān pratyāhuḥ ---
anyathābhāve 'vagate duḥkhoparamanimittaḥ sukhaśabda iti yujyate, anyathā mukhyārthataiva yuktā /
tatrāhuḥ ---
ubhayathā vyapadeśasya darśanādupapatteśca na vyapadeśamātrādarthasiddhirityalamativistareṇa /
children.translated_text: Nor is there a recognition "this is pleasure" in an experience that is otherwise. Nor is there anything other than the self to be experienced there. And thus, the daily attainment of <s>Brahmaloka</s> (the world of Brahman) is heard in scripture. Regarding this, others say: Since recognition is established even from the mere cessation of suffering, the establishment of being happy is not absolute. To them it is replied: When the absence of an alternative is understood, it is proper that the word 'pleasure' is occasioned by the cessation of suffering; otherwise, the primary meaning itself is appropriate. To this they say: Since usage is seen in both ways, and since both are logically possible, the establishment of meaning cannot be determined from usage alone — enough of excessive elaboration.

To this we reply: There is no fault in the designation of a distinguished [entity]—delight in its own nature and luminosity—through two words, just like moonlight. For example: 'Eminent brilliance is the sun.' The words 'eminent' and 'brilliance' are not synonyms. Yet a single specific meaning—a specific [kind of] brilliance—is conveyed by both. For eminence in the sun is not something other than the nature of brilliance, nor is the brilliance-nature [something] other than eminence; rather, a [specific] distinction of brilliance is understood through the two words as a means. Likewise, from '<s>vijñānamānandaṃ brahma</s>' ('consciousness-bliss is <s>Brahman</s>'), a distinction of bliss or a distinction of consciousness is understood as the nature of <s>Brahman</s> through the two words. [We shall demonstrate] its supremacy also

children.translated_text: Verse 7 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:

iti /

syādetat ---
aikātmye tadvadeva dehāntarabhogānusandhānaṃ syāt /
anyadidānīmetat /
asti tāvadbhogavyavasthā /
api ca tatrāpi na pradeśaḥ pradeśāntaravedanāmanusaṃdadhāti, tathehāpi na jīvo jīvāntaravedanāmanusaṃdadhātīti samānam /
tathā maṇikṛpāṇadarpaṇādiṣu sukhādīnāṃ varṇasaṃsthānabhedavyavasthānamupalabhyate bhedābhāve 'pi /
evaṃ ca muktasaṃsārivibhāgo 'pyupapannaḥ /

yathā malīmase darpaṇatale malīmasaṃ mukhaṃ viśuddhe viśuddhaṃ darpaṇarahitaṃ ca gamyamānaṃ tadupādhidoṣāsaṃpṛktam /

na copacaritātkāryamupapadyate /
na hyupacaritāgnibhāvo māṇavako dahati /
udāhṛtā tu vyavasthā /
satyam /
vibhramo hi saḥ /
atrāpi vibhramatvaṃ na daṇḍavāritam /
kalpito 'pi cāhidaṃśo maraṇakāryāya kalpate, pratisūryakaśca prakāśakāryāya /
children.translated_text: As for the argument from the regularity of experience, to that it is replied: Since the regularity of experience is established even from an imagined difference, this argument is worthless. For instance: Even in a single, all-pervading self, the regularity of experience based on imagined difference is observed, whether the self is of the size of the body or atomic in size — 'I have pain in my foot, I have pain in my head.' For the foot or the head has no connection with sensation, being non-conscious. Even for those who hold the self to be body-sized, it is not the parts alone that are the locus of sensation, for then the self would be devoid of it. One might say: If there is a single self, then there would be recollection of experiences in other bodies just as there is within one body. This is a different matter. The regularity of experience exists in any case. Moreover, even there a part does not recollect the sensation of another part; likewise here too, one <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) does not recollect the sensation of another <s>jīva</s> — the situation is the same. Similarly, in gems, swords, mirrors, and the like, the regularity of different colors and shapes of pleasure and other experiences is observed even in the absence of real difference. And thus the distinction between the liberated and the bound is also explained. For even a single self, being associated with pleasure, pain, and the like in certain locations, is understood as if bound there and as if liberated elsewhere — just as a face appears dirty in a dirty mirror surface, clean in a clean one, and when perceived without a mirror, is understood as untouched by the defects of those limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>). One might object: Imagination is a property of the cognizer's cognition and cannot establish a real entity. Surely things do not transform in accordance with the cognizer's cognition. Nor can an effect arise from what is merely figurative — a boy who is figuratively called fire does not burn. But the regularity cited is established. True. For that is an illusion. And here too, the status of being an illusion is not barred by any rule. Even an imagined snakebite can produce the effect of death, and a reflected sun can produce the effect of illumination.

Here some argue: Because of the regularity of experience, because the distinction between the liberated and the bound is logically possible, because the power of seeing has purpose, because of the contradiction of its operation upon itself, because the seer is inferred from the seen, and because distinctions of sound and the like are perceived just as the distinctions of pleasure, pain, and delusion in the seen — they consider the scripture of oneness to be figurative, based on the absence of distinction of class, space, and time. 'The self alone is all this' — this too is figurative, based on the relation of purpose. To them it is replied: It is one. '<s>Indra</s> through <s>māyā</s> (illusion) moves in many forms' — here the apprehension of manifold forms is clearly shown to be rooted in <s>māyā</s>. How then can oneness be said to be figurative? Likewise, the negation of plurality is explicit: 'There is no plurality whatsoever here.' And there is censure of the perception of plurality: 'He goes from death to death.' And the non-existence of the perception of difference — the perception of difference is like an illusion — 'He who sees as if there were plurality here' — the word 'as if' (<s>iva</s>) reveals this, not that oneness is figuratively superimposed. Let there be oneness through figurative usage if you wish, but there is no removal of real plurality. If it be said that it too is spoken of only figuratively — no, because there is no purpose. Figurative usage requires both an occasion and a purpose. And we see no purpose in the figurative expression of the removal of plurality. And from the converse: The removal of plurality would be figuratively expressed either for worldly prosperity or for ultimate liberation. For it, by removing the distinction of means and end, and by manifesting the sense of self everywhere, would be contradictory to those very goals. For one who has withdrawn from everything, that it is liberation — this is non-contradictory. Likewise, from 'One only, without a second' — through the emphatic particle (<s>eva</s>) and the word 'second' (<s>advitīya</s>), by the repeated statement of that very meaning, the scripture is seen to aim at the negation of difference in every respect. For in repetition, there is emphasis of meaning, as in 'Oh how beautiful, oh how beautiful!' — not diminution. Thus the claim of figurative usage is far-fetched.

children.translated_text: Verse 8 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
vivitkasvabhāvayorasaṃsṛṣṭaparasparasvarūpayorasambaddhayoḥ kīdṛśo draṣṭṛdṛśyabhāvaḥ /
na hi cityāsaṃsṛṣṭaṃ cetitamiti yujyate /
ekāntaḥkaraṇasaṃkrāntāvastyeva sambandha iti cet, na, citeḥ śuddhatvādapariṇāmādapratisaṃkramācca /
dṛśyā buddhiścitisannidhestacchāyayā vivartata iti cet, atha keyaṃ tacchāyatā? atadātmanastadavabhāsaḥ /
na tarhi paramārthato dṛśyaṃ dṛśyate /
paramārthataścādṛśyamānaṃ draṣṭṛvyatiriktamastīti durbhaṇam /
yo 'pi manyate ---
dṛśyatayaiva dṛśyaṃ vyavasthāpyate, na sambandhena /
darśanaṃ ca ‘idam'iti parāgrūpaviṣayam /
sa vaktavyaḥ ---
satyaṃ parāgrūpaviṣayam /
tattvekasyaivātmanastathā tathā vipariṇāmādvivartanādvā darpaṇatala ivātmanaḥ /
tathā hi darpaṇatalasthamātmānaṃ vibhaktamivātmanaḥ pratyeti /
citestu vibhaktamasaṃsṛṣṭaṃ tayā cetyata iti duravagamam /
evaṃ ca draṣṭuravyatireko dṛśyasyāmnāyate ---
‘ātmani vijñāte sarvamidaṃ vijñātaṃ bhavati'; iti /
tasmātsuṣṭhūktamekamiti /
children.translated_text: What kind of seer-seen relation can there be between two things that are of distinct natures, whose mutual essences are unmixed, and that are unconnected? For it is not proper that what is unmixed with consciousness should be cognized. If it be said that there is indeed a connection through their both entering one inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) — no, because consciousness is pure, does not undergo transformation, and does not transmigrate. If it be said that the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), being seen, appears to transform through the proximity of consciousness as if by its reflection — then what is this 'being a reflection of it'? It is the appearance as that which is not its nature. Then the seen is not truly seen in the ultimate sense. And it is difficult to maintain that what is not ultimately seen exists as separate from the seer. Even one who thinks that the seen is established by its very nature of being seen, not by any relation, and that seeing has an object that is external in form — to him it should be said: True, the object is external in form. But that is through the transformation or apparent modification of a single self in various ways, like a mirror surface. For one perceives oneself reflected in a mirror surface as if separate from oneself. But that consciousness should cognize something separate and unmixed with it — that is difficult to comprehend. And thus the non-difference of the seen from the seer is declared in scripture: 'When the self is known, all this becomes known.' Therefore it is well said: it is one.

As for the claim that the seer is inferred from the seen, and therefore there is difference between seer and seen, and that plurality follows from the perception of distinctions of pleasure and the like in the seen — that too is unfounded. It has been said that when the seer is not self-luminous, there can be no establishment of the seen. And the perception of distinction in the seen does not exist, because the means of knowledge does not delimit — this will be explained later. And the power of seeing has purpose through its use for the self itself. Nor is there contradiction in its operation upon itself — as with a lamp, and as with the means of knowledge and its result, as has been stated. Moreover, this very relation of seer and seen is possible only in oneness, through the transformation or apparent modification (<s>vivartana</s>) of the seer, who is of the nature of consciousness, in various ways. But in plurality,

children.translated_text: Verse 9 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
athāvidyā na brahmaṇaḥ svabhāvaḥ, arthāntaraṃ brahmaṇa āpadyeta /
na vā syāt, tatra kiṃ nivartyam? atha matam ---
agrahaṇamavidyā, sā kathamarthāntaraṃ syāt? na cānivartyā, sarvapramāṇavyāpārāṇāmagrahaṇanivṛttyarthatvāt /
tadapyayuktam /
tattvāgrahaṇātmikayā vidyayā nivartyate /
sā ca nityā brahmaṇi /
na ca brahmaṇo 'nyo 'sti, yasya tattvāgrahaṇaṃ brahmaṇi prayatnalabhyayā vidyayā nivartyeta /
brahmaṇi tu yugapadgrahaṇāgrahaṇe vipratiṣiddhe /
avipratiṣedhe vā na kadācidavidyā nivartyeta /
yasya tu viparyayagrahaṇamavidyā, tasya brahmaṇaḥ svabhāvaścetsa nityaḥ kathaṃ nivartyeta? asvabhāvaścedarthāntaramāpadyeta /
kasya ca taditi vācyam, brahmaṇo 'nyasyābhāvāt /
brahmaṇa eveti cet, vipratiṣedhaḥ, tasya vidyāsvarūpatvāt /
avipratiṣedhe vā kena nivṛttiḥ?
children.translated_text: Now, if <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is not the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, it would become something other than <s>Brahman</s>. Or it would not exist at all — in that case, what is to be removed? If one thinks that non-apprehension is <s>avidyā</s>, how could it be something other? Nor is it irremovable, because the operation of all means of knowledge is for the purpose of removing non-apprehension. But this too is improper. It is removed by knowledge whose nature is the non-apprehension of reality. And that is eternal in <s>Brahman</s>. And there is no one other than <s>Brahman</s> whose non-apprehension of reality in <s>Brahman</s> could be removed by knowledge obtained through effort. In <s>Brahman</s>, apprehension and non-apprehension simultaneously would be contradictory. Or if there is no contradiction, then <s>avidyā</s> would never be removed. For one who holds that erroneous apprehension is <s>avidyā</s>: if it is the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, then being eternal, how could it be removed? If it is not its nature, it would become something other. And it must be said whose it is, since there is nothing other than <s>Brahman</s>. If it is <s>Brahman</s>'s itself, there is a contradiction, since <s>Brahman</s>'s nature is knowledge. Or if there is no contradiction, by what would it be removed?

Those who hold the doctrine of momentary consciousness (<s>kṣaṇikajñāna</s>) as the self say that the attainment of <s>Brahman</s> consists in the cessation of knowledge, characterized by the complete eradication of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) along with their latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>). And thus it is heard in scripture: 'After death there is no consciousness.' Others, however, say it is characterized by the arising of pure knowledge, freed from the surge of object-forms, due to the complete destruction of all latent impressions. For if it is beginningless and endless, then there is nothing to be removed or added, and thus the scriptures aimed at that and the practices directed toward that would be purposeless. For if its nature is knowledge, then nothing needs to be removed or attained, since ignorance is absent and knowledge is present. If its nature is ignorance, then since that is eternal, there would be abandonment of its former nature and no advent of another nature. Likewise even if it has both natures — since knowledge is already attained and ignorance cannot be destroyed. To them he replies: It is immortal and unborn. Nor is there purposelessness of the scriptures aimed at liberation and the practices directed toward it, because ignorance is removable. And in all philosophical systems, ignorance, though beginningless, is accepted as capable of being destroyed. We do not say that what is beginningless cannot be destroyed — rather, that the nature of the eternal <s>Brahman</s> cannot be destroyed.

children.text:
atrocyate ---
nāvidyā brahmaṇaḥ svabhāvaḥ, nārthāntaram, nātyantamasatī, nāpi satī /

avabhāsamātraṃ tu syāt /

children.translated_text: Verse 10 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
śūnyatve svayaṃ nivṛttatvāt /
evaṃ ca nādvaitahānam, na nivartanīyasyābhāvo vā /
children.translated_text: In the case of voidness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), it is self-annulled. And thus there is neither loss of non-duality, nor absence of that which is to be removed.

To this it is replied: <s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance) is not the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, nor is it something other, nor is it absolutely non-existent, nor is it existent. Thus this <s>avidyā</s> is called <s>māyā</s> (illusion), <s>mithyā</s> (falsity), false appearance. If it were the nature of something, whether different or non-different, it would be ultimately real — and then it would not be <s>avidyā</s>. If it were absolutely non-existent, like a sky-flower, it could not be a factor in practical activity. Therefore it is indescribable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>). And all philosophical schools must accept this. For instance: For the <s>Śūnyavādin</s> (Mādhyamika), if it exists, perception would be veridical — it would not be <s>avidyā</s>. If it were equal to a sky-flower, it could not be a factor in practical activity. Even for the <s>Vijñānamātravādin</s> (Yogācāra), given the reality of knowledge as it appears, there is no denial of objects; since the external appearance of the knowable form — blue, yellow, and so forth — cannot be denied, and if it were absolutely non-existent, external appearance would be impossible, like a sky-flower. Even for the proponents of external objects (<s>Bāhyārthavādin</s>), the apprehensions of permanence and the like in what is impermanent, and illusions such as silver — these would not constitute <s>avidyā</s> if the appearing form were real. And if absolutely non-existent, no practical activity based on them would be possible. One might say: Let the appearing form not exist, but the appearance itself is real, and that is called <s>avidyā</s>. This is not sound. Without the appearing thing, its appearance too is difficult to account for as ultimately real. There would only be bare appearance. And even 'its appearance' is itself an illusion. Therefore <s>avidyā</s> is neither existent nor non-existent. And precisely because of this, its removal is possible, since it has no firm nature, being mere <s>māyā</s>. Otherwise, how could what is firmly established in its own nature become otherwise? For that would mean loss of its nature.

children.text:
yattu kasyāvidyeti /
jīvānāmiti brūmaḥ /
nanu na jīvā brahmaṇo bhidyante /
evaṃ hyāha ---
‘anena jīvenātmānupraviśya'; iti /
satyaṃ paramārthataḥ /
kalpanayā tu bhidyante /
kasya punaḥ kalpanā bhedikā? na tāvad brahmaṇaḥ, tasya vidyātmanaḥ kalpanāśūnyatvāt /
nāpi jīvānām, kalpanāyāḥ prāk tadabhāvāditaretarāśrayaprasaṅgāt ---
kalpanādhīno hi jīvavibhāgaḥ, jīvāśrayā kalpaneti /
children.translated_text: As for the question 'Whose is <s>avidyā</s>?' — we say: it belongs to the <s>jīvas</s> (individual souls). But do not the <s>jīvas</s> differ from <s>Brahman</s>? For thus it is said: 'Having entered by means of this <s>jīva</s> (living self).' True, in the ultimate sense. But through imagination they are differentiated. Whose then is the imagination that differentiates? Not <s>Brahman</s>'s, for <s>Brahman</s>, being of the nature of knowledge, is devoid of imagination. Nor the <s>jīvas</s>', for prior to the imagination there is no existence of <s>jīvas</s> — and thus there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>): the distinction of <s>jīvas</s> depends on imagination, and imagination depends on the <s>jīvas</s>.

children.translated_text:
Showing the distinction of attachment and aversion through the division of completeness and incompleteness of parts—
or like painters who produce various pictures through the distinction of complete and incomplete [forms] and other differences, and like children playing with various models made of clay and so forth—there is no partiality or cruelty in those [actions].
And [<s>Īśvara</s>] arranging variety in accordance with the dispositions of <s>karma</s> is no fault—so say the teachers.
And not—

Here some say:
The fault lies in the establishment of a [real] entity—
An unestablished entity is not capable of producing another entity, but [there is no problem] in mere illusion.
For there is no impossibility in illusion.
Illusion is precisely that whose meaning is impossible.
If its meaning were possible, then due to being a real thing, it would not be illusion.
But others say:
Since both <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) are beginningless, like the succession of seed and sprout, there is no mutual dependence.

Objection: But the <s>jīvas</s> (individual souls) too, due to their non-difference from the reality of <s>Brahman</s>, are of pure nature.
Then how is there room for <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) in them? This is [merely] talk.
For a reflection in a sword and such is not different from a clean mirror-image.
Yet impurity such as darkness finds scope there.
If [you say] that is an error—then equally, the impurity of the <s>jīvas</s> is also an error.
Otherwise, purification would be extremely difficult to attain.
'The natural <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) indeed, no one is capable of destroying;
For if something of a different character were to arise, the natural [quality] would sometimes perish.'
<s>KKS</s> 12

'But for those who accept oneness of the self, there is no cause of a different character.'
Thus [ends the objection].

And it itself decays; just as one poison neutralizes another poison and itself becomes neutralized.
As it has been said:

Here it is replied:
What has been stated is that the <s>jīvas</s> (individual souls) are tainted by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), not <s>Brahman</s>.
For that [<s>Brahman</s>] is eternally pure, of eternal luminosity, and without adventitious purpose.
Otherwise, even for one who has attained the state of <s>Brahman</s>, <s>avidyā</s> would not cease.
In that case there would be no liberation.
If <s>Brahman</s> itself transmigrates and <s>Brahman</s> itself is liberated, then the liberation of one would entail the liberation of all.
Since <s>Brahman</s> itself transmigrates through the vision of difference,
'He who knows both <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) and <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) together—
Having crossed death through <s>avidyā</s>, he attains immortality through <s>vidyā</s>.'

One might [object]: This is real in its own form; it is not void.

This is what is meant:
<s>Vidyā</s> (knowledge) and <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) are two things united through the relationship of means and end.
Without <s>avidyā</s>, there is no arising of <s>vidyā</s>.
[Objection:] Then it must be produced, and being produced, it is impermanent due to being an effect. Therefore it says: 'Having crossed death through <s>avidyā</s>.'
The meaning is this:
<s>Avidyā</s> is not the cause of <s>vidyā</s>.
Rather, through <s>avidyā</s> characterized by hearing and so forth, <s>avidyā</s> itself is removed.
By 'death' is meant <s>avidyā</s> itself,

Moreover, the means to the vision of non-difference are also not false in their own form, since <s>Brahman</s> itself is their own form.
Therein, <s>Brahman</s> itself, bound by <s>avidyā</s>, is the means to attaining <s>Brahman</s>; that which—

children.translated_text: —just those two. Is this that we are stating not acceptable to you? This has been stated: <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) are merely imagined objects, not [existing] in the supreme reality. Moreover, even if momentary consciousness is accepted, liberation and transmigration are accepted only of the beginningless and endless continuum. For thus: because the continuum is beginningless, and because <s>saṃsāra</s> is unreal, there is no origination; nor is there annihilation, because of its unreality and because a final moment is impossible. For that final moment would either initiate some effect, or not. If it initiates, it is not the final [moment]—hence from its absence there is no annihilation. If it does not initiate, then due to the absence of all potency, being characterized by non-existence, it [itself] is non-existent. When that is non-existent, all continuum-possessors too would be non-existent by this very sequence. In the absence of that, there is no continuum at all—whose annihilation [would there be]? But if the final [moment] does indeed initiate an effect in another continuum—in omniscient [knowledge]—then given the causal relation, how [can there be] another continuum? Nothing other than the causal relation establishes the unity of a single continuum. The unity of a single continuum is not established by the mere causal relation, but rather by the material-cause (<s>upādāna</s>) relation. And the final moment of omniscient knowledge does not serve as the material cause. For that [final moment] is [merely] the object-condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>). The immediately-preceding-condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>) is the material cause. And omniscient knowledge is produced from the immediately-preceding-condition falling within its own continuum. The final moment is its object-condition. If [one requires that] the material cause be of the same class (<s>tulyajātīya</s>)—there is no same-class relation between the liberated mind and omniscient knowledge. As for one who holds that annihilation of the continuum occurs when the effect is of a different kind—for him, in the continuum of form-cognition, there would be the absurd consequence of <s>nirvāṇa</s> from cognition of a different object. How, given the sameness of mind-nature, can there be non-<s>nirvāṇa</s>?—enough of this over-extension.

For the one whose self is momentary consciousness, due to the impossibility of anything to be adopted or rejected, the liberation-<s>śāstras</s> and activities aimed at liberation become purposeless.
Because the momentary [consciousness] naturally ceases of its own accord, and because it cannot be endowed with any additional excellence.
Because in a single moment there is no distinction between the particular and the universal, and because a moment cannot be divided.
If it is thought that in a continuum there is something to be adopted and something to be rejected—that is wrong.

children.translated_text: though transparent and of the nature of illumination, display only that which is placed near [them] and is suitable, through the reflection of its image—so too this <s>puruṣa</s> (person), situated in the body which is the abode of experience, enjoys sounds and the like brought by the senses which are the instruments of experience, through the reflection of their images, even though eternally conscious. And therefore there is no absurd consequence that everyone perceives everything. Nor is there enjoyment of external objects in liberation. One might object: for an omnipresent [self], everything exists as an object; what then needs to be brought near? It is replied: even for one who holds that the ignorant self's knowledge is produced from contact with the mind and the like—since all selves are in contact with all minds—how is there a determinate order of experience? All [objects] exist as its objects by way of mind-contact. But if the determinate order of experience is due to <s>karma</s> being its foundation, that [determination] by <s>karma</s> is not denied to the proponent of the self as consciousness either. Moreover, when, through the completion of non-difference-perception, everything has become the self, there is no perception precisely because of the absence of the perceivable—even for one whose nature is seeing—just as there is no burning for fire when there is nothing to burn, and just as there is no illuminating power for light when there is nothing to illuminate. Thus it is stated: '<s>na hi draṣṭur dṛṣṭer viparilopo vidyate, avināśitvāt; na tu tad dvitīyam asti tato 'nyad vibhaktam, yat paśyet</s>' ('For there is no cessation of the seeing of the seer, because of its imperishability; but there is no second thing separate from it that it could see'); '<s>yatra tv asya sarvam ātmaivābhūt</s>' ('But where everything has become his very self'); and so on. And liberation, characterized by the cessation of the particular qualities of consciousness and the like, does not differ from the annihilationist position. For even if something exists, the absolute absence of perception is not distinguishable from non-existence. And who would desire the non-existence of the self, which is the dearest of all?—thus liberation would be purposeless for persons. One might say: since it is the cessation of manifold sufferings, even the annihilation of the self is desired by a person. For we observe those afflicted with severe sins and diseases striving for their own destruction. True—those whose every happiness has been uprooted by an aggravated disease, as if bearing a form made entirely of suffering [may desire this]. But not so for transmigrating beings who partake of the various and wonderful joys of gods and the like. There, just as [liberation] has purposefulness because it is the cessation of manifold sufferings, so too it has purposelessness because it is the cessation of manifold pleasures. But for one whose state is the experience of supreme bliss with all taint of suffering wiped away—for that alone is there absolute purposefulness for persons. Enough of this over-extension.

Some, however, holding that the self-principle (<s>ātmatattva</s>) has knowledge as its quality but is not of the nature of knowledge, maintain that its abiding in its own nature—with all particular qualities completely uprooted—is the attainment of <s>Brahman</s>. For that state of it, unconditioned by the limiting adjuncts of body, senses, and the like, being vast, is celebrated as <s>Brahman</s>. But if it were of the nature of knowledge, then, being omnipresent, independent of body and senses, eternal in its knowledge-nature, and with manifold knowable distinctions present before it, [its] <s>saṃsāra</s> would be greater [rather than less]. If, alternatively, it does not know anything, then it is not of the nature of knowledge. For the meaning 'knows' requires a grammatical object; without an object-relation it is not appropriate. To these [thinkers] he replies: '<s>vijñānam</s>' (consciousness). Why? Because it is heard in scripture: '<s>satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma</s>' (Truth, knowledge, infinite is <s>Brahman</s>); '<s>vijñānam ānandam</s>' (consciousness, bliss); and so on. Nor does the stated fault [apply]. Just as fire, though a burner, burns [only] fuel that is brought near, not what is not brought near or what is non-combustible; and just as crystal, mirror, and the like,

children.translated_text: then [is its] word-nature [established]? From <s>śrutis</s> such as '<s>paraṃ cāparaṃ ca brahma yad oṅkāraḥ</s>' ('The supreme and the non-supreme <s>Brahman</s> is that which is <s>Oṅkāra</s>'). And this is not dependent on the signified [object], since the <s>kāra</s>-suffix designates the nature of the sound itself. The <s>kāra</s>-suffix is observed to denote what is beyond even syllables and combinations of syllables: '<s>evakāraḥ kimarthaḥ?</s>' ('What is the purpose of the particle <s>eva</s>?'); '<s>kimarthaś cakāraḥ?</s>' ('What is the purpose of the particle <s>ca</s>?'). Objection: This is explained otherwise—since <s>Brahman</s>, which transcends all distinctions, cannot be meditated upon [directly], this is a teaching of a symbol (<s>pratīka</s>): '<s>Brahman</s> is to be meditated upon in this support'—just as, since direct worship of a deity is impossible, worship is prescribed of a wooden or stone [image] bearing its mark, with the notion of [it being] that [deity]; thus the deity meditated upon is pleased. Or, by this designation, that [<s>Brahman</s>] is to be meditated upon, since <s>praṇava</s> (Oṃ) is its designation. It is replied: where it is heard as an auxiliary to <s>yoga</s>—'<s>om ity ātmānaṃ dhyāyatha</s>' ('Meditate on the self with Oṃ'); '<s>om iti yuñjīta</s>' ('One should concentrate with Oṃ')—there [the explanation] may be thus. But where '<s>yuñjīta</s>' and the like are not heard, and the sentence concludes in identity, there it is not so—as in '<s>om iti brahma, om itīdaṃ sarvam</s>' ('Oṃ is <s>Brahman</s>; Oṃ is this all'). For here, by showing that <s>Oṅkāra</s> is the truth of speech through its following all speech and not being abandoned [by any utterance], and then through the abandonment of the speech-form, from which [follows the abandonment] of the manifest world of forms, it concludes: '<s>oṅkāra evedaṃ sarvam</s>' ('Oṅkāra alone is this all'). And even where it is heard: '<s>etenaiva paraṃ puruṣam abhidhyāyīta</s>' ('By this alone one should meditate on the Supreme Person')—that too is preceded by the teaching of the all-self-nature. And it is not proper [to say] that the all-self-nature is figurative, meant for praise, since there is no contradiction even with the primary meaning. For this nature of everything, unknowable by perception and the like, knowable [only] through scripture—is not contradicted. For the non-cognizability by one means of knowledge does not negate the domain of another means of knowledge. And thus '<s>tasmād vidvān</s>' ('Therefore the knower')—the instruction of meditation through that [Oṃ] is for one who already knows the all-self-nature. And not for anyone else. Therefore the subsequent sentence concludes in that very [identity]. Hence, for one who has already attained the knowledge of all-self-nature, the instruction of meditation [follows]. Or alternatively: in '<s>vāg eva viśvā bhuvanāni jajñe, vāg edaṃ bubhuje vāg uvāca</s>' ('Speech alone gave birth to all worlds; speech enjoyed this; speech spoke') and the like, the all-self-nature of speech is heard. Similarly, in the <s>Vāksūkta</s>, the all-self-nature and all-lordship of speech is demonstrated: '<s>ahaṃ rudrebhir vasubhiś carāmi</s>' ('I move with the <s>Rudras</s>, with the <s>Vasus</s>')—by speech itself. Just as by one who has realized [himself] in the Self—

children.translated_text: by <s>Vāmadeva</s>: '<s>ahaṃ Manur abhavaṃ Sūryaś ca</s>' ('I became <s>Manu</s> and <s>Sūrya</s>'). Moreover, modifications are pervaded by the nature of their material cause. And the world is pervaded by the nature of speech. Therefore, either a real transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) or an apparent transformation (<s>vivarta</s>) of speech is to be concluded. How is this pervading [by speech established]? Because [the world] is cognizable through knowledge colored by that [speech]. For thus: from smoke, 'here there is fire'—the difference of the cognition of objects from words is clearly experienced by everyone as being in different substrates. And furthermore, this is so: the qualifier-qualified relationship understood between two words—'blue lotus'—belongs to the objects [not the words]. Otherwise, just as from 'the post [is above] from the crow's nest,' two mutually exclusive objects give rise to the cognition of a third object, so it would be [here]. Moreover, in words as the cause of cognition—like smoke—there would not be certainty in the form of the [signified] thing. And the certainty regarding fire [gained] from another means of knowledge, [apart] from smoke, does not bear the form of smoke. But the certainty regarding objects [gained] even from another means of knowledge does bear the impression of the word-form. From observing this, we conclude that in cognition from words too, the cognition is likewise [word-tinged]—it is not a mere error caused by temporal succession. And the activity of even infants toward the breast and the like, with rejection of other things—that cannot occur for those who do not ascertain 'this [is the breast].' There is no activity directed at a post or a person when it is undetermined [which it is]. And since certainty without word-coloring [is not possible], even for them—who are partakers of word-impressions (<s>bhāvanā</s>) from previous births—knowledge is determined to be colored by the word-form. And thus the world, being graspable through that form, is its transformation—thus we hold. Moreover, there are conventional objects that have no reality other than being transformations of words. By analogy with those, other [objects] too should be so regarded. Such as: injunction and prohibition—'one should do, one should not do'—sentence-meaning, aggregates, and non-existent things like fire-circles, hare's horns, and the like. Now, injunction and prohibition are not activity and withdrawal in the past, nor in the present, nor will they be in the future—because of the absurd consequence of being no different from 'he cooked,' 'he cooks,' 'he will cook.' If [one says they concern] what is to be done (<s>kārya</s>)—no, because what-is-to-be-done cannot be determined apart from the three times. Therefore, injunction and prohibition would be a mere appearance (<s>pratibhā</s>), without [real] substance, conforming to activity and withdrawal. And an appearance without a support is not proper, since it has the nature of cognition. Nor is that [appearance] devoid of word-form impression. Therefore, conforming to activity and withdrawal, the word-reality itself

children.translated_text: thus variously appears—this is correct. Similarly with sentence-meaning: connection (<s>saṃsarga</s>) is nothing apart from the connected things; nor is there anything beyond the connected and the unconnected. Knowledge is not devoid of the knowable. The conceptual cognition is not free from word-form coloring—therefore it is proper that the word-reality itself variously transforms. The same reasoning should be applied to aggregates, to non-existent things like forests and the like, and to fire-circles and similar [things]. Moreover, although there is cognition of musical notes like <s>ṣaḍja</s> and the like, and of cows and the like, prior to words, nevertheless it is not of such [a clear] kind as [the cognition] at a later time after the imposition of words.

'<s>Akṣaram</s>' (the Imperishable)—he states [<s>Brahman's</s>] nature as being of the essence of word (<s>śabda</s>), since the universal is defined by its particularization. children.translated_text: For the prior cognition is undifferentiated, [while] the later [cognition] is clearer, possessing discrimination. And thus cowherds and shepherds impose names for the purpose of discriminating knowledge. And since, when there is contact with words, an enhancement of understanding is observed regarding an object, and when that [verbal contact] is removed, even things once cognized become as if uncognized—like grass and such [seen but not noticed] by one walking on a road—the awareness-nature of consciousness is dependent on the word-form alone. Or, the power of speech itself is consciousness (<s>citi</s>). Even when that is withdrawn, there is a subtle speech-power—so say some. In every case, the cognition of knowable objects is dependent on the word-form; therefore all knowable things are understood as pervaded by the word-form—hence they are either its transformation or its apparent manifestation (<s>vivarta</s>). Just as pots and the like [are transformations] of clay; just as [reflections of] the moon in water-waves [are apparent manifestations] of the moon. Others, however, from observing the illustration of clay and the like, hold that <s>Brahman</s> [really] transforms. This is refuted: '<s>Akṣaram</s>' (the Imperishable). Why? Because of <s>śruti</s> passages here and there: '<s>dhruvaḥ</s>' (eternal); '<s>nityaḥ</s>' (permanent). But if it is thought: even with transformation, since the essential nature is not destroyed, permanence is not contradicted—as stated: 'That too is permanent, in which, even when it is being modified, the essential nature is not destroyed'—true. Nevertheless, since the pure self-nature [of <s>Brahman</s>] would be absent [in total transformation], there would be impermanence in complete transformation; in partial transformation, being-composed-of-parts would contradict both permanence and oneness. This very purity, permanence, and oneness is inconceivable in <s>Brahman</s>, which is like space. In imagined limitation, even unlimited space, [itself] without imagined limitation, does exist. But if [one says] that the imagined partial transformation is by imagination alone—well said: '<s>Akṣaram</s>' (the Imperishable) [is established].

children.translated_text: Some, based on the <s>śruti</s> '<s>sarvagandhaḥ sarvarasaḥ</s>' ('all-fragrance, all-taste') and so forth, have accepted the all-selfhood (<s>sarvātmatā</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>. And thus, since the enjoyment of sense-objects is possible, and since objects are [apprehended by] the self whose nature is luminosity (<s>prakāśa</s>), it is fitting that they should be illuminated. But if [the objects] were different [from the self], the illumination of inert things would be inconceivable.

children.translated_text: In reply to them, [the author] says: 'Not-all' (<s>asarvam</s>). Why? Because the <s>śruti</s> 'not gross, not fine, not short' negates the taint of all differentiation. And since [<s>Brahman</s>] is inseparable from all differentiations, there would be no liberation. For a thing cannot be separated from its own nature, just as fire [cannot be separated] from heat. Moreover, even if it were somehow separated, still, since the continuity of the manifold of differentiation (<s>bhedaprapañca</s>) is unbroken, due to the absence of separation, there would be perpetual <s>saṃsāra</s>. In every way, the manifold of hunger, thirst, and so forth would be its self. And the cessation of that manifold is not accepted [by them]. Therefore, for the proponent of oneness (<s>ekātmyavādin</s>), there is no liberation. But for the proponent of the difference of selves (<s>ātmabhedavādin</s>), since [the manifold] is destroyed for some and not for others, there is a division between the liberated and those in <s>saṃsāra</s>. Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> is not of the nature of the manifold; it is correct that the manifold is merely the play of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).

children.translated_text: Rather, it is only for one who suffers that pleasure, insofar as it is pleasure, persists. For one who is burning, the touch of sandalwood is pleasure. To this [the author] says: 'Fearless' (<s>abhayam</s>). For the state of <s>Brahman</s> is free from all fear. And not even the slightest affliction (<s>kleśa</s>) exists therein, because of the repeated <s>śruti</s> on fearlessness: '<s>abhayaṃ vai brahma</s>' ('Fearless indeed is <s>Brahman</s>') and so forth. For there is no intrinsic fear in <s>Brahman</s>, because it contradicts [its] nature of bliss. Nor is there adventitious fear having a cause, because there is no second [entity]. As stated: '<s>dvitīyādvai bhayaṃ bhavati</s>' ('Fear arises from a second'). And pleasure does not consist in the cessation of suffering, such that pleasure would persist as pleasure only for one who suffers—this has been elaborated previously.

If, then, the manifold is merely the play of <s>avidyā</s>, then emptiness of the manifold (<s>prapañcaśūnyatā</s>) is the ultimate reality (<s>paramārtha</s>). Let that itself be <s>Brahman</s>, since it is the ultimate reality. And thus its nature is conveyed through the negation of the manifold alone: '<s>sa eṣa neti neti</s>' ('This is not this, not this'); '<s>asthūlamanaṇvahrasvam</s>' ('not gross, not fine, not short'); and so forth. To this [the author] replies: 'All' (<s>sarvam</s>). What is meant is this: <s>Brahman</s> does not have all-selfhood; but everything has <s>Brahman</s> as its self, possessing form by virtue of <s>Brahman</s>'s form—it is not mere void, because of the absurd consequence of perpetual liberation, and [consequently] the pointlessness of instruction directed toward that [liberation]. [Objection]: Even if there is perpetual liberation, <s>saṃsāra</s> is rooted in <s>avidyā</s>. [Reply]: If <s>avidyā</s> is the absence of apprehension, how then can <s>saṃsāra</s> be rooted in it? For that [absence] would be the same even in liberation; [and then], just as [before], nothing would be illuminated. But if <s>avidyā</s> is erroneous apprehension, then there is no total voidness. Because the <s>śruti</s> states: '<s>tenedaṃ pūrṇaṃ puruṣeṇa sarvam</s>' ('All this is filled by that Person'); and '<s>ātmaivedaṃ sarvam</s>' ('The self alone is all this')—[thus] the self is taught in everything; and '<s>kathamasataḥ sajjāyeta</s>' ('How could being arise from non-being?')—thus voidness itself is negated. For a real entity, when not illuminated as it truly is, appears with a superimposed unreal form. But in a void, where would superimposition be? What would be illuminated?—thus it would be without any seed [for manifestation]. And because the <s>śruti</s> teaches a positive form: '<s>vijñānamānandam</s>' ('consciousness-bliss'), <s>Brahman</s> is not the mere absence of everything, but rather the self of everything. But some think that since pleasure unmixed [with pain] is not observed, and since pleasure is inseparable from suffering, there is no state free from contact with suffering. For no being whatsoever is observed to be purely happy or purely miserable.

children.translated_text: or by its own nature, could bind [them] again, just like a worldly sovereign. And if [<s>Brahman</s>] is dependent on <s>karma</s>, then it has no sovereignty over <s>karmas</s>. Even so, since <s>karmas</s> are infinite and there is no fixed rule for the time of fruition, even after the passage of hundreds of aeons, re-bondage from <s>karmas</s> whose time of fruition has arrived is conceivable. For the store of <s>karma</s> does not belong to a single life; it is not only death that activates it, but also place, time, and other [factors]. For thus, even in a single body, the sequential experience of the fruits of <s>karma</s> is observed, since <s>karmas</s> that are causes for the enjoyment of mutually contradictory births cannot all come to fruition simultaneously, and since [otherwise] birth and death, being non-<s>karmic</s>, would entail liberation [for everyone]. To this it is replied: 'Fearless' (<s>abhayam</s>). For this attainment of safety (<s>kṣemaprāpti</s>) is declared to be supreme. In it there is no fear of renewed <s>saṃsāra</s>. First, renewed <s>saṃsāra</s> is not caused by <s>karma</s>, because through knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>)—as through an expiation (<s>prāyaścitta</s>)—even infinite <s>karmas</s> whose fruits have not yet been experienced are destroyed. For it is said: '<s>jñānāgniḥ sarvakarmāṇi bhasmasātkurute tathā</s>' ('The fire of knowledge likewise reduces all <s>karmas</s> to ashes'). Likewise: '<s>kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi</s>' ('And his <s>karmas</s> are destroyed'). Alternatively, when <s>avidyā</s> ceases through knowledge, the division into agent, action, and fruit simply dissolves. Whence would it arise? Nor is [renewed <s>saṃsāra</s>] caused by <s>avidyā</s>, because the cause of its operation is absent. For <s>avidyā</s> is beginningless; precisely because it is beginningless, it does not require a cause. For a cause operates upon prior non-existence; in the absence of prior non-existence, when would a cause operate? For there is nothing for a cause to accomplish with respect to what already exists. But [<s>avidyā</s>], once cut off by knowledge, being previously non-existent [in its cut-off state], cannot arise again without a cause. In deep sleep, however, only the projection (<s>vikṣepa</s>) ceases; its latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) and non-apprehension do not cease. Otherwise, it would not differ from the fourth state (<s>turīya</s>). But the attainment of <s>Brahman</s> is spoken of [in deep sleep] only because of the absence of projection alone. Therefore, it is well said: 'Fearless' (<s>abhayam</s>).

Another approach: Here, some hold that even for those considered liberated, there is the fear of return (<s>punarāvṛtti</s>). For here, the conscious selves (<s>vijñānātmānaḥ</s>) would either be divided from <s>Brahman</s> or undivided. They would be divided either by <s>Brahman</s> itself—for the purpose of enjoyment, or play, or the display of sovereignty, or by [its own] nature—or their division would be rooted in <s>avidyā</s>. Or the conscious selves themselves are what is denoted by the word '<s>Brahman</s>,' with no other <s>Brahman</s> [apart from them]. Their <s>saṃsāra</s> would be rooted in <s>karma</s> and <s>avidyā</s>, or rooted in the mutual fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) between seer and seen. In the case of it being rooted in fitness, since that fitness does not pass away, the fear of return would remain unremoved. And if there is no return because the purpose has been accomplished, then upon the first perception of sound and so forth, there should be no further perception of them. But if <s>prakṛti</s> has infinite modifications, it ceases upon the perception of the self of all, yet proceeds again for the perception of the remaining unmodified forms. Since [its modifications] are indeed infinite, the perception of the self of all would be impossible—thus even for one who holds the doctrine of the distinction between <s>guṇa</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>, return would be conceivable. Even if rooted in <s>avidyā</s> and prior <s>karma</s>, since in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s> <s>karmas</s> are infinite and their time of fruition is not fixed, the fear of return cannot be averted, just as in the state of dissolution (<s>pratisarga</s>), so also in the state of liberation. Even if rooted in <s>avidyā</s>, since <s>avidyā</s> operates without cause and without purpose, what prevents its repeated operation again and again? And thus, in deep sleep, return from the attainment of <s>Brahman</s> is observed. But if <s>Brahman</s> is autonomous, it is inconceivable that for the <s>jīvas</s>—whether divided or undivided—that have been divided [from <s>Brahman</s>] and provided with bodies, senses, and enjoyments, there would not again be the division into bodies and so forth by causes such as enjoyment. For an autonomous [being], through play, or through the display of autonomy,

children.translated_text: [is it capable] of comprehending the absence of the manifold, since when perception and the other [means of knowledge] exist, that [absence of manifold] is impossible. Nor does <s>āgama</s> (scripture) composed by a trustworthy author apply here, since its domain is [only] what has been ascertained by another means of knowledge. Nor is [scripture] independent [as a means of knowledge], since it has the form of injunction and prohibition, and since when the reality is [already] established, those two are impossible. Nor is its authoritativeness [directed] only at an object that is an established entity independent of those [injunction and prohibition], since if it were [merely] restating existing facts, it would be dependent on another means of knowledge. And the capacity of words is understood from ordinary usage. There, words are used with reference to things connected with an effect, only as subordinate to an action, since they are meaningful [only] in that way. For an utterance devoid of [connection to] activity or cessation has no purpose. Moreover, the relation of words [to meanings] is not traced from statements of existing facts, but from prompting statements. For it is through [observing] activity that one, having inferred the cognition of meaning, comprehends the capacity of words therein. And thus the capacity of words is not understood with respect to meanings unconnected with activity. That being so, words whose capacity is not [otherwise] ascertained—how could they convey an existing object? Moreover, if this meaning has been ascertained by another means of knowledge, then words have no authoritativeness regarding it. And if it has not been ascertained, all the less so. Or if [<s>Brahman</s>] is not a word-referent, it cannot be the object of a sentence, since it is only a word-referent that, in a qualified manner, becomes a sentence-meaning. But what is entirely unobserved, being uncomprehended from a word, cannot enter—either as subordinate or as principal—into a sentence-meaning that consists in the connection of word-referents.

But by what means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) is this reality comprehended? Not by perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), since its domain is the opposite—differentiation. Nor by inference (<s>anumāna</s>), since it is dependent on the former [perception]. Nor by analogy (<s>upamāna</s>), since its domain is similarity, and that [similarity] is based on differentiation. And <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) [operates] in the contrary case—it is not the case that no transaction is possible without differentiation. For non-difference too is difficult to comprehend without the division into knower and so forth. Absence (<s>abhāva</s>) too is not capable of [leading to] the comprehension of the reality that has a positive nature. Nor

children.translated_text: when it has a purpose, an operation terminating in activity can be posited. Moreover, a person is prompted [to act] either when he has not [yet] engaged in the means, or when, not having previously engaged in the end due to ignorance of the means, [he is prompted] through the indication of the means. Here, [the person is not prompted] to the means, namely the birth of the son, since that has already been accomplished. Nor [is he prompted] to the end, namely happiness, since there is no other effort directed toward that [happiness as a goal]. Likewise, the utterances of wicked people—unpleasant announcements—serve the purpose of producing dejection and do not instruct either activity or cessation, by the same reasoning as before. Similarly, for one who is coiled around by a rope yet thinks himself coiled by a snake, the declaration of the truth is seen [to serve] the cessation of fear; but the injunction 'Do not be afraid!' is not what is operative there. For an injunction applies where a person, having understood the purpose of the injunction, deliberately acts or desists by virtue of the injunction's force or by [his own] desire. But here, from the mere apprehension of the truth, the fear ceases for one who does not depend on the injunction, simply because of the absence of the cause [of fear]. And one who spontaneously acts upon the cessation of fear does not need to be enjoined; nor [need he be enjoined] to the means of that [cessation], namely the apprehension of the truth, since that arises from the very utterance 'It is a rope, not a snake'; and any operation subsequent to the comprehension of the word's meaning is governed by an injunction [only in other contexts]. Likewise, reports of events in distant lands, [given] to those who have asked out of curiosity, serve the purpose of removing their eager anxiety, are directed at existing facts, and are not for the sake of adoption or rejection.

It will be stated [later] that even if [scripture] describes existing reality, being authorless (<s>apauruṣeya</s>), it is not dependent [on another means of knowledge]. And not all utterances in the world are action-oriented. For example, pleasant announcements—'Fortunate you are! A son has been born to you!'—are not for the sake of activity or cessation, yet they are seen to serve the purpose of producing happiness. And it is not the case that the instruction 'Be happy!' is given therein, since that [happiness] is accomplished by the very power of the fact itself, without need of instruction. [Objection]: There is indeed a specific activity there, and the utterance has its purport in that [activity]. [Reply]: True. The purport is in the arising [of happiness], not in the cognition [as something to be done]. Rather, the cognition is directed at the existing fact alone. children.translated_text: abandon their role as factors in engagement and desistance; likewise, the word too—so nothing is vitiated. [Objection:] Engagement and desistance are intended by the speaker. [Reply:] It is not because of the speaker's intention that [something becomes] the meaning of the word, but rather because of [its] capacity. Otherwise, the attainment of various human purposes through the medium of obtaining the treasure would also be the meaning of the word, since that too is intended by the speaker. And when something is inquired about through perception and the like with the intention of engagement or desistance, even though engagement and desistance are intended, they are not the objects of perception and the rest. [Similarly,] even though engagement and desistance are intended, they are not the meanings of the word. And furthermore this is the case for this very reason: That toward which one person has the cognition of adoption, another has indifference. For if [engagement] were the meaning of the word, there would be the cognition of adoption in all persons.

Even where, in the apprehension of an existing fact, abandonment or adoption is possible—[such as] 'this road has an obstruction,' 'this piece of land has a treasure'—even there, the word operates for the sake of abandonment or adoption, [but only] on the basis of conveying the existing fact. Having apprehended the existing fact from the word, and having recollected its capacity to benefit or harm, which was known through another means of knowledge, one either engages through desire or desists through aversion. [Objection:] But the speaker, acting intentionally, uses speech for the purpose of the listener's engagement or desistance. And so [speech] culminates in engagement or desistance alone. For in such cases, what should be said is not said: [e.g.,] 'You should not go by this road'; likewise, 'Take the treasure from here.' [Reply:] This is not sound. For even speech that culminates in conveying an existing fact does not fail to serve as a factor in engagement or desistance through the medium of conveying the existing fact—just like perception and the other [means of knowledge]. Perception and the like, whose operation is completed in ascertaining an existing fact, without even touching upon engagement or desistance even slightly, do not

children.translated_text: Nor is the apprehension of the relation [between word and meaning] solely from the usage of injunctive sentences, such that the orientation toward activity alone would be understood. For it is observed otherwise as well. [Consider:] 'Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood'—one who does not know the meaning of the word 'firewood' but knows the meanings of the other words and the meanings of the case-endings, upon seeing what is the instrument in the act of cooking, understands its identity as the meaning of the stem 'firewood.' Likewise, from statements of fact whose purpose is joy, sorrow, or relief, the understanding of words for the causes of joy and the like arises. For just as from observing a particular activity, a cognition of that particular activity or a cognition of its cause is inferred, and due to the absence of any other cause and the immediate precedence of the word, the capacity of the word in that regard is postulated—so too, from the observation of joy and the like, a cognition of the cause of joy and the like is inferred, and due to the immediate precedence of the word, the capacity of the word in that regard is postulated. And since the birth of a son, which is the cause of joy, has been ascertained through another means of knowledge, and since nothing else [could be the cause], one understands that this sentence 'A son has been born to you' was used by a trustworthy person in reference to that birth of a son. And one determines that it was the birth of the son alone that was apprehended from this sentence. Thus, through both usage and understanding, one grasps the capacity of the sentence in this meaning.
