children.translated_text: When usage and understanding are explained by just that much [i.e., mutual connection of referents], there is no evidence for connection with a specific [purpose, i.e., injunction]. For whoever postulates a connection with a specific [purpose] postulates a connection with something else entirely. And so, even without any [injunctive] purpose, through the mutual connection of the referents, the cognition of a qualified existing fact is established. And this must necessarily be understood in this way. Otherwise, since in ordinary life the connection of referents [in a sentence] depends on the intention [of the speaker], in the absence of such [intention] in the <s>Veda</s>, the understanding of the meaning of the <s>Veda</s> would not be possible. Moreover, if all [words] were connected with a purpose, the referents would have no mutual connection with each other. In that case, the injunction would not be understood as having a qualified referent as its object; it would be accomplishable by the referent of a single word alone. But if the injunction does not require a separate specification [of its object], since it has a qualified object—then the specification comes first, and the injunction after. What follows from this? The word has capacity for the connection of meanings other than injunction, independently of injunction, since the referents that are mutually connected enter into connection with injunction [afterwards]. And it is not the case that the connection [of referents] is grounded in the expectancy of injunction—this will be demonstrated. And even what has not been ascertained through another means of knowledge, and whose relation has not been ascertained, can be determined through its own word by way of negating specific [alternatives], since the relation of specific words and the negative particle with their respective meanings is known. And thus it is taught in this very way: 'Not gross'—as transcending all specific determinations. [The author] states this: 'Through the door of the dissolution of the manifold of distinctions.' And this will be discussed further.

Or let it be the case that in ordinary life all speech is promotive [of action], and that from this the relation [between word and meaning] is apprehended. Even so, this must be examined: Do the words other than injunctive terms have as their purport merely their own meaning, or the connection with a purpose to be accomplished, or merely the connection of [their] referents? In the first case—[if they purport] merely their own meaning—there would be no cognition of the sentence-meaning, and the usage [of the sentence] would be pointless. Therefore, [the words have] an orientation toward connection with something else.

children.translated_text: Another meaning [is proposed]. As for what was said—'Reality that has transcended all specific determinations is beyond the scope of cognition itself'—to this it is replied: That [reality] is deposited in the mind through the word itself, by means of the negation of specific determinations, like the essence of gold. For the essence of gold is not seen apart from the contamination of distinctions of shape such as lump, bracelet, and the like. Nor are those [shapes] the essence of gold, since [the essence] persists even when [those shapes] are abandoned, in another shape. Yet even though the separation from the contamination of shape-distinctions has not been [directly] seen, [the essence] is cognized by the intellect through the door of the removal of distinctions, and is communicated to another. This method of cognition has been shown by the <s>Śruti</s> itself: 'That is [described as] 'not this, not this' (<s>neti neti</s>).' Likewise by others: 'When forms are dissolved, what remains at the end is the truth.' And by yet others: 'The non-elaborated is elaborated through superimposition and negation (<s>adhyāropāpavāda</s>).'

children.translated_text: somewhere the dissolution of some distinction is understood. For example, in '<s>svargakāmo yajeta</s>' ('Let one who desires heaven sacrifice'), the dissolution of the identity of self with the body [is understood]. For here an agent is understood who is capable of enjoying heaven as distinct from the body; hence the dissolution of the identity of self with body. Likewise, from '<s>godohanena paśukāmasya praṇayet</s>' ('One should pour the libation for one desiring cattle by milking a cow'), the dissolution of the distinction among qualified agents [is understood], since the prescribed agent goes beyond the specified agent. Likewise, in injunctions and prohibitions, the dissolution of natural tendencies rooted in passion and the like [is understood]. In prohibitions directly, and in injunctions through the implicit injunction within the activity. In ordinary life too, either directly preventing [someone] from an undesirable path, or by instructing [them] in an alternative path. And thus, through the door of the dissolution of the distinction of natural tendencies rooted in passion and the like, the ritual injunctions are, by the seen [purpose] itself, conducive to the qualification for self-knowledge. For indeed, the vision in the self is taught to one who is tranquil, self-controlled, and concentrated. And it is possible. For one who is being drawn by sense-objects and whose mind is engaged in pursuing them cannot concentrate on the self. But one who has desisted from natural tendencies, with a disciplined mind, is qualified for the vision of the self, by virtue of [his] capacity.

Now this is to be examined: Does the entire <s>Āmnāya</s> (Vedic corpus) determine <s>Brahman</s> through the door of the dissolution of the manifold of distinctions, or only some portion of it? Here some say: Throughout the entire <s>Āmnāya</s>,

children.translated_text: Yet others describe the connection of rituals with the qualification for self-knowledge in terms of the purification of the person: '<s>mahāyajñaiśca yajñaiśca brāhmīyaṃ kriyate tanuḥ</s>' ('Through great sacrifices and [other] sacrifices, the body fit for <s>Brahman</s> is fashioned'), and 'He who has these forty <s>saṃskāras</s> and eight qualities of the self.' Yet others describe this very thing in the opposite direction—that self-knowledge itself enters into the qualification for ritual action through the purification of the agent. Yet others think that rituals and self-knowledge, being mutually contradictory as pertaining to duality and non-duality respectively, have no connection whatsoever.

Others think: One whose desires are unfulfilled, whose mind is overwhelmed by desires, is not fit for the vision of supreme non-duality. But through rituals performed up to the thousand-year <s>Prājāpatya</s> rite, having eradicated desires, from [the knowledge gained through] that stage, one realizes the self as supreme non-duality. On both these views, the entire <s>Āmnāya</s> culminates exclusively in self-knowledge. The view of [yet] others [is this]: Ritual injunctions, being [productive of] separate results of their own, introduce a person into the qualification for self-knowledge, since one whose three debts have not been discharged has no qualification for that: 'Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind to liberation.' Yet others say that all rituals enter into the qualification for self-knowledge through their combined or separate [effects], based on the <s>Śruti</s>: '<s>vividiṣanti yajñena</s>' ('They seek to know through sacrifice'), and 'By whatever [sacrifice], even by the oblation with a ladle, one whose mind becomes undisturbed.'

children.text:
yatpratigrāmaṃ vaktuḥ śrotuśca satyāmarthaprāptau pramāṇāntareṇānadhigate paradeśaprāptyabhiprāye pūrvopadeśān pūrvārthāneva pārśvasthāḥ pratipattāraḥ pratipadyante, paradeśopadeśaṃ ca svārthaniṣṭham /

śabdavṛttānusāreṇa ceha tātparyam, pramāṇāntarābhāvāditi /
children.translated_text: In each village, when the speaker and listener have attained the purpose at hand, and the intention of reaching a further destination has not been ascertained through any other means of knowledge, the bystanders understand the earlier instructions as having only their earlier [immediate] purposes, and the instruction for the further destination as culminating in its own purpose. Even though, in reality, the purposes of the earlier instructions do benefit [the attainment of] the further [destination], the purport of the word is not there—just as in the case of injunctions for the acquisition of wealth and the like, even though they serve the purpose of ritual injunctions, [the purport is not there]. And here the purport [is determined] by following the operation of words, due to the absence of another means of knowledge.

Of these, the first position is not [correct]. For ritual injunctions and the like, having their own results such as heaven and the like ascertained from their own sentences, do not require any further result. Nor does the injunction of self-knowledge, being independent through its own stated means of celibacy and the like, require the ritual injunctions. In that case, how can there be a single qualification [for both]? If one thinks that the ritual injunctions and the like have not had their results ascertained, [and that they are connected to liberation] through the heaven and the like being subsidiary [to liberation]—let him explain the <s>svargakāmādhikaraṇa</s> (the topic concerning the desirer of heaven). Moreover, if all injunctions and prohibitions had as their result the dissolution of name and form leading to liberation, then the prosperity and downfall of beings would be uncaused and accidental, not caused by ritual action. And liberation too would follow [automatically], rendering the <s>śāstra</s> also pointless. [Objection:] But the entry of ritual injunctions into the qualification for knowledge is through the medium of their own results such as heaven and the like, just as instructions for reaching wayside villages enter into the instruction for reaching the desired city. [Reply:] That is not so. It is fitting for the reaching of wayside villages to enter into the instruction for reaching the undesired destination. For there is no attainment of the human purpose in the instructions for wayside villages. Therefore, being incomplete, they enter into that [instruction] where the human purpose is attained. But in the case of ritual injunctions, there is no failure to attain the human purpose, since heaven and the like are desired by persons. And when there is no incompleteness in that regard, how can there be entry into something else? [Objection:] But when one is enticed and led to a desired destination by showing the merits of progressively [better] villages, the instructions for the earlier villages, having attained their desired results, do enter into another instruction. [Reply:] That is fitting there too, because through another means of knowledge one ascertains the intention of the speaker. For there, through another means of knowledge, this has been ascertained: 'When [the listener] has reached this place, this purpose of the speaker is fulfilled; therefore, this is what he intended.' But not by merely following the operation of words. And furthermore, for this very reason—

children.translated_text:
That apprehension of cessation would have its scope removed from afar.
Alternatively, the injunctions of ritual action, by fulfilling desires, dissolve those desires and thus make one fit for the domain of knowledge.
As it has been said:

Moreover, in the case of instructions about roads and villages, it is precisely through the determination of their intent that travel there and attainment of the goal [occurs].
But in the case of intent being the attainment of another place, travel there is not obligatory.
One might go even by another route, since that attainment is what is intended.
Nor is the attainment of the goal obligatory, since even the mention of purpose in [texts] with a different intent has the nature of <s>arthavāda</s> (eulogy).
So here, if injunctions and prohibitions have some other purpose, they do not have heaven and such as their purpose.
Indeed, the purpose of heaven and so forth is not like the purpose of preliminary rites, so as to be subordinate to another purpose.
And how can one say that they serve only the visible purpose of qualifying for self-knowledge?
If through the cessation of activity directed toward visible purposes impelled by passion and so forth—let the prohibitions be of such a nature.
But how do the injunctions of ritual action restrain [desire]? This must be stated.
For they are not restrictive, nor are they determinative, since their object is entirely unattained.
An injunction whose object is already attained is understood to have the fruit of excluding other [actions].
Nor is there cessation through conflict with [actions] having the same result.
For obligatory activities with results at an indeterminate time have invisible purposes.
But those impelled by passion and so forth have visible purposes and are natural.
And there is no conflict in both service and collection being means to [reaching] a village, since the <s>śāstra</s> is authoritative only to that extent.
Wherein lies the conflict for one who desires abundant fruits and practices both service and collection, whether simultaneously or successively? Moreover, if all activity with visible purposes were stopped, even activities based on obligation would be stopped, since they are impossible for one who has not earned wealth and lacks the means.
Furthermore, when both are equally means to desire, there is no difference between activity with visible and invisible purposes in being impelled by passion and so forth.
For thus:
'He who desires heaven [should sacrifice]'—through the mention of activity impelled by passion and so forth, a specific [ritual] is enjoined.
And when attachment to the phenomenal world is equal, by what distinction does one [teaching] accord with the oneness of self, while another opposes it? For the impulse of desire in the mind is undifferentiated.
If one would not regard [rituals] as means to desire at all, then the accidentality [of their results] as described [above applies], and the reasoning stated would be reversed.
And since the conflict and so forth are based on having the same result,

Then the mortal becomes immortal—here one attains <s>Brahman</s>.'

athānyaparādapyarthādevamavasīyata iti, tadapi hastini dṛṣṭe tatpadena tasyānumānamiva /

children.translated_text:
That too is wrong.
Because desires are not dissolved by the fulfillment of desires, but rather by contemplative meditation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>) born of the cultivation of [seeing] faults.
If the mind is touched even slightly by desires, it is indeed carried away by those alluring [objects].
For it has been said:
'Desire is never pacified by the enjoyment of desired objects'; and 'Through repeated experience of pleasures, passions and the proficiencies of the senses both increase.'
Therefore, one should first turn away from desires because they are not the [proper] means.
And one should resort to self-knowledge, whose nature is the pacification of all afflictions.
But one who follows the various means indicated by the injunctions of ritual action would become attached to those very alluring pleasures that are [part of] the subject at hand.
And one would shrink from self-knowledge, whose nature is the dissolution of those [pleasures].
For the bliss in the self, though heard about, being unexperienced, is not able even to diminish—much less destroy—the longing for bliss rooted in experienced sense objects.
Therefore, contemplative meditation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>) alone is the sole means for the destruction of desires, while the injunctions of ritual action are causes of the opposite.
As for the [argument] that:
throughout the entire Vedic corpus, somewhere some [aspect of] difference is dissolved—as in 'He who desires heaven should sacrifice,' which dissolves the identification of self with the body—
that too is wrong, since [the text] does not have that as its purport.
For this statement is not aimed at the knowledge of the self as distinct from the body.
If [one argues] that this is inferred even from a text with a different purport—that is like inferring [the presence of] an elephant from its footprint when the elephant has already been seen.
For directly, beginning with 'It is not gross,' the distinction from body and senses is shown; and from the meaning [of those texts], the knot of desire and so forth would be [loosened]—the Vedic [teaching] would be rigorous.

children.translated_text: The second alternative too is untenable, for the very reason already described—desires' inability to destroy desires—and because there is no authority for the entrance of [ritual actions] that are indifferent to their own effects into [the domain of] another [effect].

children.translated_text:
Even those who in the opposite way maintain the single domain of qualification for knowledge and action must state the authority for the connection of knowledge with action.
It is not like 'He sprinkles the rice grains.'
For there, because of the context, the word 'rice' in its own form, being purposeless otherwise, conveys its connection with the <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit) that is the subject at hand.
Nor is it like 'He whose sacrificial ladle is made of leaves.'
For there, without any context, the invariable connection of the ladle with ritual action brings the ritual to mind.
There the connection is through the sentence itself.
But self-knowledge is not mentioned in the context [of ritual].
Nor is there an invariable connection of the self with ritual action.
Therefore, its connection with action is difficult to assert.
And since the mention of a result, when its subordinate purpose is unknown, does not become an <s>arthavāda</s> (eulogy)—therefore there is a separate domain of qualification.
If it is thought:
Because of the indication of the present [tense] in 'He does not return,' the result must be construed by transforming it, due to the absence of a desire-connection.
But that [transformation occurs] only when there is an expectation of that.
But there is no such expectation when a visible [result] is available.
And there is a visible result of the injunction of self-knowledge: activity in ritual actions whose fruits are to be enjoyed in another body.
Therefore, the injunction of self-knowledge is like the injunction of Vedic study.
For the injunction of Vedic study, having a visible result in the comprehension of ritual action, does not seek a result from <s>arthavāda</s>; similarly, the injunction of self-knowledge—therefore there is not a separate domain.
That too is wrong.
Because this is another person—the person of the <s>Upaniṣads</s>—who is to be inquired into in the <s>Vedānta</s>.
And knowledge of that [person] is not a cause for the undertaking of action.
For that [self] has neither agency nor enjoyership.
Thus it is said:
'It does not eat anything'; 'The other one watches without eating.'
But the one who is the agent and enjoyer of ritual actions is the very one established through all direct perception.
He is not an object of verbal testimony.
[Objection:] But the <s>jīva</s> and the supreme self are indeed identical.
Thus it is said:
'Through this living self (<s>jīva</s>)...'
True. But it is the form of that very <s>jīva</s>, apprehended through perception as bound by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), that is the cause for the undertaking of action.
And that does not depend on verbal testimony.
But that which is self-luminous, devoid of all distinctions—that is desired to be known from verbal testimony.
And that is opposed to the undertaking of action.
How could the undertaking of action be the visible purpose of knowledge of that? For thus:
For one who knows the self as the one, non-dual bliss of <s>Brahman</s>—for what purpose and how could there be activity, since all desires are fulfilled and there is an absence of means [to employ]?
[Objection:] Perhaps knowledge of the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> person is enjoined as an auxiliary to ritual action: 'What one does with knowledge and faith and with <s>upaniṣad</s>

Likewise, beginning with 'He who, having known this Imperishable, O <s>Gārgī</s>, offers in this world,' by showing the limited nature of the fruits of sacrifice and other [rituals], the subordination of <s>Brahma</s>-knowledge to those [rituals] is demonstrated.
And 'Knowledge and action both lay hold of him'—here the conjunction of knowledge and action is shown.
First, however, the subject at hand concerns the <s>udgītha</s>, since it begins with 'This syllable <s>Oṃ</s> is the <s>udgītha</s>.'
And the subsequent [portion] is praise of the knowledge of the Imperishable through censure of ritual action.
And the 'laying hold' of knowledge and action is through separation:
Knowledge lays hold of the knowledgeable, action lays hold of the one who performs action.
Therefore, even from this, there is no single domain of qualification for action and knowledge.

If there were a single domain of qualification, there would be a combination of all ritual actions.
But that is impossible.

[that consequence] would follow.
What then is the cause? It has been said: '<s>Avidyā</s> is beginningless and purposeless.'
And therein, the demand for a cause has no scope.
And there is no fault because erroneous cognition and its dispositions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) are established as mutual cause and effect.
Therefore, the cessation of erroneous cognition is to be accomplished by knowledge, and therein knowledge may require an auxiliary.
But this too is [mere] talk.
For in the case of mother-of-pearl and so forth, those in whom correct cognition has arisen preceded by erroneous cognition do not separately exert effort for the removal of that [error], nor do they require any other auxiliary.
Because the arising of an opposing positive entity is itself the prior destruction [of the error]—not a void.
Otherwise, destruction would have no cause.
And knowledge is opposed to erroneous cognition.
Upon its arising, erroneous cognition is already destroyed.
If it is said:
Ritual actions are causes of bondage. Their destruction [comes] from knowledge requiring auxiliaries.
But how is that possible when knowledge has arisen, pure, with all particularities wiped away? And ritual actions that have been contemplated upon are, like erroneous cognition and doubt, [destroyed]:

Those who hold that there is absolutely no connection between action and knowledge because of their opposition—'action pertains to duality, knowledge pertains to non-duality'—for them, the non-arising of non-dual knowledge would follow, because of the opposition between the division [inherent in] the means of knowledge and the comprehension of non-duality.
If [they say] there is no opposition because the means and the end are not simultaneous—then all division dissolves when non-dual comprehension [arises].
Nor is there opposition or unsuitability [of the means], because the means belong to an earlier time, and at that time they have not [yet] dissolved.
And it is precisely difference that is the means to the comprehension of non-difference.
Then there should be no opposition with ritual actions either, since they too are means.
[Objection:] Perhaps, since <s>Brahman</s> cannot be accomplished, ritual actions have no use.
And it is heard:
'The uncreated is not [attained] by the created.'
Nor do they serve for the arising of knowledge, since knowledge depends on the means of valid cognition.
Nor are ritual actions auxiliaries to knowledge, since knowledge has no other result to accomplish.
Liberation is not its result to be accomplished, since that would entail impermanence.
If it is said that the cessation of the cause of bondage is what is to be accomplished—when that is cut off, liberation [follows] from the absence of that.
What then is the cause of bondage? Beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). Then the cessation of that is not separately to be accomplished, since the removal of <s>avidyā</s> is the very arising of <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge).
[Objection:] Let the arising of knowledge be the removal of <s>avidyā</s> characterized by non-apprehension, since a positive entity is the removal of a negative entity.
But the arising of knowledge is not the removal of erroneous cognition.
For one positive entity is not the removal of another positive entity.
Nor are entities of the nature of mutual absence, since that would entail being non-entities.
If one thinks: erroneous cognition, having non-apprehension of reality as its cause, will cease of its own accord when the cause ceases—that is not so.
For non-apprehension, being a [mere] absence, is not the cause of anything, since in states of unconsciousness and so forth
'The knots of the heart are pierced; all doubts are cut asunder;

children.translated_text: It is established through direct vision. No other <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is needed for its establishment. Even what is seen through <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) may be inquired into by other [means of knowledge], due to the possibility of that [further inquiry], since there is no distinguishing feature [that prevents it]. The other [means of knowledge] also have the capacity to produce certainty, since they are [genuine] <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge). [Objection:] <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) has as its object what is suitable for abandonment and the like, because its object is what is proximate — not so the other [means of knowledge]. [Reply:] Then let the cause of proximity be what is required, not the <s>pramāṇa</s> itself, since the cognition is already established. And in the present subject matter, there is no such distinction. [Objection:] <s>Śabda</s> (verbal testimony) and the rest have universals as their objects, while <s>pratyakṣa</s> has particulars as its object. [Reply:] Then the object of <s>pratyakṣa</s> is simply not apprehended by <s>śabda</s> at all. Quite so. This has been stated — that <s>Brahman</s> is not the object of verbal knowledge. If then <s>Brahman</s> is not apprehended by <s>śabda</s>, how can <s>upāsanā</s> (meditation) directed toward it proceed? Nor does the direct realization of one thing occur when something else is meditated upon. And for the direct realization of what form is the injunction of <s>yajña</s> (sacrifice) and the like? The injunction of <s>yajña</s> and the like is justified for the direct realization of the self whose nature is <s>Brahman</s>, characterized by <s>niratiśayānanda</s> (unsurpassed bliss), <s>apahatapāpman</s> (freedom from evil), and so forth, as indicated by <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony). When the nature of the human goal is unknown, or when the opposite is taken to be the case, once it has become manifest from a <s>pramāṇa</s> that is free from doubt, nothing further is required. [Objection:] But even when the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>ātman</s> is apprehended from the <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) 'thou art that' (<s>tattvamasi</s>), since <s>saṃsāric</s> (worldly) properties are still perceived as before, there is a need for something else to remove them. [Reply:] This is not sound. How can one who has apprehended the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>ātman</s>, who has known the true nature of the self, be subject to properties caused by false perception? And it is heard in scripture: 'He who knows <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself.' And in <s>Brahman</s>, which is <s>apahatapāpman</s> (free from evil), there is no room for those [worldly properties]. Likewise —

If [it is said that] another [auxiliary] is needed for the purity of knowledge—
that too is futile, since in knowledge born of valid cognition there is no possibility of doubt and erroneous cognition, which are impurities of knowledge.
If it is thought:
Besides knowledge from verbal testimony, another, perceptual knowledge is posited—one from which the apprehension of distinctions has fallen away, transcending all conceptual construction.
For <s>Brahman</s> is the object of that, not of verbal knowledge which apprehends the connection of distinct word-meanings.
For its arising, an expectation of ritual action, meditation, and so forth [is needed].
But what is its distinctive feature, for which it is sought? Vividness. But that has no use.
For knowledge is for encompassing the knowable, and in verbal knowledge, once arisen, the knowable is already fully known.
If [one says] that cognition has its culmination in perception, and there is no further need [beyond that]—then what else would be sought when the object to be known has been cognized? Another means of cognition? No, because the expectation of that is for the sake of establishing the object to be known.
For the sake of establishing it again? No, because it has already been established, even repeatedly, by the previous [means].
And there is no reason for expecting [further] establishment of what is [already] established.
If [one says] there is the existence of another means—then one should expect another means.
But regarding the object to be known, there is just no further need.
If [one says it is for] a special delight—that too [arises] from the previous means of cognition.
'If a person were to know the self as "I am this,"
Desiring what, for whose sake would he cling to the body?'

children.translated_text: Here it is replied: Even when the reality is ascertained through a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), false appearances do not always cease everywhere — due to a special cause, they may persist. Just as the appearance of two moons or the reversal of directions [persists] for those who have ascertained the truth about the directions and the moon from the testimony of trustworthy persons. Similarly, for one who has apprehended the truth of the self from the doubtless <s>āmnāya</s> (Vedic scripture), false appearances continue due to the strength of <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) nourished by the practice of beginningless false perception. For their removal, something else is required. And that is the repeated practice of the vision of truth, which is well-known in the world, as well as <s>yajña</s> (sacrifice) and the like, which are grounded in <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) as their authority. For repeated practice, by strengthening [its own] <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression), overpowers the prior <s>saṃskāra</s> and extends its own effect. And <s>yajña</s> and the like [operate] through some unseen means (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>). Others say: through the removal of impurities that obstruct the highest good, since obligatory <s>karmas</s> (rituals) have the purpose of destroying accumulated sin. [Objection:] Let the false appearances continue. But certainty arises from the <s>pramāṇa</s>. And conduct follows reality as it is ascertained. Therefore, for one who has apprehended the truth of the self, no activity — whether auspicious or inauspicious — is justified. [Reply:] It is said: Even when the vision of truth has arisen, if the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) in the form of a cloth [of repetition] has not been laid down, and the <s>saṃskāra</s> born of false perception is stronger, even certainties become directed toward false objects. Just as for one confused about directions, when the trustworthy person's statement is not recalled, activity proceeds as before. Similarly, even for a rope whose nature has been correctly cognized, when the <s>pramāṇa</s> is not recalled, the sight of fear arises from the delusion of a snake. Therefore, even when the vision of truth has arisen from a <s>pramāṇa</s>, for the purpose of overpowering or destroying the stronger <s>saṃskāra</s> that has been perfected through the practice of beginningless false perception, the practice of the vision of truth is advocated. And thus it is said: 'It is to be reflected upon, to be meditated upon' (<s>mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ</s>). And there is the injunction of means such as <s>śama</s> (tranquility), <s>dama</s> (self-restraint), <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy), <s>yajña</s> (sacrifice), and the like. Otherwise, what would be the purpose of that instruction? [Objection:] It may be that the knowledge of truth arises from the <s>āmnāya</s> (Vedic scripture) only through the performance of means such as <s>brahmacarya</s> and the like. [Reply:] That is wrong. For the cognition arises from <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) alone. For the <s>āmnāya</s> dealing with the apprehension of truth is not non-signifying prior to the special means, nor is it non-ascertaining, since it removes all doubts entirely. Otherwise, the apprehension would be difficult to obtain even with the means it prescribes. Moreover, even when there is certainty otherwise, actors on stage such as <s>Bharata</s> and the like, through false appearances, become causes of grief and fear. Even when the sweetness of sugar is ascertained, a false appearance of bitterness in it causes suffering as if it were real, since one rejects it with disgust just as one would the real [bitterness]. Therefore, for the removal of those [false appearances], even for one who has ascertained the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>ātman</s>, means are required.

children.translated_text: Just as from a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) there is no producibility of liberation in the manifestation of truth, so too there is no [producibility] from the means in a particular [degree of] manifestation. The <s>śrutis</s> (Vedic texts), however, may be understood as pertaining to the stage where perfection is attained through repeated practice, or as requiring knowledge that is grounded in <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony), since the latter is the cause of the former. Enough of this excessive elaboration.

The connection with the body is caused by false self-identification (<s>mithyābhimāna</s>). When that is removed through the vision of truth, there is bodilessness. Therein, the absence of connection with pleasure and pain is declared. Therefore, one who has apprehended the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>ātman</s> does not partake of <s>saṃsāric</s> (worldly) properties as before. And he who does so has not [truly] apprehended the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>ātman</s>.

children.translated_text: As for the [objection] that the injunctions of <s>karma</s> (ritual action), having their own separate effects, [merely] qualify one for knowledge, since one whose three debts are discharged has eligibility for that — that too is not [established] from injunction, because the option regarding <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life) is mentioned in <s>smṛti</s> (tradition): 'Some [teach] an option regarding <s>āśramas</s> for him'; 'let him abide in whichever [<s>āśrama</s>] he wishes'; and from hearing: 'One may renounce directly from <s>brahmacarya</s> (studentship).' And from the observation of the abandonment of <s>karma</s>: 'Verily, the wise of old did not offer the <s>agnihotra</s> (fire offering)'; likewise, 'What shall we do with progeny?'; and 'For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we sacrifice?' For one who has entered <s>gṛhastha</s> (householder) life and who considers himself fulfilled through self-knowledge alone, disregarding the repayment of debts, the text shows that the sin resulting from non-performance of prescribed duties obstructs the arising of knowledge: 'Having discharged the three debts.'

children.translated_text: But this is proper: Even for <s>karmas</s> (rituals) that have no expectation of any other result, due to the separability of their conjunction [with knowledge], as in 'The <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> seek to know it through the study of the <s>Vedas</s>, through <s>yajña</s> (sacrifice)' — their being auxiliaries to knowledge [is established]. And this auxiliaryship is for the purpose of the arising [of knowledge], not for bodily utility like the preliminary offerings (<s>prayāja</s>) and the like. Because knowledge has no other result [to produce]. Or the view of <s>saṃskāra</s> (purification), as per <s>smṛti</s> (tradition). For knowledge arises in one who has been purified. As it has been stated: 'Because the <s>āśrama karmas</s> (duties of one's stage of life) are also enjoined.'

tathā cordhvaretasāṃ cāśramiṇāṃ vināpi tairviśuddhavidyodaya iṣyate /
kiṃ tu kālakṛto viśeṣaḥ /
sādhanaviśeṣāddhi sā kṣipraṃ kṣiprataraṃ ca vyajyate /
tadabhāve cireṇa ciratareṇa ca /
taduktam ---
‘sarvāpekṣā ca yajñādiśruteraśvavat'; /

children.translated_text: KKS_37

children.text:
eṣo 'rthaḥ ---
‘yajñena dānena'iti śravaṇātkarmāṇyapekṣyante vidyāyāmabhyāsalabhyāyāmapi, yathāntareṇāpyaśvaṃ grāmaprāptau siddyantyāṃ śaighryāyākleśāya vāśvo 'pekṣyate /
children.translated_text: This is the meaning: From hearing 'through <s>yajña</s> (sacrifice), through <s>dāna</s> (charity),' <s>karmas</s> (rituals) are required even for knowledge that is attainable through practice alone — just as even when the arrival at a village is achievable even without a horse, a horse is required for speed and ease.

But the arising of knowledge has [only] perceptible means. In that case, let perceptible factors alone be required as the subsidiary conditions — the specific means such as <s>śama</s> (tranquility), <s>dama</s> (self-restraint), and so forth counteract the distraction of the mind, since for one whose mind is composed, the clarity of knowledge arises effortlessly. But <s>yajña</s> (sacrifice) and the like [are not needed], since that [knowledge] can arise through practice even without them. True. And thus for <s>ūrdhvaretas</s> (celibate ascetics) and [other] <s>āśramins</s> (those in stages of life), the arising of pure knowledge is accepted even without those [sacrifices]. However, there is a difference due to time. For through special means, it manifests quickly or more quickly. In the absence of those [means], [it manifests] slowly or more slowly. As it has been stated: 'And all [means] are required, from the <s>śruti</s> (scripture) regarding <s>yajña</s> (sacrifice) and the like, like a horse.'

children.text:
nanu vidyārūpaṃ brahmaiva /
na vidyā brahmaṇo 'nyā /
tacca nityamakāryam /
tatra kathaṃ kiñcidapekṣyeta? ucyate ---
yathopadhānatirohitarūpasphaṭikamaṇirupadhāvakarṣaṇaṃ svarūpābhivyaktaye 'pekṣate tathehāpi draṣṭavyam /
na hi sphaṭikamaṇeḥ pūrvarūpaṃ vinaṣṭamupadhānasannidheḥ, tadapagame vānyadutpannam /
na hyakasmādanekavisabhāgakṣaṇavyavahitasya pūrvasabhāgakṣaṇasyotpattiḥ sambhavati /
na hyagnivigame 'ṅgārebhyaḥ punaḥ kāṣṭhasantatipravṛttiḥ /
tasmādyathaivākāryaṃ sphaṭikarūpamupadhānāvakarṣaṇamapekṣate tathātmarūpamapi /
syadetat ---
jñānaṃ tatra sāpekṣam /
tacca sphaṭikādbhinnaṃ kāryam /
puruṣaprayatno hi tatra jñānārthaḥ /
kiṃ punarjñānaṃ svarūpeṇaivārthitam, āhosvidarthasvabhāvasiddhaye? na tāvatsvarūpeṇa, arthena vyavahārat /
na vijñānamātranibandhano vyavahāraḥ, mithyājñānenāpi prasaṅgāt /
athārthasvabhāya jñānamarthyeta, tadartho vyāpārastenārthito bhavati /
na ca jñānādarthe kaścidvikāraḥ, tayorasaṃbandhāt /
yogyadeśatāyāḥ sarvatra bhāvāt /
sarvapratipattṛṇāṃ ca viditatvaprasaṅgāt /
dhvastānāgateṣu ca tadasaṃbhavāt /
tasmādyathātirohitamapi tirohitamivābhivyajyata iva prayatnāpekṣam, tathātmatattvamapyatirohitaṃ tirohitamiva prayatnādabhivyajyata iveti puṣkalam /
children.translated_text: But knowledge itself is <s>Brahman</s>. Knowledge is not other than <s>Brahman</s>. And that is eternal and uncreated. How then could anything be required for it? It is replied: Just as a crystal gem whose form is concealed by a covering (<s>upadhāna</s>) requires the removal of that covering for the manifestation of its true form, so too it should be viewed here. For the prior form of the crystal gem is not destroyed by the proximity of the covering, nor is another form produced when that [covering] is removed. For it is not possible that a prior homogeneous moment should arise after being separated by many dissimilar moments without any cause. For when fire departs, the continuity of wood does not resume from the embers. Therefore, just as the uncreated form of the crystal requires the removal of the covering, so too does the form of the <s>ātman</s> (self). [Objection:] It may be said: Knowledge there requires something [else]. And that [knowledge] is different from the crystal and is a product. For human effort there is directed toward knowledge. But is knowledge desired for its own sake, or for establishing the nature of the object? Not for its own sake, since practical activity depends on the object. Nor is practical activity based merely on cognition [alone], for [otherwise] there would be the absurd consequence of [activity based on] even false cognition. If knowledge is desired for [establishing] the nature of the object, then since the purpose is the activity [directed at the object], that [activity] is what is desired. But from knowledge, no modification occurs in the object, since there is no connection between the two. Because the fitness of location exists everywhere. And because it would follow that [the object] is known by all cognizers. And because that [knowledge] is impossible with regard to things destroyed or not yet arisen. Therefore, just as what is not concealed, yet appears as if concealed and as if manifested, requires effort, so too the truth of the <s>ātman</s> (self), though not concealed, appears as if concealed and as if manifested through effort — this is sufficient.
Thus the <s>ātman</s> (self), with all differences subsumed within, has been described as the universal self,
Like gold indicated through the subsumption of differences such as bracelets and the like. [End of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> 1.3]

children.text:
yataśca viśeṣapratyastamukhena tannirūpaṇam, ato 'nyairbrahmavidyābhiyuktaiḥ sāmānyarūpaṃ brahma nirūpitam ---
‘sa eva mahānaja ātmā sattālakṣaṇaḥ'; tathā ‘sattaiva sarvabhedayoniḥ prakṛtiḥ parā'; iti /
yathā suvarṇatattvaṃ kaṭakāṅgulīyādiviśeṣopasaṃhāreṇa nirūpyamāṇaṃ tatsāmānyamiti /
ye vā ---

children.translated_text: KKS_38

children.text:
‘nirviśeṣaṃ na sāmānyaṃ bhavecchaśaviṣāṇavat'ityabhāvamāhuḥ, tān pratyucyate ---
saṃhṛtākhilabheda iti /
yadi tāvadasāmānyatvaṃ sādhyate siddhasādhanam /
viśeṣāṇāmabhāve keṣāṃ tatsāmanyam? sāmanyaṃ tūktaṃ brahmavādibhirviśeṣapratyastamukhena nirūpaṇādupacārataḥ /
athābhāva eva sādhyaḥ, viśeṣairevāsya nirviśeṣairvyabhicāra iti /
children.translated_text: 'That which is without particulars cannot be a universal — it would be like a hare's horn' — [for those who] declare its non-existence, to them it is replied: 'With all differences subsumed.' If what is being proved is that it is not a universal, then it is proving what is already established. In the absence of particulars, of what would it be the universal? But the term 'universal' was used by the proponents of <s>Brahman</s> figuratively, because the characterization is through the negation of particulars. If what is to be proved is [its] non-existence itself, then there is deviation [of the proof] through the very particulars, which are themselves without particulars.

And since its characterization is through the negation of particulars, therefore other masters devoted to <s>Brahmavidyā</s> (knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>) have described <s>Brahman</s> as having a universal nature: 'That great unborn self, characterized by being (<s>sattā</s>)'; likewise, 'Being itself is the supreme <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), the source of all differences.' Just as the nature of gold, when characterized by subsuming the particulars such as bracelet, ring, and so forth, is [understood to be] that universal. Or those who —

children.text:
iti śrīmanmaṇḍanamiśraviracitāyāṃ brahmasiddhau brahmakāṇḍaḥ samāptaḥ /
-- edition; Originally Brahma- and Tarka-kāṇḍas were together; Vacaspati does not know this division.
children.translated_text: Thus ends the <s>Brahmakāṇḍa</s> (Chapter on <s>Brahman</s>) in the <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> composed by the revered <s>Maṇḍana Miśra</s>. — Edition note: Originally the <s>Brahmakāṇḍa</s> and <s>Tarkakāṇḍa</s> were together; <s>Vācaspati</s> does not know this division.
KKS_39
<s>Tarkakāṇḍa</s> (Chapter on Reasoning)

children.text:
nanu pratyakṣādibhirvyāvṛttānāṃ bhāvasvabhāvānāmavagamānnaikasminnadvaye śabdaḥ pramāṇam, pratyakṣādivirodhāt, grāvaplavanādyarthavacovat /
ucyate ---
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Since entities whose natures are known from <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and the like as distinct are apprehended, <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) cannot be a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) regarding oneness and non-duality, because it would contradict <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the like — like the statement about floating stones and the like. It is replied:
The wise declare that <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is an establisher, not a denier.
<s>Āgama</s> (scripture) regarding oneness therefore does not contradict <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception). [<s>Brahmasiddhi</s> 1.4]

children.text:
nanu pramāṇāntaraparatantrāṇāṃ puruṣavacasāṃ tadvirodhādyuktamapramāṇatvam /
svatantrasya tvāmnāyasyānapekṣitapramāṇāntarapravṛttestadvirodhe 'pi kasmādapramāṇatvam? āmnāyavirodhādeva tu pratyakṣādīni pramāṇatāyāḥ kimiti na cyavante? tulye 'napekṣatve na viśeṣaheturasti /
tatra vṛthā pramāṇāntaravirodhaparihārapariśrama iti /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] For human statements, which are dependent on other <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), it is reasonable that they are not authoritative when they contradict those [other <s>pramāṇas</s>]. But for the <s>āmnāya</s> (Vedic scripture), which is autonomous and operates without dependence on other <s>pramāṇas</s>, why should it be non-authoritative even when it contradicts them? Why should not <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and the like rather lose their authority due to contradicting the <s>āmnāya</s>? When both are equally independent, there is no distinguishing reason. In that case, the effort to resolve the contradiction with other <s>pramāṇas</s> is futile.

children.text:
tatra kecidāhuḥ ---
pratyakṣādivirodhe āmnāyasya daurbalyam, sāpekṣatvat /
tathā hi svarūpasiddhyarthameva tāvatpratyakṣādīnyāmnāyo 'pekṣate /
tathā ca teṣāṃ prāmāṇyamanumantavyam, tadapabādhane svarūpasyaiva tāvadasiddheḥ /
na tvevamāmnāye pratyakṣādīnāṃ kācidapekṣā /
dṛṣṭavyabhicāratvācca śabdasya, pratyakṣasya cādṛṣṭavyabhicārāt /
api ca sāvakāśānavakāśayoranavakāśaṃ balavat /
anavakāśāśca pratyakṣādayaḥ, sāvakāśastu śabdo gauṇenārthena /
tathā hi ---
śakyamekatvamabhedaśrutīnāmupacaritamavakāśo varṇayitum /
avivakṣitārthānāṃ vā vedāntānāṃ japopayogo 'vakāśaḥ /
upaniṣado vedāntā iti varṇitam /
kiṃ ca vyākulatvādāmnāyasyāvyākulatvātpratyakṣādīnām /
karmavidhayo hi bhedāśrayā abhedāśrayāśca vedāntāḥ parasparaparāhatā asatyapi pramāṇāntaravirodhe durlabhaprāmāṇyāḥ /
kiṃ punaravyāhatapratiṣṭhitaprāmāṇyādivirodhe /
tasmādidamavirodhāya prayatyata iti /
mukhyatvācca /
mukhyā hi pratyakṣādayaḥ /
jātasya jantoraparakāla āmnāyaḥ /
sa taiḥ pratiṣṭhitārthairapahṛtaviṣayaḥ kalpanīyārtho bādhyate, tadanusāreṇa vārthakalpanāmarhati /
arthato 'pi ca mukhyatā pratyakṣādīnām /
padapadārthavibhāgādhīna āmnāyārthaparicchedaḥ, sa ca pratyakṣādiṣvāpatate /
ato 'virodhāya prayatyata iti /
children.translated_text: Regarding this, some say: When there is conflict with perception and the like, scripture is weaker, because it is dependent. For scripture depends on perception and the like for the very establishment of its own nature. And thus their validity must be accepted, since if they are sublated, the very nature of scripture itself would be unestablished. But perception and the like have no such dependence on scripture. And because verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) has been observed to deviate, while perception has not been observed to deviate. Moreover, between that which has scope for alternative interpretation and that which does not, the one without scope is stronger. Perception and the like are without scope for reinterpretation, while verbal testimony has scope through secondary meaning. For it is possible to describe the oneness stated in the non-difference scriptures as figurative — that is the scope for reinterpretation. Or the <s>Vedānta</s> texts whose intended meaning is not taken literally have the scope of being useful for recitation (<s>japa</s>). The <s>Upaniṣads</s> are <s>Vedānta</s> — this has been explained. Furthermore, because scripture is internally conflicted while perception and the like are not. For the injunctions of ritual action presuppose difference, while the <s>Vedānta</s> texts presuppose non-difference — being mutually contradictory, their validity is difficult to establish even without conflict with other means of knowledge. How much more so when there is conflict with means of knowledge whose validity is firmly established and uncontradicted. Therefore, an effort is made toward reconciliation. And because of primacy. For perception and the like are primary. Scripture comes at a later time for the being already born. It, being deprived of its subject matter by those whose objects are firmly established, is sublated as having a meaning that must be construed, or it warrants construal of meaning in accordance with them. And the primacy of perception and the like is also from the standpoint of meaning. The ascertainment of scriptural meaning depends on the division of words and their meanings, and that falls within the domain of perception and the like. Therefore, an effort is made toward reconciliation.
Verse 40 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
anye manyante ---
tulyabalatve 'pi pratyakṣādīnāmāmnāyasya ca vastuni vikalpānupapattervirodhe saṃśayaḥ syāt /
tenāvirodha upapādyata iti /
children.translated_text: Others think: Even if perception and the like are equal in strength to scripture, in the case of conflict there would be doubt, since the alternatives cannot be resolved regarding the real nature of the object. Therefore, reconciliation is established.

na tvevamapauruṣeye śabde kāciddoṣāśaṅkā /
satyāṃ vā pramāṇameva na syāt /
pratyakṣādīnāṃ tu vyāvahārikaṃ prāmāṇyam, avidyāsaṃskārsya sthemnā vyavahāraviparyayābhāvāt /

śabde tu saṃbhāvitadoṣe na tattvāvedanena prāmāṇyam /
na vyavahārāviparyayeṇa /
adṛṣṭārthatvāddoṣebhyo vyavahāravisaṃvādijñānadarśanācca /
pratyakṣādīnāṃ tu vyavahāre saṃvādānna śakyate vyavahāravisaṃvādijñānaheturdoṣaḥ kalpayitum /
vyavahāraviparyayāddhi sa kalpyeta /
tattvadarśanasya tu vedāntajanmanaḥ pratipakṣatvāttattvapratihatimātraheturevānādiravidyānubandhaḥ kalpyate /
tato doṣānubandhaḥ prāmāṇyaṃ ceti na virodhaḥ /
śabdastu saṃbhāvitadoṣo durlabhaprāmāṇya eva syāt /
dṛśyate hi doṣebhyo vyavahāravisaṃvādijñānotpattiḥ /
tatra doṣāśaṅkayā vyavahāravisaṃvādasya śaṅkitatvāttattvapratighātasya ca, na tattvāvedanalakṣaṇaṃ prāmāṇyam, na vyavahārāvisaṃvādalakṣaṇamiti /
tasmācchabdasya prāmāṇyābhyupagame pramāṇāntaravirodhe 'pi tasyaiva balavattvamiti sāṃpratam /
yattu pratyakṣādyapekṣaṇāditi, tatrocyate ---
na pramitāvapekṣāvattā śabdasya pratyakṣādiṣu, kiṃ tu svarūpasiddhau /
anyathā pramāṇameva na syāt /
tathā ca svakārye 'pekṣatvānna pratyakṣādibhyo hīyate /
pratyakṣādayo pi svarūpasiddhau nānyānapekṣāḥ /
kārye hi sāpekṣatvaṃ

children.translated_text: Verse 41 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
sāmarthyamapakarṣatīti /
yattveteṣāṃ prāmāṇyamanumātavyamiti, ko vānyathāha? vyavahārāvisaṃvādilakṣaṇaṃ tu tat, na tattvāvedanalakṣaṇam /

svayameva vyāhatā vedāntārthapratipattiḥ /
nābhedo bhedamantareṇa śakyo 'vasātum /
bhedopāyā hi tasya pratipattiḥ /
tatrābhedaḥ samākṣiptabheda eva pratāyata iti vyāghātaḥ ---
tadapāstam /
yata upāyamākṣipati pratipattiḥ /

itarayorapi tulyamavyabhicāritvam /
tathānavakāśatvamapi /
yadi khalvekamadvayaṃ vedāntārthaḥ, kasteṣāmanyo 'vakāśaḥ? athaupacārikatvamekatvaṃ tadartho 'vivakṣitārthatā vā japopayoginām, tatra virodha eva nāstīti balābalacintā nāvatarati /

‘dṛṣṭo hi tasyārthaḥ karmāvabodhanam'; ‘aviśiṣṭastu vākyārthaḥ'iti ca avivakṣitārthatā? pramāṇāntaravirodhāditi cet, vārtametat /
na pramāṇasya pramāṇāntarāpekṣaṃ prāmāṇyam, yena tadvirodhe svarasaṃ jahyāt /
tadapekṣatve hi tadanuguṇatayā varteta /
nirapekṣasya kaḥ pramāṇāntarānusaraṇe
children.translated_text: diminishes the capacity. As for the statement that the validity of these must be inferred — who says otherwise? But that validity is characterized by non-discordance with convention, not by revealing ultimate truth. From perception and the like, which possess conventional validity, the established scripture provides the vision of truth; due to conflict with that, it sublates only the aspect of truth-vision in them, not the aspect of non-discordance with convention. And it is observed that a later cognition is stronger than an earlier one, even when the earlier was relied upon as a cause — as in the case of trees at a distance, where the cognition that they are trees is stronger than the cognition that they are elephants. For the cognitions of elephants were relied upon as causes for the clear cognition that they are trees. For that cognition does not arise from the mere contact of sense organ and object, since it is absent at the initial moment. Nor from a particular location, since it arises only for one who is at that location. Therefore, it should be understood that for one who has directed attention toward the trees in front, that cognition is produced by the contact of the sense organs aided by latent impressions following from the earlier erroneous cognition. Similarly, cognitions of twenty and the like, which sublate the cognitions of one and the like, can also be cited as examples. And thus what some describe — that the understanding of <s>Vedānta</s> meaning is self-contradictory, that non-difference cannot be established without difference, that its understanding requires the means of difference, and that non-difference as understood necessarily involves difference, hence a contradiction — that is refuted. For the understanding sublates the means. It does not require the ultimate reality of the means, since even from false knowledge, true understanding can arise. And the conventional reality of difference is indeed accepted. The observation of deviation is the same for both verbal testimony and perception, which are born from defective causes. The non-deviation of both is likewise equal. And so too is the absence of scope for reinterpretation. If indeed the meaning of <s>Vedānta</s> is that reality is one and non-dual, what other scope is there for them? And if oneness is figurative, or the meaning is unintended, or they are useful only for recitation, then there is no conflict at all — and so the inquiry into relative strength does not arise. Then how is there weakness from having scope for reinterpretation? And how can a figurative scope be accepted by passing over the primary meaning? And how, when verbal testimony has a subordinate relation to its meaning as established by convention — 'For its purpose is seen to be the communication of action'; 'But the sentence meaning is undifferentiated' — can there be non-intended meaning? If it be said: because of conflict with other means of knowledge — this is exactly the point. The validity of a means of knowledge does not depend on other means of knowledge, such that it would abandon its natural meaning in case of conflict with them. For if it depended on them, it would operate in conformity with them. For one that is independent, what is the reason for following another means of knowledge?
Verse 42 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.translated_text: What is the reason? Ordinary words express their meanings in dependence on other means of knowledge, so it is proper that their usage follows those. But when the independence is equal, why not the reverse? Or, from the contradiction of both, invalidity of both? Or, 'in a sequence of earlier and later, the earlier is weaker' — sublation of the earlier, like the cognition of silver? Surely the cognition of mother-of-pearl is not rendered objectless or directed to another object because of its conflict with the cognition of silver. How then is there secondary meaning (<s>guṇavāda</s>) in the <s>Veda</s>? Where the establishment of the meaning of a valid means of knowledge is impossible through the scriptural meanings alone, there, because a secondary usage of words is also observed, the valid object is obtained through that secondary meaning. But where words obtain their object naturally, they do not turn away because of conflict with other means of knowledge. For their meaning is not dependent on other means of knowledge, such that they would turn away under their control.

Another view: Scripture alone is stronger when there is conflict. 'In a sequence of earlier and later, the earlier is weaker, as is natural.' 'The arising of the later is indeed established by the non-sublation of the earlier.' For instance: Everyone's determination of distinct objects, which is innate and based on perception and the like, is well known. But the non-dual understanding, which depends on that, is preceded by it, is not innate, and belongs only to some — that understanding, being unable to arise without first crushing the former, arises through the sublation of the former. Furthermore: Because perception and the like can be causes of various possible errors, while scripture is free from all suspicion of defects. For the defects that reside in persons are impossible in verbal testimony when no person is involved. Indeed, from scripture itself, a beginningless latent impression of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) can be posited and ascertained as the cause of error in perception and the like — just as the false identification of the body with the self. But in scripture, which is not of human origin (<s>apauruṣeya</s>), there is no suspicion of any defect. Or if there were, it would not be a valid means of knowledge at all. The validity of perception and the like is merely conventional (<s>vyāvahārika</s>), because the latent impression of <s>avidyā</s> is firmly established and there is no reversal of conventional activity. But where there is reversal of conventional activity, there is no validity. In the case of scripture, where defects can be posited, there is no validity in the form of revealing ultimate truth — nor through non-discordance with conventional activity, since its objects are unseen, and because knowledge discordant with convention is observed even from defects. But for perception and the like, since there is concordance in conventional activity, a defect that causes knowledge discordant with convention cannot be posited. For such a defect would be posited from reversal of conventional activity. But the continuous association with beginningless <s>avidyā</s> is posited as merely the cause of obstruction of the vision of truth, since the vision of truth born from <s>Vedānta</s> is its opponent. Therefore, the association with defects and validity are not contradictory. But scripture, where defects can be suspected, would indeed have difficult-to-establish validity. For the arising of knowledge discordant with convention from defects is observed. There, because of the suspicion of defects, both discordance with convention and obstruction of truth are suspected — so there is neither validity in the form of revealing truth nor in the form of non-discordance with convention. Therefore, when the validity of scripture is accepted, even when there is conflict with other means of knowledge, it is scripture alone that is stronger — this is proper.

By this, the following claim is also refuted: In the world, when verbal testimony conflicts with other means of knowledge, it is observed to have figurative meaning or unintended meaning. Therefore, when there is conflict with perception and the like, the <s>Vedānta</s> texts must be the same — since this is observed in perception and the like as well.

If one thinks: It is construed thus for the benefit of both. For in this way, both verbal testimony and perception and the like are favored. Otherwise, perception and the like would be completely sublated. This is not sound. With respect to the object of knowledge, some construal may be made following the capacity of the means of knowledge. But with respect to the means of knowledge itself, there is no basis for construal by abandoning what is naturally established. Therefore, the arrangements of combining alternatives are construed following the means of knowledge, not for the benefit of both. There is no means of knowledge that dictates that both must be favored. If those themselves are the means of knowledge — if this is the view: the validity of a means of knowledge is not to be supported by another means of knowledge, but rather by itself alone. For it is precisely because of being a valid means of knowledge that it establishes objects in a certain way. Then the object should be established just as it is understood from that means. Thus it is favored. Otherwise it would be sublated. And the establishment of objects without valid means would not follow, since there is no cognition from that naturally, and because of the absence of any other basis, and because of the fallacy of mutual dependence — validity is to be construed from the impossibility of explaining it otherwise when an object different from what is cognized from established validity is cognized, and the validity follows from that cognition. But when the object is obtained naturally, validity follows from the cognition itself — so there is no mutual dependence. Therefore, in conflict, sublation of the earlier follows the means of knowledge, since that is how cognition operates. Not the construal of an alternative object for the later. Surely, to favor the cognition of silver, one does not construe another object for the cognition of the mother-of-pearl fragment. Nor is there absence of scope for perception and the like such that they have no other recourse. Whatever recourse the illusions of silver and the like have, that same recourse is theirs too. If the object of those is figurative or construed, then the object of perception and the like is likewise. children.translated_text: As for the argument that because of primacy, scripture is deprived of its subject matter by those whose objects are firmly established — precisely for that reason, it is the sublator, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl. Nor does it warrant the construal of meaning in accordance with them, because it is independent. No — its being a valid means of knowledge does not depend on those. It does not act in conjunction with them; there is no syntactic unity between scripture and perception and the like. For in both cases, the arising of cognition is mutually independent. Therefore, the greater strength of the later is proper. As it has been said:
'Let the greater strength of the later over the earlier be acknowledged there,
where the arising of cognitions is mutually independent.'

And so, how can those [ritual injunctions] defeat the <s>Vedānta</s> [texts], or the <s>Vedānta</s> [texts] defeat them? Moreover, defeat is observed even among perception and other [means of knowledge] themselves, from the observation of the relationship between the sublatable and the sublating in cognitions of silver, shell-fragments, and the like, and from the apprehension of both difference and non-difference everywhere.
Thus, even though the scripture is authoritative, if some dull-witted person, seeing that worldly statements are given figurative meaning when they contradict perception and the like, thinks that verbal usage in the <s>Veda</s> too is like that of the world; or if someone, because of the deeply entrenched darkness of the perception of difference, thinks that perception and the like alone are more authoritative, and because sublation of worldly statements is seen through those [means]—to awaken such a person, the [alleged] contradiction is refuted. For it is not the case that one who dies from being bitten by a scorpion with mild venom is therefore not to be treated.

But where there is joint operation through syntactic unity, since the primary meaning stands firm due to the absence of contradiction through natural function, the subordinate words—unable to comprehend the syntactic unity through the primary function because of the impossibility of supplying the required meaning—supply the meaning required by the preceding [words] through the secondary function, by the force of syntactic unity. Thus the primacy of the primary [meaning] is [established].
As for the objection regarding confusion, it is replied:
There would be confusion only if the injunctions of ritual action were aimed at establishing difference.
But they, relying on already established difference, are primarily concerned with instruction for human welfare, [saying] 'one should accomplish this by this means in this manner.'
It may be objected:
In the absence of difference, whence instruction for welfare, since all three components would be nullified? It is replied:
Just as in [rites like] the <s>Śyena</s> and others, even though the component of what is to be accomplished is nullified by the prohibition 'one should not harm any beings,' there is still instruction—so too everywhere, even when all three components are nullified.
For consider:
How could <s>hiṃsā</s> (violence), which produces prohibited harm, be something to be accomplished? Yet it does occur for someone whose inner nature is seized by fierce anger, whose discriminative knowledge is obscured by the risen darkness, who sees even what is harmful as beneficial and transgresses the teaching of scripture. Similarly, in the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> and other [rites], all three components are presented to the unawakened through innate <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), and instruction is given to them relying on those [apparent components].
But the awakened are not instructed by injunctions of ritual action,
just as those who have conquered the enemy of anger [are not instructed] by the injunctions of the <s>Śyena</s> and similar [rites].

children.translated_text:
Regarding perception, there are three alternatives:
[perception involves] affirmation (<s>vidhi</s>) of the intrinsic nature of an entity, exclusion (<s>vyavaccheda</s>) of other entities, or both. And in each of these three, there is a further threefold division:
simultaneity, exclusion preceded by affirmation, and affirmation preceded by exclusion.
Among these, if [perception's scope includes] exclusion of other entities or both, then difference falls within the range of perception, and there is a contradiction [with non-duality].
But if [perception involves] mere affirmation of intrinsic nature, devoid of any exclusion, then difference is not established by a means of valid cognition, for without exclusion there is no establishment of difference.
And if perception has the function of mere affirmation, then there is no contradiction. How is this explained? It is said:
In something that has acquired its form, something of that very nature is negated;
Therefore without affirmation (<s>vidhāna</s>), negation (<s>viṣedha</s>) is impossible. // <s>MBs</s> 1.5 //

Others, however, explain that the external negation is made of things that have acquired their form in the mind through some cause. Otherwise, what negation could there be of something whose form has not yet obtained [in cognition], being precluded by fate? Or if its form has obtained, how could there be absolute negation? Moreover, if exclusion negated without regard to its object, <s>śūnyatā</s> (voidness) would be the meaning of valid cognition, not difference, since everything would be negated everywhere without distinction.
But the exclusion that serves difference requires the establishment of both things to be differentiated, and that [establishment] is not possible without affirmation. Therefore, affirmation must be prior, and negation preceded by affirmation alone is accepted.

Now, mere exclusion is not the function of perception, nor are both [affirmation and exclusion] simultaneous, nor is affirmation preceded by exclusion. For what is negated in an established object is an already established form:
'This is not here,' 'this is not that'—in an established ground, an established pot [is negated], or in a cow, a horse.
Without the object to be negated and the locus of negation, negation cannot take place.
Then how is there negation of absolutely non-existent things like <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), sky-flower, and the like? For there is no negation of them in any place or time, since [their non-existence] is absolute; nor is there any establishment from anywhere, since they are absolutely non-existent.
Regarding this, some say:
As for sky-flowers and the like—in the established [substrates] such as the sky and so forth, flowers and the like of that kind are negated; 'there is no <s>pradhāna</s>' means that in the cause of the world, [properties such as] having the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, being an undifferentiated [material cause], and the like are denied.
Nor is exclusion preceded by affirmation [tenable], because:
Sequence is not logically consistent for the operations of a single cognition;

And because the object and the thing to be excluded are attained through prior cognition, there is no impossibility [of exclusion]. And since the object to be excluded has been manifested in the prior cognition, the occurrence of exclusion does not entail the manifestation of a non-present object, because that [exclusion] arises in dependence on the prior [cognition].
And it is precisely through dependence on the prior [cognition] that it arises with a dual nature; otherwise it would arise with a single nature alone.
Moreover, if [affirmation] does not accomplish all exclusions, which exclusion is intended, on the basis of which one would take a stand? If [it is said] 'that which is established in the world'—then is this too not established in the world:
'A horse is not a cow, a cow is not a horse'?

Indeed, affirmation and exclusion, being operations of a single means of valid cognition, cannot logically have sequence, because [cognition] is momentary. For if the two operations were sequential, the latter one would not be an operation of that [same cognition], due to the intervening gap.
Moreover, the very arising of cognition is its operation, since cognition has the nature of apprehending an object. And if this [cognition] arises in the form of affirming an object, then its operation is affirmation alone, since simultaneity has been rejected, and since what has already arisen does not arise again.
Furthermore, perception, having a present object as its support, cannot manifest an object that is not present; and it cannot exclude what does not appear [in it]. For if the object to be excluded does not appear, there would be mere exclusion [in the abstract], not the exclusion of anything specific—or it would be the exclusion of everything.
Therefore there is no exclusion when the object to be excluded does not appear, and it is not proper for perception, which rests on present objects, to manifest what is not present.
How then does sublating perception [work]? For in that case, negation of the prior object is admitted as preceding the affirmation of another in a single cognition, and there is manifestation of what is not present as the object to be negated. Therefore, this restriction [that negation requires prior affirmation] does not hold, since negation can come first, and there can be sequence within a single cognitive operation, and perception can manifest a non-present object.
This is not sound. Even there, regarding silver and the like posited by a prior cognition, the negation is preceded by affirmation in the general [cognition] 'this' which rests on a present object. The affirmation of shell, however, is said to be preceded by the negation arising from contradiction. And the rule that negation is preceded by affirmation is stated with respect to negation, not that affirmation cannot be preceded by negation. Nor is there, in that case, a single cognition's

As for the view that:
Affirmation of one thing alone is the exclusion of others.
That is to say:
Just as perception, by [taking on] the form of that [object], posits that form, so too, because of its restriction to that single form, it excludes the other, [thinking] 'that alone, not another.' And the conceptual constructions 'this' and 'not this,' produced by the power of that [restriction], initiate the practical activity of existence and non-existence.
For there is no exclusion of others apart from the cognition that is restricted to a single form and does not associate with anything else.

Therefore, even for the exclusion of visible [entities], another reason must be sought—not the mere restriction of perception.
And thus the exclusion of other selves too does not attain establishment from that [restriction alone].
Granted, because the nature of affirmation is the exclusion of the non-existence of what is to be affirmed, the absence of that [entity] would be excluded, but not the existence of another self—just as the existence of things not perceived at that place and time [is not excluded].
If [it is said that] one entity does not have many selves—then the exclusion would be due to contradiction from another [source],

And in the absence of exclusion, whence multiplicity, or whence contradiction—or would there be mutual dependence? Therefore, the affirmation of one thing is not the exclusion of another.
Moreover, if the exclusion of others [followed] from restriction to one, then in variegated [objects] such as paintings, the difference of blue and the like, which share a single perception, would not be established, since there is no restriction of cognition to one [color] when there is association with a single cognition.

The restriction to one [object] is not the cause of the ascertainment of the absence of another, because there would be the undesirable consequence of exclusion without distinction of this other [entity] that fulfills the defining characteristic of being perceivable. For the restriction to that [one object] is the non-association of another with it.
And thus, if exclusion [follows] from non-association, the exclusion of both the visible and the invisible would follow, since there is no distinction [between them in this regard].

The defining characteristic of perceivability serves as the distinguishing factor for ascertaining the exclusion of [entities at] the same place and time. Objection: Entities are different by their very nature (<s>prakṛti</s>). Perception, in positing them as they are, thereby differentiates them from one another. For <s>vyāvṛtti</s> (exclusion/distinction) is not something other than the entity possessing exclusion.
In positing what possesses exclusion, that [exclusion] too is posited, since whatever entity has a certain nature must be posited with that very nature; otherwise there would be no positing of it [at all]. And entities whose nature is to be distinct manifest in their respective perceptions accordingly, and therefore are posited just as they are.
Even against this, the same problem remains: since there is no contact [of perception] with [the other entity's] manifestation, there is no [contact with] its nature, and the exclusion of both visible [entities] follows without distinction.

Difference (<s>bheda</s>) is not the nature of an entity, because its absence would follow;

children.translated_text: The method [of argument is as follows]: If difference is the own-nature of a thing, no single thing would exist, because of the contradiction between difference and oneness. Even an atom, being manifold due to difference, would not be one. And likewise, the self of a manifold [thing], being of the form of an aggregate of those [atoms], does not hold [as one either]; since both oneness and manyness are impossible in that case, and a third mode is not possible, the consequence would be that the thing has no own-nature. An alternative explanation of the second half [of the verse]: [The verse] stands firm against the alternatives of separateness and non-separateness; this division pertains to the thing itself—namely, being of that nature and being of another nature—and does not admit of application to an unreal difference whose body is fabricated by conceptual construction. For indeed, [difference is] inexpressible as either identical or different, having its body displayed by conceptual construction whose basis is beginningless latent impressions of conceptualization. 'This is different from that; this is the difference between them'—thus it engenders conventional usage. Difference is not some real thing whose identity or otherness could be investigated. Herein this further stands firm: And the differentiation of a thing through what is formless does not hold. If then difference is formless and without own-nature—if indeed it does not exist in reality and is merely displayed by conceptual constructions—then there is no real differentiation of things, because of the absence of difference in the ultimate sense. For it is not fitting that an ultimate possession of that [difference] could hold through a constructed own-nature; it would itself be merely constructed. This very thing, being stated by us, why does your honor not assent to it? We too say this very thing: Difference does not exist in reality; this is the play of beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).

<s>Vyāvṛtti</s> (exclusion) is not the intrinsic nature of a thing. For it is acknowledged and recognized as having both single and multiple substrates.
And thus, if this single [exclusion] with multiple occurrences were the intrinsic nature of things, there would be no difference among things either, for it is not logical that what has a nature undifferentiated from one [exclusion] could be different—it would be just like [that one exclusion].
If, to avoid this fault, <s>vyāvṛtti</s> is held to be something entirely different [from the entity], even then, since <s>vyāvṛtti</s> is not the [entity's] nature, entities would not be distinguished by their own nature.
Another alternative:
If <s>bheda</s> (difference), whose nature is the mutual non-selfhood [of entities], were the intrinsic nature of a thing, then the non-existence of things would follow, since one would be asserting that their nature is [essentially] non-existence.
Another [alternative]:

children.translated_text: As for what was said—'If difference is the nature of a thing, there would be no single thing; and given its existence, the other [oneness] too [would be negated], hence no thing [at all]'—to this they reply: We speak of the difference-nature of a thing as relative to another, not relative to itself, by which [latter], due to contradiction, there would be no single thing. Rather, a thing is one in its own form but different in relation to another. To this it is replied:
A thing does not conform to a dependence that is merely personal [i.e., subjective].
