children.translated_text: Because of the consequence of mutual dependence in the establishment of the own-nature of things. Alternatively, as for what was said—'Because of non-separateness from a single [thing], there is the consequence of the absence of difference in things'—to this they reply: Difference is not one, because of the contradiction of [its] forms; and if it were one, by that reason all things would become one. Therefore, difference is differentiated with respect to each entity. How then does it have multiple substrata? Through dependence. For its own form is established in dependence on the counter-correlate. And thus things are different through differences that are relative to counter-correlates and are identical [with the things themselves], each in their respective way.

Dependence is not any real property of a thing by which things could be determined. For in things whose arising has been brought about by their own causes and whose natures are established [independently], it is not fitting that there be dependence on another thing for the establishment of their own nature. Hence this [dependence] is a property of personal cognition. And things do not conform to personal cognition, since their own natures are established from their own causes. Therefore, the form of a thing is not determined in accordance with that [personal cognition]. It is proper that its determination follows the established own-nature of the thing, since [cognition] presupposes that [thing].

children.translated_text: An alternative explanation: Difference is not the form of a thing, for it is cognized as relative. And in the matter of dependence, a thing does not conform to personal cognition, because [cognition] presupposes the established thing.

It might be [objected]: An entity arises from its causes with its form complete. Therein, the form called 'difference' is dependent on the counter-correlate, [but] since [the entity] at no time lacks it, being of that nature, it arises together with that nature—hence there is no manifestation of an incomplete form. To this it is replied: Let there be the manifestation of one of that nature. But the purpose of the dependence must be stated. For whatever pertains to something with respect to something else, that is said to be dependent on that; no other distinguishing mark that separates the dependent from the independent is identified. Now, [one might say]:

children.translated_text: How then [do relations such as] father and the like [function]? For they too do not exist without dependence, nor are they comparable to the sky-flower or the city of the <s>Gandharvas</s> and the like, since they are established in the world by virtue of being factors in non-deceptive practical activity. It is replied: Is difference too not equally established in the world? Moreover,
Dependence in the case of father and the like is brought about by procreation and the like. (<s>MBs</s> 1.9)

children.translated_text: The capacities of being produced and producing are already established as the referents of the words 'father' and 'son'; however, those [words] are applied [more broadly] to objects of the same generative activity, through their own-nature difference. Hence, the dependence is with respect to that in which there is commonality. What is meant is this: The word-meaning there is dependent, not the thing. And the cause of dependence there—a common activity—exists even for things whose [own-natures are already] established. But in [the case of] difference of entities, this investigation concerns the real nature of things, and no cause of dependence is apprehended. Even in the case of the short and the long, [the dependence is] with respect to a single class.

children.translated_text: If dependence arises even from difference of effects—well then, the mutual relative difference of entities will be established simply from the difference of causal efficacy! Moreover, since even without direct perception, difference is established through inference by difference of effects alone, we infer the difference of causes from the difference of effects—this being the sole operation of inferential reasoning. In the case of oneness, difference of effects is not tenable, because the difference of effects depends on the nature of the cause. If producing that is its nature, it does not produce another. Therefore, the other effect has its origin from something else. Thus, this [difference of effects is established] only through difference itself.

children.translated_text: Very well, but burning and cooking are both from touch alone. And these two are distinguished in ordinary experience even when there is commonality in the modification of the substance in contact. And a single action is the cause of conjunction, disjunction, and momentum; the self [is the cause] of desire and the like; <s>sattva</s> and the rest, individually and without difference, [are causes] of lightness, illumination, and the like; color and the like [are causes] of specific cognitions and of moments of the same class—thus it should be considered. [Objection:] But we do not assert difference merely from difference of causal efficacy, but rather from [causal efficacy] that is unprecedented and inconceivable [in a single entity]. Just as, when the eye is present but [the capacity is] unprecedented, and in the case of a deaf person, that [incapacity is established]

children.translated_text: Similarity of effects is [also] applicable—who would prevent the birth of a heterogeneous [effect] from a homogeneous [cause]? Therein, just as from conventional non-difference there is similarity of effects, so too from conventional difference there is difference of effects—hence no distinction [between the two positions]. It might be [objected]: If difference is constructed and yet capable of [producing] difference of effects, then it is not constructed. For there is no other mark of the ultimately real than the capacity for causal efficacy. This [objection] applies equally to [the position of] non-difference as well.

From the difference of causal efficacy, no mutual difference of form among entities is cognized, nor can it be inferred. There would be merely a difference of designation, since difference of effects such as burning and cooking is observed even in a single fire. If it is thought: Fire is an aggregate of color and the like; therein, illumination is from color, burning is from touch—

children.translated_text: properties, even while inhering in an unlimited, infinite object, do not pervade it. Therefore, there is no contradiction of presence and absence even in a single entity. As for one who thinks that difference of causal function is the regularity of causal function, and from that the apprehension of difference follows — for in unity there can be no regularity; and thus from milk too there would be oil, and from sesame seeds there would be curd; likewise, when one thing is born everything would be born, and when one perishes everything would perish; otherwise difference would merely be stated by another word — as it has been said: 'Simultaneous production and destruction, and everything would serve for everything' — to him also, the same reply applies: 'By the distinction of burning and cooking.' If the regularity is the plurality of effects, one does not thereby understand the difference of sesame seeds and milk. If the regularity is that curd is born from milk and not from anything else — the difference that is sought to be proven cannot enter into the definition of a regularity that is yet to be established, since that would lead to the non-establishment of the regularity itself. Therefore, the regularity consists in the capacity to produce curd and its absence. From that, difference follows. For the capacity and incapacity regarding the same object cannot belong to one and the same thing — but this argument from contradictory properties as a ground for difference has been refuted just above. Just as objects of long duration, when associated with properties of limited duration, are both possessors and non-possessors of those properties without being subject to contradiction, so too are objects of vast extent with those of limited extent, and infinite with finite. If one asks how an infinite entity can have a finite property — when there is either distinction or indescribability, there is no room for impossibility. Even without distinction, it is like a short-duration property of a long-duration entity. For one who does not accept long-duration entities, this must be recited again: 'By the distinction of burning and cooking.' Even a single fire burns only some things and cooks them. And thus it is both a burner and a non-burner, yet is not differentiated. Likewise, it does not produce other burnings or other cookings in that very thing being burnt or cooked. Similarly, seeds and the like, though individually capable, do not produce other sprouts, nor does the aggregate. And thus there is the capacity to produce and the incapacity to produce. If in one and the same thing there is the capacity to produce, why does it not produce another — one that has perished or one yet to come? Because their capacity is directed only there and not elsewhere, even in things of the same class. Why? Because only that arises, and because capacity is inferred from the effect. And thus there is no contradiction of capacity and incapacity. Even without difference then, if from milk there is no production of curd from sesame seeds, there is no contradiction. For it is not the case that in the milk from which curd is born there is non-production from sesame seeds such that from the contradiction of capacity and incapacity

children.translated_text: difference would follow. Why? Because of the non-difference of sesame seeds and milk. If the contradiction is the non-production of another curd — that too is not so, because of the incapacity elsewhere but capacity right there, just as with seeds and the like. For it is not the case that whatever is capable as a cause produces everything of the same class, since that would lead to the absurd consequence that all effects of the same class would arise from a single cause. If one thinks: We ascertain difference from the differentiated assignment in causal functions — for milk is assigned to curd, not sand — that too is inconclusive, because differentiated assignment is observed even in unity. That very real entity, together with its auxiliaries, is assigned — not by itself alone. If one thinks: That itself is differentiated, due to the difference of limiting conditions created by the presence of auxiliaries — then the difference is merely adventitious, resting on cognition alone, not ultimate. And such a difference of entities is indeed accepted. Even one who asserts difference through momentariness — since his difference too is of the same kind, either everything serves for everything, or nothing serves for anything, because the capacity is equally unobserved. If the establishment follows from a difference beyond the reach of conceptual construction, then from a non-difference of the same kind too — there is no distinction, as has been stated. Even one who affirms both of a single entity — both difference and non-difference — by accepting the presence of contradictory properties in one thing, finds it equally difficult to establish the division of sesame seeds and milk by the capacity and incapacity to produce curd.

Even one who thinks that the apprehension of difference arises from the simultaneous observation of contradictory functions — for instance, the universe is perceived at one time as endowed with various mutually contradictory properties such as birth, death, growth, decay, staying, going, sorrow, joy, and the like, and therefore it is understood as having difference — to him also, the same reply applies repeatedly: 'By the distinction of burning and cooking.' How so? First, this person must be asked: What is 'contradictory function'? If it means impossibility in one thing, that is unestablished. If it means mutual exclusion of natures — that birth and the like are defined by the negation of each other's form — then from this, the establishment of difference does not follow, since even in a single fire, the capacities of burning and cooking are observed. For without mutual exclusion, there is no plurality of properties. And if difference followed from that, nothing possessing multiple properties would be one. If contradiction is merely the nature of mutual absence — that in one thing the same property both exists and does not exist — and from that one concludes difference — that is wrong. For there are no such two properties at all; how then can apprehension of difference arise from their contradiction? And in the case of sky-flowers and the like, since both are absent, both conclusions would follow. If contradiction is the relation of victim and destroyer — joy destroys sorrow and sorrow destroys it, and similarly for others — even there, one that is unborn does not destroy another, nor does it destroy what is in a different substratum. Therefore, it must be said that it destroys after becoming co-located in the same substratum. And thus, since the co-location of both in one substratum is observed, the inference of difference of substrata from observing them is not invariable. If the contradictory properties are those that are positive in nature and defined by the exclusion of each other — such as permanence and impermanence, corporeal and incorporeal — and difference is understood from their connection — that too is not valid. For it is not necessarily the case that whatever exists somewhere pervades it entirely. For chariots and the like, and their contacts, do not pervade space, nor other conjoined things like earth and the like, because they are limited. Similarly, limited
Thus indeed:
This alone is the greatness of the one, which is incapable of being matched by the production of difference.
When the imagining of difference in entities is like that of fire, it is in vain.

children.translated_text: then the imagining of difference is causeless, since that is established even from a single entity — this is the conclusion of the preceding section. This very point has been expressed by the Vedic verse: 'Such is his greatness.' This is the measure of his capacity — that even though one, he is 'of a thousand heads,' and 'whatever has been and whatever will be.' How does the one become the substratum of the various mutually contradictory functions and effects indicated in the preceding two verses? 'From this' — meaning from what is presented through perception — '<s>Puruṣa</s> alone is all this' — meaning from what is indicated by the unseen (scripture). Or, 'and of immortality' — <s>Puruṣa</s> is greater than the manifest world, taken individually and collectively, as elaborated through the division of the worlds of gods and men. Therefore, there is nothing improper in the infinite one containing limited and seemingly contradictory properties. That very greatness is shown: 'One quarter of him is all beings.' Even the entire manifest world is his lesser portion — how much more so each individual thing. Thus: His 'three-quarters' — the unlimited, infinite form, devoid of the properties of the manifest world such as death and the like — 'abides in heaven,' in the state of radiance, or in the state of supreme bliss, or in the orb of the sun, or in the celestial realm. For there it is to be meditated upon. For that is said to be the place of its realization. Another interpretation: Even if in an imagined or established difference of substrata based on difference of effects, why is there no different effect? Why is there no confusion, or an inverted regularity? Even with difference, why is it that oil comes from sesame seeds and not from sand? And though different, the eye, light, and the like produce a single effect, and arrows and horns likewise. And with difference too, why is oil from sesame and curd from milk, but not oil from milk and curd from sesame? If one thinks: Because of the inconceivable capacities of things — the inconceivable and inexplicable capacities of things, to the question 'why? how?', have their regularity to be inferred from the observed effects — from these come the difference, regularity, and non-reversal of effects. If so, let that surplus of capacity belong to the one alone — that the effects are many, regular, and non-reversed. By that alone its establishment is achieved; the postulation of difference among entities is without valid basis.

Because the distinction of functions is observed in a single entity; because the impossibility in one is unestablished; because the observation of the unseen lacks the capacity to sublate non-difference; because it is merely a cause of particularity and that particularity is indescribable as either identical or different, being a ground for conceptual construction; because non-difference of effects is possible from a non-difference of the same kind just as difference of effects from a difference of that kind; because contradiction is inconclusive or because regularity is unestablished; because the differentiation of assignment is inconclusive; and because its establishment follows from an imagined difference just as from non-difference — this alone is some inconceivable surplus of capacity belonging to the one, capable of producing the entire elaboration of difference, just as the power of fire is the cause of the distinction of cooking, burning, and the like, when it is demonstrated that

children.translated_text: The difference of capacities is postulated because of the supposed contradiction of one thing being connected with many effects. But if one thing cannot be connected with many, how is one thing connected with many different capacities? Just as the one entity of a certain nature is associated with many capacities, why is its association with many effects not likewise accepted? If there is contradiction in association with many effects but not in association with many capacities, the reason for the distinction must be stated. Moreover, since the capacities are non-different from their substrate, the one is accepted as having many natures. There, the oneness is contradicted by the plurality that inheres in the same substrate. But it is well said that it is contradicted by that which inheres in another substrate as known through effects! If the capacities are entirely different entities, their substratum must be explained. If by contact — in the case of truly different things, there can be no contact characterized by non-separation of forms; difference itself would not exist. Not by contiguity, for then another substance conjoined with a substance conjoined with that capacity would also have that capacity. For there is nothing intervening between the substance and its capacity. Just as there is nothing between the eye-substance and color that is not immediately adjacent. And because space and the like are all-pervading, since there is no intervening absence of any capacity of any object, there would be the absurd consequence that everything has every capacity. Therefore, the substratum is based on some specific benefit. There, just as in the case of different capacities, one entity of a certain nature performs different benefits due to the difference of those capacities, why is it not accepted that it likewise produces effects? Thus, even through inference there is no apprehension of difference, nor through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption).

For the difference of entities consists in the aspect of mutual absence, and that is not within the range of the senses. Therefore, beyond the means of knowledge that establish positive entities, a separate means of knowledge must be resorted to for the establishment of absence. Or a separate means of knowledge called 'absence' serves as the delimiter, distinct from the means that establishes positive entities. Based on that,
'And the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends on the validity of that means of knowledge.' To them it is replied:
Difference, because of mutual dependence, is not established by a separate means of knowledge.

children.translated_text: It is said: This is not sound. If there is no cognition of an undifferentiated form, then the means of knowledge would simply be without an object. For there is no cognition of difference without exclusion. Exclusion is not [possible] alone, nor accompanied by a positive [cognition], nor does the means of knowledge operate after the positive [cognition]—nor is the positive [cognition] itself the exclusion: this has been expounded. In that case, if not even one [thing] is cognized, there would simply be objectlessness [of cognition]. And if the non-recognition [of identity] is said to be due to the dissimilarity of cows, even though the form of mere being is apprehended throughout, then even in another cow there should be no [recognition], due to dissimilarity from <s>Devadatta</s>. For the cognition of oneness upon re-seeing <s>Devadatta</s> is not of the same kind as [the recognition] in another cow.

Furthermore, when the form of mere being (<s>sanmātra</s>) is apprehended everywhere, in entities whose nature is that [being], the non-arising of means of knowledge accepted by each [disputant] regarding what is accepted by the other [does not lead to absence-cognition], since both have the nature of being. And because everywhere there is a means of knowledge for 'being' (<s>sat</s>). [Objection]: And from the absence of a means of knowledge [comes] the cognition of mutual absence. [Reply]: But no form of entities is undifferentiated. For that [undifferentiated form] is understood through recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>). And for one who has perceived a mere object, there is no recognition 'this is the very same' in another object, as [there is] for one who has seen one cow in another cow. But the recurrence of the word 'being' and the concept [of being] is, like [the concept of] 'cook' and the like, based on convention (<s>yoga</s>). For [the concept] 'being' is the object of a means of knowledge.

children.translated_text: perception is not sublated by reasoning. True. It has been indicated that the cognition of difference is not [genuinely] perceptual—just as [the cognition] of a firebrand-circle produced by extremely rapid contact in all directions [is not genuinely perceptual]. That [cognition], even though existing, is not produced by a means of knowledge; [yet] being similar in form to perception, like the cognitions of dream-objects, firebrand-circles, and the like, it does not [lead to] the ascertainment of reality. [Objection]: But as has been stated, the arising of the cognition of difference from [a source] other than a means of knowledge is also impossible. [Reply]: Who says otherwise? For there is no ultimate apprehension of difference. If there were, how could difference be denied? And if denied, how could there be apprehension of it? That it is not apprehended yet exists, and that it is apprehended [yet does not ultimately exist]—this is hard to reconcile. What then is this? It is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), error (<s>vibhrama</s>). And when the existence of the object [of cognition] is [accepted] in accordance with its appearance, it is not error, but rather correct cognition. Yet the apprehension of what is non-existent is impossible. Therefore, it is not characterized as ultimately existent, nor as non-existent, since it is established in ordinary experience in all [philosophical] doctrines—so it has been said.

[One might think]: There exist two cognitions—of recurrence (<s>anuvṛtti</s>) and exclusion (<s>vyāvṛtti</s>). For without those two, the transactions of recurrence and exclusion would be impossible. And there is no other cause for the determination of objects than the form of cognition. If [cognition] is not the cause, then non-difference too would not be established. [Reply]: This is not sound. For cognition does not determine the reality of an object merely because it is a cognition. For that [cognition] too must be examined: does it conflict with reasoning, or not? Is it produced by a means of knowledge, or not? For surely the reality of objects is not determined from cognitions such as [the perception of] a firebrand-circle and the like. [Objection]: This may be so, but—

children.text:
api ca jñānadvaye 'smiṃścatasraḥ kalpanāḥ saṃbhavanti ---
jñānabhedātsāmānyavyaktivibhāgena vastudvayam, yathāhuḥ saṃsargavādinaḥ /
ekaṃ vā sāmānyaviśeṣātmakaṃ vastu, yathāhuranekāntavādinaḥ /
viśeṣā eva vā vastūni /
teṣāmātyantikabhedaniścayāsāmarthyāttadupādānastadviṣaya evābhedaḥ kalpanājñānagocaraḥ /
dṛṣṭā hi bhinneṣvabhedakalpanā ‘vanam'; iti ---
yathāhurātyantikabhedavādinaḥ /
abhedo vā paramārthaḥ /
tasyānavacchinnasyānantasya tathā niścetumaśakteranāditvāccāvidyāyāstadupādānāstadviṣayā bhedaparikalpanāḥ /
dṛṣṭā hi taraṅgabhedādabhinne candramasi bhedakalpanā /
tannāparīkṣya tattvaniścayaḥ /
tatra parīkṣāyām ---
children.translated_text: Moreover, given these two cognitions, four theoretical possibilities arise: [1] Two entities—universal and particular—distinguished by the difference of cognitions, as the proponents of conjunction (<s>saṃsargavādins</s>) maintain. [2] Or a single entity having the nature of universal and particular, as the proponents of manifoldness (<s>anekāntavādins</s>) maintain. [3] Or only particulars are real entities; due to the inability to ascertain their absolute difference, non-difference that has those [particulars] as its substrate and as its object is the domain of conceptual construction (<s>kalpanā</s>)—for the conceptual construction of non-difference in what is different is observed, as in [the concept] 'forest': so say the proponents of absolute difference. [4] Or non-difference is the ultimate reality; due to the inability to ascertain it as it is—unlimited and infinite—and due to the beginninglessness of <s>avidyā</s>, the conceptual constructions of difference that have it as substrate and object [arise]—for the conceptual construction of difference in the undivided moon [due to] the difference of waves is observed. Therefore, without examination, there is no ascertainment of reality. Now, upon examination:
First, [there are] not two [entities], because of the non-difference of appearance in [apparent] oneness. (<s>MBs</s> 1.15)
If that [non-difference of appearance] is due to <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), [it fails] because difference is not abandoned.

children.text:
na tāvaddve vastunī sāmānyaviśeṣau, prakhyābhedāt /
samānādhikaraṇatvena hīme prakhye jāyete ‘san ghaṭaḥ, gauḥ svastimatī'; iti /
na vyadhikaraṇatvena yathā nīlapītaprakhye, yathā vā ‘daṇḍo devadattaḥ'; iti /
nāpi viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvena yathā ‘daṇḍī'iti, saṃbandhasyāpratibhāsanāt /
na ca vastubhedaviṣayatve sāmānādhikaraṇyamavakalpate satyapi saṃbandhe /
saṃbandhidvayaṃ viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatvena dvābhyāmekayā vā buddhyā gṛhyate, na tu parasparātmatvena /
parasparātmatvena ceha pratipattiḥ pratyātmavedanīyā /
vipratipatteśca sāmānyaviśeṣayor

children.translated_text: <s>KKS</s> 61

children.text:
bhede /
nānyathā vipratipadyeran /
sāmānyapratyakṣe ca viśeṣapratyakṣābhimānāt /
anyathā dhūmadṛṣṭāvivāgnau parokṣābhimānaḥ syāt /
syādetat ---
na saṃbandhamātrādbhedapratipattiḥ, api tu saṃbandhaviśeṣātsamavāyāt /
sa hi vastusaṃśleṣātmakaḥ /
tanna, samavāye 'pi tābhyāṃ rūpabhedasyānapāyāt, anyathā bhedābhāvādasaṃbandhāt /
tathā ca naikātmyena prakhyā yujyate /
asti ceyam /
atastayā viruddhaḥ prakhyābhedo na vastubhedavyavasthāyai prabhavati /
svayaṃ vā vyāhatatvāt, ekādhikaraṇatvenotpatteḥ (ekādhikaraṇatvenopapatteḥ edition) /
children.translated_text: [it is clear that there is disagreement precisely] regarding their difference. They would not otherwise disagree. And in the perception of a universal, there is the conviction that it is the perception of a particular. Otherwise, as in the case of [inferring] fire from seeing smoke, there would be the conviction that [the fire] is imperceptible. [Objection]: The cognition of difference does not arise from mere relation, but from a specific relation, namely <s>samavāya</s> (inherence). For that [inherence] has the nature of the coalescence of entities. [Reply]: That is not so, because even in <s>samavāya</s>, the difference of form between those two does not disappear; otherwise, there being no difference, there would be no relation. And thus the appearance as having a single identity is not tenable. Yet this [appearance] exists. Therefore, [the fact that] the non-difference of appearance conflicts with [the hypothesis of] the difference of entities does not serve to establish the distinction of entities; or [the hypothesis] is self-contradictory, since [the unified appearance] arises as having a single locus.

First, the universal and the particular are not two entities, because their appearances are non-different. For these two appearances arise as co-referential (<s>samānādhikaraṇa</s>): 'the pot exists,' 'the cow is auspicious.' Not as having different referents (<s>vyadhikaraṇa</s>), like the appearances of blue and yellow, or like 'the stick [and] <s>Devadatta</s>.' Nor as qualifier and qualified, as in '<s>daṇḍin</s>' ('one with a stick'), because the relation [between them] does not appear [in cognition]. And if [universal and particular] are objects of different entities, co-referentiality is not tenable even when there is a relation. For two relata are apprehended as qualifier and qualified, by two or by one cognition—but not as being each other's self. Yet the cognition of [them] as each other's self is experienced in one's own awareness. And from the disagreement [among philosophers] regarding the universal and the particular,

children.text:
nanu bhede 'pi parasparātmatvena pratipatternimittaṃ samavāyaḥ /
tasya khalveṣa sāmarthyātiśayaḥ, yena bhedavatāmarthānāṃ bhedaṃ tirodadhāti /
tathā ca te 'bhedena prakāśante /
atrocyate ---
children.translated_text: [Objection]: But even given difference, <s>samavāya</s> is the cause of the cognition of [them as having] each other's nature. That indeed is the special capacity of <s>samavāya</s>, by which it conceals the difference of different entities. And thus they appear as non-different. To this it is replied:
If the capacity to conceal difference is held [to belong to inherence] even in [the case of] difference, (<s>MBs</s> 1.16)
well then, why should not the same [capacity belong] to a single [entity] that appears in this way?

children.text:
samavāyasāmarthyāccedbhedavatorabhedavatorabhedāvabhāsaḥ, hantaikasyaiva vastunaḥ sāmarthyaviśeṣānnānāvabhāso 'bhyupeyatām /
vyarthā vastubhedakalpanā /
na hyasti viśeṣaḥ ---
yato bhinnayorabhedaprakāśasaṃbhavaḥ, naikasya nānāvabhāsasaṃbhava iti /
children.translated_text: If, due to the capacity of <s>samavāya</s>, there is the appearance of non-difference for things that are different, then let it be accepted that, due to a special capacity, a single entity alone has a manifold appearance. The postulation of a real difference of entities is pointless. For there is no distinguishing [reason] such that the appearance of non-difference for two different things is possible, but the manifold appearance of one [thing] is not.

children.text:
nanu jvalanāyoguḍādiṣu dṛṣṭamevaṃvidhaṃ saṃsargasya sāmarthyam /
tatra darśanātsaṃbhavī saṃsargādbhedavatsvabhedāvabhāsaḥ /
naikasminnānāvabhāsaḥ, adarśanāt /
ucyate ---
children.translated_text: [Objection]: But in the case of fire and a ball of iron or jaggery and the like, such a capacity of conjunction is directly observed. From that observation, the appearance of non-difference for things that are [actually] different is possible due to conjunction. But a manifold appearance for a single [entity] is not [possible], since it is not observed. [Reply]: It is said:

children.text: dṛṣṭaḥ saṃsargadharmo 'yaṃ yadyekamapi vai tathā // MBs_1.17 //
children.translated_text: If this property of conjunction is observed, then indeed a single [entity] too likewise (<s>MBs</s> 1.17)
appears as manifold—a single variegated form, and likewise cognition.

children.text:
dṛṣṭaṃ khalvekamapi vividhāvabhāsam, yathā citraṃ rūpam /
taddhi khalu na nīlādisamāhāramātram /
teṣāmavayavasamavāye rūpāntarānabhyupagame cāvayavino nīrūpatvaprasaṅgāt /
na ca nīrūpatvamevāvayavinaḥ /
rūpasaṃskārābhāve hi na sa cākṣuṣaḥ syāt /
na ca rūpisamavāyātsaṃkhyākarmādivaccākṣuṣatvam /
evaṃ hyuktam ---
‘mahatyanekadravyasamavāyādrūpāccopalabdhiḥ'; iti /
sarvaścetthamavayavī nīrūpaḥ syāt /
atha nārūpaḥ pratīyata iti nāyaṃ prasaṅgaḥ,

children.translated_text: KKS_62

children.text:
citro 'pi tatheti nārūpaḥ /
taccāsya rūpaṃ nīlapītādinirbhāsaḥ /
children.translated_text: — even the variegated one is likewise, and therefore is not colorless. And its color is precisely the appearance as blue, yellow, and so forth.

It is indeed observed that even a single thing has variegated appearance, as in the case of a variegated color. For that is certainly not a mere aggregate of blue and other colors. Because if <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) of parts is accepted, and a distinct color of the <s>avayavin</s> (composite whole) is not admitted, there would be the undesirable consequence of the composite whole being colorless. And the composite whole is not simply colorless. For in the absence of the impression of color, it would not be perceptible by the eye. Nor is its visual perceptibility due to inherence in something possessing color, as in the case of number, action, and the like. For it has been stated thus: 'In the case of a large thing, perception is due to color arising from inherence in multiple substances.' If so, every composite whole would be colorless. If it is argued that it is not perceived as colorless and therefore this undesirable consequence does not arise —

children.text:
tathā nagaratrailokyādibuddhayo vividhaviṣayākārā nirbhāsante bhedābhāve 'pīti viṣayākārajñānavādino manyante /
na caikabuddhitattvāvyatirekādviṣayākārāḥ parasparato 'pi vyāvartante, prāgeva buddheḥ /
syādetat ---
citramapi rūpaṃ saṃsargādevaikārthasamavetasamavāyalakṣaṇāttathāvabhāsate /
tadasat /
yataḥ ---
children.translated_text: Similarly, cognitions of a city, the three worlds, and the like appear with variegated object-forms even in the absence of difference — so the <s>viṣayākārajñānavādins</s> (proponents of the doctrine that cognition takes the form of its object) maintain. And since the object-forms do not differ from one another apart from the single reality of cognition, still less do they differ from the cognition itself. [Objection:] It may be said that even a variegated color appears as such due to connection — namely, the connection characterized by <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) subsisting in a single locus. That is wrong. Because —

children.text: na ca saṃbandhisaṃbandhaḥ saṃsargo vyavadhānataḥ // MBs_1.18 //
children.translated_text: Contact, which is the connection of the related terms, does not occur through intermediaries. // MBs_1.18 //

children.text:
saṃśleṣo hi saṃsargaḥ /
tataśca paraspararūpāvabhāsaḥ /
sa cāvyavadhāne yujyate /
na tu svāśrayābhyāṃ vyavadhāne /
avayavāvayavirūpayorekavyavadhāne 'pyasaṃśleṣaḥ, kimu dvayavyavadhāne /
children.translated_text: For contact means close conjunction. And from that arises the mutual appearance of each other's form. That is possible only without intermediaries, but not when there is intermediation by their own substrata. Even with a single intermediary between the forms of the part and the composite whole there is no close conjunction — how much less when there are two intermediaries.
Moreover —
When conventional usage is based on extrinsic limiting adjuncts, every cognition is merely conventional;
When it is not in accordance with reality, the superimposition of difference among entities is futile. // MBs_1.19 //

children.text:
yasya khalu ‘śuklo gauḥ'; ityādibuddhayo vyavahārāṅgabhūtā dravyeṣu guṇajātyupādhinibandhanāḥ tasyaitā na yathāvastu, jātiguṇadravyāṇāmanyonyamarthāntaratvāt /
tathā ca na vastunibandhano vyavahāraḥ, buddhyānupadarśitasyāvyavahārāṅgavādbuddhyupadarśitasya ca tathābhāvāt /
evaṃ ca pratyayaviracitenaivāyamarthena vyāvṛtto vyavahāro 'nuvṛttaśceti vyarthā vastubhedakalpanā, kalpitasyāpi tasya vyavahāre 'nupayogāditarasya copayogāt /
yathārthatvāya hi vyāvahārikīṇāṃ buddhīnāṃ vastubhedaḥ kalpyate /
kalpite ca tasmin paropādhitvāttāsāṃ nāyathārthatvaparihāraḥ /
children.translated_text: For one who holds that cognitions such as 'the cow is white' and the like, which serve as instruments of conventional usage, are based on the limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhis</s>) of <s>guṇa</s> (quality) and <s>jāti</s> (universal) in substances — for such a person, these cognitions do not correspond to reality, since <s>jāti</s>, <s>guṇa</s>, and <s>dravya</s> (substance) are mutually distinct entities. And thus conventional usage is not grounded in reality, since what is not presented by cognition is not an instrument of conventional usage, and what is presented by cognition is likewise [not grounded in reality]. And thus, since this conventional usage — both inclusion and exclusion — operates through an object constructed by cognition alone, the postulation of real difference is pointless, since even a constructed [difference] serves the purpose of conventional usage while the other [i.e., real difference] does not. For real difference among entities is postulated in order to make conventional cognitions veridical. But when that [difference] is postulated, since those cognitions are based on extrinsic limiting adjuncts, the problem of their being non-veridical is not resolved.

children.text:
syādetat ---
asati vastubhede 'yathārthamapyanuvṛttavyāvṛttāvagrahaṃ vyāvahārikaṃ vijñānaṃ nodetumarhati, bījābhāvāt /
na khalu sthāṇuśakalādiṣu puruṣarajatādivibhrāntayo nirbījāḥ, sāmānyanibandhanatvāt /
ucyate ---
children.translated_text: [Objection:] It may be said — even in the absence of real difference, a conventional cognition that grasps inclusion and exclusion, though non-veridical, ought not to arise, due to the absence of a cause. For surely the illusions of a person or silver with respect to a post or a piece of shell are not without a cause, since they are grounded in similarity. It is replied:
The cause of a non-veridical cognition is not necessarily external alone;
for an internal disturbance too is observed, such as a visual defect (<s>timira</s>), desire, and the like. // MBs_1.20 //
KKS_63

children.text:
na viṣayadoṣādeva sādṛśyāderayathārthajñānam, ādhyātmikebhyo 'pi tu doṣebhyastimirakāmaśokādibhyaḥ /
tatrāsati vastubheda ādhyātmiko doṣo 'vidyālakṣaṇo vyāvahārikajñānabījamiti nārtho vastubhedena /
children.translated_text: Non-veridical cognition does not arise only from a defect in the object, such as similarity, but also from internal defects such as a visual defect (<s>timira</s>), desire, grief, and the like. In this case, in the absence of real difference, the internal defect characterized by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is the cause of conventional cognition — thus there is no need for real difference.

children.text:
astu tarhyekaṃ dvyātmakam /
evaṃ hi parasparātmapratipattiśca sāmānyaviśeṣayoḥ kalpate /
vastuviparītaśca nārthasāmarthyātiśayaḥ kalpayitavyaḥ /
vastunibandhano vyavahāraḥ, na vyāvahārikajñānānāmayathārthā vṛttiḥ /
syādetat ---
ekasya dvyātmakatā virodhavatī /
ekaṃ ca dvyātmakaṃ ceti vipratiṣiddham /
api ca sāmānyaṃ bhedāntarānuyāyi /
tato vyāvṛttasvabhāvo bhedaḥ /
tayorekatvaṃ hi virodhādaśakyāvaham /
naitatsāram /
viruddhamiti naḥ kva saṃpratyayaḥ? yatpramāṇaviparyayeṇa vartate /
yattu yathā pramāṇenāvagamyate tasya tathābhāve viruddhatvābhidhāne kaṃ batāyamāśritya hetuṃ viruddhatvāviruddhatve vyavasthāpayet? pramāṇaṃ caikasya sāmānyaviśeṣātmakatāmavagamayati, vyāvṛttyanuvṛttibhyāṃ prakhyārūpabhedātsāmānādhikaraṇyāvagamācca (aikādhikaraṇyāvagamācca edition) /
tadidamasāṃpratam, yato nedṛśāṃ vipratiṣiddhārthajñānānāṃ prāmāṇyameva yujyate saṃśayajñānavat /
anyathā saṃśayaviṣayo 'pi dvyātmā syāt, dvyābhāsatvāttasya sāmānādhikaraṇyācca tadavabhāsayoḥ /
children.translated_text: Let it then be that one thing has a dual nature. For in this way, the mutual identification of the universal and the particular is possible. And an extraordinary capacity not opposed to reality need not be postulated. Conventional usage is grounded in reality, and conventional cognitions do not function non-veridically. [Objection:] It may be said — the dual nature of one thing involves a contradiction. 'One' and 'having a dual nature' are mutually opposed. Moreover, the universal pervades different instances. Difference has a nature that is excluded from that. The oneness of these two is indeed impossible to maintain because of contradiction. [Reply:] This is not sound. 'Contradictory' — where does our conviction lie regarding this? In what conflicts with a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). But that which is apprehended by a <s>pramāṇa</s> as it is — if one calls it contradictory when it is so established, on what basis would one then determine what is contradictory and what is not? And the <s>pramāṇa</s> reveals the dual nature of a single thing as possessing both universal and particular, through exclusion and inclusion, through the distinction of manifest forms, and from the apprehension of co-location (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>). [Objection:] This is improper, since the validity of cognitions with mutually contradictory contents is not tenable, just as with doubt. Otherwise, the object of doubt too would have a dual nature, since doubt has a dual appearance and its two appearances share co-location.

children.text:
atha matam ---
na saṃśayite rūpasamuccayāvagamaḥ, yathā sāmānyaviśeṣavati, ‘ayaṃ vā, ayaṃ vā'iti pratīteḥ /
mā bhūtsamuccayaḥ, vikalpaḥ syāt /
so 'pi na, vastuno vikalpānupapatteḥ /
ekamapi tarhi na dvyātmakam, ekasya dvyātmakatāvirodhāt /
tatra yathā saṃśayajñānaṃ vipratiṣedhādapramāṇaṃ tathā sāmānyaviśeṣapratipattirapi, aikādhikaraṇyāt /
children.translated_text: If it is thought: In the case of doubt, there is no apprehension of a combination of forms, as there is in the case of what possesses a universal and a particular — because the cognition takes the form 'either this or this.' [Reply:] Let there be no combination; there may be an alternative. [Objection:] That too is not possible, since an alternative is untenable with respect to a real thing. [Reply:] Then a single thing too does not have a dual nature, because of the contradiction of one thing having a dual nature. [Objection:] In that case, just as the cognition of doubt is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> due to contradiction, so too the apprehension of universal and particular [as one] is not valid, because of co-location.

children.text:
syādetat ---
na saṃśayajñānaṃ vipratiṣedhādapramāṇam, nirṇayajñānena tu bādhanāt /
yatra tarhi na nirṇayastatra vikalpātmatā syāt /
api ca yathā bādhāyāmekasyāprāmāṇyaṃ nirākaraṇāt, evaṃ virodhe 'pi dvayorekasya vā jñānasya viruddharūpopagrahe tadrūpādhigatyoranyonyanirākaraṇāt /
tatraikanirākaraṇe

children.translated_text: KKS_64

children.text:
itarasmānniścayaḥ /
parasparanirākṛtau tulyabalatve sandeha iti na saṃśayajñānādekasya sāmānyaviśeṣapratipattirviśiṣyate /
tasmādihānaikāntikaṃ vastvityevaṃ jñānaṃ suniścitamiti svapakṣopavarṇanam /
children.translated_text: there is certainty from the other. When both are negated and of equal strength, there is doubt. Thus the apprehension of universal and particular is no different from the cognition of doubt. Therefore, the position is described thus: 'Here, the thing is indeterminate' — this cognition is firmly established.

[Objection:] It may be said — the cognition of doubt is not invalid because of contradiction, but because it is sublated by a determinate cognition. Where there is no determination, there would be an alternative nature. Moreover, just as in the case of sublation, one [cognition] is rendered invalid because it is negated, similarly in the case of contradiction too, when one or both cognitions apprehend contradictory forms, through the mutual negation of the apprehension of those forms — in such a case, upon the negation of one,
Moreover —
If the oneness of difference and universality is without contradiction,
there would be no dual nature, just as in the case of an undivided part of one of them. // MBs_1.21 //

children.text:
avaśyamanena padārthānāṃ bhedābhedau vyavasthāpayatā ---
yathā tāvatsāmānyamabhinnaṃ viśeṣā bhidyanta iti ---
bhedābhedayorlakṣaṇaṃ vācyam /
tatra rūpavirodho 'nyonyābhāvo bhedalakṣaṇam /
viparyayo 'bhedalakṣaṇam /
rūpavirodhāddhyanyonyābhāvaparyāyādviśeṣā bhidyante /
bhidyamāneṣvapi teṣu sāmānyamabhinnam, viparyayāt /
tatra sāmānyaviśeṣayoryadi svarūpavirodho 'nyonyābhāvaḥ, naikatvaṃ bhedānāmiva parasparam /
atha sāmānyaviśeṣabuddhyeraikādhikaraṇyenotpatteḥ svarūpavirodho 'bhyupeyate, na tarhyekaṃ dvyātmakam /
sāmānyaviśeṣayoḥ svarūpavirodhābhāvādasati bhede dvitvānupapatteḥ /
yathā na sāmānyāṃśo dvirūpo viśeṣāṃśo vā rūpavirodhābhāvāt ---
tatraikasminnirbhakte dvitvābhāvāt ---
tathā sāmānyaviśeṣayorapi sāmānādhikaraṇyabuddheryadi na rūpavirodhaḥ, na parasparātmābhāvaḥ (Ms B; parasparābhāvaḥ edition) /
dvitvaṃ na yujyate /
atha rūpavirodhaḥ, naikatvamiti /
children.translated_text: For one who establishes both difference and non-difference of entities, the defining marks of difference and non-difference must necessarily be stated. There, opposition of forms — that is, mutual absence — is the defining mark of difference. The opposite is the defining mark of non-difference. For it is due to opposition of forms, which is synonymous with mutual absence, that particulars are different. Even when those are different, the universal is non-different, by virtue of the opposite [i.e., absence of form-opposition]. Now, if there is opposition of forms — mutual absence — between the universal and the particular, then they are not one, just as particulars are not one with each other. If, on the other hand, it is accepted that there is no opposition of forms because the cognitions of universal and particular arise with co-location — then a single thing does not have a dual nature, since in the absence of difference, duality is untenable, because the universal and particular lack opposition of forms. Just as neither the universal-aspect alone nor the particular-aspect alone has a dual form due to the absence of form-opposition — since in one undivided [aspect] there is no duality — so too, if the co-locational cognition of universal and particular involves no form-opposition, there is no mutual non-existence. Duality is not tenable. If there is form-opposition, there is no oneness.

children.text:
yadi matam ---
na svarūpavirodhānnānātvam, tadabhāvāccaikatvam, yena sāmānyaviśeṣayoḥ svarūpavirodhābhāvāddvitvaṃ na syādanyatarasyeva bhāgasya /
kiṃ tu buddhe rūpabhedābhedābhyām /
sāmānyaviśeṣayośca parasparātmatvena pratipatterasatyapyanyonyābhāvalakṣaṇe svarūpavirodhe buddhe rūpabhedāddvitvam /
aṃśe tu rūpābhedādekatvam /
ato vastuno dvirūpabuddhigrāhyatvād dvyātmateti /
tatrocyate ---
children.translated_text: If it is thought: Multiplicity does not arise from opposition of forms, nor does oneness arise from the absence thereof, such that the duality of universal and particular would not follow from the absence of form-opposition, as in the case of one aspect. Rather, [multiplicity and oneness arise] from the difference and non-difference of forms in cognition. And since the universal and particular are apprehended as having each other's nature, even in the absence of the defining mark of mutual absence as form-opposition, there is duality due to the difference of forms in cognition. And in the case of an [undivided] aspect, there is oneness due to the non-difference of forms. Therefore, because the thing is grasped by a cognition of dual form, it has a dual nature. To this it is replied:
If the cognition of oneness [establishes non-difference] in the case of an aspect, then it should do so for the thing as well;

children.text: na cetkutastyamekatvamasti ced dvyātmatā katham // MBs_1.22 //
children.translated_text: if not, whence comes oneness? And if there is [oneness], how can there be a dual nature? // MBs_1.22 //
KKS_65

children.text:
tatrāpi buddhiḥ kimekarūpopagrāhiṇī na veti /
tatra yadi naikarūpopagrāhiṇī vastuni buddhiḥ ---
sāmānyaviśeṣātmakaṃ hi vastu ---
taddvirūpabuddhyupagrāhyam, kathamekatvaṃ vastunaḥ? buddhirūpābhedasyābhedalakṣaṇasyābhāvāt, rūpabhedasya ca bhedalakṣaṇasya bhāvāt /
athaikarūpopagrāhiṇyeva vastuni buddhiḥ, na dvyātmakatvamaṃśavadeva /
atha matam ---
buddhirūpabhedaḥ parasparātmābhāvaśca (Mss AB; parasparātmatābhāvaśca -- edition) bhedalakṣaṇam /
tatra gavādayo bhedā bhinnarūpabuddhyupagrāhyāḥ parasparānātmānaśca, na tu sāmānyaviśeṣau, buddhirūpabhede 'pi parasparātmatvena pratipatteḥ /
evamapi sāmānyaviśeṣayorbhedalakṣaṇena virahānna dvyātmatā, aṃśavadityuktam /
children.translated_text: Does cognition there too grasp it as having one form or not? If cognition does not grasp the thing as having one form — for the thing possesses both universal and particular nature — and it is grasped by a cognition of dual form, how can there be oneness of the thing? Because the non-difference that is the defining mark of non-difference — namely, the non-difference of cognitive form — is absent, while the difference of cognitive form, which is the defining mark of difference, is present. If, on the other hand, cognition indeed grasps the thing as having one form, then there is no dual nature, just as with an [undivided] aspect. If it is thought: The defining mark of difference is both the difference of cognitive form and the absence of having each other's nature. Among these, cows and the like, which are different, are grasped by cognitions of different forms and do not have each other's nature. But the universal and the particular are not so, because despite the difference in cognitive form, they are apprehended as having each other's nature. Even so, since the universal and particular lack the defining mark of difference, there is no dual nature — just as with an aspect, as stated.
If, then, non-difference of an aspect is established because cognition grasps it as having one form, the thing must be examined:

children.text:
yadi manyeta ---
buddhirūpābhedaḥ (Ms B; buddheḥ rūpābhedaḥ -- edition) parasparātmapratipattiśca dve abhedalakṣaṇe /
tatrāṃśasya rūpābhedādekatvam, ubhayostu parasparātmatvapratīteḥ /
viśeṣāṇāṃ tu na buddhe rūpāvibhāgaḥ, na parasparātmapratipattiriti bhinnā iti /
evamapyabhedalakṣaṇe sati parasparātmapratipattau, ubhayābhāve ca bhedalakṣaṇe 'vidyamāne, na dvyātmatā /
na caikasyābhedasya dve lakṣaṇe yujyete /
lakṣaṇābhedo hyabhedaṃ vyavasthāpayati, tadbhedaśca bhedam /
lakṣaṇabhede 'pi cettattvam, anyatvaṃ ca lakṣaṇābhede 'pi yadi, vyarthataiva lakṣaṇasya syāditi /
children.translated_text: If one should think: The non-difference of cognitive form and the mutual apprehension of having each other's nature are the two defining marks of non-difference. Among these, the oneness of an aspect is due to the non-difference of form. But in the case of the two [universal and particular], it is due to the apprehension of mutual identity. As for particulars, there is neither non-distinction of cognitive form nor apprehension of mutual identity — hence they are different. Even so, when the defining mark of non-difference — namely, the apprehension of mutual identity — is present, and when the defining mark of difference is absent [since] neither condition [is met], there is no dual nature. Nor is it tenable that one non-difference has two defining marks. For it is the non-difference of the defining mark that establishes non-difference, and the difference of the defining mark that establishes difference. If identity [of the thing] holds even when the defining marks differ, and otherness holds even when the defining marks are non-different, then the defining mark would be entirely purposeless.
Moreover, if the universal and the particular are non-different,
the purposelessness of a separate cognition would follow, just as in the case of a single aspect;
if purposefulness is due to multiplicity, why not purposelessness from oneness? // MBs_1.23 //

children.text:
buddhyantarapravṛttireva sāmānyaviśeṣayorekavastvātmatāmapākaroti /
sā hi nānātmatve bhedeṣvivārthavatī, anadhigatādhigamāt /
ekatve tu yathā sāmānyaviśeṣavibhāgayoḥ svabuddhisamadhigatayorna vilakṣaṇaṃ buddhyantaramarthyate, tathā sāmānyabuddherna buddhyantaraṃ vilakṣaṇaṃ viśeṣādhigamāya prārthyeta /
tathā viśeṣabuddherna sāmānyādhigamāya /
atha nātyantamavyatirekaḥ sāmānyaviśeṣayoḥ, vyatireko 'pi tu /
tatra vyatirekādarthavatteti /
tadasat /
evamapi kuta etat ---
vyatirekādarthavattvaṃ bhedavat, na punaravyatirekādekāṃśavadvaiyarthyam?

children.translated_text: KKS_66

children.text:
tulyayorhi bhedābhedayoḥ kuta etat ---
bhedādekayā buddhyā na grahaṇam, na punarabhedādgrahaṇamiti buddhyantaravaiyarthyam? autsargikaśca hetvabhāve phalābhāvaḥ svabhāvasiddhaḥ /
tasya hetubhāve phalabhāvo 'pavādaḥ /
tatrābhede hetubhāvādekayaiva buddhyobhayādhigamo yuktaḥ /
naikatve 'nyatarādhigamaheturnāstīti śakyaṃ vaktum /
athāpi kathañcinnāstītyucyeta /
tathāpyasti tāvat, ekatvāt /
tatra hetubhāvāt phalabhāvaḥ syāt, tasya kāraṇatvāt /
na tvabhāvo 'bhāvasya kāraṇam /
svabhāvasiddhastvabhāvaḥ phalasya /
tasya hetunibandhanaḥ phalabhāvo nivartakaḥ /
sa ca heturubhayatrāsti tāvat /
asattvaṃ tvanupayogam, akāraṇatvāditi /
children.translated_text: For when difference and non-difference are equal, how is it that apprehension by one cognition does not occur due to difference, but apprehension does occur due to non-difference — [such that] the separate cognition becomes purposeless? And by default, the absence of an effect in the absence of a cause is naturally established. The presence of an effect when a cause is present is the exception. In the case of non-difference, since a cause is present, apprehension of both by a single cognition is proper. It cannot be said that in the case of oneness there is no cause for apprehending the other. Even if it were somehow said that there is not — still, there is, due to oneness. In such a case, from the presence of a cause, the effect should follow, since [the cause] is productive of [the effect]. But an absence is not the cause of an absence. Rather, the absence of an effect is naturally established. The presence of an effect due to a cause is what removes [that default absence]. And that cause is present in both cases. The non-existence [of the cause], on the other hand, [would entail] purposelessness — but [that non-existence] is not established, since it is not a cause.

The very occurrence of a separate cognition undermines the claim that the universal and the particular are of one and the same nature. For that [separate cognition] is purposeful in the case of multiplicity, as with [distinct] particulars, because it leads to the apprehension of what was not previously apprehended. But in the case of oneness, just as a separate cognition different from either the universal-aspect or the particular-aspect is not needed when each has been apprehended by its own cognition, so too a separate cognition different from the cognition of the universal would not be sought for apprehending the particular. Likewise, from the cognition of the particular, [a separate cognition] would not [be sought] for apprehending the universal. If it is said: The non-separation of the universal and the particular is not absolute; there is also separation. And from that separation, [the separate cognition] has purpose. That is wrong. Even so, how is it that purposefulness is due to separation, as with difference, but not purposelessness due to non-separation, as with a single aspect?
Moreover —

children.text: sāmānyaṃ na hi vastvātmā na bhedaścitra eva saḥ /
children.translated_text: The universal alone is not the nature of the thing, nor is difference alone — it [the thing] is variegated.

Since it [the universal] does not carry over [to other instances], the doctrine of difference [follows]; this [claim of dual nature] is [merely] from another word [i.e., a verbal distinction]. // MBs_1.24 //

children.text:
yasyaikamubhayātmakaṃ vastu na tasya sāmānyamātraṃ vastuna ātmā na viśeṣamātram /
tanmātratve vastubhedaprasaṅgāt /
tasmāt saṃbhinnobhayarūpaḥ śabalo vastvātmā /
na ca śabalasyānyatrānugamaḥ /
yasya tvanugamaḥ sa vasturūpaṃ na bhavati /
tathā ca śabdāntaramavalambya bhedā eva satyā ityetatpratipādyate śabdāntareṇa vā hetunā dvyātmakamekamiti /
anuganturavastusvabhāvatve kalpanāviṣayatvāt /
children.translated_text: For one who holds that a single thing has a dual nature, the nature of the thing is not merely the universal, nor merely the particular. For if it were merely one of those, there would be the undesirable consequence of real difference in the thing. Therefore, the nature of the thing is variegated (<s>śabala</s>), a composite of both forms. But what is variegated does not carry over to other instances. And that which does carry over is not the real form of the thing. And thus, relying on a different word or a different reason, what is being taught is just that differences alone are real — or that one thing has a dual nature. Since what carries over, not being of the nature of the real thing, falls within the domain of conceptual construction.

children.text:
syādetat ---
mā bhūdvastu tadaṃśatvaṃ tu na vāryate /
anyathā nirbījā kalpanāpi na bhavet /
kaḥ punarayamaṃśo nāma /
na tāvadvastveva /
tanmātrarūpatve vastuno bhedaprasaṅga ityuktam /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] It may be said — let it not be the real thing, but its being an aspect is not denied. Otherwise, even an unfounded conceptual construction would not be possible. But what is this 'aspect'? It is not the real thing itself. For it has been stated that if its form were merely that [universal or particular alone], there would be the undesirable consequence of real difference in the thing.

children.text:
nāpi vastuno 'nyatsvayaṃ vastu, sāmānyaviśeṣatadvatāṃ trayāṇāṃ vastūnāṃ prasaṅgāt /
atha na vastveva nānyatsvayaṃ vastu /
pariśeṣāt kalpanāviṣayastattvānyatvābhyāmanirvacanīyaḥ /
nanu nāṃśoṃ 'śino 'rthāntaraṃ nāpi sa eva, ubhayathānaṃśatvāt /
nāpyavastu, ata eva /
na hi khapuṣpaṃ kasyacidaṃśo bhavati /
tatrāṃśānugame vastvevānugataṃ bhavati tasya tadavyatirekāt /
naitatsāram /

children.translated_text: KKS_67

children.text:
ananugamādaṃśāntarasya kiṃ na vastuno 'nanugamaḥ /
api tvananugama (api tvananugama -- edition) eva tasya samudāyātmakatvādekābhāve 'pyabhāvāt /
tathā hi ---
itaretarāpekṣau vā sāmānyaviśeṣau vastu, tatsamāhāro vā /
ubhayathārthāntare viśeṣasyābhāvānna vastvanvayaḥ /
pratyekamanapekṣayorvastutve nobhayātmakamekaṃ vastu syāditi suṣṭhūcyate ---
children.translated_text: From the non-persistence of a different part, why not [conclude] the non-persistence of the real thing [itself]? Rather, there is indeed non-persistence of it, because being of the nature of an aggregate, it is absent when even one [component] is absent. For consider: Either the universal and the particular are mutually dependent as a real thing, or [the real thing is] their aggregate. In either case, since the particular is absent in another object, there is no continuity of the real thing. If each independently were a real thing, then there would be no single thing of a dual nature—thus it is rightly said:

Nor is a part a real thing different from the whole, because there would be the consequence of three real things—the universal, the particular, and the possessor of those. Now, [if one says] it is not a real thing at all, nor different from itself as a real thing— then by elimination, it is a conceptual construct, inexpressible (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) as either identical or different. [Objection:] A part is neither something different from the whole nor identical with it, for in either case it would be partless. Nor is it unreal, for that very reason—a sky-flower (<s>khapuṣpa</s>) is never a part of anything. In that case, if the part persists [in the whole], what persists is a real thing itself, because of its non-difference from that [whole]. This is not sound.
Because of its non-continuity, the doctrine of difference [follows]; this [conclusion comes] from a different formulation.
Or alternatively, if because of the non-difference of all entities, that [non-difference] is their true nature,
then the adoption of the doctrine of non-difference would follow through a statement of a different kind. // MBs_1.25 //

children.text:
aṃśānuvṛttyā vā vastvanugame 'dvaitavādaḥ /
tathā hi ---
gauḥ svatastāvadgauḥ, saddravyādirūpānugamādaśvavastuno 'nugamādaśvaḥ /
tadevaṃ gaurgauścāśvaśca /
aśvo 'pi tāvadaśvaḥ saddravyādirūpānugamena govastuno 'nvayādgauḥ /
tadevamaśvo 'pyaśvo gauśca /
tadevaṃ sarvabhāvānāṃ tadbhāvānyabhāvābhyāmabheda ityadvaitaṃ jagadityuktamanyaprakārayā vācā /
satyam, dvaitamapyasti /
yatastadbhāvānyabhāvābhyāmabhedaḥ /
naitatsāram /
gaurapi cedaśvo gauścāśvaśca /
tatkuto 'nyatvam? gauraśva ityapi (gauścāśvaścetyapi -- edition) bhedābhidhānamanibandhanameva /
siddhe hi gavāśvabhede etadupapadyate /
gavāśvasya tu pratyekaṃ gavāśvatve bhedābhāvādanibandhanameva tat /
nanu viśeṣāṃśānāṃ vyāvṛtteranyatvasiddhiḥ /
tathā ca dvaitādvaitātmakaṃ jagaditi /
atha viśeṣavyāvṛtteranyatvasiddhiḥ /
kimubhayarūpatvādvastuno vastvantare 'nugamo nāsti? aśvavastu govastu na bhavati /
athāstyanugamaḥ, aśvo 'pi gaurbhavati? tatra pūrvasminkalpe vastuno 'nanvayādanuyataścāvastutvādbhedavāda ityuktam /
atha viśeṣavyāvṛttāvapi tadvastvanugatam, bhavatyaśvo gauḥ (bhavatyaśvo 'pi -- edition) /
kuto 'nyatvasiddhiḥ? yadi matam ---
anugataṃ cānanugataṃ cāśve govastu /
bhavati cāśvo gauḥ /
gaustu gaureva /
bhavatyeva hi tatra govastu /
tato 'nyatvasiddhiriti /
atha govastu kathaṃ vaktavyam? kiṃ yadgaurbhavatyeva, atha yanna bhavatyapi? tatra pūrvasyāṃ kalpanāyāṃ na vastuno 'nugama ityananvitāni vastūni /
dvitīyasyāṃ

children.translated_text: KKS_68

children.text:
vastuno vastvantare 'nvayādadvaitam /
sarvathā yena viśeṣeṇāyamaśvādgovastu vyavasthāpayatyanyat tadviśeṣayujastu tasyānanvayādbhedavādaḥ /
athānanvayadoṣānna viśeṣamāśrayati abhedavāda iti na dvaitādvaitakalpanopapadyata iti /
children.translated_text: because of the continuity of one real thing in another, there is non-duality. In every way, that particular by which one determines cow-thing as different from horse—if that particular [itself] does not persist [in the other], then the doctrine of difference [follows] because of its non-continuity. But if [one says] the doctrine of non-difference does not resort to the particular because of the fault of non-continuity—then the construction of duality-cum-non-duality is not tenable.

Or, if there is continuity of the real thing through the persistence of parts, [then there follows] the doctrine of non-duality (<s>advaitavāda</s>). For consider: A cow is first of all a cow by its own nature; through the continuity of the form of existence, substance, etc., and through continuity with the real thing 'horse,' it is a horse. Thus a cow is both a cow and a horse. A horse too is first of all a horse; through the continuity of the form of existence, substance, etc., and through continuity with the real thing 'cow,' it is a cow. Thus a horse too is both a horse and a cow. In this way, through the identity and otherness of all entities, there is non-difference—hence the world is non-dual, [when] stated in a different manner of speech. True, duality also exists, since through the identity and otherness of those [entities] there is non-difference. This is not sound. If a cow is also a horse, and is both a cow and a horse, then whence comes difference? The expression 'cow and horse' as a statement of difference would be entirely groundless. For this [statement] is appropriate only if the difference between cow and horse is already established. But if each [entity] is individually both cow and horse, then because of the absence of difference, that [statement] is entirely groundless. [Objection:] The difference is established through the exclusion of the particular aspects. And thus the world has the nature of both duality and non-duality. Now, [is it that] the difference is established through the exclusion of the particular? Then does the real thing not persist in another real thing because of its dual nature? Does the real thing 'horse' not become the real thing 'cow'? Or does it persist, [so that] a horse also becomes a cow? In the first alternative, because the real thing does not persist, and because what follows [the thing] without persistence would be unreal, the doctrine of difference [results]—as was stated. But if even when the particular is excluded, that real thing still persists, [so that] a horse becomes a cow—then whence is the establishment of difference? If it is thought: The cow-thing both persists and does not persist in the horse. And [so] a horse does become a cow. But a cow is simply a cow—the cow-thing certainly exists there. Hence the establishment of difference. Now, how should 'cow-thing' be described? As that which simply is a cow, or as that which also is not [simply a cow]? In the first alternative, there is no persistence of the real thing—hence the real things are without continuity. In the second alternative,
The doctrine of those who hold the meaning of substance and modes (<s>dravya-paryāya</s>) is also refuted by this [argument].

children.text: teṣāmapi dravyanayaḥ paryāyanaya eva vā // MBs_1.26 //
children.translated_text: For them too, it is either the substance-standpoint or the mode-standpoint alone. // MBs_1.26 //

children.text:
ye ca ---
dravyaṃ nityaṃ mṛtsuvarṇādi /
tasya (tasya tu Ms A; tasya ca -- edition) ghaṭarucakādayaḥ paryāyā viśeṣākhyā apāyina upāyinaścāvyatirekāḥ /
na ca te dravyameva, tasya sthitimattvāt /
na ca tato 'tyantaṃ vyāvartante, bhedenānupalabdheḥ /
dravyasyaiva rucakādirūpeṇa pratyayāt /
evaṃ dravyaparyāyarūpaṃ vastu /
atha (Ms B; atha -- edition) tu dravyameva syāt, vardhamānakabhaṅgena rucakakriyāyāṃ na kiñcidutpannaṃ naṣṭaṃ veti prītiśokau tadarthinorna syātām /
atha tu paryāyamātram, hemārthino madhyasthatā na syāt /
paryāyamātre hi hemni hemno vināśātparyāyavināśe kathaṃ madhyasthatā? utpāde vā? tasmāddravyaparyāyarūpatvādvastuna utpattisthitibhaṅgānāmekatra saṃbhavāddravyarūpasthitermādhyasthyam, paryāyayorutpattivināśābhyāṃ prītiśokāvavakalpete iti ---
manyante /
tannītirapyanenaiva nirākṛtā prakāreṇa /
tathā hi ---
teṣāmapi vastuno vastvantarānvaye 'pi bhāgābhāvāddravyamātraṃ syāt /
atha na vastvanveti dravyaparyāyarūpatvādvastunaḥ, paryāyāntare ca paryāyāntarasyānanugamādananvitāni tarhi vyāvṛttasvabhāvāni vastūni /
yasyānugamaḥ kalpyate tanmātrarūpasyāvastutvātparyāyamātram /
avasthitaṃ hi dravyamucyate /
na caivamavasthitaṃ kiñcidekaṃ vastvasti /
vastunastvapoddhṛtasyāṃśasyāvasthānakalpanā kalpanaiva /
vastunaścitratvāt, tasya cātathābhāvāditi /
children.translated_text: And those who [hold]: The substance (<s>dravya</s>) is permanent—clay, gold, and the like. Its modes (<s>paryāya</s>), called 'particulars' (<s>viśeṣa</s>), such as pot and bracelet, are perishable and arising, yet non-different [from the substance]. They are not simply the substance, because that [substance] is enduring. Nor do they entirely differ from it, because they are not apprehended as separate. For the substance itself is cognized in the form of bracelet, etc. Thus the real thing has the nature of substance-and-mode. Now, if it were simply substance, then when a bangle is destroyed and a bracelet is fashioned, nothing would have arisen or perished—and so there would be no joy or sorrow for one who desires them. But if it were mere mode, there would be no indifference for one who desires gold—for if gold is mere mode, then upon the destruction of gold through the destruction of the mode, how could there be indifference? Or upon [its] arising? Therefore, because the real thing has the nature of substance-and-mode, and because origination, persistence, and destruction coexist in one [entity], from the persistence of the substance-aspect comes indifference, and from the origination and destruction of the modes come joy and sorrow—so they think. That doctrine too is refuted by this very same method. For consider: Even when their real thing persists in another real thing, because there is no [distinct] part, it would be substance alone. But if the real thing does not persist, [then] because the real thing has the nature of substance-and-mode, and because in another mode the [previous] mode does not persist—then the real things are discrete, with exclusion as their nature. That which is postulated as persisting, being of the nature of mere [abstraction], is unreal—[hence] it is mere mode. For what is called 'substance' is that which is stable. But nothing that is a single [enduring] real thing exists in this way. The postulation of stability for an abstracted part of the real thing is mere postulation—because the real thing is variegated, and that [abstracted part] does not truly exist as such.
Moreover,
from the coexistence of origination, persistence, and destruction in one [entity],
that joy, indifference, and sorrow would [simultaneously] exist and not exist—that is untenable. // MBs_1.27 //
KKS_69

children.text:
yasya khalu dravyātparyāyā bhidyante tasya ---
dravyamātrārthino dravyasya sthitervināśābhāvādapūrvasyānutpādānmadhyasthatā, rucakārthinastasyāpūrvasyotpatteḥ prītiḥ, vardhamānakārthinastasya vināśācchokaḥ ---
iti vyavasthā kalpate /
yasya tu na paryāyebhyo 'nyaddravyaṃ

children.translated_text: For one who indeed distinguishes the modes from the substance, the following arrangement is possible: For one who desires only the substance, there is indifference because there is no destruction of the substance's persistence and no origination of anything new; for one who desires a bracelet, there is joy because of the origination of that new [form]; for one who desires a bangle, there is sorrow because of its destruction. But for one who holds that the substance is not different from the modes, nor the modes different from the substance—for such a person, when origination, persistence, and destruction coexist in one [entity], the one who desires the substance would and would not have indifference; joy and sorrow would and would not arise. For that substance neither simply endures nor simply perishes, and something new arises. From the destruction and the origination of the new, there would be joy and sorrow, not indifference. And from persistence there would be indifference—thus an untenable [situation] would result. Likewise, for one who desires a bangle, there would be sorrow from its destruction; and yet there would not be, because of persistence. There would be joy from the origination of that new [form]; and yet there would not be, because the former [thing] still persists. And there would be sorrow from the destruction—and so on. [Objection:] But if difference also exists, this is not a fault. [Reply:] Then does non-difference also not exist? [Objection:] The non-difference is not absolute, hence there is no confusion. [Reply:] If the non-difference is not absolute, then the arrangement [of joy, indifference, and sorrow] is also not tenable. For one who accepts non-one-sidedness everywhere in all respects, there is nothing anywhere that is absolutely one-sided, by which this distinction could be stated: 'The non-difference is not absolute, hence there is no confusion.' And thus:
If there is no one-sidedness of all entities in all respects,

children.text: apravṛttinivṛttīdaṃ prāptaṃ sarvatra hī jagat // MBs_1.28 //
children.translated_text: then this world would have attained [the state of] neither activity nor cessation in all matters. // MBs_1.28 //

children.translated_text: For when entities are non-one-sided in all respects, then: This world would not undertake activity anywhere, having determined the mode of being a means to a desired [end], because [the thing] is not simply like that. Nor would it desist, because [the thing] is not simply not like that. Likewise, one would not desist from a cause of suffering, because it is not simply like that. Nor would one not desist, because it is not simply not like that—thus one would arrive at a most distressing state indeed.

children.translated_text: when [things are] non-one-sided: One who desires joy would not undertake [activity] toward the means of joy, because joy already exists. Nor would one not undertake [such activity], because of its [simultaneous] absence. Likewise, one who desires the cessation of suffering would not avoid contact with the causes of suffering, because it [i.e., suffering] does not [simply] exist. Nor would one not avoid it, because it does exist—thus the entire world would arrive at [a state of] neither activity nor cessation, alas!

Alternatively, regarding what was said—'that joy, indifference, and sorrow would and would not exist is untenable'—to this they might reply: Since all modes are non-one-sided in all things, what is untenable about it? For consider: Joy, indifference, and sorrow absolutely exist and absolutely do not exist. To this it is said: 'There is no one-sidedness of all entities'—for if the existence and non-existence of joy and the rest [are themselves non-one-sided],

children.text:
evaṃ tāvanna dve vastunī, naikaṃ dvyātmakam /
tatra dvayamavaśiṣyate ---
bhedaḥ satyaḥ, tadupādānābhedakalpanā /
abhedo vā satyaḥ, tadupādānā bhedakalpaneti /

children.translated_text: Thus, so far, two real things [are untenable], nor is one thing of a dual nature [tenable]. Two [options] remain: Either difference is real, and the construction of non-difference is based upon it; or non-difference is real, and the construction of difference is based upon it. Regarding this:
Since difference is relative (<s>āpekṣika</s>), it presupposes the apprehension of [another entity as] different.

children.text: naikajñānaṃ samīkṣyaikaṃ na bhedaṃ tattvahānataḥ // MBs_1.29 //
children.translated_text: One cognition apprehending one [thing] does not [apprehend] difference; [to maintain otherwise would involve] abandonment of the true nature [of cognition]. // MBs_1.29 //

children.text:
na bhedamupādāyābhedakalpanā /
kutaḥ? āpekṣiko hi bhedo nānyamanapekṣya śakyate grahītum /
na cāgṛhīto bhedo 'bhedakalpanāyā upādānaṃ bhavati /
parāpekṣatve cāsya grahaṇamanupapannam /

nāpi bhedagrahaṇāpekṣam, abhedahānaprasaṅgāt /
na hi bhede gṛhīte 'bhedasyāvakāśo 'sti /
tatrābhedaṃ gṛhītvā tamupādāya tasya yathāvanniścayāśaktau vyavacchedakalpanopapadyate, yathaikabuddhinirgrāhyeṣu ghaṭādiṣvavayavavibhāgakalpanā /
na tatra bhedopādānābhedakalpanā /

te cātīndriyāḥ /

bhedāsparśe (bhedāsaṃsparśe -- edition) hi kiṃ kenānusandhīyatāmiti /
pratyuktametat ---
nedānīmabhinnadeśakālo 'rtha ekaḥ syāt /
asati caikasmin kimāśrayā bhedāśaṅkā syāt, yasyānusaṃdhānādekatvamucyata iti /
children.translated_text: The construction of non-difference is not based upon difference. Why? Because difference is relative—it cannot be apprehended without reference to another. And difference that has not been apprehended cannot serve as the basis for the construction of non-difference. Moreover, its apprehension is untenable if it [itself] depends on another, since when difference has not been apprehended, self and other are not established. And there is no apprehension of difference without the establishment of self and other—as was elaborated earlier. But the apprehension of non-difference is not dependent upon the apprehension of non-difference [in a circular way]. Nor is it dependent upon the apprehension of difference, because there would be the consequence of the negation of non-difference—for when difference has been apprehended, there is no room for non-difference. Therefore, having first apprehended non-difference and taking that as the basis, when there is inability to determine it as it truly is, the construction of distinction becomes tenable—just as in the case of pots and the like, which are apprehensible by a single cognition, [yet] there is the construction of the division of parts. In that case, the construction of non-difference is not based upon difference. For difference is established [only] at the level of atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>), and those are beyond the senses. [Objection:] But unity too must be ascertained through a cognition of synthesis (<s>anusandhāna-pratyaya</s>), and that [synthesis] is not possible without difference—for without any contact with difference, what would be synthesized with what? [Reply:] This has been answered: A thing that is not separated in place and time is one. And in the absence of a single [thing], what basis would there be for the suspicion of difference, from the resolution of which unity is said [to obtain]?

children.text:
api ca sarvapratyātmavedanīyametadabhedopādāno bheda iti /
tathā hi ---
children.translated_text: Moreover, this is verifiable by everyone's own experience (<s>pratyātmavedanīya</s>)—that difference presupposes non-difference. For consider:
A mere object is apprehended by cognition that arises spontaneously (<s>āpāta-janman</s>).
That difference, though not being cognized, still shines forth—this is sheer audacity. // MBs_1.30 //
KKS_71

children.text:
vastumātraviṣayaṃ prathamamavikalpakaṃ pratyakṣam /
tatpūrvāstu vikalpabuddhayo viśeṣānavagāhanta iti sarvapratyātmavedanīyam /
syādetat ---
viśiṣṭarūpopagrāhyeva pratyakṣam /
sa tu bhedaḥ śabdenāsaṃsparśānna tathopalakṣyate, yathā vikalpabuddhau /
tadayuktam, vipratiṣedhāt /
na copalakṣyate pratyakṣabuddhau viśeṣaḥ prakāśate ceti vipratiṣiddham /
ato 'tisāhasamucyate /
yastu saṃvittāveva vipratipadyate sarvānātmavyāvṛttaspaṣṭapratibhāsaṃ pratyakṣamiti vadan, tasyottaram ---
‘āhurvidhātṛpratyakṣam'; ityādyuktameveti /
children.translated_text: The first non-conceptual (<s>avikalpaka</s>) perception has for its object the mere thing. And conceptual cognitions (<s>vikalpa-buddhi</s>), which presuppose that [non-conceptual perception], do not grasp particulars—thus this is verifiable by everyone's own experience. [Objection:] It may be said: Perception apprehends only a qualified form. But that difference, because it has no contact with language, is not so discerned as in conceptual cognition. This is untenable, because of contradiction. That [the particular] is not discerned in perceptual cognition and yet it is manifest—this is contradictory. Therefore it is called sheer audacity. But to one who disputes the very nature of awareness, saying that perception has a clear appearance of each [thing] as excluded from everything other than itself—the reply to such a person is: 'They declare it to be the perception of the creator (<s>vidhātṛ</s>)'—and so on, as already stated.
Furthermore,
cognition that rests on the mere object is well-established;
but there is instability even in sense-cognitions with respect to differences. // MBs_1.31 //

children.text:
vastudvayānupapatterekasya ca dvyātmatāyogādavaśyakalpanīye 'nyatarasya mithyātve yuktaṃ viśeṣāvabhāsasya mithyātvam, rajatādivibhrāntiṣu darśanāt /
na ca vastumātrāvabhāsasya /
