dṛṣṭatadbhāvasyaiva tatkalpanā laghvī, kḷptatvādyogyatāyāḥ, itaratra tu kalpyatvāt /
children.translated_text: Since two real things are untenable, and since a single thing cannot have a dual nature, when the falsity of one of the two must necessarily be postulated, it is reasonable that the appearance of distinction is false, because this is observed in illusions such as [mistaking shell for] silver and the like. But [it is not reasonable that the appearance of] the mere object [is false]. For no deviation from the mere object has ever been observed in any cognition whatsoever, since even there, that very object itself appears. The postulation [of falsity] for that which is observed to be present is simpler, because its capacity [for falsity] is already established; whereas for the other [i.e., the mere object], it would need to be postulated [afresh].

children.translated_text: Moreover, according to one whose doctrine is: Entities have their own-characteristics as exclusion (<s>vyāvṛtta-svalakṣaṇa</s>). By that [account], they must be explained either as having the nature of mutual absence (<s>anyonyābhāva</s>), or as being qualified by that [mutual absence]. Otherwise the word 'exclusion' (<s>vyāvṛtta</s>) would have no meaning, since it is occasioned by mutual absence. In that case,
The nature of mutual absence does not apply to all things.

children.text: tatropādhau pratīyantāṃ tathā bhinnā na rūpataḥ // MBs_1.32 //
children.translated_text: Let them be cognized as different through limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>), but not in their essential nature.

children.translated_text: Verse 72 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
syāt /
nanu nānyonyābhāvo nāma kaścit, yo bhāvānāṃ tattvaṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ vā syāt arthasiddhirevaiṣā /
na cedanyonyābhāvo kaścit, siddhastarhyabheda iti /
children.translated_text: There would be no essential difference. Objection: There is no such thing as mutual absence that could be the reality or qualifier of entities — this is merely an accomplished fact. Reply: If there is no mutual absence whatsoever, then non-difference is established.

When one thing stands independently, another, having the nature of its absence, is established. But all things cannot be conceived as having the nature of mutual absence, because they depend on each other for their existence. If mutual absence is a qualifier — very well, let them be understood as such through the attraction of the qualifier, even though they are not of that nature. But there is no real difference of nature.

children.text:
api ca bhedatvādeva viśvasya bhedo 'bhedopādāna iti śakyate 'numātum /
dṛṣṭo hi maṇikṛpāṇadarpaṇādiṣvabhinnamukhopādānastadbhedaḥ /
na ca tatra bhāvāntarotpattiḥ, viruddhapariṇāmatvāt /
syādetat ---
abhedo 'pi śakyo bhedopādāno 'numātum, vanābhedasya tarubhedopādānatvāt /
na, bhedābhāvaprasaṅgāt /
evaṃ hi na kaścideko 'bhinnaḥ paramāṇurapi /
tadabhedo 'pi hi bhedopādānaḥ syādvanādivat /
tathā tadaṃśābhedo 'pītyanavasthāyāmekasyābhāvāttatsamuccayarūpo 'bhedo na syāt /
atha kvacidavatiṣṭhate sa ekaḥ /
tadabhedo na bhedopādāna iti vyabhicāraḥ /
tadidamucyate ---
children.translated_text: Moreover, since difference itself belongs to the universe, it can be inferred that difference depends on non-difference. For in gems, swords, mirrors, and the like, the difference of the face is observed as depending on the undivided face. Nor is there the production of another entity there, because it would involve contradictory transformation. One might say: Non-difference too can be inferred as depending on difference, since the non-difference of a forest depends on the difference of trees. No, because that would lead to the absence of any difference. For thus, nothing would be one and undivided — not even an atom. For even its non-difference could depend on difference, as in the case of a forest. And the non-difference of its parts too — and so, due to infinite regress, since no single thing would exist, non-difference, which is of the nature of their aggregate, would not exist either. But if at some point that one thing stands firm — then its non-difference does not depend on difference, and so there is deviation from the rule. This is stated thus:
Just as the difference of the face in a mirror and the like depends on non-difference,
non-difference does not similarly depend on difference, because of the absence of such a case.
Moreover,
Because each individual thing is pervaded by non-difference, difference is considered false,

children.text: bhedo yathā taraṅgāṇāṃ bhedādbhedaḥ kalāvataḥ // MBs_1.34 //
children.translated_text: just as the difference of the moon's reflections in waves arises from the difference of the waves.

children.text:
abhedānuviddhatvātpratyekaṃ viśvasya bhedo mṛṣā /
yathā jalataraṅgeṣu candramasaḥ /
tatra hi pratyekaṃ candramā ityabhedānvayaḥ, tathā viśvasya bhede 'pi pratyekam ‘idam'; ‘tat'; ‘arthaḥ'; ‘vastu'ityabhedānvayaḥ /
tarubhedastu yadyapi na mṛṣā, vanamityabhedānugamaśca na pratyekam /
na hi pratyekaṃ taruṣu vanamiti buddhiḥ /
ato na tena vyabhicāraḥ /
etadarthaṃ ca pratyekamityuktam /
children.translated_text: Because each individual thing in the universe is pervaded by non-difference, difference is false — just as with the moon's reflections in water-waves. For there, in each wave there is the connection with non-difference, 'it is the moon'; likewise, even in the difference of the universe, in each thing there is the connection with non-difference — 'this,' 'that,' 'an object,' 'a thing.' The difference of trees, though not false, is not accompanied by the non-difference 'forest' in each individual tree. For there is no cognition 'this is a forest' in each individual tree. Therefore there is no deviation from the rule. And for this reason the word 'each individual' was used.
Moreover:
Let the greatness belong to the one alone, that it appears as many;
but it is not the case that different things appear as undifferentiated — for parsimony favors the former, not the latter.

children.text:
idaṃ tāvadayaṃ bhedavādī praṣṭavyaḥ ---

children.text:
iti /
tadasat /
vyāvṛttasvabhāvasya tadagrahe grahaṇameva hi na syāt /
atha niścayapratyakṣayorātmabhedādaniścayāt /

tathā hi ---
kālākṣyāṃ gosāmānyanibandhanaśca vyavahāro gavāntaravyāvṛttiśca dṛśyate /
na ca gavāntaravyāvṛtteraniścaye sa yujyate /

tadapyayuktam, niyamāt /

tasmātprakṛtyaiva kecitkasyacidabhedāvamarśasya yogyāḥ kecinneti svabhāvaviparītā bhāvānāṃ sāmarthyātiśayā kalpayitavyāḥ /
tathā satyevaṃ gauravātkalpanāyāḥ /
ekasyaivāstu māhātmyaṃ yadeko 'pi nānevāvabhāsate (nāneva bhāsate -- edition), laghutvātkalpanāyāḥ /
na tu bhinnānāṃ te sāmarthyātiśayāḥ, yadamī abhinnā iva bhāsante (ivāvabhāsante -- edition) /
children.translated_text: This is wrong. For if something whose nature is distinct is not apprehended as such, there would be no apprehension at all. If it is because of the difference between determination and perception, and hence lack of determination — that too is wrong, because both kinds of usage are observed. For instance, in a black cow, both the usage based on the genus 'cow' and the distinction from other cows are observed. And without the determination of distinction from other cows, the latter usage would not be proper. If it is because they produce the same effect, and because the exclusion from non-producers of that effect is equal — that too is improper, because the effects too are different, so the equality of exclusion from non-producers of that effect does not hold. The effect of one is not accomplished by another, so the exclusion of non-producers cannot be equal. And exclusion, being the inherent nature of things, is not equal, due to the difference of each thing. If they are non-essential, how can they be equal? If it is due to beginningless latent impressions, not dependent on any distinction in things — that too is improper, because of the regularity. For the appearance occurs only in certain individuals and only of a certain kind, and this would not be proper if it depended on latent impressions alone. Therefore, one must postulate inconceivable surpluses of capacity in things that are contrary to their nature — that some by nature are suitable for the non-difference cognition of something and some are not. This being so, because of the cumbersomeness of the postulation: Let the greatness belong to the one alone, that even though one, it appears as manifold — because of the simplicity of the postulation. But the surpluses of capacity should not be attributed to different things, such that they appear as if undifferentiated.

First, the proponent of difference must be asked: How is there this appearance of non-difference and the practice of generalization among things whose individual characteristics are distinct? If it is due to similarity — that is impossible in things that are entirely unconnected. If it is due to the non-apprehension of distinction — who is able to apprehend the distinction of redness among berries, corals, and the like?

children.text:
bhedavyavahāraśca (bhedavyavahārāśca -- edition) yathāvabhāsaṃ bhedavādināmivābhedavyavahāra upapadyate (@vyavahārā upapadyante -- edition) /
tathā hi ---
ātyantikabhedavādināṃ yathāvabhāsamabhedavyavahāraḥ, na yathāvastu /

ye 'pyanarthāntaravādinaḥ, teṣāmapi śabalatvādvastunastasya cānanvayādyathāvabhāsamevobhayavyavahāraḥ /
na vastvanupātīti darśitamiti /
children.translated_text: And the practice of difference, like the practice of non-difference for the proponents of difference, is established in accordance with appearance. For instance: For the proponents of absolute difference, the practice of non-difference is in accordance with appearance, not in accordance with reality. Even for the proponents of inherence, since the universal, as a real entity, is something different, the practice of non-difference in different things is merely in accordance with appearance. Even for those who deny the universal as a separate entity, since things are variegated and the universal does not actually connect with them, both practices are merely in accordance with appearance. It has been shown that they do not follow reality.
Just as the externalists explain the establishment of the practice of generalization as being in accordance with appearance,
so too the discerning followers of <s>Vedānta</s> explain the propriety of the practice of difference.
Thus ends the <s>Tarkakāṇḍa</s> (Chapter on Reasoning) in the <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> composed by the revered <s>Maṇḍana Miśra</s>.
<s>Niyogakāṇḍa</s> (Chapter on Injunction)
Verse 74 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
evaṃ pratyakṣādivirodhātkarmavidhivirodhācca śrutārthaparigrahe ye manyante vedāntānāmupacaritārthatvaṃ tatpratibodhanāya vihitaḥ prayatnaḥ /
saṃprati tu ---
kārya evārthe vedasya prāmāṇyam, na bhūtarūpe /
evaṃ hyuktam ---
‘codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ'; /
codanāpramāṇako vedārtha iti yāvat /
codanā ca pravartakaṃ vacanam, tasmātkārye 'rthe vedaḥ pramāṇam /
vedāntānāmapi tu pratipattikartavyatāpramāṇabhājāṃ tanmukhena tadanugatabhūtātmatattvaviṣayabodhakatvam /
ataste 'pi kāryaniṣṭhatāṃ nātivartante /
tathā ca kathaṃ tarhi mantrārthavādāḥ sopaniṣatkā ityāśaṅkya ‘codanā hi bhūtaṃ bhavantam'; ityādyuktam /
etaduktaṃ bhavati ---
kāryamarthamavagamayantī codanaiva bhūtādikamapyarthamavagamayatīti ---
ye manyante tatpratibodhanāya prayatyate /
tisraśca pratipattayo brahmaṇi /
prathamā tāvacchabdāt, anyā śabdātpratipadya tatsantānavatī dhyānabhāvanopāsanādiśabdavācyā, anyā tato labdhaniṣpattirvigalitanikhilavikalpā sākṣātkaraṇarūpā /
tatra prathamāmadhikṛtyocyate ---
children.translated_text: Thus, because of conflict with perception and the like and with injunctions of ritual action, those who think that the <s>Vedānta</s> texts have figurative meaning when their stated meaning is accepted — the effort has been made to awaken them. Now, however: The <s>Veda</s> has validity only regarding what is to be done (<s>kārya</s>), not regarding what already exists. For thus it has been said: '<s>Dharma</s> is that which is characterized by <s>codanā</s> (injunction)' — meaning that the object of the <s>Veda</s> has injunction as its means of valid knowledge. And <s>codanā</s> is a statement that prompts action; therefore the <s>Veda</s> is a valid means of knowledge regarding what is to be done. Even the <s>Vedānta</s> texts, inasmuch as they are means of knowledge for what is to be cognized as a duty, communicate the truth about the nature of the self through that function. Thus, they too do not transgress their orientation toward duty. And accordingly, anticipating the question 'How then are <s>mantras</s> and <s>arthavādas</s> together with the <s>Upaniṣads</s>?' — it has been stated: 'For injunction communicates the past, the present...' and so on. The meaning is: It is injunction itself that, while communicating what is to be done, also communicates what already exists and the like. Those who think thus — the effort is directed at awakening them. And there are three kinds of cognition regarding <s>Brahman</s>. The first is from the scriptural word (<s>śabda</s>); the second, arising after understanding from the word, is continuous and is called meditation, cultivation, <s>upāsanā</s>, and the like; the third, having reached completion from that, free from all conceptual construction, is of the nature of direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>). Regarding the first, it is said:
The knowledge of the self that arises from the scriptural word — that is not enjoined;
for it arises for one who has studied the <s>Veda</s>, just like the understanding of ritual action.

children.text:
brahmaṇo hi pramāṇāntarānadhigamanīyarūpatvācchabdādhigamyasvabhāvaviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ vidheyam /
tatra yacchabdādeva jñānaṃ tadavidheyam, vidhimantareṇa bhāvātkarmāvabodhavat /
yathaiva ‘svargakāmo yajeta'; iti śrutavākyasya vākyārthāvabodhastadvākyaprāmāṇyādeva bhavati, na vidhyantaramapekṣate, tathātmasvarūpābhidhāyivākyaprāmāṇyādātmāvabodho vidhyanapekṣaḥ

children.translated_text: Verse 75 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
saṃjāyate, sati pramāṇe tatsāmarthyenaiva prameyabodhotpatteḥ /
na khalu sopakaraṇe samagre pramāṇe satīcchāpi puruṣasyāpekṣyate jñānaṃ prati, aniṣṭānāmapyavabodhāt, prāgeva vidhiḥ /
children.translated_text: It arises, because when the means of knowledge is present, together with its instruments and complete, the understanding of the object to be known arises by its own capacity. Indeed, when the means of knowledge is fully equipped, not even the desire of the person is required for knowledge, since even undesired things are understood — let alone an injunction.

Since the nature of <s>Brahman</s> cannot be ascertained by any other means of knowledge, the knowledge whose object is the nature ascertainable from the word must be the subject of injunction. But the knowledge that arises from the word itself is not to be enjoined, since it comes into being without an injunction, just like the understanding of ritual action. Just as, when one hears the sentence 'One who desires heaven should sacrifice,' the understanding of the sentence-meaning arises from the validity of that very sentence and does not require any further injunction, so too the understanding of the self arises from the validity of the sentence that declares the nature of the self, without requiring an injunction.
He shows that very independence from injunction in the case of understanding ritual action:
'One who desires heaven should sacrifice' — in the understanding of this, no other
injunction is required. There is no infinite regress, nor does this injunction serve to establish the ritual action.

children.text:
na karmavidhivākyārthajñānapravṛttau vidhirapekṣyate 'nyaḥ, na tadgata eva vā /
anyasminnanavasthādoṣāt, tadarthajñāne 'pi vidhyantarasyāpekṣaṇīyatvāt, tadgatasya ca karmaviṣayatvena tadbodhaṃ vidhātumasāmarthyāt /
children.translated_text: No other injunction is required for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence enjoining ritual action, nor is one contained within that very injunction. Not another one, because of the fault of infinite regress — since for the knowledge of its meaning too, yet another injunction would need to be required. Nor the one contained within it, because being directed at action, it lacks the capacity to enjoin the understanding of that action.

children.text:
nanu yathaiṣāṃ grahaṇe vidhyantaramapekṣyate ‘svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ'; iti, na cānavasthā, tadvattadarthabodhe 'pi syāt /
asti ca vidhiḥ ---
‘vedaḥ kṛtsno 'dhigantavyaḥ'; iti /
children.translated_text: Objection: Just as another injunction is required for the learning of these texts — 'The sacred study must be studied' — and there is no infinite regress, so too there may be one for the understanding of their meaning. And there is such an injunction: 'The entire <s>Veda</s> must be comprehended.' Reply: The comparison is improper. For even one who has not yet commenced, upon hearing the injunctive sentence about sacred study from another person who has studied it, proceeds to study that and other sentences, just as one assembles auxiliary rites from other Vedic branches upon merely hearing them. It is not the case that only a sentence one has studied oneself prompts one. Just as one person hears from others, the study being beginningless like the <s>Veda</s> itself. But an injunction whose meaning is not yet understood cannot prompt one to understand. And if the understanding of its meaning requires an injunction, that very injunction cannot prompt, since its meaning too is not understood. There would be mutual dependence: understanding comes from engagement, and engagement comes from understanding. Therefore another injunction would be required — leading to infinite regress. And 'The entire <s>Veda</s> must be comprehended' is not an injunction establishing something unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>). 'For its purpose is observed to be the communication of action' — here the naturally established purpose is being indicated. Even if this is an injunction, it would not state the knowledge of meaning that is already implied by the injunction to study; and even so, for the understanding born from the Vedic sentences declaring the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, no separate injunction need be required, just as with the sentence enjoining ritual action. Just as when the general injunction 'One who desires heaven should sacrifice' has established the matter, no further injunction is required — because of infinite regress, and because even when an injunction exists, yet another would need to be required —

children.text:
viṣama upanyāsaḥ ---
apravṛtto 'pi hi svādhyāyādhyayanavidhivākyādhyayane puruṣāntarādhītāttatastasya cānyeṣāṃ ca vākyānāmadhyayane pravartate, śākhāntarīyāṅgopasaṃhāra iva śravaṇamātrāt /
na khalu svādhītameva vākyaṃ pravartayati /
yathaikastathā puruṣāntarāṇyapi, anāditvādvedavattadadhyayanasyāpi /
anavabuddhārthastvavabodhavidhirnāvabodhe pravartayati /
tadarthabodhaścedvidhyapekṣaḥ, na tatra sa eva pravartayati, anavabuddhārthatvāt /
itaretarāśrayaṃ syāt ---
tadarthabodhātpravṛttiḥ, pravṛttasya ca tadarthabodha iti /
tasmādvidhyantaramapekṣitavyamityanavasthā /
na ca ‘vedaḥ kṛtsno 'dhigantavyaḥ'ityapūrvārthavidhiḥ /
‘dṛṣṭo hi tasyārthaḥ karmāvabodhanam'; iti nyāyaprāpto 'rthaḥ pradarśyate /
athāpyeṣa vidhiḥ, svādhyāyādhyayanavidhinārthākṣiptamarthajñānaṃ nocyeta (@jñānamucyeta -- edition, alternative reading in Tattvasamīkṣā), tathāpi brahmasvarūpābhidhāyivedavākyaprabhave bodhe na pṛthagvidhirapekṣitavyaḥ, karmavidhivākyavat /
yathaiva ‘svargakāmo yajeta'; iti sāmānyavidhinā siddhe nānyo 'pekṣyate, anavasthānāt, satyapi vidhāvanyasyāpekṣaṇāt,

children.translated_text: Verse 76 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
na caitadgata eva, karmaviṣayatvāt /
evaṃ tattvapratipattipareṣvapi vākyeṣu na vidhirapekṣitavyaḥ, vākyasāmarthyādeva tattvabodhotpādāditi /
children.translated_text: nor is one contained within that very injunction, because it is directed at action. Similarly, even in sentences aimed at the knowledge of reality, no injunction need be required, since the understanding of reality arises from the capacity of the sentence itself.

The objection [raised] is improper. For even one who has not yet commenced, upon [hearing] the injunctive sentence about the study of sacred recitation studied by another person, proceeds to the study of that [sentence] and of other sentences as well, just as the assembling of auxiliary rites belonging to another Vedic branch [proceeds] from mere hearing. It is surely not the case that only a sentence well studied [by oneself] prompts [one to act]. As with one [person], so too with other persons [it occurs]; and the study of that [Veda] is also beginningless, like the <s>Veda</s> [itself]. But an injunction to understand whose [own] meaning has not been understood does not prompt toward understanding. And if the understanding of its meaning depends upon an injunction, then that very [injunction] does not prompt there, because its meaning has not [yet] been understood. There would be mutual dependence: engagement [follows] from the understanding of its meaning, and the understanding of its meaning [follows] for one [already] engaged. Therefore yet another injunction would have to be depended upon — hence infinite regress. Nor is 'The entire <s>Veda</s> must be comprehended' an injunction [enjoining] an unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>) matter. 'For its purpose is observed to be the communication of action' — [thus] a purpose obtained by [this] reasoning is being indicated. Even granting that this is an injunction, [and] even if the knowledge of meaning implied by the injunction to study sacred recitation be not [separately] stated, still, for the understanding arising from the Vedic sentences that declare the very nature of <s>Brahman</s>, no separate injunction need be depended upon, just as [is the case] with the sentence enjoining ritual action. Just as, when [the matter] is established by the general injunction 'One who desires heaven should sacrifice,' no other [injunction] is depended upon — because of infinite regress, [and] because, even when an injunction exists, another would [then] have to be depended upon —
Furthermore:
The result is the activity that follows from understanding what is enjoined, and that is the purpose of the injunction.

children.text: anyonyasaṃśrayānnaiṣa śābdo bodhaḥ sa no paraḥ // MBs_2.3 //
children.translated_text: Due to mutual dependence, this understanding from the word is not that separate understanding.

children.text:
śabdādavagamya vidheyaṃ yā pravṛttiḥ sā vidheḥ prayojanam, na tu śabdaprabhavo vidheyāvagama eva, anyonyasaṃśrayāt ---
avagate śabdārthe pravṛtteḥ, pravṛttasya cāvagamāt /
śabdārthabodhādeva vā śabdārthabodha ityātmāśrayaḥ /
anyonyasaṃśrayastu tulyānupapattitvāduktaḥ /
yastu tattvāvabodhaparādvākyāttattvāvabodhaḥ, nāsau śabdārthabodhātparācīnaḥ, kintu sa eveti /
children.translated_text: The activity that follows upon understanding the enjoined object through the word — that is the purpose of the injunction, not the understanding itself that arises from the word. This is because of mutual dependence: activity follows from understanding the meaning of the word, and understanding comes from engagement. Or, the understanding of the word's meaning from the understanding of the word's meaning would be self-dependent. Mutual dependence is stated because of equal impossibility. But the understanding of reality that comes from a sentence aimed at the understanding of reality is not something beyond the understanding of the word's meaning; rather, it is that very understanding.
Moreover,

children.text: jāte bodhe na pravartyo natarāṃ khalvabodhake /
children.translated_text: Once understanding has arisen, there is nothing to prompt; still less when the word does not produce understanding.

children.text: śabde na (śabdena -- edition) niścaye tasmādanyasmādanyavāñchanam // MBs_2.4 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the desire for something else from something other than the word-generated certainty is unjustified.

children.text:
udapādi cet ‘sadeva somyedamagra āsīdekamevādvitīyam'; ityupakramāt ‘tattvamasi'ityantādvākyādātmatattvāvabodhaḥ, padānāṃ parasparānvitārthatvāt, kimanyadvidhiḥ kariṣyati? na pravṛtta eva pravartyaḥ /
atha padārthasamanvayamātrānna tattvabodhotpādaḥ, sutarāmapravartyaḥ /
śābdasya tattvāvabodhasyāsaṃbhavāt /
syādetat ---
utpanne 'pi tattvāvabhāse śabdāt, niścaye pravartyaḥ ‘evamidam'; iti /
tanna /
yadi tasmācchabdānniścayaḥ, sa jāta eva /
athānyato niścayaḥ, anyavāñchanaṃ pramāṇāntarāpekṣā, na tatra tattvaniścayanibandhanaṃ śabdaḥ syāt /
evaṃ tāvanna tattvaniścayāya vidhirarthyate /
children.translated_text: If the understanding of the truth of the self has arisen from the sentence beginning with 'In the beginning, dear one, this was Being alone, one only, without a second' and ending with '<s>Tat tvam asi</s>' (That thou art), because the words have mutually connected meanings — what will another injunction accomplish? What is already in operation need not be prompted. But if understanding of reality does not arise from the mere syntactic connection of word-meanings, then all the more it cannot be prompted — because verbal understanding of reality would be impossible. One might say: Even when an appearance of reality has arisen from the word, one may be prompted regarding certainty — 'It is indeed so.' No, that is not right. If certainty comes from that very word, it has already arisen. But if certainty comes from something else, then one desires something else — requires another means of knowledge — and the word would not be the basis for certainty about reality. Thus, no injunction is needed for certainty about reality.
If an injunction is sought in order to remove the possibility of unintended meaning —

children.text: artho jñātavya ityukte jñeyaḥ syānnāvivakṣitaḥ // MBs_2.5 //
children.translated_text: when it is said 'The meaning must be known,' it becomes something to be known, not something unintended.
Verse 77 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
yadapi matam ---
satyapi vākyādarthopaplave tātparyaṃ durlabham, bhūtārthaparasya vaiyarthyāt /
sāṃśayikatvaṃ vā, atātparyasyāpi darśanājjapamantreṣu /
vidhau tu satyarthajñānasya coditatvānnārtho 'vivakṣito bhavitumarhati /
tasmādvivakṣitārthatvāya vidhiḥ prārthyaḥ /
children.translated_text: As for the view: Even when a flood of meaning arises from the sentence, the intended purport is difficult to ascertain, because a sentence about what already exists would be purposeless. Or there is doubt, because lack of intended purport is also seen, as in <s>mantras</s> used for recitation. But when there is an injunction, since the knowledge of meaning is enjoined, the meaning cannot be unintended. Therefore an injunction is to be sought for the sake of establishing intended meaning.
That is settled: the orientation of words toward meaning is the same in ordinary language and in the <s>Veda</s>,
since 'But the sentence-meaning is undifferentiated' is a general rule.

children.text:
autsargikaḥ śabdānāmarthaṃ prati śeṣabhāvaḥ /
nimittāntarāttu svarūpapradhānatvamavivakṣitārthatvamapavādo loke /
tathā vede 'pi, lokāvagamyatvācchabdasāmarthyasya /
taduktam ---
‘aviśiṣṭastu vākyārthaḥ'; iti /
children.translated_text: The default relation of words is subordination to their meaning. But through another cause, the predominance of [the word's] own form—i.e., the non-intention of meaning—is the exception (<s>apavāda</s>) in ordinary usage. So too in the <s>Veda</s>, since the capacity of words is understood from ordinary usage. As stated: 'The sentence-meaning is not different [from ordinary usage].'
Moreover:
And the purposefulness (<s>dṛṣṭārthatā</s>) of the injunction to study (<s>svādhyāyavidhi</s>) is not contradicted here.
Otherwise, the entire [content] would be that injunction's object, with [its] meaning unintended. (<s>MBs</s> 2.7)

children.text:
yathaiva karmavidhīnāṃ ‘dṛṣṭo hi tasyārthaḥ karmāvabodhanam'; iti nāvivakṣitārthānāmadhyayanātphalāntarakalpanā tathā dṛṣṭatvādātmatattvāvabodhasya vedāntānām /
na ca bhūtārthapratipattau vaiyarthyamiti vakṣyate /
pratipattividhau ca tulyam /
avaśyaṃ caitadevaṃ vijñeyam /
anyathā saha vidhāyakena kṛtsnasyāvivakṣitārthatā syāt /
yato vidhāyakaśabdanibandhanamanyeṣāṃ vivakṣitārthatvam, vidhāyakasya tu na tannibandhanamasti /
evaṃ ca tasyāvivakṣitārthatve itare 'pi tathā syuḥ /
atha vidhāyakaḥ prakṛtyā dṛṣṭārthatvena cārthaparaḥ, itare 'pi tatheti vyartho 'sau vidhiḥ /
children.translated_text: Just as, for injunctions of ritual actions, 'its purpose is seen, [namely] the comprehension of the ritual'—so no additional fruit need be postulated from the study of [texts] whose meaning is not unintended—likewise for the <s>Vedānta</s> [texts], since the comprehension of the truth of the self is their observed [purpose]. And it will be stated that there is no purposelessness in the apprehension of existing fact. And the same [applies] to the injunction of apprehension [itself]. And this must be understood in this way. Otherwise, along with the injunctive [element], the entire [content] would have unintended meaning. For the intended meaning of the other [words] is based on the injunctive word; but the injunctive [word] itself has no such basis. And thus, if its meaning is unintended, the others too would be likewise. But if the injunctive [word] is meaningful both by its nature and by having an observed purpose, then the others are likewise—and so that injunction is pointless.
An injunction is sought in order to establish the purposefulness for a person of [that] knowledge.
But [to say that] everywhere the purposefulness for a person [comes] from an injunction is also not fitting. (<s>MBs</s> 2.8)

children.text: vidhyadhīnaḥ puruṣārthasādhanatāvabodhaḥ, tacchabdato labdhajanmano 'pyātmatattvāvabodhasya puruṣārthasādhanatvāvagamo vidherityetadapi na śobhanam /
children.translated_text: The comprehension that [knowledge] is a means to the human goal is dependent on an injunction; [and thus] even for the comprehension of the truth of the self, though born from those words, the understanding of its being a means to the human goal [requires] an injunction—this too is not sound.
Since no fruit other than cognition is accepted, due to the pervading of the knowable by [the knower],

children.text: iṣyate mokṣa iti cetsādhyastattvacyuterna saḥ // MBs_2.9 //
children.translated_text: if [it is said that] liberation [is that separate fruit]—that [liberation] is not [separate], because it would lapse from the [nature of the] reality to be realized. (<s>MBs</s> 2.9)
<s>KKS</s> 78

children.text:
jñānasya hi dṛṣṭameva phalam ---
jñātrā jñeyābhivyāptiḥ, jñātāraṃ prati tasya prakāśanam (prakāśatā -- edition) ---
na tvadṛṣṭaṃ kālāntarabhāvi, yadartho vidhiḥ syāt /
syādetat ---
ātmajñānasya phalāntaramapīṣyate mokṣaḥ /
tanna, asādhyatvāt /
na hetujanyo 'sau mokṣaḥ, tattvacyuteḥ /
kāryatve vināśāttasya punaḥsaṃsārāt /
ātyantikī ca saṃsāranivṛttirmokṣa ityucyate /
nanu kāryo 'pi nāśo na naśyati /
satyam, bhāvarūpaṃ tu mokṣaṃ niratiśayānandalakṣaṇaṃ niratiśayaiśvaryalakṣaṇaṃ cābhipretyaitaducyate, bhāvasya kāryasya vināśenāvinābhāvāt /
āgāmiśarīrendriyabuddhisaṃyogābhāvasya prāgabhāvasya kāryatvamanupapannameva /
bandhahetunivṛttistu yadyapi kāryā, kāryatve 'pi ca nāsyā anityatvaprasaṅgaḥ, tathāpi nāsau tattvajñānātpṛthagiti na tena sādhyā /
avidyā hi bandhahetuḥ, tattvajñānodaya eva ca tannivṛttiḥ /
children.translated_text: For the fruit of knowledge is observed directly: the pervading of the knowable by the knower, the illumination of it for the knower—not an unseen [fruit] arising at a later time, for which an injunction would be needed. [Objection]: But liberation is also accepted as a different fruit of the knowledge of the self. [Reply]: That is not so, because [liberation] is not something to be accomplished. That liberation is not produced by a cause, because [it would lapse from] the reality [of the self]. If [liberation] were an effect, since it would be destructible, there would be renewed <s>saṃsāra</s>. And the absolute cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s> is called liberation. [Objection]: Even an effect, [namely] destruction, does not perish. [Reply]: True, but this is said with respect to liberation as a positive entity characterized by unsurpassed bliss and unsurpassed sovereignty—because a positive entity that is an effect is invariably accompanied by destruction. And the prior non-existence of the future non-conjunction with body, senses, and intellect being an effect is entirely untenable. Although the cessation of the cause of bondage is indeed an effect, even if it is an effect, there is no consequence of its being impermanent; nevertheless, it is not different from the knowledge of reality, and so it is not [separately] to be accomplished by it. For <s>avidyā</s> is the cause of bondage, and the cessation of that is simply the arising of the knowledge of reality.

children.text:
athavā ‘paraṃ jyotirupasaṃpadya svena rūpeṇāvatiṣṭhate'; iti svarūpasthitirmuktiruktā /
sādhyatve ca na svarūpasthitiḥ syāt /
ato mokṣatvāccyaveta /
yattu ---
‘na sa (na ca --edition) punarāvartate'; iti śruteḥ prāmāṇyātkāryasyāpi mokṣasya nityatvamiti, dṛṣṭaviparītamapi tadāśrīyeta, ananyagatitve śruteḥ /

children.translated_text: Alternatively, the <s>śruti</s> '<s>paraṃ jyotirupasaṃpadya svena rūpeṇāvatiṣṭhate</s>' ('Having reached the supreme light, [the self] abides in its own form') states that liberation is abiding in one's own form. If [liberation] were something to be accomplished, there would be no abiding in one's own form. Hence it would lapse from being liberation. As for the [argument] that from the authoritativeness of the <s>śruti</s> '<s>na sa punarāvartate</s>' ('He does not return again'), even liberation as an effect would be permanent—[we reply that] even what contradicts experience would be relied upon [from <s>śruti</s>], if <s>śruti</s> had no other recourse. But when one who has known the truth of the self sees the self as non-dual, pure luminosity, and when <s>avidyā</s> has been completely uprooted without remainder—since renewed bondage is inconceivable due to the absence of a cause—the <s>śruti</s>, by use of the present tense, simply restates what is already established, as an <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage). In that case, how can infinite fruit [be derived] from its authoritativeness? For precisely because of the use of the present tense, non-return is not understood as something to be accomplished. Nor is there any connection with desire, from which accomplishability could be understood. Therefore it is an <s>arthavāda</s>. And even the postulation of a fruit from an <s>arthavāda</s> is untenable when knowledge, having the observed fruit of the manifestation of the knowable reality, is free from expectation [of further fruit]. And its purposefulness for a person will be stated [later].
Others, however, say:
Without an injunction, a statement about an existing fact, devoid of [reference to] what is to be done, would be a mere reiteration (<s>anuvāda</s>).
And reiteration is [confined to] what is within the domain of another means of knowledge. (<s>MBs</s> 2.10)
<s>KKS</s> 79
Its authoritativeness, being dependent on another means of knowledge, is surpassed [by that other means].
But in the case of the object of an injunction, which is not within the domain of another means of knowledge, it is firmly established. (<s>MBs</s> 2.11)
[Scripture] attains independent authoritativeness, like injunctive statements about ritual actions.
Even in the absence of [prompting another's] activity, that injunction is [present] precisely for the sake of authoritativeness. (<s>MBs</s> 2.12)

children.translated_text: Without an injunction, there is no apprehension of the instruction regarding what is to be done. The thing as it exists is understood to be merely a reiteration by that injunction. And since reiteration has its object within the domain of another means of knowledge, and [since] an existing fact that is dependent [on another means of knowledge] is not said to [independently] convey meaning—therefore, due to dependency, there is no authoritativeness. But since the object of an injunction is not within the domain of another means of knowledge, [scripture that is] directed at that [injunctive object] is an independent means of knowledge, like injunctive statements about ritual actions. And the object of an injunction is not within the domain of another means of knowledge. For there is no apprehension [of what is to be done] from anything other than the verbal cognition 'do [this].' And this being so, even though in a statement directed at the apprehension of reality there is activity subsequent to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, there is no fruit of an injunction. Rather, its being directed at an injunction should be accepted precisely for the sake of [establishing] authoritativeness. To this it is replied:
Does the [fact of] having its meaning ascertained by another means of knowledge [constitute] reiterativeness (<s>anuvādatā</s>)?

children.text: uta bhūtārthatā tatra siddhārthamapi yadvacaḥ // MBs_2.13 //
children.translated_text: Or is it [merely] the [fact of] stating an existing fact? For [is] even a statement about an established matter [a reiteration]? (<s>MBs</s> 2.13)
It is not the case that because [its] meaning has been obtained by another means of knowledge, [scripture] is [merely] an informer of that [already-known meaning].
If [scripture] is not dependent on that [other means of knowledge], then this is the intended [sense of] reiterativeness. (<s>MBs</s> 2.14)

children.translated_text: What then is reiteration (<s>anuvāda</s>)—is it having its meaning mixed with another [prior] cognition, i.e., the [mere] communication that '[this] has been cognized by another means of knowledge'; or is it merely the [fact of] stating an existing fact? In the first alternative, let it be that what has its meaning mixed with another [prior] cognition is dependent [on another pramāṇa]. But that which conveys that even an existing fact has not been cognized by another means of knowledge—that is not a reiteration, not dependent, because there is no cognition with contact with a prior cognition.
Now the other alternative:

children.text: sāpekṣatāyāḥ ko hetuḥ śuddhā siddhārthatā yadi /
children.translated_text: What is the reason for dependency, if [it is] pure [statement of] an established fact?
The contact with another means of knowledge is the cause of dependency [on it]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.15)
In [scripture] not born from human intellect, there is no such [contact] even regarding an existing fact in <s>Vedic</s> [statements].

For from that [human origin], the cognition is of a meaning that is mixed with that [prior cognition], not [a cognition that is] independent of prior cognition, [operating] autonomously regarding the object. As stated: 'From a statement originating from a person, the cognition arises that "this person knows thus," not that "the object is thus."' But in <s>Vedic</s> speech, since it does not originate from human intellect, even regarding an existing fact there is no reason for dependency, since the mixing with prior cognition is caused by the connection with a person.

If mere [statement of] existing fact is reiterativeness, there is no reason for dependency. children.translated_text: [Objection]: Even in the case of authorless (<s>apauruṣeya</s>) [scripture] regarding an existing fact, there is dependency on another means of knowledge, because of the possibility of another means of knowledge regarding that same domain. For when another means of knowledge is possible regarding that domain, even contradiction with it might be suspected. Therefore, to [confirm] the absence of that [contradiction], agreement [with that other pramāṇa] must be looked for. But when the object is [something] to be done, no suspicion of contradiction from any [other source] arises, so there is nothing to depend on. To this it is replied:
Dependency is not established by the mere possibility [of another pramāṇa]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.16)

children.translated_text: <s>KKS</s> 81

children.text:
atha śabdasaṃbhave 'pi na tatsāpekṣam /
tatsaṃbhave 'pi na śabdasya sāpekṣatā, viśeṣābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: Even when [another pramāṇa] is possible, that [other pramāṇa] is not dependent on scripture. And even when [scripture] is possible, there is no dependency of scripture [on the other pramāṇa], since there is no distinguishing [reason].

When both [pramāṇas] can have the same object, why [should we conclude] that scripture (<s>śabda</s>) is dependent on that [other pramāṇa], but not that the other means of knowledge would be dependent on scripture? If [the answer is] that scripture is seen in ordinary usage to have its object [already] ascertained by another means of knowledge—then all the more so, regarding what is not within the domain of another means of knowledge, it would have no authoritativeness. For regarding what is within the domain of another means of knowledge, [scripture's authoritativeness] would at least [be possible] despite the possibility of another means of knowledge; but elsewhere, due to its absence, that [authoritativeness] would be hard to obtain. But if the [fact of] having one's object already ascertained by another means of knowledge is a property caused by human origin, not caused by the capacity of words [themselves]—[and if] the capacity of words is [operative] only regarding an object not mixed with another means of knowledge—then it is not the case that, merely because another means of knowledge is possible, scripture alone is dependent; that [other pramāṇa] too, because of the possibility of scripture, would be dependent on scripture. What [follows] from its being dependent? It would be non-authoritative. [Reply]: Dependency on scripture is not tenable for it. For if [the other pramāṇa] has authoritativeness, agreement and disagreement with it would [need to] be sought. But if scripture lacks authoritativeness, then that [other pramāṇa] is not [rendered] authoritative by dependency on scripture. It is authoritative [simply] because it is independent. [Opponent]: Whence [comes] the non-authoritativeness of scripture? [Reply]: From its dependency on another means of knowledge. [Opponent]: And the authoritativeness of that [other pramāṇa comes] from its independence, and its independence from the non-authoritativeness of scripture—[this is] mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>). For if scripture is authoritative, and [another pramāṇa] is possible regarding the same domain, that [other pramāṇa] too would be dependent on scripture's possibility, just as scripture [is dependent on it]—since there is no distinguishing [reason].
Moreover:
If perception and inference can operate in each other's domain, (<s>MBs</s> 2.17)
the absurd consequence of mutual dependency would follow, without distinction.
Even a sense organ would be dependent [on another sense organ] when [it operates] within the domain of another sense organ. (<s>MBs</s> 2.18)

children.text:
saṃbhavamātreṇa sāpekṣatve pratyakṣānumayorekasmin viṣaye saṃbhavādanyonyāpekṣatvādaprāmāṇyaprasaṅgaḥ /
tathā sattāguṇatvadravyeṣvanekendriyagrāhyeṣvindriyāntarāṇāmindriyāntarasāpekṣatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
atha śabdasyaiva pramāṇāntarasaṃbhave sāpekṣatvam, viśeṣaheturvācyaḥ /
pramāṇāntarādhigatārthatvadarśanāditi cet, uktamatra ---
yadi śabdamātradharmo 'yamasaṃbhavādeva tadviṣaye pratyakṣāderbuddhādivākyavadaprāmāṇyaṃ prāpnoti, saṃbhave tvindriyaviṣaye pratyayitapuruṣavacovadyujyate prāmāṇyam /
yathoktam ---
‘taccetpratyayitātpuruṣādindriyaviṣayaṃ vā, avitathameva tat'; iti /
atha pauruṣeyadharmo 'yam, na saṃbhavatpramāṇāntaraviṣayasyāpyapauruṣeyasya śabdasya sāpekṣatvam /
api ca pratyakṣādhigataviṣayaṃ kiñcidanumānamiti na sāmānyatodṛṣṭasya tathā pratyakṣasāpekṣatā, yathā cāgamapūrvakaṃ ṣaḍjādivivekaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣamiti na sarvaṃ pratyakṣaṃ tathā, evaṃ puruṣavacasāṃ pramāṇāntarādhigataviṣayatvadarśane 'pi nāpauruṣeyasya tathābhāvo bhūtārthasyāpi /
anyathā sutarāṃ pramāṇāntarāsaṃbhavādaprāmāṇyaṃ syādityuktam /
children.translated_text: If mere possibility [of another pramāṇa] entails dependency, then since perception and inference are both possible regarding the same object, mutual dependency would result in the consequence of both being non-authoritative. Likewise, regarding entities such as existence, quality, and substance that are apprehensible by multiple sense organs, the absurd consequence would follow that each sense organ is dependent on the others. [Objection]: But the dependency of scripture alone when another means of knowledge is possible [is due to] a specific reason, which should be stated. [Reply]: If [the answer is] 'because scripture is seen to have its object [already] cognized by another means of knowledge'—[then] it has been addressed: if this is a property of words as such, then regarding a domain where perception and the like are impossible, [scripture] would be non-authoritative, just like the statements of the <s>Buddha</s> and others—since there is impossibility [of verification]. But if [another pramāṇa] is possible, regarding a sense-domain, authoritativeness is tenable, like the words of a trusted person. As stated: 'If [the statement is] from a trusted person, or [regarding] an object of the senses—then it is certainly non-deceptive.' But if this is a property [only] of human-originated [speech], then when another means of knowledge is possible regarding the same domain, there is no dependency for <s>Vedic</s> speech that is authorless (<s>apauruṣeya</s>). Moreover, just as some inference has an object [already] cognized by perception, yet inference by general observation (<s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s>) is not thereby dependent on perception; and just as some perception regarding the discrimination of <s>ṣaḍja</s> and other [notes] is preceded by scripture, yet not all perception is thereby [dependent on scripture]—so too, even given the observation that human speech has its object [already] cognized by another means of knowledge, it does not follow that authorless [scripture] is likewise, even regarding an existing fact. Otherwise, all the more so, from the impossibility of another means of knowledge [in scripture's unique domain], there would be non-authoritativeness—as has been said.
Moreover:
The independence of the injunction of medicines and the like is due to the impossibility [of another pramāṇa regarding the means-end relation].
But regarding worldly [injunctions], [they are] preceded by human cognition. (<s>MBs</s> 2.19)
The specific application [of means to ends] there [is what constitutes] that dependency. But in <s>Vedic</s> [injunctions],
since that [application] too is not preceded by [human] intellect, independence is said [to obtain]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.20)
