children.translated_text: even worldly statements that are directed at what is to be done would, being independent, attain authoritativeness. [Reply]: But the means-end relation there is preceded by human intention (<s>puruṣavivakṣā</s>); hence there is dependency there. In the <s>Veda</s>, however, even the means-end relation is not preceded by human intention; hence independence. Or: the relation among the object, the person to be enjoined, and the injunction is fashioned by human intellect in worldly statements. But in the <s>Veda</s>, even the bare injunction is not preceded by human intellect. That too [establishes] independence. It is replied:

If the independence of <s>Vedic</s> statements directed at injunctions—[i.e.,] at an action to be done—is due to the impossibility of another means of knowledge regarding that [injunctive content], then [worldly statements such as] 'one who desires freedom from fever should drink this medicine,' 'one who desires heaven should eat sand grains'—
The very fact of being preceded by human intellect is thus indeed the basis of dependency,
since even where another means of knowledge is impossible, there is dependency there [in worldly speech]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.21)

children.text:
asaṃbhavatpramāṇāntarakāryaniṣṭhe 'pi cedvākye puruṣasaṃbandhātsāpekṣatvam, puruṣabuddhipūrvataiva tarhi pramāṇāntaravyapekṣākāraṇamanvayavyatirekābhyām /
tadbhāve loke sāpekṣatvāt, tadabhāve vede nirapekṣatvāt /
na viṣaye pramāṇāntarasaṃbhavaḥ, tadabhāve 'pi lokaniyoge sāpekṣatvadarśanāt /
children.translated_text: If in a statement directed at what is to be done—where another means of knowledge is impossible—there is still dependency due to the connection with a person, then it is precisely the being-preceded-by-human-intellect that is the cause of dependency on another means of knowledge, by [the methods of] agreement and difference (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>). When that [human origin] is present, in ordinary usage there is dependency; when it is absent, in the <s>Veda</s> there is independence. [The cause] is not the possibility of another means of knowledge regarding the domain, since even in its absence, dependency is observed in worldly injunctions.
Now it is thought:
In the <s>Veda</s>, [verbal testimony] culminates in <s>niyoga</s> (injunction); <s>viniyoga</s> (application to a specific object) is primary.

children.text: loke vede na vyapekṣā talloke ca vyapekṣaṇam // MBs_2.22 //
children.translated_text: In worldly [speech], there is no dependence on the <s>Veda</s>; but in the <s>Veda</s>, there is dependence on that [worldly usage]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.22)

children.text:
niyogaparyavasitaṃ vaidikaṃ vacaḥ, sa ca pramāṇāntarasyāgocara ityanapekṣatvam /
sādhyasādhanabhāvaniṣṭhaṃ tu laukikaṃ vacaḥ, sa pramāṇāntaraviṣaya iti sāpekṣatā /
children.translated_text: Vedic speech culminates in <s>niyoga</s> (injunction), and since that [injunction] is not within the scope of any other <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), there is independence. Worldly speech, however, culminates in the relation of end and means (<s>sādhya-sādhana-bhāva</s>), and since that is within the scope of other <s>pramāṇas</s>, there is dependence.
This kind of division of capacity does not belong to words as such.
A word whose capacity is known from worldly [usage] is informative in the <s>Veda</s> as well. (<s>MBs</s> 2.23)

children.text:
na tāvadayaṃ śabdamātrasyānapekṣitapuruṣasaṃbandhāsaṃbandhasya śaktipravibhāgaḥ ---
yadekatra niyogaḥ śabdārthaḥ /
anyatra viniyogaḥ, yathā gośabdasya sāsnādimān, aśvaśabdasya kesarādimān /
yato lokādhigatasāmarthyo vede 'pi pratipādakaḥ /
loke cedviniyogaḥ śabdārthaḥ, tatraivāsya sāmarthyamadhigatam, na niyoge /
tatra vede 'pi viniyoga eva pramāṇārthaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: To begin with, this is not a division of the capacity of words as such—words whose connection or non-connection with persons is not taken into account—such that in one case <s>niyoga</s> (injunction) is the meaning of the word and in the other case <s>viniyoga</s> (application), just as the word 'go' (cow) [denotes] one possessing a dewlap and so forth, and the word 'aśva' (horse) [denotes] one possessing a mane and so forth. For a word whose capacity has been ascertained in worldly [usage] is informative in the <s>Veda</s> as well. If in the world <s>viniyoga</s> (application) is the meaning of a word, and its capacity has been ascertained precisely in that [domain], not in <s>niyoga</s> (injunction), then in the <s>Veda</s> too, <s>viniyoga</s> alone should be the meaning established by the <s>pramāṇa</s>.
Now, having known [a thing] through another <s>pramāṇa</s>, a person employs speech,
regarding that object; hence [worldly speech] is grounded in that [object]. The other [i.e., Vedic speech] stands otherwise. (<s>MBs</s> 2.24)
<s>KKS</s> 83

children.text:
atha matam ---
naiṣa śabdamātrasya sāmarthyavibhāgaḥ /
śabdasya hi nijaṃ sāmarthyaṃ kāryaniṣṭhataiva /
tathā hi ---
kāryo niyogārthaḥ /
kāryāya cānyasyānvayaḥ pratīyate /
na tu kāryasyānyārtho 'nvayaḥ /
tasmātkāryatvānniyogasya tatpradhānatā /
puruṣastu pramāṇāntarādavagamyārthaṃ tatra prayuṅkte vacanam /
na ca niyogaḥ pramāṇāntaragocaraḥ /
tasmānna tatra prayoktumarhati /
viniyogasya tu tathābhāvāttatra yujyate prayogaḥ /
tasmādviniyogapradhānaṃ puruṣavacaḥ /
vaidikaṃ tu sāmarthyena kāryatvānniyogasya tatpradhānamiti /
children.translated_text: Now, if it is held: this is not a division of the capacity of words as such. For the inherent capacity of a word is precisely its orientation toward what is to be done (<s>kārya</s>). For thus: <s>niyoga</s> (injunction) is the meaning of <s>kārya</s> (what is to be done). And the connection of other [word-meanings] is understood as being for the sake of <s>kārya</s>. But the connection of <s>kārya</s> is not for the sake of something else. Therefore, because <s>niyoga</s> has the nature of <s>kārya</s>, it is primary. A person, however, having ascertained the object through another <s>pramāṇa</s>, employs speech regarding it. And <s>niyoga</s> is not within the scope of another <s>pramāṇa</s>. Therefore, one cannot employ [speech] regarding that. But since <s>viniyoga</s> is not of that nature, its employment there is fitting. Therefore, human speech has <s>viniyoga</s> (application) as its primary [content]. Vedic [speech], however, by its own capacity, has <s>niyoga</s> (injunction) as primary, since <s>niyoga</s> has the nature of <s>kārya</s>.
To this we reply:
Because of dependence on another <s>pramāṇa</s>, [the object] is one for which another <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible.
Alas, its object is [simply] not [the ground] for dependence on another <s>pramāṇa</s>. (<s>MBs</s> 2.25)

children.text:
yadi puruṣo 'dhigate viṣaye vacaḥ prayuṅkte iti viniyogaviṣayatā tasya kalpyate pramāṇāntarāpekṣatvāt, tarhi saṃbhavatpramāṇāntaro 'sya viṣayaḥ /
na tu saṃbhavatpramāṇāntaraviṣayatvātpuruṣavaco 'pi sāpekṣam, sāpekṣatvanimittatvāttadvidhasya viṣayasya /
children.translated_text: If the <s>viniyoga</s>-character of [human speech's] object is postulated on the ground that a person employs speech regarding an already known object, and thus because of dependence on another <s>pramāṇa</s>, then its object is one for which another <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible. But it is not the case that human speech is dependent [on another pramāṇa] merely because its object is one for which another <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible, since [the availability of] such a type of object is the ground for dependence.
Therefore, having known [the object] through another <s>pramāṇa</s>, for the understanding of another [person],

children.text: vacaḥ prayuṅkte puruṣo nākasmāttena tadgiri // MBs_2.26 //
children.translated_text: a person employs speech—not without reason; hence that [person's] speech [is so characterized]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.26)
The intermixture with another <s>pramāṇa</s> is due to dependence, not due to [mere] possibility.

children.text:
svopalabdhikhyāpanāya puruṣasya gīḥ, tatastasyāṃ pramāṇāntarasaṃbhedaḥ, ‘mayopalabdho 'yamarthaḥ'ityarthaḥ /
tena tatropalabdhe saṃbhavāsaṃbhavāvevāpekṣyeyātām /
yatropalabdherniścayaḥ ‘saṃbhavatyasyopalabdhiḥ, na cānupalabhyāyaṃ bravīti'; iti tatra prāmāṇyam, yathāptapuruṣasya pramāṇaviṣaye /
yatra tūpalabdherasaṃbhava eva yathā dṛṣṭārthe buddhādivākye, yatra cānupalabhyāpi vacanapravṛttisaṃbhāvanā, tatrāprāmāṇyāt /
na tu pramāṇāntarasaṃbhavātpuruṣavacane 'pi tadapekṣā /
children.translated_text: A person's speech is for the purpose of communicating one's own cognition; hence in it there is intermixture with another <s>pramāṇa</s>—the meaning being 'this object has been cognized by me.' Therefore, in that [speech], what should be examined is the possibility or impossibility of [the speaker's] cognition. Where there is certainty of [the speaker's] cognition—'his cognition is possible, and he does not speak without having cognized'—there [speech] is authoritative, as in the case of a trustworthy person regarding an object within the scope of a <s>pramāṇa</s>. But where there is impossibility of cognition, as in the case of <s>Buddha</s> and others' statements about objects already established [by perception], or where there is the suspicion that one might speak even without having cognized, there [speech] is not authoritative. However, it is not the case that because another <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible, human speech too requires dependence on it.
Hence, non-human authorship (<s>apauruṣeyatā</s>) and indeed human authorship (<s>pauruṣeyatva</s>) (<s>MBs</s> 2.27)
[have] independence and dependence as their respective grounds, as described by the wise.
Even [speech] concerning an existent object is dependent [on another pramāṇa]; therefore it is not [necessarily] born of non-human intelligence. (<s>MBs</s> 2.28)
<s>KKS</s> 84

children.text:
ata eva pauruṣeyatvāpauruṣeyatve sāpekṣatvānapekṣatvakāraṇe nyāyavidbhirdaśite pauruṣeyatvanirākaraṇaprayatnena ---
‘autpattikastu śabdasyārthena saṃbandhaḥ'; iti /
autpattike śabdārthasambandhe 'svātantryācchabdasya na puruṣabuddhipūrvakatvamiti na pramāṇāntarasaṃbhinnā śabdādarthāvagatiriti nirapekṣatvam /
children.translated_text: Precisely for this reason, since dependence and independence have been shown by logicians to be the grounds of human authorship (<s>pauruṣeyatva</s>) and non-human authorship (<s>apauruṣeyatā</s>) respectively, in the effort to refute human authorship [of the Veda], [<s>Jaimini</s> states]: 'The relation of the word with its meaning is innate (<s>autpattika</s>).' When the word-meaning relation is innate, due to the word's lack of independence [from a human speaker], there is no dependence on human cognition—thus the cognition of meaning from words is not intermixed with another <s>pramāṇa</s>—and hence there is independence.

children.text:
nanu pramāṇāntarāsaṃbhave 'pi kṛta eva yatnaḥ ---
‘satsaṃprayoge'; iti /
satyam /
codanaiva pramāṇam, nānyat ---
ityavadhāraṇasiddhaye /
na tu pramāṇameva iti /
children.translated_text: [Objection]: But even when another <s>pramāṇa</s> is impossible, the effort has already been made [by <s>Jaimini</s>]—[in the sūtra] 'when there is contact with an existent [object]' (<s>satsaṃprayoge</s>). True. [The purpose is] to establish the restriction that <s>codanā</s> (Vedic injunction) alone is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, and nothing else—not [to establish] that it is a <s>pramāṇa</s> [at all].

children.text:
atha pramāṇāntarasaṃbhave 'pi yadi codanāprāmāṇyaṃ na vyāhanyate, ko 'rthaḥ pramāṇāntaranirākaraṇena? dharmatattvajñānam /
pramāṇāntarasaṃbhave hi sarvajñābhimatabuddhādyupadiṣṭo 'pi dharmaḥ pratīyeta tatra na dharmatattvamavadhāritaṃ syāt /
tadavadhāraṇārthaścāyaṃ yatnaḥ /
codanāprāmāṇyamapi tadarthaṃ mṛgyate, nādṛṣṭāya /
athavā tadvirodhāccodanāyā bādhaḥ syāt, saṃśayo vā tulyabalatve, tena tasyāsaṃbhavaḥ pratipādyate /
na tu tatsaṃbhavātsāpekṣateti /
nanu tadabhāvo 'pekṣaṇīyaḥ syāt /
kāmam /
na tu śabdaḥ pramāṇāntarāpekṣamarthaṃ pratipādayati /
yataḥ yadarthasya pratipādakam, na tu tadapekṣyate /
yadapekṣyate na tadarthaṃ pratipādayati /
na hi virodhipramāṇābhāvaḥ pratipattihetuḥ /
virodhasaṃbhavamātreṇa cāprāmāṇye pratyakṣādīnāmapi tatsyāt /
api ca virodhisaṃbhavādaprāmāṇyaṃ kāryaniṣṭhatve 'pyaparihāryam, kartavyatādvāreṇa bhūtārthapratipatteriṣṭatvāt /
tatra tu pramāṇāntaravirodhisaṃbhāvanāt /
bhūtārthasya pramāṇāntaraviṣayatvāttena kāryaniṣṭhatā varṇyate /
pramāṇāntaraviṣayatve kilānuvādatvātpramāṇāntarāpekṣamarthaṃ pratipādayati ---
pramāṇāntareṇāyamadhigataḥ ---
iti na svātantryeṇa /
kāryaniṣṭhatve tu svātantryeṇa, tasya pramāṇāntarāgocaratvāt /
uktena prakāreṇa na sāpekṣatvamiti ‘bhūtārthamapi sāpekṣaṃ nāto 'puruṣabuddhijam'iti suṣṭhūktam /
children.translated_text: Now, even if another <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible, if the authoritativeness of <s>codanā</s> (Vedic injunction) is not contradicted, what is the purpose of refuting other <s>pramāṇas</s>? [Answer]: The ascertainment of the true nature of <s>dharma</s>. For if another <s>pramāṇa</s> were possible, then <s>dharma</s> as taught by <s>Buddha</s> and others claiming omniscience would also be accepted, and in that case the true nature of <s>dharma</s> would not be ascertained. This effort is for that ascertainment. The authoritativeness of <s>codanā</s> too is sought for that purpose, not for [establishing] the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>). Alternatively, due to conflict with that [other pramāṇa], there would be sublation of <s>codanā</s>, or doubt in the case of equal strength; therefore the impossibility of that [other pramāṇa] is demonstrated. But it is not that dependence follows from the [mere] possibility of that [other pramāṇa]. [Objection]: But its absence would need to be ascertained. Granted. But a word does not convey a meaning that depends on another <s>pramāṇa</s>. For that which conveys a certain meaning does not depend on that [meaning being independently established]. That which is depended upon does not convey that meaning. For the absence of a conflicting <s>pramāṇa</s> is not the cause of cognition. And if mere possibility of conflict would entail non-authoritativeness, the same would apply to perception and other [pramāṇas] as well. Moreover, non-authoritativeness due to the possibility of a conflicting [pramāṇa] is unavoidable even when [Vedic speech] is oriented toward what is to be done (<s>kārya</s>), since the cognition of an existent object is accepted as occurring through the medium of what is to be done. In that case too, there is the possibility of conflict with another <s>pramāṇa</s>. Because an existent object is within the scope of another <s>pramāṇa</s>, orientation toward <s>kārya</s> is posited [as the solution]. When [Vedic speech] is within the scope of another <s>pramāṇa</s>, being a restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>), it conveys a meaning dependent on another <s>pramāṇa</s>—'this has been ascertained by another <s>pramāṇa</s>'—and thus not independently. But when oriented toward <s>kārya</s>, [it conveys meaning] independently, since that [kārya] is not within the scope of another <s>pramāṇa</s>. By the manner explained, there is no dependence—thus 'even [speech] concerning an existent object is dependent; therefore it is not born of non-human intelligence' is well stated.

children.text: atha saṃsargabhājo no padārthāḥ kriyayā vinā /
children.translated_text: Now, [if one objects]: word-meanings do not enter into mutual connection without a <s>kriyā</s> (verbal action).

children.text: kimāyātaṃ vidheḥ sāpi tvastyādiḥ sulabhā kva na // MBs_2.29 //
children.translated_text: What gain comes from [postulating] an injunction (<s>vidhi</s>)? That [kriyā] too, such as 'exists' (<s>asti</s>) and the like, is easily available everywhere. (<s>MBs</s> 2.29)
<s>KKS</s> 85

children.text:
yadi matam ---
ākhyātapadārthamantareṇa na nāmapadārthānāṃ saṃsargaḥ /
kriyā hi padārthasaṃśleṣahetuḥ tadabhāve sākāṅkṣatvāt /
ataḥ siddho 'rtho brahmādirna śabdagocaraḥ padasyāviditasaṃgatitvenānavabodhakatvāt /
na vākyārthaḥ tasya saṃsargātmakatvāt /
kriyārahitānāṃ ca padārthānāmasaṃsargāt /
evamapi kriyābhyupeyatām /
taddvāreṇa ca padārthasaṃsargasiddhirāśāsyatām /
na vidheḥ kaścidarthaḥ /
sāpi ca kriyā sarvatra sulabhaivāśrūyamāṇāpyastyādiḥ ‘astirbhavantīparaḥ prathamapuruṣo 'prayujyamāno 'pi gamyate'; iti /
tatra brahmasvarūpapratipattiparaṃ vākyamastyarthaniṣṭham /
tannibandhanastatra padārthasaṃśleṣaḥ /
sattāyāśca prakṛtyaiva satpradhānatvāt taddvāreṇa viśiṣṭavastusiddhiriti /
children.translated_text: If it is held: without the meaning of the verbal [element] (<s>ākhyāta</s>), there is no connection among the meanings of nominal words (<s>nāma-pada</s>). For <s>kriyā</s> (action) is the cause of the conjunction of word-meanings; in its absence, there is expectancy (<s>sākāṅkṣatva</s>). Therefore, an established entity such as <s>Brahman</s> is not within the scope of words, since the word's connection [with meaning] is unknown and hence it is non-informative; nor is it a sentence-meaning, since sentence-meaning has the nature of connection, and the meanings of words devoid of action have no connection. Even so, let <s>kriyā</s> (action) be accepted. And let the establishment of the connection of word-meanings through its medium be hoped for. [But] there is no [specific] purpose of <s>vidhi</s> (injunction) [here]. And that <s>kriyā</s> too—even when not heard [explicitly]—is easily available everywhere as 'asti' (exists) and the like: 'the root <s>as</s> (to be), synonymous with <s>bhū</s> (to become), [in] the third person, even when not [explicitly] used, is understood.' In that case, the sentence aimed at conveying the nature of <s>Brahman</s> is grounded in the meaning of existence (<s>astyartha</s>). The conjunction of word-meanings is based on that. And since existence (<s>sattā</s>) is primarily characterized by being (<s>sat</s>) by its very nature, through that medium, the establishment of a qualified reality [is achieved].

children.text:
atrāhuḥ ---
na pramāṇāvagamyatāyā anyā kācana sattā /
tathā hi ---
yat pramāṇenāvagamyate tatra ‘asti'; iti vyavahāro laukikānām viparyaye ‘nāsti'; iti /
na khalvanyaḥ sadasadvibhāgaheturlakṣyate /
arthakriyābhāvābhāvau cet /
na tayorapi pramāṇabhāvābhāvādhīnatvāt /
tathā hi ---
kārye 'pi sadvyavahāro yadi kāryāntaranibandhanaḥ anavasthā /
tasmādante 'pi pramāṇādeva sadvyavahāraḥ tadviparyayāccāsadvyavahāraḥ /
evaṃ cedādāveva pramāṇābhāvābhāvanibandhanau sadasadvyavahārau stām /
tathā cāstyarthaniṣṭhaṃ vākyaṃ pramāṇāntarāpekṣamevārthaṃ bodhayati pramāṇaviṣayatāyā astyarthatvāt /
children.translated_text: To this they say: There is no existence other than being cognizable by a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). For thus: whatever is cognized by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, regarding that, worldly people use the expression 'it exists'; in the contrary case, 'it does not exist.' No other ground for the distinction between existent and non-existent is observed. [Objection]: Perhaps [the ground is] the presence or absence of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>)? No, for even those [causal efficacy and its absence] depend on the presence or absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>. For thus: if the usage of 'existent' even regarding an effect depends on another effect, there is infinite regress. Therefore, ultimately, the usage of 'existent' derives from a <s>pramāṇa</s> alone, and the usage of 'non-existent' from its contrary. If so, let the usages of 'existent' and 'non-existent' be grounded in the presence and absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> from the very start. In that case, a sentence grounded in the meaning of existence (<s>astyartha</s>) conveys a meaning that is dependent on another <s>pramāṇa</s>, since being the object of a <s>pramāṇa</s> is itself the meaning of existence.
To this we reply:
And being cognizable by a <s>pramāṇa</s> is not regarded as the object [of the cognition] 'it exists.'
For from a <s>pramāṇa</s> itself arises the cognition: '[it] existed,' '[it] exists,' '[it] will exist.' (<s>MBs</s> 2.30)
For when [something] has been ascertained through smoke and so forth, with respect to fire and so forth, this [cognition 'it exists'] would be otherwise [i.e., only present-tense];

children.text: bhidyetottarakāle vā bhavantī na khalu tridhā // MBs_2.31 //
children.translated_text: or it would differ at a subsequent time—but [the cognition] 'it exists' is certainly not threefold. (<s>MBs</s> 2.31)

children.text:
na pramāṇāvagamyatvamastyarthaḥ na ‘asti'; iti buddhestadviṣayaḥ /
yataḥ pramāṇādeva tridhā buddhirbhavati ---
‘dhūmādastyatrāgniḥ'; ‘nadīpūraviśeṣādabhūdvṛṣṭiḥ'; ‘meghodayaviśeṣād

children.translated_text: <s>KKS</s> 86

children.text:
bhaviṣyati vṛṣṭiḥ'; iti /
tatra yadi buddhiḥ pramāṇaviṣayatāṃ gocarayati pramite hi syāt na pramāṇādeva /
na hi prāk pramāṇotpatteḥ san pramāṇasaṃbandhaḥ /
pramāṇasaṃbandhanibandhanā ceyaṃ buddhiḥ /
atha vaiyātyāduttarakālatāmevāsyā brūyāt /
traividhyamanupapannam, pramāṇasaṃbandhasyābhedādbhinnakāleṣvapyartheṣu /
children.translated_text: there will be rain.' Now, if cognition has as its object the fact of being within the scope of a <s>pramāṇa</s>, then in the case of what has been ascertained, [the cognition] would be [only 'it exists'], not [arising] from the <s>pramāṇa</s> itself. For prior to the arising of the <s>pramāṇa</s>, the connection with the <s>pramāṇa</s> does not [yet] exist. And this cognition is grounded in the connection with the <s>pramāṇa</s>. Alternatively, if one were to say that [the cognition 'it exists'] is only subsequent [to the pramāṇa], the threefold division would be unjustified, since the connection with the <s>pramāṇa</s> is undifferentiated even with respect to objects in different times.

Being cognizable by a <s>pramāṇa</s> is not the meaning of 'exists,' nor is the cognition 'it exists' directed at that [cognizability]. For from a <s>pramāṇa</s> itself, cognition arises in three ways: 'From smoke, fire exists here'; 'From the particular nature of the river-flood, there was rain'; 'From the particular nature of the cloud-formation,
If, alternatively, [one holds that] the <s>pramāṇa</s> cognizes the object as related to itself,

children.text: tathāpi naiva bhidyeta netthaṃ cānyavyapekṣatā // MBs_2.32 //
children.translated_text: even so, there would be no differentiation, and in this way there would be no dependence on another [pramāṇa]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.32)

children.text:
atha matam ---
ātmasaṃbandhitayaiva pramāṇenārtho 'vagamyate /
ato na ‘asti'iti buddheruttarakālatā pramāṇasaṃbandhaviṣayāyā api, svātmasaṃbandhitayaivārthasya pratīteḥ /
evamapyastītyeva sarvatra syāt /
na traividhyam, sarvasya pramitau pramāṇasaṃbandhasya vartamānatvāt /
na cetthaṃ pramāṇāntaravyapekṣatvamastyarthaniṣṭhe vacasi tatpramāṇasaṃbandhasyaivāstyarthatvāt /
children.translated_text: If, alternatively, it is held that the object is cognized by the <s>pramāṇa</s> precisely as related to itself, and therefore there is no subsequence of the cognition 'it exists' even when it has as its object the relation with the <s>pramāṇa</s>, since the object is cognized as related to [the pramāṇa] itself—even so, 'it exists' alone would apply everywhere. There would be no threefold division, since the connection with the <s>pramāṇa</s> is present [as current] in every act of cognition. Nor, in this way, would there be dependence on another <s>pramāṇa</s> in speech grounded in the meaning of existence, since the connection with the <s>pramāṇa</s> itself constitutes the meaning of existence.
If, alternatively, cognizability by another <s>pramāṇa</s> is held to be threefold on the basis of an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>),

children.text: syālliṅgamapi sāpekṣaṃ tatsiddhestata eva cet // MBs_2.33 //
children.translated_text: then the inferential mark too would be dependent [on another pramāṇa], if its establishment [depends] on precisely that [other pramāṇa]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.33)
If that independence does not [hold], that [rule] is not prohibited in the <s>Veda</s> by [any] punishments.

children.text:
atha matam ---
pramāṇāntaragamyataiva liṅgenādhigamyate /
tena nottarakālatā /
tacca pramāṇaṃ trikālamiti traividhyam /
kiṃ punastat? pratyakṣam /
tathā hi ---
bhūtāyāṃ dṛṣṭau kasyacidbhūtaṃ pratyakṣam, bhaviṣyantyāṃ bhaviṣyat, vartamāne 'gnau vartamānamiti /
etacca vārtam, nityānumeye tasyābhāvāt /
api ca liṅgamapyevaṃ pramāṇāntarāpekṣatvādapramāṇaṃ syāt /
atha liṅgādeva pramāṇāntarasadbhāvasya siddhernirapekṣatvam /
tathā hi ---
pramāṇāntarasadbhāva evedānīṃ liṅgaṃ pramāṇam /
na ca tatrānyadapekṣyate /
pramāṇasadbhāvadvārā prameyasiddhiriti /

children.translated_text: <s>KKS</s> 87

children.text:
nāyaṃ vidhirvede daṇḍavāritaḥ /
vaidikamapi vaco 'styarthaniṣṭhaṃ viśiṣṭārthapramāṇasadbhāva eva pramāṇam /
tatra nirapekṣam /
tatpramāṇadvārā ca viśiṣṭārthasiddhiriti samānam /
children.translated_text: This rule is not prohibited in the <s>Veda</s> by [any] punishments. Even Vedic speech that is grounded in the meaning of existence is a <s>pramāṇa</s> precisely through the existence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> for a specific object. In that regard, it is independent. And the establishment of a specific object is through the medium of that <s>pramāṇa</s>—the situation is the same.

If, alternatively, it is held that cognizability by another <s>pramāṇa</s> is ascertained through an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>), and therefore there is no subsequence [of the cognition 'it exists'], and that <s>pramāṇa</s> [operates across] three times, hence the threefold division—what then is that [other pramāṇa]? Perception. For thus: when perception has occurred for someone regarding a past [object], the perception is past; regarding a future [object], it will be future; regarding a present fire, it is present. But this is false, because in the case of what is always inferred (<s>nityānumeya</s>), that [perception] is absent. Moreover, in this way, even the inferential mark would be non-authoritative because of dependence on another <s>pramāṇa</s>. Alternatively, [one might say] there is independence because the existence of another <s>pramāṇa</s> is itself established through the inferential mark. For thus: the very existence of another <s>pramāṇa</s> is now what makes the inferential mark a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And nothing else is required for that. The establishment of the object to be known is through the medium of the existence of the <s>pramāṇa</s>.

The possibility of that [other pramāṇa] does not [apply] in the case of a supra-worldly object (in the case of an inferred object—according to the edition), unlike the meaning of <s>Buddha</s>'s statements. (<s>MBs</s> 2.34)
Here, because direct perception is accepted as the means, [this position] is incoherent.

children.text:
syānmatam ---
yuktaṃ liṅgasya prāmāṇyamevam, arthe tasya pramāṇāntarasya saṃbhavāt /
saṃbhavati hi vṛṣṭyādiṣu pramāṇāntaram /
tatastaddvārārthagatiḥ /
na tu sarvaviśeṣātīte brahmaṇyāmnāyaikanibandhane 'bhyupagamyate /
tatra yathaiva buddhādivākyānām ‘evamayaṃ puruṣo veda'; iti jñānaniṣṭhānāmatīndriyārthe jñānasyāsaṃbhavānnārthe prāmāṇyamatīndriyārthopadeśinām, tathātrāpi syāt /
saṃbhavipramāṇaviṣayāptavacanavattu liṅgasya pramāṇaniṣṭhatve 'pi yujyate prāmāṇyam /
tadasat, brahmaṇyapi sākṣātkaraṇasyābhyupagamādavidyāsaṃhāre /
avidyāvatāṃ tu tadāmnāyaikanibandhanamucyate /
api ca
children.translated_text: It may be held: the authoritativeness of the inferential mark is fitting in this way, because of the possibility of another <s>pramāṇa</s> for its object. For another <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible in [cases like] rain and so forth. Hence the cognition of the object is through that medium. But in the case of <s>Brahman</s>, which transcends all particularities and is grounded solely in scripture (<s>āmnāya</s>), [another pramāṇa] is not accepted. In that case, just as the statements of <s>Buddha</s> and others—which culminate in [claims of] knowledge, such as 'this person knows thus'—are not authoritative regarding a supersensory object because knowledge [of such objects] is impossible for those who teach about supersensory objects, so too it would be here. But just as in the case of trustworthy testimony concerning an object for which a [confirming] <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible, even though the inferential mark culminates in [establishing] the <s>pramāṇa</s>, its authoritativeness is fitting. That is wrong, because even for <s>Brahman</s>, direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) is accepted upon the destruction of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). It is only for those who possess <s>avidyā</s> that [<s>Brahman</s>] is said to be grounded solely in scripture. Moreover,

children.text: meyatvameva sattā cenmāne trividhatā kutaḥ // MBs_2.35 //
children.translated_text: If being a knowable object (<s>meyatva</s>) is itself existence, then whence the threefold division in [its being] a <s>pramāṇa</s>? (<s>MBs</s> 2.35)
From [mere] connection with that [pramāṇa], therefore, threefold division in the object is not tenable.

children.text:
yadi ca liṅgena pramāṇameva mīyate, mīyamānataiva ca sattā, tatra pramīyamāṇatvātpramāṇaṃ sarvaṃ sadeva /
sacca vartamānamityucyate /
tatra vartamānatvātpramāṇasya sarvatrārthe ‘asti'; ityeva syāt /
na pramāṇatraividhyādarthe traividhyam, mīyamānasya sattvātsataśca vartamānatvāditi /
children.translated_text: And if through the inferential mark only the <s>pramāṇa</s> itself is measured, and being measured is itself existence, then since every <s>pramāṇa</s> is being measured, all [pramāṇas] are existent. And what is existent is said to be present. In that case, since the <s>pramāṇa</s> is [always] present, everywhere with respect to the object there would be only [the cognition] 'it exists.' There would be no threefold division of the object from the threefold division of the <s>pramāṇa</s>, since what is being measured is existent, and what is existent is present.

children.text:
api ca idamayaṃ praṣṭavyaḥ ---
kiṃ vartamānapramāṇayogaḥ pramāṇasaṃbandhaḥ sattā, tadviparyayo 'sattā, āhosvit pramāṇayogamātramanāśritakālaviśeṣam? tatra ---
children.translated_text:
Moreover, this person should be asked —
Is <s>sattā</s> (existence) the connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) that is presently operative, and <s>asattā</s> (non-existence) the opposite of that, or is it merely the connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s> without reference to any particular time? In that regard —
If contact with a presently operative <s>pramāṇa</s> is <s>sattā</s> (existence), and <s>asattā</s> (non-existence) is its opposite, // MBs_2.36 //
then, if that is accepted, non-existence would follow for what is within the range of <s>smṛti</s> (memory);
KKS_88

children.text:
na smaryamāṇasya vartamānapramāṇasaṃbandhaḥ /
nanu smaryamāṇe vināśasaṃbhavānnaiva ‘asti'; iti vyavahāraḥ /
satyam /
‘nāsti'; ityapi nāsti /
yadi vartamānapramāṇayogaḥ sattā tadviparyayo 'sattā, ‘nāsti'; ityeva syāt na ca ‘asti'; iti /
tasmādanye sadasattve /
children.translated_text:
For what is being remembered has no connection with a presently operative <s>pramāṇa</s>.
Objection: Since destruction is possible for what is being remembered, the usage 'it exists' does not apply.
True.
But 'it does not exist' also does not apply.
If contact with a presently operative <s>pramāṇa</s> is <s>sattā</s> (existence) and its opposite is <s>asattā</s> (non-existence), then only 'it does not exist' would apply, and not 'it exists.'
Therefore, existence and non-existence must be defined differently.
If mere connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s> is <s>sattā</s> (existence), and <s>asattā</s> (non-existence) is its opposite, // MBs_2.37 //
then the capacity to hold honey would be obtained from a pot that was once cognized but has since been destroyed;

children.text: pramite ca na jijñāsā punaḥ syātsadasattvayoḥ // MBs_2.38 //
children.translated_text: and there would be no further inquiry regarding the existence or non-existence of what has already been cognized. // MBs_2.38 //

children.text:
anāśritakālaviśeṣe pramāṇayogamātre sattve pramitanaṣṭamapi vastu saditi tenārthakriyāprasaṅge 'naṣṭeneva, sattvāviśeṣāt /
naṣṭānaṣṭayorviśeṣānnaivamiti cet, sa eva tarhi viśeṣaḥ sadasadvyavahāravyavasthāyā hetuḥ kāryavyavasthāyā iva, na pramāṇayogaḥ /
children.translated_text:
If <s>sattva</s> (existence) consists in mere connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s> without reference to any particular time, then even a thing that was once cognized and has since perished would be existent, and the undesirable consequence would follow that <s>arthakriyā</s> (causal efficacy) could be performed by it just as by something not destroyed, since there is no difference in existence.
If it be said that this does not follow because of the difference between what is destroyed and what is not destroyed — then that very difference is the basis for the determination of the usage of 'existent' and 'non-existent,' just as it is for the determination of effects, and not the connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text:
tadanusāriṇyevaiṣā dṛśyate loke /
na khalu pramitanaṣṭaṃ ‘sat'ityupacarati lokaḥ /
kiṃ ca pramite 'rthe sadasattve jijñāseranna punarlaukikāḥ, siddhatvātpramāṇayogamātrasya tallakṣaṇatvācca sattvasya /
children.translated_text:
Indeed, this [usage of 'existent' and 'non-existent'] is seen in the world to follow that [difference between destroyed and non-destroyed] alone.
Surely the world does not figuratively apply the term 'existent' to what has been cognized and destroyed.
Moreover, ordinary people would not inquire again about the existence or non-existence of an object already cognized, since the mere connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s> is already established, and existence is defined by that [on the opponent's view].

children.text: atha pramāṇayogyatvaṃ sattā (Mss AB; sattvaṃ -- edition) naṣṭācca taccyutam /
children.translated_text: Now, if <s>pramāṇayogyatā</s> (fitness for valid cognition) is <s>sattā</s> (existence) (Mss AB; sattvaṃ — edition), and that is lost from what is destroyed,
and in the case of what is being remembered, it is said to be 'partially displaced' — that too is unsatisfactory. // MBs_2.39 //

children.translated_text: KKS_89
Since the sentence whose principal meaning is the object denoted by 'exists' — whence comes its dependence [on a <s>pramāṇa</s>]? Because there is no essential connection with the <s>pramāṇa</s>.

Suppose it is held —
Existence is not contact with a presently operative <s>pramāṇa</s>, nor is it mere connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s> without reference to time.
Rather, it is fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) for a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
And that fitness is lost from what is destroyed, so there is no undesirable consequence of its being existent.
But in the case of what is being remembered, [the fitness] is displaced with respect to some [means of knowledge] and not displaced with respect to others, so it is not the case that everything [about the remembered object] is non-existent.
This too is not satisfactory, because of the abandonment of what was admitted. For —
In this way, existence is being described as nothing other than the intrinsic nature of the object itself.
The intrinsic nature of the object that is fit for a <s>pramāṇa</s> is existence; the distinction between the usage of 'existent' and 'non-existent' is grounded in the intrinsic nature of the object alone, and is not conditioned by the <s>pramāṇa</s> or its absence.
The <s>pramāṇa</s> is merely the means of stating it, not its essential connection — just as when one says 'an object fit for blue-aspect cognition is blue,' the word 'blue' is not conditioned by the cognition of blue.
And thus it [existence] is denoted by the word 'is' and is grounded in the intrinsic nature of the object.

children.translated_text:
there would be doubt arising from the diversity of occasions, not definite cognition.
For those who cognize 'the pot exists' do not entertain doubt regarding the diversity of occasions.
Just as 'the cloth is white' leaves no desire [for further specification], so too 'the pot exists.'
As for the doubt — 'Is it substance, quality, action, form, or cognition?' — that does not belong to ordinary people.
Ordinary people apprehend only a single, undifferentiated occasion.
Moreover, doubt arises from the object, not from the word.
Why? Because even without apprehension of a specific [occasion], the cognizer has no further expectation.
For where doubt arises from the capacity of the object, as in 'let the tree be cut' [which may involve an axe, hatchet, etc.], there, even without apprehension of a specific alternative, there is no further expectation, since any one [instrument] may be employed and otherwise there would be infinite regress.
But where [doubt arises] from the word, there, without a basis for apprehending the specific meaning, there is necessarily expectation.
Thus, the word 'existent' is not a common word occasioned by diverse causes.
Nor can a <s>pramāṇa</s> serve as a single qualifier.
And this has already been stated to be untenable, even before the arising of the cognition pervaded by the word 'existent' —
as elaborated in 'since cognition arises from the <s>pramāṇa</s> alone.'
Moreover, from the effect also, only a past <s>pramāṇa</s> is ascertained.
So whence comes the qualification by it?
Surely an object is not qualified by a qualifier that is not present.
And when the absence of the qualifier has been ascertained, there is no doubt pervaded by a word denoting what is qualified — just as when the absence of a staff is ascertained, there is no doubt 'does he have a staff or not?'
Yet in the case of deserted cities and treasures long buried, even when the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> is ascertained, there is doubt 'do they exist or not?'
Therefore the meaning of 'existent' is something other than connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s> — that being the locus of this doubt.
Nor can the <s>pramāṇa</s> serve as an indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), because the word 'existent' is not applied to what has been cognized and destroyed, and because in the case of what is being remembered there is doubt pervaded by the word 'existent.'

It may be objected —
Let the intrinsic natures of objects, which are diverse and fit for <s>pramāṇa</s>, be the referents of the word 'existent,' rather than a single <s>sattā</s> (existence).
Let it be so — this is not what needs to be established.
In any case, the word 'exists,' which denotes the intrinsic nature of the object, is not occasioned by the connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
For if it depended on the connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s>, there would be [the fault of] dependence.
But multiplicity does not bring any defect.
Moreover, if it [existence] is multiple, how is there a single application of the word? For —
A single word would apply relying on a common qualifier or indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) among diverse things, or it would be a common word occasioned by different causes, like the word 'eye' (<s>akṣa</s>) [which denotes dice, axle, etc.].
Now, commonality among infinitely diverse intrinsic natures of objects is not tenable, given the capacity for grasping their relations.
For words like <s>akṣa</s> pertain to a limited number of classes or are characterized by a limited indicator.
It may be objected — the word 'existent' is common to objects characterized by the three universals such as <s>dravyatva</s> (substance-ness).
That is wrong.
For one who denies <s>sattā</s> (existence) [as a universal] would equally deny <s>dravyatva</s> and the rest.
Surely one who has seen fire does not have an apprehension of that [fire-nature] in water.
Moreover, <s>sāmānya</s> (universal), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) are themselves also existent.
The word 'existent' applied to them is not figurative, since the cognition [of them as existent] is not different in character.
And there is no figurative usage without a [prior] universal.
If there is such a universal, then that itself is the meaning of the word 'existent.'
And that itself is <s>sattā</s> (existence), since the cognition is the same.
Suppose it is held —
In every philosophical system, all categories are subsumed under certain limited properties.
The word 'existent' is common to objects, however infinite, that are characterized by those [limited properties].
That is wrong.
For subsumption is impossible without a single [underlying universal].
In that case, if the subsumption is under the meaning of the word 'existent' — 'this much variety is the meaning of the word existent' — there would be no exclusion of other things.
Thus there would be no comprehensive inclusion of all objects, just as [the statement] 'the word cow has nine referents' does not entail the non-existence of others.
In that case, no knowledge of the true nature of things would follow from philosophical systems.
Objection: The meaningfulness of philosophical systems is not what needs to be proven.
We do not say that the meaningfulness of philosophical systems needs to be proven.
But the proponents of these systems do apprehend a single intrinsic nature of the object, of which this enumeration as 'five, six' and so on is a classification.
Because without a single subsuming principle, there is no basis for the arrangement of subordinate enumerations.
If the subsumption is under fitness for <s>pramāṇa</s> or under <s>arthakriyāsāmarthya</s> (capacity for causal efficacy) — 'this much is fit for <s>pramāṇa</s> or capable of causal efficacy' — then let the meaning of the word 'existent' be indicated by those alone; the mention of limited properties is pointless.
In that case, the word would have universal reference, not [merely] common reference.
And if it were occasioned by different causes, then as with words like <s>akṣa</s>,
