kāryakāraṇayośca yaugapadyābhāvādviśiṣṭatānupapattiḥ /
athopalakṣaṇam, atītasyāpi

children.translated_text: KKS_91

children.text:
sattvaprasaṅgaḥ /
smaryamāṇe ca saṃśayo na syādityuktam /
tasmādyathaiva nīlādiśabdārtho 'rthasvabhāvaḥ, na kāryalakṣyaḥ, na pramāṇalakṣyaḥ, anavasthānāt /
svarūpavyavasthastu yathāpramāṇamavasīyate /
tathā sadarthasvabhāvo 'pīti yuktam /
kāryapramāṇasadasadbhāvanibandhane hi sadasadvyavahāravibhāge tasyāpravṛttireva kāryapramāṇasadasadvyavahāravibhāgasyāpi tannibandhatvaprasaṅgāt, anavasthānāt /
tasmādarthasvabhāva ekā satteti (@svabhāva ekaḥ satteti -- edition) brahmavido manyante /
children.translated_text:
would absurdly be existent.
And it has been said that there would be no doubt regarding what is being remembered.
Therefore, just as the meaning of words like 'blue' is the intrinsic nature of the object, not something indicated by an effect, not something indicated by a <s>pramāṇa</s> — since there would be infinite regress —
but its specific character is ascertained in accordance with whatever <s>pramāṇa</s> [is available],
so too it is proper that the meaning of 'existent' is the intrinsic nature of the object.
For if the distinction between the usage of 'existent' and 'non-existent' were grounded in effects and <s>pramāṇas</s>, there would be no application [of the word 'existent'] at all to that [distinction based on effects and pramāṇas], since the distinction between existent and non-existent usage regarding effects and <s>pramāṇas</s> themselves would also have to be grounded in the same, leading to infinite regress.
Therefore, the knowers of <s>Brahman</s> hold that <s>sattā</s> (existence) is one, being the intrinsic nature of the object.

If the qualification is by a <s>pramāṇa</s>-connection that has already occurred, then there would only be existence, never non-existence, and no doubt.
As for one who distinguishes or indicates the meaning of the word 'existent' by <s>arthakriyā</s> (causal efficacy) — for him too, prior to the observation of the effect, the word 'existent' would not apply.
If one were to say that the generation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> itself is the <s>arthakriyā</s>, then the cognition 'it exists' would not arise from the <s>pramāṇa</s> [since the pramāṇa would need to already exist to produce the cognition that establishes existence].
If it is held that this [cognition 'it exists'] is optional and arises after the <s>pramāṇa</s>, then it would not arise from an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>).
If it is said that what is inferred through an inferential mark is only that which has an already-ascertained connection with an effect — then in that case there would be nothing left to cognize.
For —
The meaning of 'exists' is the possession of effects, and that has already been ascertained.
To ascertain possession-of-effects through possession-of-effects itself is circular.
And since cause and effect are not simultaneous, the qualification [of something as existent by its effect] is untenable.
If [the effect] is an indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), then even what is past

children.text:
atha matam ---
nārthasvabhāvo yogyatā, pramāṇahetusadbhāvastu /
na cāsatāṃ pramāṇahetavaḥ santīti /
tadayuktam ---
children.translated_text:
Suppose it is held —
<s>Yogyatā</s> (fitness) is not the intrinsic nature of the object, but rather the presence of causes for a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
And those causes of a <s>pramāṇa</s> do not exist for non-existent things.
That is wrong —
That which is buried in the ground, without any mark, unknowable, beyond all evidence,
and whose perceiver has perished — all that transcends fitness for every [<s>pramāṇa</s>]. // MBs_2.40 //

children.text:
bhūmau nikhātamavidyamānendriyasaṃbandhamadṛśyamānāvinābhūtamasaṃvedyamānānyathānavakalpamānaṃ vastu pralīnadraṣṭṛkaṃ yattasya na pratyakṣānumānārthāpattyāgamahetavaḥ santi /
sādṛśyaviṣayaṃ hyupamānam, tasya heturdūrāpeta eva /
sarvapramāṇayogyatāmatikrāmati, na ca tadasat /
nanu sattvamapyasya katham? evamapi saṃśayaḥ /
tatra pramāṇahetubhāvalakṣaṇayogyatārūpe sattve pramāṇahetvabhāvasya niścayātsaṃśayo na syāt /
atha svabhāvaviśeṣaḥ kaścitpramāṇaṃ prati yogyaḥ sattvam, prakṛtahānādasundaramityuktam /
atha vā pramāṇaviśiṣṭaḥ sacchabdārtha ityetadanena nirākriyate /
na niścite viśeṣaṇābhāve viśiṣṭābhidhāyiśabdānuviddhaḥ saṃśayo yukta iti /
children.translated_text:
A thing buried in the ground, having no contact with any sense organ, invisible, not occurring together [with anything from which it could be inferred], unknowable, and not conceivable as being otherwise, and whose perceiver has perished — for such a thing, the causes of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), and <s>āgama</s> (scripture) do not exist.
For <s>upamāna</s> (analogy), which pertains to similarity, its cause is far removed indeed.
It transcends fitness for all <s>pramāṇas</s>, and yet it is not non-existent.
Objection: But how can its existence be [established] either? Even so, there is doubt.
In that case, if existence has the form of fitness characterized by the presence of causes for a <s>pramāṇa</s>, then since the absence of <s>pramāṇa</s>-causes is certain, there should be no doubt.
If some specific intrinsic nature that is fit for a <s>pramāṇa</s> is existence — it has been said that this is unsatisfactory, since it abandons the [original] thesis.
Alternatively, this [verse] refutes the view that the meaning of the word 'existent' is qualified by a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
For when the absence of the qualifier has been ascertained, a doubt pervaded by a word denoting what is qualified is not proper.

children.text:
api cābhāvasyāpi prameyatvānna pramāṇayogyatā sattālakṣaṇam /
tathā hi ---
children.translated_text:
Moreover, since <s>abhāva</s> (absence) too is an object of valid cognition, fitness for <s>pramāṇa</s> is not the defining mark of <s>sattā</s> (existence).
For —
The non-existent too is an object of valid cognition; yet this [opponent] establishes it as it is [i.e., as non-existent].

children.text: amitaṃ hi tathā kasmāttathā na punaranyathā // MBs_2.41 //
children.translated_text: For what has not been [positively] cognized — why should it be thus and not otherwise? // MBs_2.41 //

children.text:
avaśyaṃ khalvanena sadasadvyavahāravibhāgamicchatā asatkathañcidvyavasthāpyam, anyathā vyavahārasaṃkarāt /
tatra yadi pramāṇasyāviṣayaḥ, yadi

children.translated_text: KKS_92

children.text:
sarvaśaktiviraho vāsadbuddherviṣayaḥ /
sarvathā tathā prameyam /
aparicchinnaṃ hi tathā pramāṇena kimiti tadvidham, na punaranyathā syāt? na cettasya tathābhāve 'tathābhāve vā pramāṇavyāpāraḥ kiṃnimitta ekapakṣānurāgaḥ?
children.translated_text:
the absence of all capacity is the object of the cognition 'non-existent' —
in every case it is equally an object of valid cognition.
For if it has not been delimited by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, why should it be of such a nature and not otherwise? And if the <s>pramāṇa</s> does not operate with respect to its being thus or not being thus, what is the basis for its partiality toward one alternative?

One who wishes to maintain the distinction between the usage of 'existent' and 'non-existent' must necessarily establish the non-existent in some way; otherwise there would be a confusion of usages.
In that case, if [the non-existent] is not an object of any <s>pramāṇa</s>, or if
Moreover —
How does one place one's foot without having cognized the absence of thorns?
It is not [merely] from the non-apprehension of something else; and if [that absence] existed prior [to cognition], there would be an undesirable consequence. // MBs_2.42 //
Inquiry would not proceed if [the absence were established merely] from the non-occurrence of cognition.

children.text:
‘dṛṣṭipūtaṃ padaṃ nyaset'; iti kīṭakaṇṭakādyabhāve 'pramite kathaṃ tannyāsaḥ? tathā hi ---
kīṭakaṇṭakādyarthāntarabhūtalādiparicchedātsa syāt, kīṭādyaparicchedāt, abhāvaparicchedādvā /
tatra na tāvadarthāntaraparicchedāt, kaṇṭakādibhāve 'pi prasaṅgāt /
tatrāpi vastvantaraparicchedasya sattvāt /
prāgapi ca bhūbhāgaparicchedāt prasajyeta, yasya kasyacidvastvantarasya paricchittervidyamānatvāt /
atha kīṭakaṇṭakādyaparicchedāt, na tadbhāvābhāvajijñāsā syāt /
jijñāsāpūrvamapi ( jijñāsāpūrvakādapi -- edition) prayatnāttadaparicchedamātrameva prāpyate yasyābhāvo na prameyaḥ /
tacca prāgapi tato 'sti /
abhāve tu prameye 'bhāvaniścayāya jijñāsā yujyate /
na cāpariccheda eva jijñāsyaḥ, svataḥ siddhatvāt /
paricchedena hi sa nivartyate /
aprameyatvācca so 'pi khalvabhāva ityaprameyaḥ /
children.translated_text:
'One should place one's foot [only] where the eye has purified [the path]' — when the absence of insects, thorns, and the like has not been cognized, how can one place one's foot? For —
This [placement of the foot] would be either from the ascertainment of something else such as the ground apart from insects, thorns, etc., or from the non-ascertainment of insects and the like, or from the ascertainment of [their] absence.
Now, it is not from the ascertainment of something else, because the same consequence would follow even when thorns and the like are present.
For the ascertainment of some other entity exists there too.
And [on that view], the consequence would follow even before [looking], since the ascertainment of some other entity is always available.
If it is from the non-ascertainment of insects, thorns, and the like — then there would be no inquiry into their presence or absence.
Even from effort preceded by inquiry, what is obtained for one for whom absence is not an object of valid cognition is merely the non-ascertainment of those [things].
And that [non-ascertainment] existed even before [the inquiry].
But if absence is an object of valid cognition, then inquiry for the purpose of ascertaining the absence is justified.
Nor is non-ascertainment itself what is to be inquired about, since it is self-established.
For it is removed by ascertainment.
And since [non-ascertainment] is not an object of valid cognition, that absence too would be — absurdly — not an object of valid cognition.

children.text:
atha matam ---
satsūpalambhahetuṣu pramāṇaviṣayasyāparicchedāt pravṛttiḥ /
tadasat ---
children.translated_text:
Suppose it is held —
The activity [of placing one's foot] arises from the non-ascertainment of an object of <s>pramāṇa</s> when the conditions for apprehension are present.
That is wrong —
The usefulness of being an object of <s>pramāṇa</s> is not seen here. // MBs_2.43 //
For in the cognition of non-existence, it serves by appearing as having no other cause.

children.text:
aparicchedāccetpravṛttirna pramāṇaviṣayatvasyopayogaḥ, itaratrāpyaparicchedasya tulyatvāttataśca pravṛtteḥ /
yasya svabhāvaḥ prameyaḥ, tatparicchedātpravṛttiḥ,

children.translated_text: Verse 93 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

and its being an object of a valid means of knowledge is useful precisely because there is no other cause for it. This non-ascertainment is not due to deficiency of causes when the object exists, because those causes are complete. Therefore it is due to the absence of the object.

If activity arises from non-ascertainment, then being an object of a valid means of knowledge has no utility, since non-ascertainment is equal in the other case too, and activity would follow from that as well. That whose nature is knowable — from its ascertainment arises activity,

children.text: atha yatra pravṛttiḥ syāttatra kevalasaṃvidaḥ // MBs_2.44 //
children.translated_text: Now, where there would be activity from mere cognition alone:

children.text: jijñāseta na sūkṣmārthaṃ kaivalyaṃ saṃvido yadi /
children.translated_text: One would not investigate subtle matters if the isolation of cognition alone sufficed.

children.text: kevalo viṣayo neṣṭo rūponmiśre 'pi tadyataḥ // MBs_2.45 //
children.translated_text: A bare object is not accepted, because that form exists even in a mixture.
And for what is qualified, there is no qualifier other than the absence of other things.

children.text:
yadi matam ---
yatra bhūbhāgādau caraṇanyāsādilakṣaṇā pravṛttiḥ, tasya kevalasya sā jñānāditi /
tatrāpi saṃpradhāryam ---
kimidaṃ jñānasya kaivalyamabhisaṃhitamekaviṣayapratiniyamo viṣayāntarāsaṃsargaḥ, āhosvidviṣayasya /
yadi vijñānasya, pramite 'pi bhūbhāgādau sthūle sūkṣmakīṭakaṇṭakādibhāvābhāvaparīkṣā na syāt /
pravartetaiva, kevalabhūtalāvagrahajñānāt /
atha viṣayasya, tatrāpi saṃpradhāryam ---
svarūpeṇa vā viṣayasya kaivalyam, viśeṣaṇayogena vā /
tatra na tāvatsvarūpeṇa, miśre 'pi tasya bhāvāt /
viśeṣaṇayogena kaivalye prāptā kīṭakaṇṭakādyabhāvaviśiṣṭaparicchedātpadanyāsādilakṣaṇā pravṛttiḥ /
yato nānyābhāvādviśeṣaṇamanyādṛśaṃ kiñciddṛśyate, yadviśeṣaṇaṃ vastu kevalaṃ syāditi /
children.translated_text: If it is thought that the activity of placing one's foot and the like on a piece of ground occurs from the knowledge of that ground alone — even there it must be considered: Does this 'isolation' of knowledge mean restriction to a single object and non-association with other objects, or does it pertain to the object? If it pertains to cognition, then even when a gross piece of ground is ascertained, there would be no examination of the presence or absence of subtle insects, thorns, and the like — one would simply proceed, from the mere apprehension of the ground alone. If it pertains to the object, even there it must be considered: Is the isolation of the object in terms of its own nature, or in terms of its qualifiers? Not in terms of its own nature, since that exists even in a mixture. When isolation is in terms of qualifiers, activity characterized by placing the foot and the like follows from the ascertainment qualified by the absence of insects, thorns, and the like. Because no qualifier other than the absence of other things is seen that would make a thing isolated.
On what object do the cognition and the usage 'it does not exist' depend?

children.text: mānābhāvaṃ yadi kṣuṇṇaṃ meyābhāvasya tatra kim /
children.translated_text: If the absence of the means of knowledge is already established, what then of the absence of the object to be known?

children.text:
api cānena ‘nāsti'iti buddhiśabdayorviṣayo vācyaḥ /
sa na vastusvarūpeṇa, miśre 'pi prasaṅgāt /
na kevalam, abhāvādanyasya viśeṣaṇasyābhāvādityuktam /
nanu ‘nāsti'ityayamarthaḥ ‘nedaṃ pramīyate'; iti, na punarabhāvo 'vagamyate /
viruddhamidam ---
nāstyavagamyate ceti /
yadyevaṃ pramāṇābhāvo viṣaya uktaḥ syāt ‘nāsti'; iti dhīśabdayoḥ, tatra ko 'parādhaḥ syātprameyābhāvasya, yena

children.translated_text: Verse 94 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text: tamatilaṅghya pramāṇābhāvo viṣaya ucyate? na hi tayornirupākhyatve kaścidviśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: it is bypassed and the absence of the means of knowledge is declared to be the object? For between the two, being both without positive content, there is no distinction.

Moreover, the object of the cognition and the word 'it does not exist' must be stated. It cannot be the thing's own nature, because that would apply even in a mixture. It cannot be bare, because there is no qualifier other than absence, as has been said. Objection: The meaning of 'it does not exist' is 'this is not ascertained by any means of knowledge' — absence itself is not cognized. This is contradictory — to say it does not exist and yet it is cognized. If so, then the absence of the means of knowledge would be the object of the cognition and the word 'does not exist' — then what fault is there in the absence of the object to be known, that
If it is thought:
In the non-apprehension of an existent, the cognition of non-existence is an error; the usage of absence is a delusion.
And in the absence of seeing the usage of absence, it is like seeing darkness.

children.text:
naiva stāṃ ‘nāsti'; iti buddhivyavahārau /
kathamimau sarvajanānāṃ pratītāvapahnūyete? ucyate ---
bhramo 'yaṃ sadbuddhyabhāve tadviparyayapariccheda iti /
tathā sadvyavahārābhāve tadviparyayavyavahārabhramaḥ yathālokadarśanābhāve ‘tamaḥ paśyāmi'iti vibhramaḥ /
na hi tamo nāma kiñciddṛśyamasti /
children.translated_text: Let neither the cognition nor the usage 'it does not exist' stand. How can these, which are known to all people, be denied? It is said: This is an error — in the absence of the cognition of existence, the determination of its opposite. Likewise, in the absence of the usage of existence, the delusion of the usage of its opposite — just as in the absence of seeing light, 'I see darkness' is a delusion. For there is no such thing as darkness that can be seen.
This is not sound:
In that case, in deep sleep and the like, there would be the erroneous perception of the absence of the three worlds.
And for one who does not ascertain anything, there can be no error.
One who does not know both the locus of superimposition and the thing superimposed is not one who has the illusion of silver.
The usage is not different from absence, and the absence of that is also a mental verbal act.
But the seeing of darkness apprehends either the shadow of the earth or the very absence of light,
and it is not the case that one who has not seen anything has a delusion of seeing.

children.text:
yadi khalvadarśane viparyayadarśanabhramo bhavati suṣuptādyavasthāsu viśvābhāvadarśanabhramaḥ syādālokādarśanabhramavat /
na ca kiñcidaparicchindato vibhramaḥ /
tathā hi ---
āropasya viṣayaṃ purovarti vastu āropaṇīyaṃ ca rajataṃ jñānenānāpnuvan na rajatabhramavān bhavati /
anyathāpratipattiḥ, smṛtiḥ, sāmānyapratipattirvā /
na ca buddhyabhāvo jñānasya viṣayo na vyavahārābhāvaḥ, nābhāvabuddhirnābhāvavyavahāraḥ, viśeṣaṇasyābhāvasya jñānāviṣayatvāt /
tatrobhayorviṣayāropaṇīyayoragrahaṇe na mithyājñānamiti /
children.translated_text: If indeed there is the delusion of seeing the opposite when there is no seeing, then in states like deep sleep there would be the delusion of seeing the absence of the entire universe, like the delusion of not seeing light. And for one who does not ascertain anything, there can be no error. For one who does not reach through knowledge both the object before one that is the locus of superimposition and the silver that is to be superimposed does not have the illusion of silver — otherwise it would be mere non-cognition, memory, or general cognition. And neither the absence of cognition is the object of knowledge, nor is the absence of usage, nor is the cognition of absence, nor is the usage of absence — because absence as a qualifier is not an object of knowledge. Therefore, when both — the locus of superimposition and the thing to be superimposed — are not apprehended, there is no false knowledge.
Accepting the fitness to be a valid object as existence, the absence of fault is stated:
Or let fitness to be a valid object be existence, and let that be what is known.

children.text: astu vā mānayogyatvaṃ sattvaṃ tacca pramīyatām // MBs_2.51 //

children.translated_text: When that is known, the existence of the thing becomes the object of scripture.
And there is no dependence on another means, nor do they declare a difference from the internal object in this.
Even those who do not assert a separate existence —

children.text:
bhavatu vā pramāṇayogyatā sattā /
saiva ca prameyāstu /
tatprameyaṃ vastusattvamāgamārthaḥ /
na ca pramāṇāntarāpekṣatā doṣaḥ, pramāṇāntarasaṃbhedasyābhāvāt /
‘pramāṇayogyaḥ'ityetāvanmātrādhigateḥ /
tathā hi ---
ye 'pi pramāṇayogyatāṃ sattāmāhurna tadvyatirekiṇīm, te 'pi nātrāntarārthasaṃsparśamicchanti /
tatsaṃsparśe hyanyatpramāṇamanveṣyaṃ syāt /
kathaṃ nānveṣyam? yadā vacaḥ pramāṇayogyatāyāṃ paryavasitaṃ na viśiṣṭārthasattvaṃ bodhayati, tatra yasya pramāṇasya yogyo viśiṣṭo 'rthastadavaśyāpekṣaṇīyam /
kimarthaṃ tadapekṣyate? viśiṣṭavastusattvādhigamāya /
kaṃ punarviśiṣṭasya vastunaḥ sattvam? pramāṇayogyatvam /
adhigatameva tarhi tadastyarthaniṣṭhādvacanāt, pramāṇayogyatāyā astyarthatvāt /
children.translated_text: Or let fitness to be a valid object be existence. And let that itself be what is to be known. The knowable object is the existence of the thing, which is the meaning of scripture. And dependence on another means of knowledge is not a fault, because there is no admixture of another means of knowledge. Only this much is ascertained: 'it is fit to be validly known.' For instance: Even those who say that fitness to be validly known is existence and do not assert it as something different from that — even they do not wish for contact with a different object here. For if there were such contact, another means of knowledge would have to be sought. How would it not need to be sought? When the word has reached its end in fitness to be validly known and does not communicate the existence of a specific object, then the specific means of knowledge for whose specific object it is fit must necessarily be relied upon. For what purpose is that relied upon? For ascertaining the existence of the specific thing. But what is the existence of the specific thing? Fitness to be validly known. Then that has already been ascertained — it exists, from the word that concludes with this meaning, since fitness to be validly known is the meaning of 'exists.'
He shows that even when admixture with another means of knowledge is accepted, there is no fault of invalidity:

children.text: pramāṇāntarabhinnārthamapi mānaṃ na no vacaḥ // MBs_2.53 //
children.translated_text: Even if the word is a means of knowledge whose object is distinct from another means of knowledge, it is not invalid for us.
It is independent with respect to the object 'this thing has been ascertained by me';
but with respect to the mere object it is dependent, because it communicates the object depending on something else.
Even when not sublated with respect to the object, due to sublation in the aspect of the means of knowledge,
it comes to lack validity there — like the words of a <s>Buddha</s> or a trustworthy person.

children.text:
na khalu pramāṇāntarasaṃbhinnārthamapi vaco na pramāṇam, pramāṇameva hyāptavākyam /
kathaṃ punaḥ pramāṇaṃ sāpekṣamiti cet, ucyate ---
nirapekṣameva tat ‘pramito 'yaṃ mayārthaḥ'ityasminnarthe /
kevale hyarthe ‘evamayamarthaḥ'ityapratīteḥ ‘evamayaṃ puruṣo veda'iti ca pratīteḥ puruṣajñānāpekṣam /
tatropalabdhau tāvadanapekṣatvātprāmāṇyamaśnute tatsiddhidvāraśca paścādartha iti /
kathaṃ tarhi puruṣavacaḥ kiñcidabādhitārthamapi sāpekṣatvenāpramāṇaṃ kathyate? ucyate ---
yadyapyarthe bādho nāsti, yadapekṣaṃ tvasyārthe prāmāṇyaṃ yatsiddhimukhena taṃ sādhayati tatra pramāṇāṃśe bādhyate /
tasyāsiddhestaddvāreṇa nārthasiddhirityarthe 'pramāṇam, yathātīndriyārthe buddhavacaḥ puruṣasya darśanāsaṃbhavāt /
yathoktam ---
‘puruṣāśaktitastatra sāpavādatvasaṃbhavaḥ'; /
iti /
yathā ca vipralambhakavākyam, ayathādṛṣṭārthavāditvasya pramāṇāvagatatvāt /
children.translated_text: It is not the case that a word whose object is combined with another means of knowledge is not a valid means — for the statement of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is indeed a valid means. But how can a valid means be dependent? It is said: It is independent with respect to the meaning 'this object has been ascertained by me.' For regarding the bare object, since there is no cognition 'the object is such' and since there is the cognition 'such a person knows thus,' it depends on a person's knowledge. In that, since it first attains validity through being apprehended, and the object is established through that as a subsequent step — how then is a person's statement, even when its object is not sublated, declared to be invalid due to dependence? It is said: Even though there is no sublation of the object, that on which its validity regarding the object depends, and through whose establishment it establishes the object — in that aspect of the means of knowledge, it is sublated. Because that is unestablished, the object is not established through it — hence it is invalid regarding the object, like the word of a <s>Buddha</s> regarding supersensory objects, because of the impossibility of that person's perception. As it has been said: 'Because the person lacks the capacity there, the possibility of contradiction arises.' And like a deceptive statement, because it is known through valid means that the speaker does not speak of things as they are seen.
The statement of a trustworthy person, however, is not sublated either in the object or in the aspect of the means.
Being independent in the aspect of the means, how otherwise would there be activity based on verbal testimony?

children.text:
āptavacaḥ punarnārthe nāpi pramāṇāṃśe saṃbhavatpramāṇagocaraṃ bādhyate /
pramāṇāṃśe cānapekṣaṃ tanmukhena cārthasiddhiṃ vidadhannāpramāṇaṃ bhavitumarhati /
anyathā śabdanibandhano vyavahāro na syāt /
children.translated_text: The statement of a trustworthy person, however, is not sublated in the object nor in the aspect of the means of knowledge when there is a possible object within the range of the means. Being independent in the aspect of the means, and establishing the object through that, it cannot be invalid. Otherwise, activity based on verbal testimony would not exist.
'By me' — due to the absence of a speaker, it is free from admixture with that;
it is self-knowledge in which the distinction between knowledge and the knowable has dissolved.
Let the <s>Vedānta</s> texts reveal a non-worldly means of knowledge,
and for that whose object is established through the establishment of that, it will be like a person's statement.

children.text:
evaṃ ca pramāṇāntarasaṃbhinnārthatve 'pi vedāntavacasāṃ na prāmāṇyavyāhatiḥ, āptavākyavat /
tathā hi ---
tānyapi jñānajñeyavibhāgavikalaṃ svaprakāśarūpamalaukikaṃ kāmamavagamayantu pramāṇāntaram, taddvārā cārthasiddhirāptavacanavat /
iyāṃstu viśeṣaḥ syāt ---
vede vakturabhāvāt ‘mayā'iti saṃsparśo na syāt /
children.translated_text: And thus, even when the object of the <s>Vedānta</s> statements is combined with another means of knowledge, there is no violation of their validity — like the statement of a trustworthy person. For they too may freely communicate, as another means of knowledge, the self-luminous nature in which the distinction between knowledge and the knowable is dissolved, which is non-worldly; and through that, the object is established, as with trustworthy statements. But there would be this difference: In the <s>Veda</s>, due to the absence of a speaker, there would be no admixture with 'by me.'

children.text:
abhyupagamavādaṃ parisamāpya prakṛtamupasaṃharati ---
evaṃ na meyatā sattā
paraḥ punaḥ pratyavatiṣṭhate ---
nanvanyāpi na yujyate /
children.translated_text: Concluding the argument by way of provisional acceptance, he returns to the main topic: Thus, existence is not being an object of knowledge. The opponent further insists: But that too is not proper.
For without a prior recognition, the construction of a universal does not arise.

children.text: na hi pūrvāvamarśena vinā sāmānyakalpanā // MBs_2.59 //

children.translated_text: For one who has seen a single cow, the kind of recognition that arises elsewhere —

children.text: avamarśo dṛṣṭasatastathā na hi sadantare // MBs_2.60 //
children.translated_text: such a recognition of something seen as existing does not arise in another existing thing.
Let the application of a single word be accepted as being like 'one who carries a stick' and the like.

children.text:
dṛṣṭarūpāvamarśaḥ sāmānyakalpanāyāṃ pramāṇam /
yathā ---
bāhuleyaṃ dṛṣṭavataḥ śābaleye ‘sa evāyam'; iti /
na ca kiñcitsadgṛhītavato 'nyatra sa bhavati /
ekaśabdapravṛttistu vināpi sāmānyenārthāntarayoganimittā, daṇḍipācakādiśabdavat /
atrocyate ---
children.translated_text: The recognition of a previously seen form is the means of knowledge for the construction of universals. As when one who has seen a tawny cow, upon seeing a spotted one, thinks 'this is the same.' But for one who has apprehended something as existent, that recognition does not arise in another existent thing. The application of a single word, however, even without a universal, is occasioned by the connection with something else, like the words 'staff-bearer,' 'cook,' and the like. To this it is replied:

children.text: ko nu pūrvāvamarśo 'yaṃ pūrvarūpānvayo dhiyaḥ // MBs_2.61 //
children.translated_text: What then is this prior recognition — is it the connection of the cognition with a previously seen form?
Even in another existing thing, that exists, at least to some degree.

children.text: sarvātmanā tvanugamo na dṛṣṭaḥ khaṇḍamuṇḍayoḥ // MBs_2.62 //
children.translated_text: But complete identity is not observed between a bald person and one with a topknot.
If it is not of that kind, then self-denial known merely from difference alone is not justified.
A cup lacking the genus 'clay' is not established merely from the difference from a pot.
For the kind of formal connection that exists in the cognition regarding pots,

children.text: na dṛṣṭamallakasyāsti maṇike khalu tādṛśaḥ // MBs_2.64 //
children.translated_text: that same kind is indeed seen in a pot with respect to a cup.

children.text:
kaḥ punarayaṃ pūrvāvamarśaḥ ---
pūrvarūpāvabhāso buddheḥ, atha ‘so 'yam'; iti pūvārparānusandhānam /
tatra yadi pūrvaḥ kalpaḥ, so 'styeva sadantare mātrayā /
tathā hi ---
nirupākhyavailakṣaṇyena satāṃ tulyarūpatā prakāśate /
anyathā nirupākhyavatsanto 'pyatyantavilakṣaṇāḥ prakāśeran /
atha sarvarūpānugamaḥ, so 'bhiprete 'pi sāmānyagocare nāsti /
na hi khaṇḍamuṇḍayoḥ sarvātmanānvayaḥ, ekatvaprasaṅgātsāmānyābhāvāpatteḥ /
atha na tādṛśo yādṛśaḥ khaṇḍādiṣu /
tadasat /
na viśeṣamātreṇa saṃvedyānvayirūpapratyākhyānaṃ yujyate, gotvāderapi tatsaṃbhavāt /
na hi devadattasya dvitīyadarśane yādṛśo rūpānugamaḥ,

children.translated_text: Verse 98 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
tādṛśaḥ khaṇḍaṃ dṛṣṭavato muṇḍadarśane /
sāmānyagocare 'pi ca na sarvatra tulyaḥ /
nānāmaṇikavilakṣaṇo hi maṇikaśarābayo rūpānvayaḥ /
na ca tāvatā mṛjjātihīnatā tayoḥ, kiñcittulyatayāvabhāsamānatvāt /
children.translated_text: that same kind does not exist when one who has seen a bald person sees one with a topknot. And even in the domain of universals, it is not equal everywhere. For the formal connection between a pot and an arrow-rest is different from that between different pots. And that does not make the two devoid of the genus 'clay,' because they appear as having some degree of similarity.

What then is this prior recognition? Is it the appearance of a previously seen form in the cognition, or is it the connecting together of the prior and later as 'that is this'? If the first alternative: that exists even in another existent thing, to some degree. For the equal formlessness of non-existents reveals the similar form of existents. Otherwise, like non-existents, existents too would appear as entirely dissimilar. But if it is the connection of all forms, that does not exist even in the intended case of universals. For there is no complete identity between a bald person and one with a topknot, since that would lead to the absurd consequence of identity and the absence of the universal. If it is not of the same kind as between bald and topknotted persons — that is wrong. It is not proper to deny the cognizable connection of form merely from difference, since that would be possible even for cow-ness and the like. For the kind of formal connection that exists in the cognition when <s>Devadatta</s> is seen a second time,
Now for the second alternative, to this it is replied:

children.text: pūrvāvamarśaḥ sa iti prakhyetyapi na śobhate /
children.translated_text: The prior recognition as the awareness 'that' is also not satisfactory.

children.text: maṇikaṃ vīkṣitavataḥ so 'pi nodeti mallake // MBs_2.65 //
children.translated_text: For one who has seen a pot, that awareness 'that' does not arise regarding a cup.

children.text:
pūrvāparānusandhānātmikā ‘so 'yam'ityabhedamavagamayantī bhinneṣvapi sāmānyakalpanāheturbuddhiḥ pūrvāvamarśa ityucyata ityetadapi na śobhate /
yato nānusandhānādevābhedasiddhiḥ /
abhinnarūpāvabhāsādapi /
anyathā nābhinnadeśakāla eko 'rthaḥ syāt /
na hi tatra deśakālabhedābhāve ‘saḥ'; ityanusandhānam /
api ca dṛṣṭamaṇikasya mallake na bhavati drāgiva ‘saḥ'ityanusandhānaṃ khaṇḍamuṇḍavat /
na caivaṃ mṛjjātihīnatā /
vimṛśatastu ‘tajjātīyamidam'iti buddhiḥ sadantare 'pi samānā /
children.translated_text: To say that the prior recognition is a cognition that, through connecting the prior and the later as 'that is this,' communicates non-difference and serves as the ground for the construction of universals even among different things — this too is not satisfactory. Because the establishment of non-difference does not come from connecting alone. It also comes from the appearance of an identical form. Otherwise, a single object would not exist in different places and times. For where there is no difference of place and time, there is no connecting as 'that.' Moreover, for one who has seen a pot, the connecting 'that' does not immediately arise regarding a cup, as it does between a bald and a topknotted person. And yet there is no absence of the genus 'clay.' But for one who reflects, the cognition 'this is of that class' is the same even in another existent thing.

children.text: tulye tarhi sāmānyayoge kasmātkvacit ‘saḥ'ityavamarśaḥ nānyatra? ucyate ---
children.translated_text: If the universal connection is equal, then why is there the recognition 'that' in some cases and not in others? It is said:
When the common forms predominate, therefore the identity is manifest;
when the dissimilarity is slight, it shines forth, because of the non-arising of those common forms when they are few.
Because even when there is a universal connection between a pot and an arrow-rest,

children.text:
na /
‘saḥ'iti prakhyā maṇikāntare ca bhavati bhūyiṣṭhasāmānyayukte /
tasmātsāmānyarūpāṇāṃ bhūyiṣṭhatvenodbhavāt ‘saḥ'; iti tattvaprakhyā /
alpatve tu na tathā, teṣāmanudbhavāt /
children.translated_text: the awareness 'that' does not arise; but it does arise in another pot, which shares abundant common features. Therefore, when common forms predominate, the awareness of identity 'that' arises. But when they are few, it does not arise so, because those forms do not manifest.
And it is not the case that the application of a single word is like 'staff-bearer' and the like — he says:
The means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) is to be known through its effect; the cognition that exists without conjoining [word-meanings] // MBs_2.67 //
arises first; therefore there is no analogy with [the case of] the staff-bearer and the like.
KKS_99

children.text:
nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇā viśiṣṭabuddhiḥ /
na ca viśiṣṭabuddheḥ prāk (sadbuddheḥ prāk --edition) pramāṇagrahaṇaṃ tatkālaṃ vā /
tathā hi pramāṇādeva sā bhavati /
pramāṇaṃ ca pramitikāryonneyatvātpaścātsatpratipattergṛhyate /
tasmādagrahātpramāṇasya tatsaṃyojanavikalā sā na pramāṇayoganimittā /
yadi tarhi na pramāṇayogo 'styarthaḥ, kathaṃ tatkālānuvidhāyinī kālapravṛttirastyarthe ---
‘kūpo 'sti'; ‘kūpo 'bhūt'; ‘kūpo bhaviṣyati'; iti? tadupādhiprakalpitabhedatvāt, devadattasattāyā iva pāṭaliputrasaṃyogopādhikalpitabhedāyā iti /
children.translated_text: A qualified cognition (<s>viśiṣṭabuddhi</s>) does not arise without its qualifier being apprehended. Nor is there apprehension of the <s>pramāṇa</s> prior to (or simultaneous with) the qualified cognition. For that cognition arises only from the <s>pramāṇa</s> itself. And the <s>pramāṇa</s> is grasped only after the cognition of existence, since it is to be inferred from the effect of <s>pramiti</s> (resultant knowledge). Therefore, since the <s>pramāṇa</s> is not apprehended, that [cognition], lacking conjunction with it, is not caused by connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s>. If then the connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s> has no purpose in the object, how is there temporal usage conforming to time with respect to the object — 'the well exists,' 'the well existed,' 'the well will exist' — thus? Because the differentiation is projected by limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>), just as the existence of <s>Devadatta</s> [has differentiation] projected by the limiting adjunct of conjunction with <s>Pāṭaliputra</s>.

children.text: na ca ‘kriyāmantareṇa na saṃsargaḥ padārthānām'; iti śabdārthanayavidāmavigānamityāha ---
children.translated_text: And the claim 'without action (<s>kriyā</s>) there is no connection of word-meanings' is not unchallenged among those skilled in the theory of word-meaning — thus he says:
What is ascertained as mere relation, other learned ones also // MBs_2.68 //
declare as action-free speech: 'The king's servants' [and] 'fruit-bearing trees.'

children.text:
‘rājño 'yaṃ puruṣaḥ'phalitā ete vanaspatayaḥ'iti kriyārahiteṣvapi saṃsargaḥ pratīyate /
na cehāpi ‘astikriyā'; iti yujyate /
yato na nirjñātarājasaṃbandhasya puruṣasya phalavatāṃ ca vanaspatīnāṃ satteha pratipādyā gamyate /
na hyete vākye sattāyāṃ paryavasyataḥ /
kiṃ tu puruṣasya rājasaṃbandhe, drumāṇā ca phalasaṃbandhe ---
‘yo 'yaṃ puruṣaḥ, sa rājñaḥ'; ‘ya ete vanaspatayaḥ, te phalitāḥ', na ‘yo rājapuruṣaḥ, so 'sti'; ‘ye ca phalitāḥ te santi'; iti /
yadapi kecit ---
‘avadhāryatām'; iti pratipattikriyāvidhinā kriyāvattāṃ manyate, tadapi śabdādeva pratipatteḥ siddhatvātprāṅ nirastameveti /
children.translated_text: In 'this is the king's man' and 'these trees have borne fruit,' a connection is cognized even in [sentences] devoid of action. Nor is it appropriate here to say 'there is the action of existence (<s>asti-kriyā</s>).' Because the existence of the man whose relation to the king is already known, and of the fruit-bearing trees, is not what is communicated here. For these sentences do not culminate in [asserting] existence, but rather in the man's relation to the king and the trees' relation to fruit — 'this man belongs to the king,' 'these trees have borne fruit' — not 'the king's man exists' or 'the fruit-bearing ones exist.' As for those who think that the statement implies action through an injunction of cognitive activity such as 'let it be ascertained' — that too has already been refuted earlier, since cognition is already accomplished from the word itself.

children.text: athāpi na kriyārahitaṃ vākyamasti kriyāyāṃ ca sāpekṣatā, tathāpi na doṣa ityāha ---
children.translated_text: Even if there is no sentence without action and there is dependence on action, still there is no fault — thus he says:
And because [the sentence] culminates in the action of origination, a qualified [entity] can be cognized. // MBs_2.69 //
The cause — 'from such a cause this originates' — thus:
KKS_100

children.text:
īdṛkṣātkāraṇājjagajjāyate'; iti janikriyāniṣṭhādapi vākyāttadvidhakāraṇasattā śakyate pratipattum /
yathā ---
‘īdṛśāttaroridaṃ phalamajani'; iti tadvidhatarusadbhāvaḥ /
tathā ca śrutayaḥ kāścidevameva brahma pratipādayanti ---
‘sarvāṇi ha vā imāni bhūtānyākāśādeva samutpadyante'; ‘yathāgneḥ kṣudrā viṣphuliṅgā vyuccaranti evamevāsmādātmanaḥ sarve devāḥ'; ityādi /
tathā
children.translated_text: 'From such a cause the world originates' — even from a sentence culminating in the action of origination (<s>jani-kriyā</s>), the existence of such a cause can be understood. Just as from 'this fruit was born from such a tree,' the existence of such a tree [is understood]. And thus certain <s>śruti</s> passages teach <s>Brahman</s> in just this way: 'All these beings indeed originate from space (<s>ākāśa</s>)'; 'Just as from a blazing fire tiny sparks fly forth, so from this <s>Ātman</s> all the gods [emerge]'; and so on. Likewise:
Just as a spider projects and withdraws,
just as herbs spring from the earth,
just as hairs [grow] from a living person,
so from the Imperishable (<s>Akṣara</s>) the universe comes into being.' //
'Just as from a well-kindled fire, sparks
by the thousands come forth, of the same form,
so from the Imperishable (<s>Akṣara</s>), O dear one, manifold beings
are born and return into it again.' //
This too is true:
Likewise:
'The divine, formless <s>Puruṣa</s>, who is both external and internal, unborn,
without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable (<s>Akṣara</s>) —
from Him are born <s>Prāṇa</s> (breath), <s>Manas</s> (mind) and all the senses,
space, wind, light, water, and earth, the supporter of all.' //
Thus.
Now [the objector] maintains that injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) must be resorted to precisely for the connection of word-meanings:
KKS_101
Objection: In human statements, the word-meanings whose connection depends on other means of knowledge, // MBs_2.70 //
have their conjunction dependent on injunction in other [i.e., Vedic] cases.
The arrangement of words therein is for the fulfillment of the speaker's intention (<s>vivakṣā</s>). // MBs_2.71 //
And the intention is established with respect to an object knowable through another means of knowledge.
In the <s>Veda</s>, [the connection is] for the accomplishment of the injunctive purpose; in its absence, there would be incoherence. // MBs_2.72 //
The cognition of a qualified meaning is an error; where there is no apprehension, the apprehension of connection is a delusion.

children.text:
vivakṣitārthaniṣpattaye hi loke padānāṃ samabhivyāhāraḥ /
naikapadasādhyo vivakṣitārthaḥ /
pramāṇāntaropalabdhaśca vivakṣāviṣayaḥ /
tena tatra pramāṇāntarāyattaḥ saṃsargaḥ /
tathā ca tadvirodhe 'saṃsarga eva padārthānām ---
‘jaradgavaḥ pādukakambalābhyām'; iti /
vede tu pramāṇāntarābhāvādvidhinibandhano 'sau /
tadabhāve tvasaṃbhavādyeyaṃ viśiṣṭārthagatirucyate sā bhrāntiḥ, samabhivyāhārāt /
so 'yaṃ vivekāgrahe saṃsargagrahavibhramaḥ /
atredameva vicāryam ---
kathaṃ loke pramāṇāntarādhīnaḥ saṃsargaḥ? iti /
yadi pramāṇāntareṇa tadavagamāt /
tadasat, apūrvasyāpi tasya pratīteḥ /
anyathā vacanavaiyarthyāt /
anadhigataṃ hi śroturarthaṃ bodhayituṃ vacaḥ prayujyate /
atha saṃsargayogyatāmātrasya pramāṇāntareṇāvagamāt, samānametadvede /
tathā hi ---
aruṇayā krīṇātīti saṃsargaḥ, nāruṇayaikahāyanyeti /
tathā bhāvārtho niyogaviṣayaḥ, na dravyaguṇaśabdārtha iti pramāṇāntarāvasitayogyatāsāmarthyenaiva vyasthāpyate /
children.translated_text: For in ordinary usage, the co-occurrence of words serves the accomplishment of the intended meaning. The intended meaning cannot be achieved by a single word. And the object of intention is ascertained through another means of knowledge. Therefore, the connection there depends on another means of knowledge. Accordingly, when there is contradiction with that [other means of knowledge], there is no connection of word-meanings at all — as in 'the decrepit old cow [is to be purchased] with sandals and a blanket.' But in the <s>Veda</s>, due to the absence of another means of knowledge, that [connection] is grounded in injunction (<s>vidhi</s>). In its absence, since [connection] would be impossible, what is called the cognition of a qualified meaning is an error, [arising] from co-occurrence. This confusion of connection-apprehension occurs in the absence of discrimination. Here this alone must be examined: how is the connection dependent on another means of knowledge in ordinary usage? If [one says] because the connection is cognized through another means of knowledge — that is wrong, since even what is unprecedented is cognized [through sentences]. Otherwise, speech would be purposeless, for speech is employed to make the hearer understand what has not [yet] been understood. If [one says] because merely the fitness for connection is cognized through another means of knowledge — the same applies in the <s>Veda</s>. For instance, 'he purchases with a red [cow]' — the connection [is determined thus], not 'he purchases with a one-year-old [cow].' Likewise, [the meaning of] 'being' is the object of injunction, not the meaning of words for substance or quality — this is established precisely through the capacity of fitness ascertained by another means of knowledge.

children.text:
atha na vivakṣaikapadāvagamyā, tadarthamātravivakṣāyā niṣprayojanatvāt /
tasmādvivakṣāviśeṣasiddhirnāsaṃsṛṣṭeṣu padārtheṣu bhavatīti tathā vivakṣayā prayuktāḥ saṃsṛjyante /
sā ca pramāṇāntarasiddha iti /
evamapi vivakṣānibandhanaḥ syāt, tatprayuktānāṃ saṃsargāt /
na pramāṇāntaranibandhanaḥ /
yato na tattasya pratipādakam,

children.translated_text: KKS_102

children.text:
na prayojakaṃ vā /
yattu pramāṇāntarasiddhe vivakṣeti /
bhavatu /
na tu tasya saṃsarga upayogaḥ /
tathā hi (na tasya saṃsarga upayogaḥ /
tathā ca -- edition) vipralambhakavākye 'pi saṃsargapratītiḥ /
yattu virodhe na saṃsargaḥ /
kāmam /
na tu tataḥ saṃsargaḥ /
virodhe 'pi tu nāsaṃsargaḥ, pratīteḥ /
pratīto 'pi tu bādhyate pramāṇāntareṇa /
evaṃ cānṛtaṃ kiñcidvacaḥ, kiñcidanarthakam ---
daśadāḍimādi, kiñcitsatyam /
anyathānṛtānarthakavibhāgo na syāt /
children.translated_text: nor its motivator. As for the claim that 'the intention concerns what is established by another means of knowledge' — granted. But the connection [of word-meanings] has no use for that. For even in deceptive sentences, there is cognition of connection. As for [the objection] that there is no connection when there is contradiction — very well. But it is not the case that connection [arises] from that [non-contradiction]. Even when there is contradiction, there is not non-connection, because of the [actual] cognition [of connection]. But what is cognized is [subsequently] sublated by another means of knowledge. Thus some speech is false, some is meaningless — like 'ten pomegranates' [and the like] — and some is true. Otherwise, the distinction between false, meaningless, and true [speech] would not be possible.

If [one says] intention (<s>vivakṣā</s>) is not cognizable from a single word, since intending merely the meaning of that [one word] would be purposeless — therefore, the establishment of a specific intention does not occur with unconnected word-meanings, and thus [words] employed with that intention are connected. And that [intention] is established through another means of knowledge. Even so, [the connection] would be grounded in intention, since the connection arises from words employed by it, not grounded in another means of knowledge, because that [other means of knowledge] is neither the communicator of it,

children.text:
atha pramāṇāntareṇopalabhyārthaṃ vivakṣitvā parasmai pratipādayati puruṣaḥ /
tena tadvacasaḥ pramāṇāntaropalabdhirevārthaḥ /
saiva prayojikā padārthasaṃsargasya /
tasyāḥ prayojikāyā abhāvānna vede padārthasaṃsargasiddhiḥ /
mā bhūtsā /
viśiṣṭārtha eva prayojakaḥ /
atha lokāvagamyatvācchabdasāmarthyasya laukikaprayojakābhāvānna saṃsargaḥ, vidhimattve 'pi na syāt /
atha loke saṃsargamātraparatve 'rthāpattiḥ /
na tadviśeṣe, tanmātreṇapratītiprayogayorupapatteḥ /
vināpi pramāṇāntaropalabdhyā viśiṣṭārthagatisiddhiḥ /
atha pramāṇāntarālloke saṃsargasatyatāvagamaḥ /
apūrvo 'pi hi śrotuḥ saṃsargo vaktuḥ pramāṇānumānamukhena satyatāṃ labhate tadasaṃbhave 'satyatvādbuddhādivākyeṣu /
tena pramāṇāntaranibandhano loke saṃsarga ucyate /
bhavatu /
vede tu pramāṇāntarasaṃbhedābhāvātsvātantryeṇārthapratīteḥ śabdanibandhana eva /
children.translated_text: If [one argues that] a person, having perceived an object through another means of knowledge, intends [to communicate] it and conveys it to another — therefore the purpose of that speech is precisely the perception through another means of knowledge, and that alone is what motivates the connection of word-meanings; since that motivating [perception] is absent [in the <s>Veda</s>], there is no establishment of word-meaning connection in the <s>Veda</s> — let that not be so. The qualified meaning itself is the motivator. If [one objects that] because the capacity of verbal expression is known from ordinary usage, and because the motivator from ordinary usage is absent, there is no connection — then even when there is injunction, it should not be possible. If [one says] in ordinary usage, when [speech] aims at mere connection, there is <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), but not for a specific [connection], since both cognition and usage are accounted for by mere connection alone — even without perception through another means of knowledge, the cognition of a qualified meaning is established. If [one argues that] in ordinary usage, one cognizes the truth of the connection from another means of knowledge — even what is unprecedented to the hearer gains its truth for the speaker through the channel of inference from a <s>pramāṇa</s>, and in the absence of that [<s>pramāṇa</s>], it becomes untrue, as in the statements of the <s>Buddha</s> and the like. Therefore, the connection in ordinary usage is said to be grounded in another means of knowledge. Granted. But in the <s>Veda</s>, since there is no dependence on another means of knowledge, the cognition of meaning is grounded in the word alone, being independent.

children.text:
tadāstāmetat /
bhavatu yathā loke /
idaṃ tu paryanuyujyate ---
children.translated_text: Let that be set aside. Let it be as in ordinary usage. But this must be examined:

children.text: kathaṃ nu vidhyadhīnatvaṃ yadi syādanyathā vṛthā // MBs_2.73 //
children.translated_text: How can there be dependence on injunction? If it were otherwise, [the injunction] would be purposeless. // MBs_2.73 //
If the injunction is without object, the same [problem] applies when another word conveys [the meaning].
For the cognition of a qualified meaning, the other word-meaning too is employed. // MBs_2.74 //
In the absence of valid cognition regarding meaningfulness, let it be meaningless.

children.text: vidhirnaivaṃ kasya hetoratha syādaparaṃ padam // MBs_2.75 //
children.translated_text: The injunction is not thus — for what reason then should there be another word? // MBs_2.75 //
Regarding an object established by another means of knowledge, [that word] is employed [merely as an accessory], not as enjoining.
KKS_103
For the meaning of that [injunction], being not knowable by any other means, when being cognized, would subsume // MBs_2.76 //
its object; but the word-meaning established [by other means] partakes of restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>).
There would be usage without [prior] convention if the knowledge of connection were denied. // MBs_2.77 //
The word would deviate from its own function if it were otherwise [held to have] a meaning established by other means.

children.text:
na tāvadvidhiḥ sākṣātsaṃsargasāmānyaṃ tadviśeṣaṃ vā bodhayati /
athākṣipati, anyathā niyogamātraṃ nirviṣayamanarthakaṃ syāt /
padārthāntareṣvapi tulyametat /
te 'pi kevalāḥ padārthāntarasaṃsargamanāpnuvanto 'pūrvārthapratipatterabhāvādanarthakāḥ /
na ca loke padaiḥ svārthāḥ svarūpamātraniṣṭhatayaiva pratyyante /
kiṃ tu viśiṣṭārthapratyayaprayuktāḥ /
tathā vyavahāropapatteḥ /
tathā ca pratipadārthaṃ saṃsargākṣepaḥ /
children.translated_text: The injunction does not directly convey either the general connection or its specific form. If [one says] it implies it, [because] otherwise mere injunction without an object would be purposeless — the same applies to other word-meanings too. They too, being isolated, not attaining connection with other word-meanings, would be purposeless due to the absence of cognition of any unprecedented meaning. And in ordinary usage, words do not convey their own meanings as terminating merely in their own form, but rather as employed for the cognition of a qualified meaning. For only thus is practical usage accounted for. And accordingly, each word-meaning implies connection [with others].

children.text:
syādetat ---
loke buddhipūrvaprayuktānāṃ mā bhūdānarthakyamiti saṃsargārthatā /
vede tu nārthavattve pramāṇamasti /
ataḥ padārthāntaramanarthakamevāstu /
naitatsāram /
nānyathānarthakyamityapramāṇo 'rthaḥ śakyaḥ pratipattum, yasya kasyacitpratipattiprasaṅgāt /
tasmādvyavahārātsaṃsargaprayuktasvārthāvabodhasāmarthyameva padānāṃ gamyate /
tato vede 'pi saṃsargākṣepaḥ /
yadicānyapadārthānāmānarthakyam, vidhyarthasya tanna kasmāt? Atha matam ---
padāntarāṇi pramāṇāntarasiddhe 'rthe prayujyante /
tāni yathāvagatārthānuvādaparyavasitāni /
tathā hi ---
anūdyamāno 'rtho yathāvagamamanuvādānnāpūrvārthākṣepāyālam /
vidhāyakastu śabdo 'nanyagamyārthaviṣayastadarthaḥ pramīyamāṇaḥ śaknotyapūrvamarthamākṣeptumanyathānavakalpamānaḥ /
tasmādvede vidhinibandhano 'pūrvasaṃsarga iti /
tadayuktam /
pramāṇāntarāviṣayaścedvidhāyakārthaḥ, tatra saṃbandhajñānamaśakyamiti nihnūyeta /
tathā ca saṃbandhajñānānapekṣatvādavyutpanno 'pi pravarteta /
saṃbandhajñānāpekṣatā ca padadharmo vyutkramyeta /
tannirapekṣatā vākyadharma āśrīyeta /
atha saṃbandhāpekṣatā nāsya nihnūyeta, balātpramāṇāntarasiddhārthatāpadyeta /
tathā ca na viśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: One might say: in ordinary usage, let there be meaningfulness through connection, so that purposefully employed [words] are not rendered purposeless. But in the <s>Veda</s>, there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for meaningfulness [of subsidiary words]. Therefore, let the other word-meanings simply be purposeless. This is not sound. One cannot accept a meaning that lacks evidential support merely on the ground that 'otherwise it would be purposeless,' for then anything whatsoever could be accepted. Therefore, from practical usage, it is understood that words have the capacity to convey their own meaning as employed for connection. Hence in the <s>Veda</s> too, each [word-meaning] implies connection. And if there is purposelessness for other word-meanings, why not for the injunctive meaning as well? If it is held that other words are employed regarding a meaning established by another means of knowledge, and that they culminate in restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>) of what is already known — for indeed, a meaning being restated conveys it as already known and is not capable of implying an unprecedented meaning through restatement. But an enjoining word, having as its object a meaning not knowable by other means, being [itself] a <s>pramāṇa</s>, is capable of implying an unprecedented meaning, being otherwise inexplicable. Therefore, in the <s>Veda</s>, the unprecedented connection is grounded in injunction — this is unjust. If the object of the enjoining word is not within the scope of another means of knowledge, then the knowledge of connection with it would be impossible, and that would have to be denied. And since there would be no dependence on knowledge of connection, even one who has not learned [the conventions] would act [on hearing Vedic words]. Moreover, dependence on knowledge of connection, which is a property of words, would be transgressed. Independence from that [connection-knowledge] would be adopted as a property of the sentence. But if the dependence on connection is not denied for it, then it would forcibly become something whose meaning is established by another means of knowledge. And thus there would be no distinction [from ordinary usage].
KKS_104

children.text: śabdādeva mite yo 'pi manyate saṃgatigraham // MBs_2.78 //
children.translated_text: Even one who thinks the apprehension of connection is from the word itself, // MBs_2.78 //

children.text: nānyonyasaṃśrayāvadyaṃ na svayaṃ pramite hi saḥ /
children.translated_text: [faces] no fault of mutual dependence, for he does not [hold that it is] self-validated;

children.text: pareṇa śabdāvagate tatpravṛttyā ca sūcite // MBs_2.79 //
children.translated_text: rather, being understood from the word through another [speaker], and indicated by that [speaker's] usage, // MBs_2.79 //
the apprehension of connection there, as with other word-meanings, is easy.

children.text:
yo 'pi manyate ---
na pramāṇāntarasiddhe viddhyarthe saṃbandhajñānam /
api tu śabdasiddha eva /
na cānyonyasaṃśrayadoṣaḥ ---
śabdātsiddhe saṃbandhajñānam, saṃbandhajñānapūrvikā ca śabdātsiddhiriti /
yato na svayaṃ śabdātpramite taducyate /
kiṃ tu vṛddhaprayuktādvṛddhāntareṇāvagateḥ /
tadavagamācca tasya vṛddhasya yā pravṛttistayānumite ‘nūnamanena vṛddhena pratipannaḥ kaścitpravṛttiheturartho 'smācchabdāt, yenāyametacchravaṇātpravṛttaḥ'; iti /
yathā ‘gāmānaya'; iti sāsnādimadānayanadarśanāttatpratyayamanumāya tatra saṃbandhagrahaṇamiti /
children.translated_text: As for the one who holds that the knowledge of connection does not concern an injunctive meaning established by another means of knowledge, but rather one established by the word itself — nor is there the fault of mutual dependence, [namely] that the knowledge of connection depends on the word and the understanding from the word presupposes knowledge of connection — because it is not said of what is validated by the word itself. Rather, [it is] through [a word] employed by an elder (<s>vṛddha</s>), understood by another elder. And from that understanding, the usage of that elder [is observed], from which one infers: 'Surely this elder has understood some meaning from this word that motivated his activity, since he acted upon hearing it.' Just as [in the case of] 'bring the cow' — from observing the bringing of [an animal] possessing a dewlap and the like, one infers that cognition and thereby grasps the connection.
If it is thus to be inferred, how can it be the exclusive object of the word alone? // MBs_2.80 //
Since that too is preceded by the word, it is the exclusive object of inference.
Why should not verbal cognition too be preceded by inference? // MBs_2.81 //
Priority cannot be established for either — like the seed and the sprout — between these two.
For one who would understand from the word, inference is always antecedent to everything. // MBs_2.82 //
Since it is [cognized] like other word-meanings through that [inference], the word is merely a restater of it.
What is being cognized through inference is not cognized [anew] from the word. // MBs_2.83 //
Cognition through another means of knowledge does not merely restate what is known from another cognition.
And the word-meaning that is merely a cause of activity would be supramundane (<s>alaukika</s>). // MBs_2.84 //
It cannot be postulated, since it is established even from ordinary [usage].
KKS_105

children.text:
yadi pravṛttyunnīyamānapratyayaviśeṣaṇatvena vyavasthito 'numeyo vidhāyakārthaḥ saṃbandhajñānaviṣayaḥ, na tarhi śabdaikapramāṇakaḥ /
athānumānaṃ śabdapūrvakamiti tathocyate, śābdo 'pi pratyayo 'numānapūrvaka ityanumānaikagocaraḥ syāt /
na khalu bījāṅkurayorivānayorekasya prāthamyaṃ vyavasthāpayituṃ śakyam /
śabdāvagatasyānumānāt, anumitasya viditasaṃgateḥ śabdādavagamāt /
api ca sarvapratipattṝṇāmanumānapūrvā śabdātpratipattiriti teṣāṃ śabdo 'nuvādaka eva /
tathā hi ---
śabdādbuddhyamāno 'numitaṃ viditasaṃgatiṃ budhyate sarvapratipattā, na tvanumimānaḥ śabdāvagatamanumimīte /
nanu śabdāvagata evānumīyate /
satyamanena tu pratipattrā /
na cānyadīyā pratipattiranyapratipattimanuvādīkaroti /
pravṛttihetumātre ca saṃbandhavyutpattestanmātraṃ śabdārthaḥ syāt /
na cālaukikaḥ kalpayitumapi śakyaḥ, laukikādapi pravṛttisiddheḥ /
syādetat ---
vaidikīṣu pravṛttiṣu tadasaṃbhavādalaukikakalpanā /
naitat /
lokāvagatasāmarthyo hi śabdo vede 'pi pratipādakaḥ /
tatra laukikīṣu pravṛttiṣu laukike viditasaṃbandhe vede 'pi tatpratipattireva syāt /
asaṃbhave vā mithyātvam /
children.translated_text: If the injunctive meaning, established as the qualifier of the cognition inferred from activity, is to be inferred [and is thus] an object of the knowledge of a relation, then it is not known solely through scripture (<s>śabda</s>). And if it is said that inference is preceded by scripture—then the cognition [derived] from scripture too, being preceded by inference, would have inference alone as its domain. For, as in the case of the seed and the sprout, it is not possible to establish the priority of one over the other—the content understood from scripture being [confirmed] through inference, and the inferred [content], with its relation known, being understood from scripture. Moreover, for all cognizers, the cognition from scripture is preceded by inference—hence for them scripture is merely a reiteration (<s>anuvāda</s>). For thus: the one who is understanding from scripture understands the inferred [content] with its relation known—[this is true of] all cognizers; but one who is inferring does not infer what has been understood from scripture. [Objection]: It is precisely what has been understood from scripture that is inferred. [Reply]: True, but [only] by this [particular] cognizer. And the cognition of one person does not render another's cognition a mere reiteration. And if only the general cause of activity [is the word-meaning], then only that much would be the meaning of the word. And a supramundane [meaning] cannot even be postulated, since activity is accomplished even from a mundane [cause]. [Objection]: But in the case of <s>Vedic</s> activities, due to the impossibility of that [mundane cause], a supramundane [meaning] is postulated. [Reply]: That is not so. For scripture, whose capacity is understood from ordinary usage, is communicative even in the <s>Veda</s>. There, in mundane activities, where the mundane relation is known, the same comprehension would occur even in the <s>Veda</s>. Or, if [the mundane cause is] impossible, [the statement would be] false.

children.text:
atha bahuvidhatvātpravṛttihetūnāṃ vyabhicārādaśabdārthatve pravṛttihetusāmānyaṃ śabdārthaḥ /
tatra vede laukikānāṃ viśeṣaṇānāmasaṃbhavādalaukikaṃ viśeṣāntaraṃ pratīyate /
evamapi yaḥ śabdārtho vede sāmānyaṃ sa lokasiddha iti nānuvādatā vyāvartate padārthāntaravat /
yo 'pi viśeṣaḥ so 'nyāsaṃbhavena pariśeṣānumānagocara iti na pramāṇāntarāviṣayatvam /
na ca pariśeṣānumānamapi śreyaḥsādhanatāyāḥ saṃbhavāt /
atha matam ---
lokavyavahāra iva vedavyavahāro 'pyanādiḥ /
tatra vaidikīṣu pravṛttiṣu laukikapravṛttihetvabhāvādalaukike

tu pravṛttihetau vaidikānāṃ vidhāyakānāṃ saṃbandhajñānam /
na cānumeyatvam, tatpratyayasya pravṛttyānumānāt /
tatsiddhistu tatpratyayasāmarthyenaiva /
sa ca pratyayaḥ śabdottha ityananyapramāṇatā /
na ca laukikasyaiva śreyaḥsādhanatvasya saṃbhava iti yuktam /
laukikī hi pramāṇāntarāvagamyā śreyaḥsādhanatā /
tatra prayogadarśanālliṅādestadanusāreṇa ca śabdārthāvadhāraṇāt pramāṇāntaragamyatāpi śabdārthānupraveśinī /
children.translated_text: cause of activity, the knowledge of the relation of <s>Vedic</s> injunctive [words] [is established]. And there is no inferability, since the cognition of that [injunctive meaning] is [itself] inferred from activity. Its establishment, however, is by the very capacity of that cognition. And that cognition arises from scripture—hence the non-availability of another means of knowledge. [Reply]: Nor is it fitting [to say] that only a mundane means to well-being is possible. For a mundane means to well-being is knowable through another means of knowledge. There, from the observation of practice and inferential marks, and from the determination of the word-meaning in accordance with those—the knowability through another means of knowledge also enters into the word-meaning.

Now [another view]: Due to the manifoldness of the causes of activity, since there is deviation [from any specific cause] when [the general cause] is not the meaning of the word, the general [notion of] 'cause of activity' is the word-meaning. There, in the <s>Veda</s>, since mundane qualifiers are impossible, a supramundane specific qualifier is understood. [Reply]: Even so, the general [meaning] that is the word-meaning in the <s>Veda</s> is established in ordinary usage—hence its reiterative character (<s>anuvādatā</s>) is not avoided, just like any other word-referent. And whatever is specific [to the <s>Veda</s>] is within the domain of residual inference (<s>pariśeṣānumāna</s>), due to the impossibility of other [explanations]—hence it is not outside the domain of another means of knowledge. Nor is even residual inference [impossible], since [a mundane] means to well-being is possible. Now it is thought: Just as ordinary usage, so too <s>Vedic</s> usage is beginningless. There, in <s>Vedic</s> activities, due to the absence of mundane causes of activity, in a supramundane

children.text:
atrocyate ---
bhavatu nāma vedavyavahārādeva śabdārthānugamaḥ, tathāpi na pramāṇāntaragocaratā vyāvartate /
tathā hi ---
alaukike pravṛttihetau śabdasya sāmarthyajñānakāle pramito vā syāt, na vā? pramitaścet, śabdasaṃbandhasya tadaiva jñāyamānatvādavaśyaṃ pramāṇāntareṇeti vācyam /
atha na pramitaḥ, kathaṃ tatra saṃbandhajñānam? na hyapramitayoḥ saṃbandhinostadāśrayaḥ saṃbandhaḥ pramātuṃ śakyaḥ /
children.translated_text: To this it is replied: Let it be that the understanding of the word-meaning [is derived] from <s>Vedic</s> usage alone; even so, the [fact of its] being within the domain of another means of knowledge is not averted. For when the capacity of the word [is known] regarding a supramundane cause of activity, at the time of knowing [its] capacity, [that cause of activity] is either cognized [by another means of knowledge] or not. If cognized, then since the relation of the word [to its meaning] is known at that very time, it must be said that [it is known] through another means of knowledge. But if not cognized, how can there be knowledge of the relation regarding it? For the relation that depends on two relata that are not cognized cannot be ascertained.

children.text:
yo 'pi manyate ---
śaktirhi śabdasya saṃbandhaḥ /
sā ca nārthe, tasya vyavasthitatvāt /
pratyayastu tasya kāryaḥ /
sa ca pravṛttyānumitaḥ /
tatraiva sāmarthyalakṣaṇaḥ saṃbandhaḥ pramīyata iti /
sa idaṃ praṣṭavyaḥ ---
kiṃ pratyayamātre sāmarthyaṃ gṛhyate, atha viśiṣṭe pravṛttihetupratyaye? yadi pratyayamātre, yatkiñcittataḥ pratīyeta /
atha viśiṣṭe laukikavyatiriktapravṛttihetupratyaye, pravṛttipariśeṣābhyāṃ tasyānumitatvātprāptaṃ pramāṇāntaragocaratvam /
dvayī hi viśeṣaṇasya gatiḥ ---
smārtākṛṣṭaṃ viśiṣṭapramitāvaṅgatvameti, yathāgnimān dhūmāditi /
viśiṣṭagrāhipramāṇaprameyaṃ vā, yathā śuklo gauriti /
ubhayathā ca pramāṇāntaraviṣayaḥ, śabdasyānadhigatasaṃbandhatvāt /
smārtākṛṣṭatve pramāṇāntaramanveṣyam /
dvitīye 'pi kalpe viśiṣṭapratyayānumānānumitatvāt /
athānumānasya

pratyaya eva prāmāṇyam /
pratītimātraṃ tu tatra viśeṣaṇasya /
tāvatā ca tadviśiṣṭapratītyaṅgam /
viśeṣaṇapramitistvanumitātpratyayāt, yathā puruṣavacanādviśiṣṭārthapramāṇe 'numite 'rthasiddhistata eva pramāṇāt /
tatra hyarthaḥ pratītimātreṇaiva vaktṛjñānasya viśeṣaṇam /
tadetadapeśalam, smṛtipramāṇasaṃśayaviparyāsavikalpāntargamātpratīteḥ /
tatrālaukikaviśeṣaṇapratītirna smṛtiḥ, prāganadhigateḥ /
na saṃśayaḥ, koṭidvayasaṃsparśābhāvāt /
na vikalpaḥ, pravṛttihetupratyayasyāpi tathā prasaṅgāt /
tathā na viparyāsaḥ kathaṃ hi tatra yathārthatve tathābhūtagrāhiṇī tatpratītirarthaśūnyā syāt? pariśeṣātpramāṇam /
parajñānena ca paraḥ pratipadyata iti subhāṣitam /
atha matam ---
na parajñānena paraḥ pratipadyate, kiṃ tu svajñānenaiva parajñānasāmarthyāt /
atha tasya svajñānaṃ katamatpramāṇamiti vācyam, na tāvacchābdam, śabdavijñānādarthe vijñānamiti lakṣaṇāt /
na ca tacchabdajñānāt /
kutastarhi? śabdotthajñānādanumitāt /
atha tasya prāmāṇye pravṛttihetusadbhāvasiddhiḥ /
prāmāṇyaṃ ca tasya doṣarahitaśabdodbhavāt /
tena śabdasya tatra prāmāṇyamucyate /
tadadhīnastatrārthaniścaya iti /
tadapyasāṃpratam, śabdādarthajñānaṃ śābdamiti lakṣaṇāt /
puruṣavacanamapi nārthe na pramāṇam /
kiṃ tu jñānaviśeṣaṇe /
dvayī ca viśeṣaṇasya gatiruktā /
tatra smṛtyasaṃbhavātpramīyamāṇa eva sa viśiṣṭārthapramityaṅgam /
anyathārthe pramāṇāntaramanveṣyaṃ syāt /
na ca vaktṛjñānenaivārthasiddhiḥ, parajñānena na paraḥ pratipadyata ityuktam /
children.translated_text: authoritativeness is in the cognition alone. The qualifier, however, is [present] in that [cognition] only as something merely cognized. And to that extent it is an element of the cognition qualified by it. But the ascertainment of the qualifier [is derived] from the inferred cognition—just as when from a person's statement, upon the authoritative cognition of a qualified meaning being inferred, the establishment of the [qualified] object [is derived] from that very means of knowledge [i.e., the person's statement]. For there the object is a qualifier of the speaker's knowledge merely by being cognized. [Reply]: This is not sound, since [mere] cognition falls within [the scope of] memory, [authoritative] means of knowledge, doubt, error, or conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>). In that [case], the cognition of the supramundane qualifier is not memory, since it has not been previously grasped. It is not doubt, since there is no contact with two alternatives. It is not conceptual construction, since the same consequence would apply to the cognition of the cause of activity [itself]. Likewise, it is not error—for how could, if that [cognition] is veridical, the cognition of it that grasps what truly exists be devoid of an object? By elimination, it is a means of knowledge. And the [principle that] 'through another's knowledge, the other understands' is well stated. Now it is thought: The other does not understand through another's knowledge, but rather through his own knowledge, by the capacity of the other's knowledge. Then it should be stated: of what means of knowledge is his own knowledge [the product]? Not of scripture, according to the definition that 'from the verbal cognition, [arises] cognition of the object.' Nor is that [knowledge of the object produced] from the verbal cognition [directly]. From what, then? From the cognition arising from scripture, [which is] inferred. Then if that [inferred cognition] is authoritative, the existence of the cause of activity is established. And its authoritativeness [is due to] its arising from a faultless word. Hence the authoritativeness of the word regarding that [meaning] is stated. The determination of the object depends on that [word]. [Reply]: That too is not correct, since from the definition that 'the cognition of the meaning [arising] from a word is <s>śābda</s> [verbal knowledge]'—the statement of a trustworthy person too is not non-authoritative regarding the object. Rather, [it is authoritative] regarding the qualifier [viz., the speaker's knowledge]. And the two modes of the qualifier have been stated. In that [case], since memory is impossible [as its source], it is precisely as being ascertained [by another pramāṇa] that it is an element of the cognition of the qualified meaning. Otherwise, another means of knowledge would have to be sought for the object. And the object is not established merely through the speaker's knowledge—it has been said that 'through another's knowledge, the other does not understand.'

And one who thinks: The relation of a word is [its] capacity (<s>śakti</s>). And that [capacity] is not [in] the object, since that [object] is [already] established [independently]. The cognition is the [word's] effect. And that [cognition] is inferred from activity. The relation characterized as capacity is ascertained in that [cognition] alone—he should be asked: Is the capacity apprehended in the bare cognition, or in a specific cognition [viz., of] the cause of activity distinct from mundane [causes]? If in the bare cognition, then anything whatsoever would be understood from it. But if in the specific cognition of a cause of activity distinct from mundane [causes], since that [specific cognition] is inferred through activity and residual [reasoning], the consequence of being within the domain of another means of knowledge has been reached. For the qualifier has two modes: [1] it enters as an element of the qualified cognition, being drawn by memory, as in 'the mountain possesses fire, [inferred] from smoke'; or [2] it is the object of the means of knowledge that apprehends the qualified [whole], as in 'the white cow.' In both cases, [the qualifier] is an object of another means of knowledge, since the relation [of the word to the supramundane meaning] is not [directly] grasped. In the first alternative, another means of knowledge must be sought [for the qualifier]. In the second alternative too, since [the qualifier] is inferred through the inference of the qualified cognition. Now, [one might say]: of the inference's

yattūktam ---
vaktṛjñānādhīnārthasiddhiriti, tattanmithyātve tadasaṃbhave vā pramāṇapratītibādhane 'rthapratīterapi bādhanāttadabādhe cābādhāt /
na tu vacaso 'rtho na viṣayaḥ /
anyathā pramāṇāntaraparatantraṃ puruṣavaco 'rthe sāpekṣamityetadeva na syāt /
na hi yo yasyāviṣayaḥ sa tatra sāpekṣo 'napekṣo vā /
tathā ca ‘prāmāṇyasthāpanaṃ tu syādvaktṛdhīhetusaṃbhavāt'; ityuktam /
sthāpanamabādhaḥ, na tu prāmāṇyameva /
tacca vaktṛdhīhetusaṃbhavādvākyasya, na tu vaktṛdhiya eva /
śabdasya cārthena saṃbandhaḥ, na tu jñānena /
evaṃ hyuktam ---
‘autpattikastu śabdasyārthena saṃbandhaḥ'; iti /
arthagrahaṇamatra ‘arthāsaṃspaśī śabdaḥ, jñānenaiva śabdasya saṃbandhaḥ ---
iti paśyatāṃ nirākaraṇāya /
tasmādanyonyayogyatā śabdārthayoreva saṃbandhaḥ /
na cāpramite 'rthe sa śakyo grahītum /
pramite pramāṇāntaraviṣayatvamuktam /
na ca pratītimātre, arthavatyāḥ pratīteḥ smṛtipramāṇayoranyataratrāntargamāt /
ānarthakye kena saṃbandha? yadi ca śābdapratītivyatirekiṇyāpi pratītyā sa viṣayīkriyate 'pramāṇātmikayāpi, bhavatyayamaśābdasyāpi jñānasya gocara iti pramāṇāntarāśaṅkā kena vāryate? naca pramāṇāntarāvagamyatā śabdārthamanupraviśati, yato nānvayamātreṇa vyatirekamātreṇa vā śabdārthaḥ /
sati hyanyasmin prayojake 'rthe yasyābhāve na prayogaḥ so 'pi tasya śabdasya prayojaka iti gamyate, yathā satsu hetvantareṣu yasyābhāve na kāryaṃ so 'pi heturgamyate /
iha ca śreyohetuvivakṣāyāṃ liṅgāderdarśanāt, tadabhāve satyapi pramāṇāntaragamyatve 'darśanācchreyohetutvaṃ tāvacchabdārthaḥ /
pramāṇāntaragamyatve yadyapi darśanam, tadabhāve ca yadyapyadarśanam, na tu śreyohetutve sati pramāṇāntaragamyatāyā abhāvāt /
tatra saṃdigdho vyatirekaḥ ---
ubhayābhāve 'prayogāt kiṃnibandhano 'prayoga iti /
tatra śreyaḥsādhanatāyāḥ prayojakatvasyāvadhāritatvāt
children.translated_text: As for what was said—that the establishment of the object depends on the speaker's knowledge: if that [speaker's knowledge] is false or non-existent, the cognition of the object too is sublated, since the authoritative cognition [that carries it] is sublated; and if that [speaker's knowledge] is not sublated, [the cognition of the object] is not sublated either. But it is not the case that the object is not the domain of the statement. Otherwise, [the principle that] 'a person's statement is dependent on another means of knowledge regarding the object, [and thus] is dependent [on it]'—this itself would not hold. For one who is not the domain of something is neither dependent nor independent regarding it. And thus it has been stated: 'The establishment [of authoritativeness] would be due to the possibility of the speaker's intellect being the cause [of the statement].' Establishment means non-sublation, not authoritativeness itself. And that [non-sublation belongs to] the statement due to the possibility of the speaker's intellect being the cause—not [authoritativeness belonging] to the speaker's intellect itself. And the relation of a word is with its meaning, not with [the speaker's] knowledge. For it has been said: 'The relation of a word with its meaning is innate (<s>autpattika</s>).' The word 'meaning' (<s>artha</s>) here is used to refute those who hold that 'a word has no contact with the object; the relation of the word is only with knowledge.' Therefore, the mutual fitness (<s>anyonyayogyatā</s>) between word and meaning alone is the relation. And that [relation] cannot be grasped regarding an object that is not cognized [by another pramāṇa]. [But] if cognized, the consequence of being within the domain of another means of knowledge has been stated. Nor [is it grasped] in mere cognition, since meaningful cognition falls within either memory or [authoritative] means of knowledge. If [the cognition is] meaningless, what relation [could there be]? And if it is made an object even by a cognition other than the cognition from scripture—even one that is not a [valid] means of knowledge—then since this becomes an object of non-scriptural knowledge too, the suspicion of [its being within] the domain of another means of knowledge—by what is it averted? Nor does the knowability through another means of knowledge enter into the word-meaning, since the word-meaning is [determined] not by agreement (<s>anvaya</s>) alone or by difference (<s>vyatireka</s>) alone. For when another motivating object is present, that in whose absence there is no usage is also understood as a motivator of that word—just as when other causes are present, that in whose absence there is no effect is also understood as a cause. And here, when the intention of [conveying] the cause of well-being [is present], since inferential marks and the like are observed, and since they are not observed in the absence of that [intention] even when knowability through another means of knowledge is present—to that extent, being a cause of well-being is the word-meaning. And though there is observation when knowability through another means of knowledge is present, and non-observation in its absence—nevertheless, when being a cause of well-being is present, the absence of knowability through another means of knowledge [does not follow]. There, the negative concomitance is doubtful: when both are absent, non-usage [results]—but [the question remains] on what is the non-usage based? Since the motivating power of being a means to well-being has been ascertained,

tadabhāve tannibandhana iti gamyate /
tanmātreṇānvayavyatirekopapattau nānyasya śabdārthatve pramāṇam /

prayogāttadabhāve cāprayogāt /
atha śiṃśapātvasya śabdārthatvāttadabhāvanibandhana eva sattādyabhāve 'prayogaḥ, tatsadbhāvācca prayoga upapadyata iti na teṣu sāmarthyakalpanā, samānametadatrāpi /
atha śreyohetutvasya pramāṇāntaraviṣayatvāttasya ca vede 'saṃbhavādaprāmāṇyam /
tadasat /

samīpe hi bahirindriyaviṣayaḥ, dūre tvāgamānumānagamyaḥ /
