na ca pramāṇāntarānupalabdhyā pramāṇāntaragamyo bādhyate, viṣayavyavasthayāpi pramāṇapravṛtteḥ /
atha pramāṇāntaraviṣayatve tadvirodhādaprāmāṇyam, anantaraphalānupalabdheḥ /
tadaviṣaye tu śabdārthe na tadvirodha iti /
syāt, yadi virodhaḥ syāt /
na cāsau /
‘ānantaryaṃ hyacoditam'; ityuktam /
children.translated_text: in its absence, [non-usage] is based on that. When agreement and difference are established by that alone, there is no evidence for anything else being the word-meaning. Otherwise, even in the word-meaning of '<s>śiṃśapā</s>' (the Dalbergia tree), [properties such as] existence and the like would also enter, since there is usage when they are present and non-usage in their absence. [Objection]: Since '<s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness' is the word-meaning, non-usage is based on the absence of that alone, even when existence and so forth are absent; and usage is accounted for by its presence—hence there is no postulation of capacity regarding those [other properties]. [Reply]: The same applies here as well. [Objection]: But since being a cause of well-being is an object of another means of knowledge, and since that [mundane means to well-being] is impossible in the <s>Veda</s>, [scripture is] non-authoritative [regarding it]. [Reply]: That is wrong. For what is an object of a [particular] means of knowledge in one case is not thereby false in another. For in proximity, [something] is an object of the external senses; but at a distance, it is knowable through scripture and inference. Likewise, regarding sacrifices and the like whose fruits are in a remote time, being a means to well-being will be knowable from the <s>Veda</s>. And [the fact of] non-apprehension by another means of knowledge does not sublate what is [otherwise] knowable by another means of knowledge, since means of knowledge can operate with a distribution of domains. [Objection]: But if [the meaning] is within the domain of another means of knowledge, non-authoritativeness [results] from contradiction with it, since the immediate fruit is not apprehended. But regarding a word-meaning that is not within its domain, there is no such contradiction. [Reply]: That would be so, if there were contradiction. But there is none. It has been said: 'The immediacy [of the fruit] is not enjoined.'

children.text:
atha mā bhūdānantaryacodanā, mā ca bhūtpramāṇāntarāvagamyatā śabdārthaḥ /
sarvathā pramāṇāntarasiddhaścetpadārtha āśrīyate, sa yathāsiddhyāśrayaṇīyaḥ /
anyathā na tatsiddhaḥ syāt /
anantaraśreyohetutā ca tatsiddhā /
tanna /
na tāvadanantaraphalasādhanatā niyogataḥ karmaṇām, kṛṣyauṣadhapānādiṣvanyathāpi darśanāt, avāntarakāryasya yāgādāvapi pramāṇasāmarthyena siddheḥ /
api ca viśiṣṭasiddhau viśeṣaṇamapi śreyohetutvamātraṃ siddham /
tāvacca śabdārthaḥ /
na ca tāvati pramāṇavirodhaḥ /
tadevaṃ laukike 'pi pravṛttihetau doṣābhāvādvyarthā alaukikakalpanā /
sukhādivaccāsyānumeyatvāt /

tathā hi ---
mukhaprasādādyunneyasaṃvedanāḥ sukhādayastenaiva sahonnīyante /
naivaṃ sattve pṛthakpramāṇamarthyate /
yadāpīdaṃ darśanam ---
vaktṛjñānameva puruṣavacanārthaḥ /
tatra jñānaṃ nārthamantareṇa saṃbhavatītyarthāpattyānumānena vārthasiddhiḥ /
tadāpi pravṛttipramitastadhetupratyayo na tamantareṇetyāptavacanārthavadanumeyatā na vyāvartate /
athānumānahrtoḥ pratyayasya śabdasādhanatvācchabdapramāṇakatvam /
tadasat /
nāptavacanārthajñānasyākṣasādhanatvāttadarthaḥ śrotuḥ pratyakṣapramāṇako bhavati /
children.translated_text: For thus: Pleasure and the like, whose inner experience is inferred from facial expression and so forth, are inferred together with that [experience]. The [inferential] existence [of pleasure] does not require a separate means of knowledge in this way. Even when the view is this: the speaker's knowledge alone is the meaning of a person's statement; since knowledge is not possible without an object, the object is established through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) or inference—even then, since the cognition of the cause ascertained through activity cannot [arise] without it, the inferability, like the meaning of a trustworthy person's statement, is not averted. [Objection]: But since the cognition inferred from the means of inference has scripture as its instrument, it is knowable through scripture. [Reply]: That is wrong. It does not follow that the object of the meaning of a trustworthy person's statement is knowable through perception for the listener merely because the knowledge [of the speaker] is instrumentally produced by the senses.
Therefore it is well said:
'If that [injunctive meaning] is inferrable in this way, how can it be an object of scripture alone?'
Likewise:
'It cannot be postulated, since it is established even from mundane [sources].'

Now, let there be no injunction of immediacy, and let the word-meaning not be knowable through another means of knowledge. In any case, if the word-referent established by another means of knowledge is relied upon, it must be relied upon as [already] established. Otherwise it would not be established by that [other pramāṇa]. And immediate causation of well-being is [what is] established by that [other pramāṇa]. [Reply]: That is not so. It is not the case that the causation of immediate fruit is [inherent] to ritual actions from the injunction—since [immediate fruit] is also observed in cases like cultivation, drinking of medicine, and so forth [where the means-end relation is observed] otherwise [than through injunction]; and since even in sacrifice and the like, the intermediate effect is established by the very capacity of the means of knowledge. Moreover, when a qualified [entity] is established, the qualifier too—[namely,] mere causation of well-being—is established. And that much is the word-meaning. And to that extent there is no contradiction with a means of knowledge. Thus, even in the case of a mundane cause of activity, there being no fault, the postulation of a supramundane [cause] is pointless. And [the cause of activity's] inferability, like that of pleasure and the like, [is established].
Thus.
Rather, it is presented by its own word as having the nature of a means of knowledge. (<s>MBs</s> 2.85)
And it is said [that the injunction] is an evoker and independent with respect to another means of knowledge.

children.text:
athocyate ---
na brūmo vidhiranyathā vṛthā syāditi tadadhīnaḥ saṃsargaḥ /
kiṃ tu pramāṇāntmanaiva sa svaśabdena pratipādyate /
tathā ca pramāṇatvātprameyasyākṣeptāpūrvasya, pramāṇāntarānapekṣaśca /
na hyasau śabdavatsaṃbandhāpekṣatvātpūrvasiddhimapekṣata iti /
children.translated_text: Now it is replied: We do not say that the connection [between means and end] depends on the injunction, [as if] otherwise the injunction would be purposeless. Rather, it is presented by its own word as having the very nature of a means of knowledge. And thus, since it is a means of knowledge, it evokes the <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented [entity]) that is the object of knowledge, and it is independent of another means of knowledge. For it does not depend on prior establishment due to requiring a relation, as does a word [in ordinary usage].
Nevertheless, if [the injunction] is not established, the two defects stated earlier [apply]; if it is established, it is [merely] a reiteration. (<s>MBs</s> 2.86)
Wherever its authoritativeness may be, there <s>śruti</s> (scripture) [suffices]; you [i.e., the injunction] are superfluous there.

children.text:
evamapyavyutpannapravṛttipadadharmavyatikramau pramāṇātmāpi sa yadi na pramāṇāntarasiddhaḥ /
atha siddho yathāvagatānuvādānnāpūrvārthākṣepaḥ /
api ca yatrāsya prāmāṇyamiṣyate, śabdasyaiva tatrāstu /
kimanena? nanūktam ---
śabdasaṃgatijñānāpekṣatvādanuvādako nāpūrvārthāvagamāya prabhavati /
naitatsāram /
śabdaścedanuvādakaḥ /
tatprakāśyaṃ pramāṇamapyanūdyamānaṃ yathādhigataṃ kathamapūrvārthaṃ bodhayet? na prameyasaṃsparśarahitā pramāṇāvagatiḥ /
ato yathādhigataprameyameva tatpratīyate /
children.translated_text: Even so, if that [injunction], though being of the nature of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), is not established by another <s>pramāṇa</s>—[it commits] the faults of operating upon what is not etymologically derived and transgressing the properties of words. And if it is [already] established, then because it is a reiteration of what has already been ascertained, there is no implication of a novel meaning. Moreover, wherever its authoritativeness is accepted, let that belong to <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) itself—what need is there for this [injunction]? [Objection]: But it has been said—because [the sentence] depends on the knowledge of the connection of words, the reiterative [statement] is not capable of conveying a novel meaning. [Reply]: This is not cogent. If <s>śabda</s> is indeed reiterative, then the <s>pramāṇa</s> that is to be illuminated by it, being itself reiterated, how could it convey a novel meaning as [already] ascertained? A cognition of a <s>pramāṇa</s> devoid of contact with the object to be known is impossible. Therefore, what is cognized through it is only the object as already ascertained.

children.text: kva ca pramāṇameṣo 'rthe na yāgādau svaśabdake // MBs_2.87 //
children.translated_text: And where is this a <s>pramāṇa</s> regarding the object—not in the case of <s>yāga</s> (sacrifice) and the like, which have their own [designating] words? (<s>MBs</s> 2.87)
Even in worldly [statements] that are not injunctions, there is a novel connection for the hearer;
and if [the objection concerns] the capacity of being a means to a result, <s>śabda</s> is not defective there. (<s>MBs</s> 2.88)
Because [the injunction] is equal to any other word-meaning, the connection of word-meanings is grounded in the expectancy of [all word-meanings for each other, not specifically in] injunction;

children.text: na saṃsargaḥ padārthānāṃ svaśabdaistu prakāśitāḥ // MBs_2.89 //
children.translated_text: the word-meanings, illuminated by their own words, (<s>MBs</s> 2.89)
are participants in connection by virtue of their form as fit for relation;
for in ordinary usage, co-occurrence [of words in a sentence] is employed for conveying a qualified meaning. (<s>MBs</s> 2.90)

children.text: ato na viddhyabhāvena saṃsargo na prakalpate /
children.translated_text: Therefore, it is not the case that connection does not obtain due to the absence of an injunction.

children.text:
na ca niyogasya prameyaṃ nirūpyate /

nāpi teṣāṃ pramāṇāntarasyāgocaraḥ saṃsargaḥ /
tathā hi ---
avidhiṣvapi laukikeṣu vākyeṣu śroturanadhigato 'pūrvaḥ saṃsargaḥ pratīyate ‘brāhmaṇa putraste jātaḥ'ityādiṣu /
atha phalasādhanasāmarthyaṃ prameyamucyate /
na kila kāmino niyogo 'kāmopāye dhātvarthe 'vakalpate /
anupāyatve hi tasya na sa kāminyā kṛtaḥ syāditi /
tadapyasaṃpratam /
na hi śabdasya tatra kaścidaparādhaḥ, yena tamatikramyānyatpramāṇaṃ mṛgyate /
pramāṇāntarāpekṣatā pratyuktā /
anantaraphalādarśanena tu virodho niyogagamye 'pi tasminnaviśiṣṭaḥ /
ānantaryasyāpramāṇārthatvena tadabhāvaḥ śabde 'pi tulyaḥ /
atha vā śabdastatra na duṣyati phalasādhanasāmarthye, niyogastu duṣyatyeva /
na hi tataḥ puruṣarthasādhanāvabodhaḥ saṃbhavati /
taccedaṃ vidhivivekabhāvanāvivekābhyāmavagantavyam /
tasmāt saṃbandhajñānāpekṣatvena padārthāntaraiḥ samānatvādvidhāyakārthasya na śakyaṃ viśeṣeṇa vaktuṃ ---
tannibandhanaḥ padārthasaṃsarga iti /
sarva eva tu padārthāḥ saṃbandhayogyaiḥ kārakādibhāvaiḥ svapadebhyaḥ pratītāḥ sannikarṣeṇa saṃsṛjyante, yato lokācchabdavyāpārāvagamaḥ /
loke ca

padaiḥ svārthānāṃ pratipādanaṃ sannikarṣeṇa viśiṣṭārthaparatayā, na svārthamātrapratipattiparatayā /
tathā ca sarvapadārthākāṅkṣānibandhana eva saṃsargaḥ /
sarve hi te padairaparyavasitarūpāḥ svarūpamātre prakāśyante /
evaṃ padārthāntaraistulyatvādvidheḥ na viśeṣeṇa tannibandhanaḥ saṃsargaḥ /
sarvapadārthanibandhane ca saṃsarge na vidhyabhāvena saṃsargo nopapadyate /
tadevaṃ na saṃsargārthamapi vidhirupāsanīyaḥ /
kathaṃ nopāsanīyaḥ, yadā niyogaparatayaiva padānāṃ svārtheṣu saṃsargajñānam? pravartakavacanāntarapravṛttidarśanena hi taddhetupratyayamanumāya tatra tasya sāmarthyaṃ gamyate /
naitat, apravartake 'pi vākye svarūpaniṣṭhe saṃbandhagrahaṇāt /
sannidhāpitāgnivyatiriktapākyopakaraṇamagnyarthinaṃ prati yadocyate ---
‘caitragṛhe kṛśānuḥ'; iti, tadā tatastenānayanaṃ dṛṣṭvā gamyate ---
‘ihānenāgnisattā pratītā, sā cāsmādvākyāt'; na ca śakyaṃ vaktum ---
‘tata ānaya'; ‘gaccha vā tatra'; iti vākyātpratyayaḥ /
agnisattāmātrapratyayena vākyātpravṛttisiddherna vākyasya niyojane 'pi sāmarthyaṃ śakyate kalpayitum /
arthāntarānvaye ca prayogapratyayopapattau na viśeṣānvaye pramāṇam /
anyathā vedārtho niṣpramāṇaka eva syādityuktam /
children.translated_text: words convey their own meanings through proximity, with the intention of expressing a qualified meaning, not with the intention of merely conveying their own individual meanings. And thus the connection is grounded in the expectancy of all word-meanings [for each other]. For all of them, having their forms not fully determined by words alone, are illuminated only in their bare nature. Thus, because [the injunction] is equal to other word-meanings, the connection is not specifically grounded in it. And when the connection is grounded in all word-meanings, it is not the case that connection does not obtain due to the absence of an injunction. Thus, the injunction need not be resorted to even for the sake of connection. [Objection]: How can it not be resorted to, when the knowledge of connection among words in their meanings arises only through the intention of <s>niyoga</s>? For, observing the activity [of people] upon hearing another's prompting speech, one infers the cause of that [activity] and thereby understands the capacity of that [injunction] in that [context]. [Reply]: This is not so, because connection is grasped even in non-prompting sentences that are confined to [conveying] their own nature. When, for instance, someone desiring fire is told, with all other cooking implements having been gathered except fire, 'There is fire in <s>Caitra</s>'s house'—then, seeing him go to bring [fire] from there, one understands: 'Here, by this [person], the existence of fire was cognized, and that [cognition came] from this sentence.' But it cannot be said that the cognition [arose] from a sentence like 'Bring [it] from there' or 'Go there.' Since the activity is accomplished by the mere cognition of the existence of fire from the sentence, it is not possible to impute to the sentence a capacity for enjoining as well. And when the purpose of prompting cognition is served by connection with another meaning, there is no evidence for connection with a specific [injunctive] meaning. Otherwise, the meaning of the <s>Veda</s> would be entirely without a <s>pramāṇa</s>—this has been stated.

Nor is the object to be known (<s>prameya</s>) of <s>niyoga</s> (injunction) determined [as unique]. For, first, <s>yāga</s> (sacrifice) and the like are not the objects to be known [by injunction], since they are within the scope of words like <s>yajati</s> (he sacrifices) and so forth. Nor is their connection, which is beyond the scope of another <s>pramāṇa</s>, [the unique object]. For thus—even in worldly sentences that are not injunctions, a novel connection not previously ascertained is cognized by the hearer, as in 'O <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, a son has been born to you,' and so forth. Now, if it is said that the capacity of being a means to a result is the object to be known—surely an injunction does not apply to a verbal root-meaning that is not a means for the desirer. For if it were not a means, it would not have been undertaken by the desirer. That too is incorrect. For <s>śabda</s> commits no fault there, on account of which one should bypass it and seek another <s>pramāṇa</s>. The dependence on another <s>pramāṇa</s> has been answered. And the contradiction due to the non-observation of an immediate result is equally [present] even in what is to be known through <s>niyoga</s>. Since immediacy is not the object of any <s>pramāṇa</s>, its absence is equally [a problem] for <s>śabda</s> as well. Alternatively, <s>śabda</s> is not defective there regarding the capacity of being a means to a result, but <s>niyoga</s> is indeed defective. For from that [niyoga], the understanding of being a means to a human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) is not possible. This should be understood through the discrimination of injunction (<s>vidhiviveka</s>) and the discrimination of <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive operation). Therefore, because of being equal to other word-meanings in requiring the knowledge of relations, it is not possible to say with any distinction regarding the meaning of the injunctive element—that the connection of word-meanings is grounded in that [alone]. Rather, all word-meanings, cognized from their own words through [forms such as] agent-hood and the like that are fit for relation, are connected through proximity—since the operation of words is understood from ordinary usage. And in ordinary usage,
Now, if purposelessness is asserted without the knowledge of what ought to be done (<s>kartavyatā</s>)— (<s>MBs</s> 2.91)
there is no purpose of a sentence other than [producing] activity or cessation [of activity];

children.translated_text: Well then, the statement does not terminate in [conveying merely] the nature [of the object]!
This [objection] is equal [against your own position] and is concluded; [for] the sentence is subordinate to another sentence. (<s>MBs</s> 2.94)
There is entry into <s>niyoga</s> (injunction) [only] if [it is useful]; otherwise it is superfluous.
Thus far, the aspect of injunction regarding the knowledge of reality has been extracted. (<s>MBs</s> 2.95)

atha manyate ---
vastusvarūpamātrajñānaṃ kartavyatājñānarahitaṃ pravṛttinivṛttiśūnyamanarthakam /
pravṛttinivṛttiprayuktā hi vākyapravṛttiḥ /
atho 'rthavattvāya vidhiḥ /
anyathānarthakyam /
tatrocyate ---
pratipattividhāvapi tulyamānarthakyam /
tathā hi ---
‘evaṃvidhaḥ pratipattavyaḥ'ityapi na tatsvarūpajñānātiriktā kācana pravṛttirnivṛttirvā /
atha svarūpajñānameva prayojanam, tatsvarūpamātraniṣṭhe 'pi tulyam /
atha pratipattividhiḥ ‘prajñāṃ kurvīta'; ‘sa kratuṃ kurvīta'; ‘ātmetyevopāsita'ityadhikāravidhivyapekṣitaprajñopāsanāviṣayasamarpaṇenārthavān, nāvagataviṣayasvarūpā prajñā śakyeti /
svarūpaniṣṭhamapi vacastathārthavat /
tasya samarpaṇe sutarāṃ sāmarthyam /
nanvevamasya svarūpaniṣṭhā hīyate niyogānupraveśinaḥ /
svagataniyoganiṣṭhamapi tarhi tanna, niyogāntarānupraveśāt /
atha matam ---
svārthaparyavasitameva vākyaṃ vākyāntareṇaikavākyatāmupaiti /
so 'yaṃ prākaraṇikaḥ saṃbandha ucyate /
anyathā vākyalakṣaṇa eva syāt /
etadapi samānam /
niyogānupraveśe 'pi na svarūpaniṣṭhatā hīyate /
nanvasti niyogānupraveśaḥ, anyathā ānarthakyāt /
kāmam /
tattvapratipattividhistu tāvadānarthakyānnirākṛtaḥ, vidhervināpi tasmācchabdāttatvāvabodhasiddheḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, if one holds that mere knowledge of the nature of a thing, devoid of knowledge of what ought to be done, and empty of activity or cessation, is purposeless—for the operation of sentences is motivated by [producing] activity or cessation; hence [there must be] an injunction for the sake of purposefulness; otherwise purposelessness [would result]—to this we reply: the same purposelessness [applies] equally in the case of an injunction of apprehension. For thus: even in '[<s>Brahman</s>] of such a nature is to be apprehended,' there is no activity or cessation beyond the knowledge of its very nature. If, then, the knowledge of the nature itself is the purpose, the same holds even when [the sentence] is confined to [conveying] the bare nature. Now, if the injunction of apprehension is purposeful through the bestowal of the object of knowledge (<s>prajñā</s>) and meditation (<s>upāsanā</s>) required by qualificatory injunctions such as 'one should cultivate knowledge,' 'he should form the resolve,' 'one should meditate on the Self alone'—[we reply]: a statement confined to [conveying] the nature [of Brahman] is equally purposeful in that way. It has even greater capacity for that bestowal. [Objection]: But in this way, its being confined to its own nature is undermined, since [the injunction] enters into <s>niyoga</s>. [Reply]: Then that [statement] too is not confined to its own <s>niyoga</s>, because of [its] entering into another <s>niyoga</s>. [Objection]: It may be held that the sentence, terminating in its own meaning, enters into a single-sentence unity (<s>ekavākyatā</s>) with another sentence. This is called the contextual connection. Otherwise it would be a [problem of] the very definition of a sentence. [Reply]: This too is the same [for our position]. Even with the entry into <s>niyoga</s>, the termination in its own nature is not undermined. [Objection]: But surely there is entry into <s>niyoga</s>; otherwise purposelessness [would result]. [Reply]: So be it. But the injunction of apprehension of reality is, for its part, rejected due to purposelessness, since the knowledge of reality is accomplished from that <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) even without that [injunction].
But [just as] the originary injunction (<s>utpattividhi</s>) is established for the knowledge of the nature of a ritual action,
so too let the injunction of knowledge of reality remain established for [producing] that knowledge. (<s>MBs</s> 2.96)
And activity is held to [come] from the qualificatory [injunction], just as in the case of ritual-action qualification;
making known what is unknown, and hence setting in motion what has not [yet] been set in motion— (<s>MBs</s> 2.97)
the wise declare this to be an injunction (<s>vidhi</s>)—this [argument] too is of the same kind.
The knowledge of the nature of the ritual action is not the desired result of the [originary] injunction there. (<s>MBs</s> 2.98)
Rather, the connection is [between] what requires [knowledge of] what ought to be done and the result-stating sentence;
that which has a connection with qualification here is not [itself] enjoined. (<s>MBs</s> 2.99)
Reality is [the content] of the knowledge of reality; there is no entry into qualification [for it],
for direct perception regarding rice and the like does not partake of qualification. (<s>MBs</s> 2.100)

yattu tadviṣayastattvajñānam, tasya nādhikārasaṃbandhaḥ, vrīhyādipratyakṣavat /
na hi vrīhyādisvarūpagrāhi pramāṇaṃ prayogaikadeśatāṃ bhajate /
pramitānāmadhikārasaṃbandhānniṣpannānāmivānovāsaḥprabhṛtīnām /
vānatakṣaṇādirhi tatkriyā nādhikāramanupraviśatīti /
children.translated_text: And as for the objection: just as the result of the originary injunction (<s>utpattividhi</s>) is merely the apprehension of the nature of the ritual action—[as in] '<s>Āgneya</s> (the oblation to <s>Agni</s>) is [made with] eight potsherds'—from that [originary injunction] there is no [direct] activity, since activity depends on the qualificatory injunction; so too, the result of the injunction of knowledge of reality is merely the knowledge of reality, while activity [comes] from the qualificatory injunction—[such as] 'one should cultivate knowledge' and the like. And because the injunction has the two distinct purposes of apprehension and activity, they state its twofold definition: 'making known what is unknown and setting in motion what has not been set in motion.' This too is without substance. For the result desired for the injunctive [element] pertaining to origination is not merely the knowledge of the [ritual's] nature. Rather, [it is] the connection with the qualificatory sentence. For thus: when it is understood that the injunction is a means solely to a human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>), in the expectancy of a specific [goal], the connection with qualification is obtained. But the result of the injunction of apprehension of reality is not the same. For that whose connection with qualification [would apply]—namely the reality of the Self, which is the object of meditation (<s>upāsanā</s>) and the like—that, being non-active in nature, is not a proper object of injunction. And as for the knowledge of reality that has that [Self] as its object, it has no connection with qualification, just like the direct perception of rice and the like. For a <s>pramāṇa</s> that grasps the nature of rice and the like does not partake of being a component of ritual performance. [It is] like [things] such as the <s>avabhṛtha</s> (concluding bath) and the like that are accomplished [independently] from the connection with qualification of [things already] cognized. For a subsidiary act such as winnowing and the like does not enter into qualification.

children.text:
idānīṃ tṛtīyapratipattigocaro vidhiḥ parāsyate, tattvāvabodhaviṣayatvena saṃbandhāt /
dvitīyapratipattiviṣayo hi na tattvāvabodhaviṣayaḥ, kiṃ tu tadabhyāsaviṣayaḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, the injunction pertaining to the third type of apprehension is set aside, on account of [its] being connected with the knowledge of reality as its object. For the second type of apprehension is not concerned with the knowledge of reality, but rather with its repeated practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>).
Then this knowledge, [which is] other [than verbal knowledge], together with its means, is enjoined from <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony);
[it is] non-dual, [being] the apprehension in which the distinction between apprehending subject and apprehensible object has dissolved. (<s>MBs</s> 2.101)
For the reality of the Self, which is without conceptual elaboration, is not [something] that has as its basis a sentence-meaning cognition of the form of a connection of distinct meanings—
this too is flimsy. (<s>MBs</s> 2.102)
This manifestation of the non-dual Self, free from the error of limitation,

children.text: svātmasthitiḥ supraśāntā phalaṃ tanna vidheḥ padam // MBs_2.103 //
children.translated_text: this supremely tranquil abiding in one's own Self—that is the result, not a domain of injunction. (<s>MBs</s> 2.103)
For the activity of the injunctive [element] is held to be in [producing] the knowledge of the means to that [realization];
the wise hold that injunction consists precisely in [indicating] the required means. (<s>MBs</s> 2.104)
For from that [injunction comes] the resolution and so forth—not spontaneously, nor from [mere] verbal designation.

children.translated_text: from the scripture 'Knowledge is infinite.' And the truth of the self is free from all evil such as sorrow and the like — a state of universal peace — from the scripture 'free from evil' and the like. It is self-luminous, unsurpassed bliss, from the scriptures '<s>Brahman</s> is consciousness and bliss,' 'This is its supreme bliss; other beings live on a mere fraction of this bliss.' And thus, abiding in one's own true nature, through the cessation of all evil and the attainment of unsurpassed joy, is the most excellent, supremely peaceful goal of human life — the fruit. As it is said: 'There is nothing higher than the attainment of the self.' Nor is it proper to say that one does not engage in action even when the goal is known but the means is unknown, because desire is the preliminary form of activity. And thus, through that, the teaching of activity is sometimes given: 'Therefore one should inquire into <s>dharma</s>.' Likewise it has been said: 'For whatever one desires, that one does.' Moreover, if one does not engage when the means is unknown, one must necessarily be prompted toward that goal by making the means known. And since activity is established by just that much, the operation of an injunction need not be relied upon there. As it has been said: 'Its characteristic is the desire for the result.' Therefore, the operation of the injunction pertains only to the means of attaining the result. Objection: Even when there is a result, activity is characterized by purpose — so where then is the operation of the injunction? In the specific mode of action. This is not sound. For just as activity arises naturally from means in general, so too from the specific mode in general. Because no means that does not assist is effective. If one must be prompted regarding a specific means, let the same apply regarding specific modes. Moreover, the very requirement of means is the injunction, because the injunction is not characterized by prompting the unprompted, because <s>dharma</s>, which is the cause of activity, is denoted by the word 'prompting,' because there is no other cause of activity besides desirability and its being a means to that, and because desirability is ascertainable by other means of knowledge — one who acts spontaneously already knows 'I must do this,' so there is no prompting of the unprompted regarding desirability. But regarding the means to the desired end, since there is no ascertainment through other means of knowledge and it is knowable only through verbal testimony — without verbal testimony there is no cause for the activity of one who has not yet engaged. Therefore, that which is known through the verbal means of knowledge is called injunction (<s>vidhi</s>). And for one who acts,

children.text:
ca sādhanamanuṣṭheyaṃ pravṛttihetuḥ /
na svabhāvasiddham /
tenānutiṣṭhataḥ sādhanatāvidhiḥ /
ato 'nuṣṭhānaṃ sādhanaviṣayameva vidhāyakācchabdādgamyate /
children.translated_text: the means to be performed is the cause of activity. It is not naturally established. Therefore, for one who acts, the injunction is of the means-nature. Hence the performance is understood from the injunctive word as pertaining to the means alone.

We do not say that the knowledge of reality born from <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is enjoined. Rather, [what is enjoined is the process leading to] the apprehension in which the distinction between cognition and the object to be cognized has ceased. And therefore [that knowledge] is non-dual—either because of the absence of a second cognition of the same kind, or because of the absence of the duality of knower and known—[and hence] different from that [verbal knowledge]. And since the means of arising of that extraordinary [knowledge] is not ascertained from another <s>pramāṇa</s>, it is enjoined together with its means—<s>śama</s> (tranquility), <s>dama</s> (self-restraint), <s>manana</s> (reflection), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy), and the like. For the reality of the Self is not an object of verbal cognition. For <s>śabda</s> as a <s>pramāṇa</s> has the character of a sentence. And its object is of the nature of a connection of diverse word-meanings, since cognition follows accordingly. And how could the reality of the Self—which is without conceptual elaboration and untouched by even a trace of duality—be the object of that sentence-born cognition, which has the appearance of a mixture of manifold meanings? This too is without substance. For that knowledge of the reality of the Self which is non-dual and devoid of contact with even a trace of duality—that, being free from the error of limitation, is [nothing but] the abiding in its own nature. For it is due to being tainted by limitation that it appears as of a nature other than itself. But there is no knowledge of reality other than that. 'The true—

children.translated_text: Objection: Determination, intention, the initial activity, mere activity devoid of the three times, activity whose connection between action and agent is unknown — thus do the experts on injunction explain the injunction. This is not sound. Because the cause of determination and the rest is to be sought here. And that is none other than the requirement of means. Nor are they without a cause. One might say: The verbal expression is their cause. That is exactly the point. For from verbal expression there would be their cognition, not their production. It is not the case that from mere cognition, pots and the like become causes of activity — this has been explained in the <s>Vidhiviveka</s>. Or alternatively: Not from verbal expression. For determination and the like do not arise from the word, because the word is merely informative, and because the unprompted would then engage — this too has been stated there. Or to one who thinks: That from which arises the determination 'I must do this,' that from which arises the cognition 'I am enjoined' — that obligation synonymous with the word injunction — to him it is replied: It is precisely from the requirement of means that the determination 'it must be done' arises. For in the world, when the means to a desired end is recognized by the agent, the cognition 'it must be done' arises — and in its absence, 'it must not be done' — as established by positive and negative concomitance. And both are understood regarding that object. Similarly, 'I am enjoined,' 'I am prompted' — this is the cognition of the cause of one's own activity. And that is nothing other than the recognition of the means to what is desired. Surely, when a capacity is observed, it is not reasonable to say 'this is not the cause' without reason. And there is no valid means to abandon that and construe a worldly thing as non-worldly. Why? Not from verbal expression. For the expression of something non-worldly is not possible, because the connection has not been grasped — as has been said. Or alternatively, from that indeed arise determination, commencement, performance, and completion — because of the requirement of means. Only in the presence of that does one who is enjoined engage; from the injunction of some one thing, one who is not enjoined does not engage.

children.translated_text: One might say: One acts from the cognition 'it must be done.' Otherwise what must be done would not be done. And that is so — the arising of the cognition 'it must be done' is not causeless. For it is caused by the attainment of one's own purpose. One might say: The cognition of obligatoriness arises from the word itself. To that it is replied: Not from verbal expression. The cognition of obligatoriness does not arise from the word. For obligation (<s>niyoga</s>) is the meaning of the word. That would be either a property of the enjoiner or something independent. But obligatoriness is a property of the object. If one were to call obligation a property of the object, then the requirement of means is already obtained. If obligatoriness follows from obligation — even so, the word is not the means of knowledge for it, since it directly denotes obligation. Nor does it follow by implication, because obligation by a non-authoritative person is observed even regarding what need not be done. If the effectuality of obligation is understood — that its accomplishment depends on the obligatoriness of the object — that too is wrong, because in the world, the effectuality is cognized in the object. For instance: When there is the obligation 'Let the cow be milked by you,' if it has been milked by another, one does not commence milking again, because the effectuality is cognized in the object and the object has been accomplished. It is not the case that the obligation has been accomplished by another, because that other was not enjoined. For the accomplishment of the obligation, milking again would follow. This topic has been discussed at length in the <s>Vidhiviveka</s> — enough of excessive digression.

children.translated_text: Or its infinitude is because it is accomplished through infinite knowledge. And even if consciousness is momentary, its infinitude is in the form of a continuum. To this they say:

One might say: This knowledge is enjoined because it is a means to liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>). For liberation is heard as being accomplished through knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>): 'Through knowledge they ascend to that,' 'Through knowledge one attains immortality,' 'One who, having found and known that self, obtains all desires.' And because of non-difference — from the teaching that by knowing it, everything is known; from the direct declaration '<s>Tat tvam asi</s>' (That thou art); and from the designation everywhere by the word 'self' (<s>ātman</s>), which operates as the inner self; and from the rejection of the vision of difference in 'But he who considers otherwise.' children.translated_text: If lesser, the attainment of <s>Brahman</s>'s form would not be self-sovereignty. For the one denoted by the word '<s>Brahman</s>' — the supreme lord — would be their master. And thus there would be subjection to another ruler. And regarding that, finitude is heard: 'But those who know otherwise, ruled by another, their worlds are perishable.' And it is consistent, because in the world the loss of sovereignty of those with lesser sovereignty by the will of the supreme lord is observed. But equality is simply impossible. If there is one ruler of all, the governor of everything — what would another do as sovereign? And there is contradiction. For there is no reason for their unanimity. When two have conflicting purposes regarding one thing, the compliance with one's purpose makes the other non-sovereign. Compliance with both is not possible, because of contradiction. Non-compliance with both makes both non-sovereign. If the effect being unaccomplished is the ground for unanimity — like a council — otherwise that would be unestablished; therefore individually there would be non-sovereignty. If sovereignty is said to be alternating to avoid contradiction — then it is finite. And since the creation of the universe is impossible for them, sovereignty equal to <s>Brahman</s>'s does not exist. Because only the supreme one is heard in scripture regarding the creation of the universe. By worshipping him, liberation is the period after creation. Therefore, like a crystal from which coloring and the like are removed, the manifestation of one's own true nature is the attainment of <s>Brahman</s>, because the conscious self (<s>vijñānātman</s>) is of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>. And thus it has been said: 'Having reached the supreme light, it manifests in its own form' — because the word 'own' would be inapplicable if another form were manifested. If one says: Because of the non-difference or relation of what is manifesting, it is proper — no, because the qualifier would be purposeless, since everything that is manifesting would be 'its own.' There, just as a cloth that is already white is said to have 'become white' upon the removal of dirt, so upon the removal of the covering of delusion, when one's own true nature manifests, it is said 'it manifests in its own form.' Similarly, 'Being <s>Brahman</s> itself, it reaches <s>Brahman</s>.' Thus, since liberation is characterized by abiding in one's own true nature, delusion has no effectuality, since the true nature already exists. Because what is adventitious is not one's own nature. And it is not something different — because the removal of <s>avidyā</s> in the manner described is itself liberation. <s>Avidyā</s> is <s>saṃsāra</s>. And knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) alone is the removal of <s>avidyā</s> — if non-apprehension is <s>avidyā</s>, because being

children.translated_text: is itself the removal of [that] absence. Or if it is a misconception (<s>viparyāsa</s>), even so, its cessation occurs only upon the arising of the knowledge of the opposing reality. For there is no cessation of the cognition of silver other than the production of the knowledge of the nacre, nor is it to be accomplished by any other effort — because of the simultaneity of the two [i.e., knowledge and cessation] and the non-dependence on any other effort. And thus the simultaneity of <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) and <s>brahmaprāpti</s> (attainment of Brahman) is heard in scripture — 'He who knows <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself'; likewise, 'The knower of the bliss of <s>Brahman</s> does not fear'; 'He knew himself thus: I am <s>Brahman</s>. Therefore he became all this'; 'What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?' — 'knows — becomes,' 'the knower — does not fear,' 'what delusion — for one who perceives' — from the hearing of [these as having] no temporal sequence. Where there is temporal sequence somewhere, that is like [the expression] 'he yawns and sleeps.' [Objection:] But if there is oneness, simultaneity too is untenable. [Reply:] No, because even a single entity is spoken of in terms of existence and absence, as in — 'When the pot perishes, the potsherds are born.' [Objection:] How then are the scriptures on the paths, on non-separation, on creation, dissolution, and sovereignty [to be understood]? To that they say — The scriptures on paths do not pertain to the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> that is pure and unconditioned (<s>nirupādhi</s>). For where the object of meditation is <s>Brahman</s> that is free from all limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) — not gross, etc. — there [it is said]: 'Being <s>Brahman</s> itself, one attains <s>Brahman</s>'; 'The vital breaths do not depart from him; they are dissolved right here' — thus, through the non-departure of the vital breaths, the non-going of the <s>vijñānātman</s> (cognitive self) itself is stated. For when there is no going of that [self], there is no distinction of the <s>vijñānātman</s> from <s>Brahman</s> through its limiting adjunct. But where the object of meditation is conditioned (<s>sopādhi</s>) — 'consisting of mind, having the vital breath as body, having the form of light' — those [path-scriptures] pertain to that. If it is the destruction of the effect-form, there would be the consequence that liberation is annihilation. In that case there is a contradiction with 'Through knowledge one attains immortality,' since knowledge itself would lead to annihilation. And since the annihilation of the self is undesirable, there would be no fruit. And the primary cause-effect relation is negated in the word 'imperishable,' and by the scripture 'modification is a mere name, a verbal handle,' which teaches the unreality of modifications. Nor the fourth, because of non-difference itself, and because there is no distinction in the consciousness that is the nature of <s>Brahman</s>. If it is said that what is distinctive for the conscious selves (<s>vijñānātman</s>) is the absence of sorrow, delusion, and the like — even there, if sorrow and the like are the very nature of the conscious selves, they cannot be destroyed. But if they are qualities, other entities, coming and going, momentary — then because of their very momentariness they perish on their own, and no means for that need be sought. And it has been said that nothing is required for the non-arising of future ones. If it is said that liberation is a special sovereignty in <s>Brahman</s>, and its attainment through transformation into that form — from the scripture 'He becomes self-sovereign' — that is wrong, because multiple sovereigns are impossible. Would the sovereignty of the conscious selves be lesser than or equal to <s>Brahman</s>'s?

those who perform <s>dakṣiṇā</s> (ritual gifts) do not go there, nor the unlearned ascetics.' //

iti, tathā ‘tameva viditvāti mṛtyumeti'; iti vacanāt /
apunarāvṛtti śrutistarhi katham? atra kecinmanyate ---
kramamuktyāśrayaṇāttatprāpya tatrotpannanirupādhitattvajñānāḥ paraṃ padamaśnuvate /
yathoktam ---
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the statement 'Knowing Him alone, one transcends death.' How then is the scripture on non-return [to be understood]? Here some hold — By recourse to <s>krama-mukti</s> (gradual liberation): having reached that [<s>Brahmaloka</s>], those in whom unconditioned knowledge of reality has arisen there attain the supreme state. As it is said —
'Those who have ascertained the meaning through the knowledge of <s>Vedānta</s>,
the strivers purified in nature through the discipline of renunciation (<s>saṃnyāsa-yoga</s>),
they, in the worlds of <s>Brahman</s>, at the final end of time,
having become immortal, are all completely liberated.' //

children.text:
brahmalokeṣviti kāryabrahmalokanirdeśaḥ, bahuvacanāttatrāvayavadvāreṇa bahutvopapatteḥ /
parāntakālo mahāpralayo brahmaṇaḥ svādhikāraparyavasānam, tasmin parāmṛtāḥ parabrahmarūpeṇāmṛtāḥ santaḥ saṃnyāsayogādbhedena parameśvare svakṛtānāṃ karmaṇāṃ phalānāṃ ca saṃnyāsādyogācca sarvamidaṃ kartrādi brahma ityupāsanāt /
tathā ca smṛtiḥ ---
children.translated_text: 'In the worlds of <s>Brahman</s>' — this indicates the world of the conditioned <s>Brahman</s> (<s>kārya-brahma</s>), because the plural [form 'worlds'] is justified through the multiplicity of its parts. 'The final end of time' is the great dissolution (<s>mahāpralaya</s>), the conclusion of <s>Brahman</s>'s own period of authority. At that time, 'having become immortal' means having become immortal in the form of the supreme <s>Brahman</s>; 'through <s>saṃnyāsa-yoga</s>' means through the renunciation of one's own actions and their fruits separately in the supreme Lord, and through the meditation (<s>yoga</s>) that 'all this — agent, etc. — is <s>Brahman</s>.' And thus the <s>smṛti</s> states —
'All of them, together with <s>Brahman</s>, when the re-absorption arrives,
at the end of the great [cycle], those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state.' //

children.text:
anye tu manyate ---
yathā candraloke yāvatsaṃpātamuṣitvā sthita eva tasmin bhuktabhogā āvartante naivaṃ sthita eva brahmaloke tata āvṛttiḥ /
kiṃ tu tatpralayaparyavasānā

children.translated_text: KKS_124

children.text:
tatra sthitiḥ /
tatpralaye hi na tata āvṛtto bhavati /
tataścānāvṛttiḥ śrūyate /
tathā ca ‘imaṃ mānavamāvartaṃ nāvartante'; iti ‘imam(?, im edition), iha'iti viśeṣaṇam ‘amṛtatvameti'ityamṛtatvamāpekṣikam, yathā ---
‘amṛtā devāḥ'; iti /
tathā ca paurāṇikasmaraṇam ---
‘ābhūtasaṃplavaṃ sthānamamṛtatvaṃ hi bhāṣyate'; iti /
yattu manyate ---
sarvagatatve 'pi brahmaṇo vikṛtāvikṛtabhedaḥ /
tataśca deśabhedaḥ /
tathā cāvikṛtasya brahmaṇo deśabhedaḥ śrūyate ---
‘atha yadataḥ paro divo jyotirdīpyate'; iti /
ato 'vikṛtasya niyatadeśasya brahmaṇaḥ prāptaye yujyate mārgaviśeṣaḥ /
tatsaṃpradhāryam /
na tāvadanutpannādvayaviśuddhavidyasyāyaṃ mārgaḥ, brahmavidaḥ śravaṇāt /
nāpi vidyāvataḥ /
vidyodaye nikhilabhedocchedāditi /
madhunadīnidarśanāvibhāgaśrutirapi vivekajñānābhāvaparā, na tu tadvidha evāvibhāgaḥ /
children.translated_text: The stay there [lasts until] its dissolution. For at the dissolution of that [<s>Brahmaloka</s>], one does not return from there. And thus non-return is stated in scripture. And thus 'They do not return to this human cycle' — the qualifier 'this, here' [indicates a specific return]; 'attains immortality' — the immortality is relative, as in — 'The gods are immortal.' And thus the <s>Purāṇa</s>-based tradition states — 'A station lasting until the dissolution of all beings is called immortality.' As for what is held — that even though <s>Brahman</s> is all-pervading, there is a distinction between modified and unmodified [<s>Brahman</s>], and hence a distinction of place; and thus a distinction of place for the unmodified <s>Brahman</s> is heard in scripture — 'Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven' — therefore a specific path is appropriate for attaining the unmodified <s>Brahman</s> which has a definite location — that must be considered carefully. This path is certainly not for one in whom the pure knowledge of non-duality has not arisen — because the knower of <s>Brahman</s> [needs no path, as] is heard [in scripture]. Nor is it for one who possesses knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), because at the arising of knowledge all distinctions are destroyed. The scripture on non-separation illustrated by the <s>Madhu-nadī</s> (honey-river) analogy also pertains to the absence of discriminative knowledge, and does not [teach] that non-separation is of precisely that kind [i.e., a real spatial merging].

Others, however, hold — Just as in the world of the moon, having stayed until the exhaustion [of merit], those who have exhausted their enjoyments return while remaining in that very [world] — it is not so that while remaining in the world of <s>Brahman</s> there is return from there. Rather, the stay there lasts until the dissolution of that [<s>Brahmaloka</s>].

children.text:
sargaśrutayo 'pi na sargaparāḥ /
kiṃ tarhi? ekātmatattvapratipattipradhānāḥ /
children.translated_text: The creation-scriptures (<s>sarga-śruti</s>) too are not aimed at [teaching] creation. What then? They are principally aimed at the understanding of the reality of the one Self (<s>ekātma-tattva</s>).

children.text:
tatastadanuguṇatayaiva tāsāmarthavyavasthānam, na tu tadvirodhena /
tathā hi ---
kasminnu bhagavo vijñāte sarvamidaṃ vijñātaṃ bhavati? ‘sadeva somyedamagra āsīdekamevādvitīyam'; ityekatvenopakramāt ‘aitadātmyamidaṃ sarvam /
tatsatyam, sa ātmā, tattvamasi'ityupasaṃhārādekatvenaivaikātmyatattvapratipattiparamekamidaṃ vākyaṃ gamyate /
tatra yadyaparastejaḥprabhṛtitattvasargaḥ satyatayā vidhīyeta, vākyabhedaḥ syāt /
ato yathopāṃśuyājavākye 'jāmitvopakramopasaṃhāre ‘viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ'ityādīni vacāṃsi

children.translated_text: KKS_125

children.text:
vākyabhedadoṣātpṛthagvidhitvamalabhamānāni tādarthyāttadānukūlyena stutyarthatayā vyavatiṣṭhante, tathā sargaśrutayo 'pyekatvopāyatayā /
na ca viparītaṃ śakyaṃ vaktum ---
ekatvaśrutireva bhedapratipattyartheti, sarvatraikatvenopakramāt upasaṃhārācca /
yenopakramyate yena copasaṃhriyate sa vākyārthaḥ /
bhedapratipatteścāphalatvāt /
ekatvapratipattestu dṛṣṭaṃ śrutaṃ ca phalaṃ śokādinivṛttaḥ, viśuddhaikātmyadarśanena tadavagamāt ‘tatra ko mohaḥ kaḥ śoka ekatvamanupaśyataḥ'; iti śravaṇāt /
phalavadaṅgatā cāphalasya /
upāyatvaṃ ca /
na cedaṃ jagadasanmūlam /
kiṃ tarhi? advitīyaikasanmūlam /
kāraṇāvyatirekācca kāryasya sadekamevedam, ghaṭādivat /
mṛdrūpeṇa hi ghaṭādayo naikatvamatikrāmanti /
nanvevaṃ mukhya eva kāryakāraṇabhāva uktaḥ syāt /
naitat, ekatvāvatāropāyamātratvāt /
na khalvatra kāryakāraṇabhāva eva pratipādyaḥ, yenāsau yathāśabdaṃ mukhya eva gṛhyeta /
ekatvopāyattvādityuktam /
ekatvaṃ cānenopāyenāvatāryate puruṣaḥ /
sa ca mukhyaḥ pradhānavirodhī /
‘ekamevādvitīyam'iti punaḥ punaḥ śruteḥ sarvabhedanirāsaparatvānna śakyaṃ vaktum ---
kāraṇātmanaikatvam, kāryātmanā nānātvam ---
‘tatsatyam, sa ātmā'; iti ca kāraṇasyaiva satyatvāvadhāraṇāt /
anyatra ca'; ‘indro māyābhiḥ'; iti bhedasya māyāgamyatvaśruteḥ /
sākṣācca bhedābhāvasya śravaṇāt ---
‘neha nānāsti kiñcana'; iti /
bhedābhedayośca virodhātprāganupapattervarṇitatvāt /
tadavirodhena varṇyate tadupādānamātratayā bhedavikalpasya, bimbapratibimbavadvarṇapadavākyādivacca /
yathā hi na bimbātpratibimbānāmutpattirnānārūpāṇām, bimbopādānamātratayā pratibimbabhedavikalpasya /
na hi bimbāt
children.translated_text: not obtaining the status of independent injunctions due to the fault of splitting the passage, are established as having the purpose of praise in accordance with and in service of that [main purport] — so too the creation-scriptures serve as means to [the understanding of] oneness. And the reverse cannot be maintained — that the oneness-scripture is itself for the purpose of apprehending difference — because everywhere oneness is the commencement and conclusion. That with which [the passage] commences and with which it concludes is the meaning of the passage. And because the apprehension of difference is fruitless, while the apprehension of oneness has a fruit both seen and heard — namely, the cessation of grief and the like — through the perception of pure oneness, from the understanding of that: 'What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?' — thus it is heard. And the subordination of the fruitless to that which bears fruit [follows]. And [the creation accounts serve as] a means [to oneness]. Nor is this world rooted in non-being (<s>asat</s>). What then? It is rooted in the one Being (<s>Sat</s>) without a second. And because the effect is non-different from the cause, this is just Being alone, like pots and the like [are just clay]. For in the form of clay, pots and the like do not transcend oneness. [Objection:] But in this case, a literal cause-effect relationship would have been stated. [Reply:] Not so, because it is merely a means for introducing [the understanding of] oneness. It is not the case that the cause-effect relationship itself is what is to be taught here, such that it would be taken literally as the words suggest. It is a means to oneness — so it has been said. And by this means a person is brought to [the understanding of] oneness. And that [oneness] is the primary [teaching], which would be contradicted by [an independently real] subordinate [creation]. From the repeated scriptural declaration 'One only, without a second,' [the teaching] is aimed at the negation of all difference; therefore it cannot be said — oneness in respect of the cause, multiplicity in respect of the effect — because of the determination of the reality of the cause alone in 'That is the truth, that is the Self.' And elsewhere, from the scriptural statement '<s>Indra</s> [appears in many forms] through his <s>māyās</s>' — [showing] that difference is cognized through <s>māyā</s>. And from the direct hearing of the absence of difference — 'There is no multiplicity here whatsoever.' And because of the contradiction between difference and non-difference, and because the impossibility [of their co-existence] has been explained before, that [difference] is described consistently with non-difference as merely the superimposition of the differentiation of appearances, like the image and its reflection, or like phonemes, words, sentences, and so forth. For just as reflections of diverse forms do not [really] arise from the original — since the differentiation of reflections is merely the superimposition of the original — for indeed, from the original
KKS_126

children.text:
parasparato vā vyāvṛttāni kānicidvastūni pratibimbāni /
bimbopādānaṃ tu tannānā nirbhāsamātram /
tathā na varṇebhyaḥ padavākyaprakaraṇādīni kānicidvastūni santi, tadupādānamātratvāttatkalpanāyāḥ ‘varṇebhyaḥ padāni niṣpadyante, padebhyo vākyam'; ityucyate /
api ca svapne 'pi sṛṣṭiḥ śrūyate ---
‘na tatra rathā na rathayogā na panthāno bhavanti, atha rathān rathayogān pathaḥ sṛjate'iti, tadvadeṣā syāt, anyaparatvāt /
svayameva ‘vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyam'; iti vikārāsatyatayā na pāramārthikītyuktam /
children.translated_text: or from one another, reflections are not any [real] entities that are mutually excluded. Rather, the superimposition of the original is merely the appearance of that multiplicity. Likewise, from phonemes, words, sentences, chapters, and the like are not any [real] entities — because those constructions are merely the superimposition of those [phonemes]: 'From phonemes, words are produced; from words, sentences' — thus it is said. Moreover, creation is heard of even in dream — 'There are no chariots there, no yokes for chariots, no roads; yet he creates chariots, yokes for chariots, roads' — this [creation-teaching] may be like that, since it has another purport. [The scripture] itself has said 'Modification is merely a verbal handle, a name' — thus, through the unreality of modification, [the creation] is not ultimately real — so it has been stated.

Therefore the determination of the meaning of those [creation-scriptures] is in conformity with that [unity teaching] alone, and not in opposition to it. For thus — 'Revered sir, by knowing what does all this become known?' 'Being (<s>Sat</s>) alone, dear one, was this in the beginning, one only, without a second' — from the commencement with oneness, and from the conclusion 'All this has that as its Self. That is the truth, that is the Self, that thou art (<s>tat tvam asi</s>)' — this one passage is understood as having as its chief purport the understanding of the reality of oneness alone. If therein the subsequent creation of the elements beginning with <s>tejas</s> (fire) were enjoined as real, there would be a splitting of the passage. Therefore, just as in the <s>Upāṃśuyāja</s> passage, where on account of the commencement and conclusion being about the prohibited consanguineous marriage, the statements 'The <s>Upāṃśu</s> [cup] is to be offered to <s>Viṣṇu</s>' and so forth,

children.text:
aiśvaryaśrutiṣvapi svaguṇavidyāvipāko 'yaṃ śrūyate ---
‘sa ekadhā bhavati tridhā bhavati'; ‘sarvāṃśca kāmānāpnoti'; ‘sa svarāḍ bhavati'; iti, na tu mokṣaḥ /
sa hi nirupādhibrahmavidyānimitta eva /
yadapi kvacidapunarāvṛttiśravaṇam, tasyāpi dvayī gatirvyākhyātetyekaṃ darśanam /
children.translated_text: In the scriptures on sovereignty (<s>aiśvarya-śruti</s>) too, what is heard is the maturation of one's own qualities and meditation (<s>vidyā</s>) — 'He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold'; 'He attains all desires'; 'He becomes self-sovereign (<s>svarāj</s>)' — but this is not liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>). For that [liberation] is caused solely by the knowledge of unconditioned <s>Brahman</s> (<s>nirupādhi-brahma-vidyā</s>). As for the hearing of non-return in some places, two interpretations of that have been explained — this is one view.

children.text:
anye tu manyante ---
āvirbhūtabrahmarūpo brahmaṇaḥ sarvātmatvātsarveśitṛtvācca sarvopabhogānāṃ ca bhoktṛtvāttadānandamātrārūpatvāddevādyānandānāṃ ‘sa sarvāṃśca lokānāpnoti sarvāṃśca kāmān'; ‘sa svarāḍ bhavati'iti tasya tatsaṃkīrtanaṃ brahmarūpāvirbhāvalakṣaṇamokṣapraśaṃsārtham /
nanu sarvātmatvena sarvakāmāvāptau sarvaśokamohādyāptirapi syāt /
na, teṣāmabrahmarūpatvādavidyādhyastatvāt /
jñānaiśvaryānandabhogāstu brahmaṇo rūpam, ‘vijñānamānandaṃ brahma'; ‘nānyo 'to 'sti draṣṭā'; ‘etasyaivānandasyānyāni bhūtāni mātrāmupajīvanti';

children.translated_text: KKS_127

children.text:
‘sarvasyeśānaḥ'; ‘etasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane gārgi'ityādiśrutibhyaḥ /
tathā ca yatkiñcidīśvaratvaṃ yacca vijñānaṃ yaścānando brahmādiṣu sthāvarānteṣu bhūteṣu brahmaṇi tāni /
tānyāvirbhūtabrahmasvarūpaḥ samaśnuta iti yuktam /
lokādayastvavidyādhyastā na brahmarūpam /
te kathamāvirbhūtabrahmasvarūpamāskandeyuḥ? nanu prapañcaśūnyasyādvaitasya brahmarūpasya jñeyābhāvādīśitavyābhāvācca vijñānamaiśvaryaṃ cānupapannam /
tatra ‘sarvajñaḥ'; ‘sarveśvaraḥ'; ityapi śrutī samādheye eva /
naitatsāram /
yato neśitavyakṛtamīśvaratvam, jñeyakṛtaṃ vā jñātṛtvam /
kiṃ tu siddhena jñānarūpeṇa siddhayā ceśanaśaktyā jñeyamavāpnoti, īśitavyaṃ ca viniyuṅkte praśāsti ca prakāśadāhavat /
siddhena hi prakāśarūpeṇa prakāśyaṃ prakāśayati vivasvān /
na tu prakāśyādhīnaṃ tasya prakāśarūpam, dāhyādhīnā vā agnerdāhaśaktiḥ /
tathā ca taccaitanyenaiva kṛtsnasya prapañcasyāvabhāsanāt ‘tasya bhāsā sarvamidaṃ vibhāti'; ‘nānyo 'to 'sti draṣṭā'ityādiśruteḥ sarvajñatvam /
sarveśvaratvamapi tadaiśvaryeṇa yathāyathamīśvarairīśitavyānāmīśanāt /
evaṃ ca ‘eṣa bhūtādhipatiḥ'; ‘eṣa lokapālaḥ'iti brahmendrayamādīnāṃ caiśvaryamuktam /
sarvakāmāvāptiśca tadīyatvāddevādyānandasya /
kāmeṣvānandaprāptyā kāmā āptā bhavanti, na svarūpeṇa /
evaṃ ‘sa tatra paryeti jakṣan krīḍan ramamāṇaḥ strībhirvā'; iti varṇanīyam,
children.translated_text: 'The ruler of all'; 'Under the command of this imperishable [<s>Brahman</s>], O <s>Gārgī</s>' — and so forth. And thus whatever sovereignty exists, whatever knowledge, and whatever bliss in beings from <s>Brahmā</s> down to immovable things — those [all belong to] <s>Brahman</s>. That one whose nature as <s>Brahman</s> has become manifest experiences all of them — this is fitting. But the worlds and the like, being superimposed by ignorance, are not the nature of <s>Brahman</s>. How could they assail one whose nature as <s>Brahman</s> has become manifest? [Objection:] But for the non-dual nature of <s>Brahman</s>, which is devoid of phenomenal manifestation — since there is nothing to be known, and nothing to be ruled — knowledge and sovereignty are untenable. In that case, even the scriptures 'omniscient' and 'the Lord of all' would need to be reconciled. [Reply:] This is not sound. For sovereignty is not produced by things to be ruled, nor is the nature of being a knower produced by things to be known. Rather, by its intrinsic nature as knowledge and by its intrinsic power of ruling, it apprehends the knowable, governs the governable, and commands — like light and burning. For by its intrinsic nature as light, the sun illuminates what is to be illuminated. But its nature as light does not depend on what is to be illuminated, nor does the burning power of fire depend on what is to be burned. And thus, because the entire phenomenal world is illuminated by that very consciousness — 'By its light all this shines'; 'There is no other seer than this' — from such scriptures, omniscience [is established]. And omnipotence too, because by that sovereignty, the various rulers are enabled to rule their respective domains. And thus 'This is the lord of beings'; 'This is the guardian of the worlds' — the sovereignty of <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Indra</s>, <s>Yama</s>, and others has been stated. And the attainment of all desires [follows] because the bliss of the gods and others belongs to that [<s>Brahman</s>]. Desires are attained through the attainment of the bliss in [those] desires, not through their actual forms. Thus 'There he moves about, eating, playing, rejoicing with women' — this is to be explained
KKS_128

children.text:
tadviṣayānandabhogāt, na tu stryādiyogaḥ /
yathā ‘ātmaratirātmakrīḍa ātmamithunaḥ'; iti, na hi mukhyamātmakrīḍatvamātmamithunatvaṃ vā saṃbhavati /
yataścānavacchinnāni tadīyānyeva sarvabhūteṣu jñānādīni kalpitāvacchedāni, ato yatra yatra nātyantamavacchedaḥ samutkarṣātteṣāṃ tāni tāni pratyāsatterbhūtānyātmatvena bhagavānuktvā ---
‘munīnāmapyahaṃ vyāsaḥ'ityādi, upasaṃjahāra ---
‘yadyadvibhūtimatsattvam'; iti /
tathā ‘adṛṣṭaṃ draṣṭṛ, aśrutaṃ śrotṛ'ityādi, sarvabhūtadarśanādīnāṃ taccaitanyanibandhanatvāt /
children.translated_text: as the enjoyment of the bliss pertaining to those [objects], and not as actual union with women and the like. Just as 'delighting in the Self, sporting in the Self, united with the Self' — for a literal self-sporting or self-union is not possible. And because the knowledge and other [attributes] belonging to that [<s>Brahman</s>], which are undivided, are [present] in all beings with imagined limitations, therefore wherever there is no extreme limitation — due to the excellence of those [attributes] and their proximity [to <s>Brahman</s>] — the Lord, having mentioned those beings as [representing] His own Self — 'Among sages, I am <s>Vyāsa</s>' and so forth — concluded: 'Whatever being has power and splendor.' Likewise, 'The unseen seer, the unheard hearer' and so forth — because all seeing and the like of all beings are grounded in that consciousness.

Others, however, hold — Since <s>Brahman</s> is the Self of all and the ruler of all, and since it is the experiencer of all enjoyments and those [divine] joys are merely the form of its bliss — 'He attains all worlds and all desires'; 'He becomes self-sovereign' — the glorification of that [<s>Brahman</s>] in those [scriptures] is for the purpose of praising liberation characterized as the manifestation of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>. [Objection:] But if [<s>Brahman</s>] is the Self of all, then along with the attainment of all desires there would also be the attainment of all grief, delusion, and the like. [Reply:] No, because those [grief, etc.] are not the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, being superimposed by ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). But knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), sovereignty (<s>aiśvarya</s>), bliss (<s>ānanda</s>), and enjoyment are the nature of <s>Brahman</s> — from the scriptures: '<s>Brahman</s> is knowledge and bliss'; 'There is no other seer than this'; 'Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this bliss';

children.text:
anye tvāhuḥ ---
yāvān kaścitparasminnāmarūpāśrayo vyapadeśaḥ sarvo 'sāvādhyānāya /
yathā ‘yo 'sāvāditye puruṣaḥ'; ‘hiraṇyaśmaśruḥ'; ityādi /
na hi svamahimapratiṣṭhasya parasya deśaviśeṣāvarodhaḥ, sarvaviśeṣātigasya ca rūpaviśeṣayogaḥ /
paraścaiṣaḥ, sarvapāpmodayaśruteḥ ---
‘uditaḥ sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ'; iti, ādhyānaṃ tu tathā vidhīyate /
tathā sarvajñatvādapi draṣṭavyamiti /
tadevaṃ brahmātmanastadrūpāvirbhāvastatprāptiḥ, sa mokṣaḥ /
sā ca vidyaiva /
tasmānna sādhyo mokṣaḥ, na ca vidyayā anya iti puṣkalam /
children.translated_text: Others, however, say: Whatever designation regarding the supreme [<s>Brahman</s>] depends on name and form—all that is for the purpose of meditation (<s>ādhyāna</s>). For example: 'The person who is in the sun'; 'the golden-bearded one'—and so forth. For the supreme, whose greatness is self-established, is not confined to a particular location; and that which has transcended all distinctions cannot have a specific form. And this [<s>Brahman</s>] is supreme, because of the <s>śruti</s> on the transcendence of all evil: 'He has risen above all evils.' But meditation is thus enjoined. Likewise, from [the teaching of <s>Brahman</s>'s] omniscience, it is to be contemplated. Thus, for one whose self is <s>Brahman</s>, the manifestation of that nature is that attainment; that is liberation. And that [manifestation] is knowledge itself. Therefore, liberation is not something to be accomplished, nor is it different from knowledge—this is sufficient.

atha matam ---

anyatra ca ‘naitaṃ setumahorātre tarato na jarā na mṛtyurna śoko na sukṛtaṃ na duṣkṛtam'; ityupakramya

ato 'vaśyakartavyaḥ /

tatrocyate ---
children.translated_text: the conclusion is: '<s>sarve pāpmāno 'to nivartante</s>' ('All evils turn back from it'). And without the destruction of those [<s>karmas</s>], there is no attainment of safety. Therefore [knowledge] must necessarily be undertaken. And it is not the case that a <s>karma</s> whose fruit has not [yet] been received is not destroyed, since expiatory rites (<s>prāyaścittas</s>), being enjoined in connection with faults, have the destruction of those [faults] as their fruit. Therefore, just as through expiatory rites, the destruction of the cause of bondage is accomplished through knowledge. And that itself is liberation, since the root <s>muc</s> means the unfastening of a bond. And thus there is no fault of finitude, since even destruction, being an effect, does not perish. To this it is replied:

Now it is thought: Let liberation not be something to be accomplished. But the destruction of the cause of bondage is to be accomplished. The means of that would be the vision of the self. And the <s>śruti</s> declares its fruit to be the destruction of <s>karmas</s> that are causes of bondage: '<s>kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin d���ṣṭe parāvare</s>' ('His <s>karmas</s> are destroyed when that supreme-and-inferior is seen'). Likewise: '<s>tadyatheṣīkātūlamagnau protaṃ pradūyeta evaṃ hāsya sarve pāpmānaḥ pradūyante</s>' ('Just as a tuft of <s>iṣīkā</s> grass thrust into fire is burnt up, so all his evils are burnt up'). The word '<s>pāpman</s>' (evil) includes merit (<s>puṇya</s>) as well, because [merit too] has blameworthy fruit. And elsewhere, having begun with '<s>naitaṃ setumahorātre tarato na jarā na mṛtyurna śoko na sukṛtaṃ na duṣkṛtam</s>' ('Day and night do not cross this bridge, nor old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor bad deeds'),
Even the destruction of the cause of bondage, in the manner of expiation, does not [result] from that [knowledge].
When all <s>avidyā</s> dissolves, nothing remains to be cut off. (<s>MBs</s> 2.107)
The cause of bondage, whose nature is <s>avidyā</s>, has set [completely] when knowledge [arises].

children.text:
bandhahetudhvaṃso 'pi nātmadarśanasādhyaḥ /
taddhi vidadhadeva nikhilāvidyāvyavahārapravilayamudīyate /
karmaphalabhogavibhāgaścāvidyopādānaḥ /
tatrānavayavenonmūlitāyāmavidyāyāṃ na cchettavyamasti /
avidyādhyastāni hi karmāṇi tatsamucchede vidyayā samucchinnānyeva bhavanti /
tadvipākasyāvakāśa eva nāstyadvaitamātmatattvaṃ paśyataḥ, bhedadarśanāśrayatvāttasya /
yataścāvidyocchedenaiva karmocchedaḥ /
atastulyavatsaṃśayaviparyāsābhyāṃ prasaṃkhyātāni karmāṇi ---
children.translated_text: The destruction of the cause of bondage too is not to be accomplished by the vision of the self. For that [knowledge], while coming into being, arises [simultaneously with] the dissolution of the entire domain of <s>avidyā</s>. And the division of <s>karma</s>, its fruits, and their experience has <s>avidyā</s> as its material cause. When <s>avidyā</s> has been uprooted without remainder, there is nothing [left] to be cut off. For <s>karmas</s>, being superimposed by <s>avidyā</s>, are themselves destroyed by the complete eradication of that [<s>avidyā</s>] through knowledge. And for one who sees the non-dual truth of the self, there is simply no scope for the fruition of those [<s>karmas</s>], since [fruition] depends on the perception of difference. And since the destruction of <s>karma</s> is [accomplished] by the very destruction of <s>avidyā</s>, therefore, like doubt and error, <s>karmas</s> that have been discerned [as unreal by knowledge] are—
'The knot of the heart is pierced, all doubts are cut asunder,

children.text: kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare'; //
children.translated_text: and his <s>karmas</s> are destroyed when that supreme-and-inferior is seen.'

children.text:
nanvevaṃ karmakṣayāmyupagame tattvadarśanasamanantarameva muktiḥ syāt, na dehapātapratīkṣā /
‘tasya tāvadeva ciraṃ yāvanna vimokṣe 'tha saṃpatsye'; iti dehapātapratīkṣāśrutirbādhyeta /
yasya tu vidyā tatkṣayasādhanaṃ śāstrādgamyate tasya

tadanusāreṇa keṣāñcitkṣayo vidyayā, keṣāñcidupabhogena /

na hi sarvakṣaye dehapātapratīkṣopapadyate /
taduktam ---
‘anārabdhakārye eva tu pūrve tadavadheḥ'; ‘bhogena tvitare kṣapayitvā saṃpadyate'; iti /
vidyayā tvavidyoccheda karmavipākavyavahārocchittāvaviśeṣātsarvoccheda iti sapadyeva mucyeta /

yathā kaścitkṣepīyastaṃ pratipādayan bravīti kvacitkārye ---

anyathā ‘tāvadeva'iti na vācyaṃ syāt /
‘ciram'; ityeva brūyāt /
‘tāvadeva'iti tu vacanātkṣaipryaparatā gamyate /
ataḥ kṣipraiva muktiḥ, na pratīkṣaṇīyamasti /
dehapātapratīkṣā tu tatra nāntarīyakatvādbhavatyeva /
children.translated_text: in accordance with that, the destruction of some [<s>karmas</s>] is through knowledge, and of others through experience. There, when the <s>śruti</s> '<s>kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi</s>' ('his <s>karmas</s> are destroyed') [is taken] without qualification, and the consequence of total destruction [is drawn], then from the hearing of '<s>tasya tāvadeva ciram</s>' ('for him, [the delay is] only so long')—with the fall of the body as the limit—it is understood that liberation [does not arise] from that [knowledge alone, since <s>karmas</s>] whose effects have begun and whose experience has commenced are not destroyed by it, but are destroyed only through experience. For the waiting for the fall of the body is not possible if all [<s>karmas</s>] are destroyed. As stated: 'Only those [<s>karmas</s>] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed by knowledge]; for that is the limit.' 'But the others are exhausted through experience, and then [one] attains [liberation].' [Reply]: But when <s>avidyā</s> is destroyed through knowledge, since there is no distinction between the cessation of the fruition of <s>karma</s> and the cessation of the dealings [of <s>saṃsāra</s>], all would be destroyed, and one would be liberated at once. [This is] not a fault. For this <s>śruti</s> does not say that the fall of the body is the limit of liberation, qualified by a long duration; rather, [it speaks of] swiftness. Just as someone, describing something very quick to another, says regarding some task: 'This much is my delay—just until I bathe and eat'—so too this [<s>śruti</s>]. Otherwise, the word '<s>tāvadeva</s>' ('only so much') would not be used. It would simply say '<s>ciram</s>' ('long'). But from the use of '<s>tāvadeva</s>,' swiftness is understood. Therefore, liberation is swift indeed; there is nothing to be awaited. The waiting for the fall of the body, however, occurs there as an inevitable [consequence].

[Objection]: If the destruction of all <s>karma</s> is accepted in this way, liberation would occur immediately after the vision of reality—there would be no waiting for the fall of the body. The <s>śruti</s> '<s>tasya tāvadeva ciraṃ yāvanna vimokṣe 'tha saṃpatsye</s>' ('For him, [the delay is] only so long until he is freed; then he will attain') indicates waiting for the fall of the body, [and this] would be contradicted. But for one who understands from the <s>śāstra</s> that knowledge is the means of destroying those [<s>karmas</s>],

children.translated_text: is awaited through experience. In that [case], for some, liberation occurs at that very time. For others, there is some delay. Just as trembling and the like, born from fear arising from the superimposition of a snake on a rope, cease for some immediately upon the vision of the truth when the fear is removed, but for others continue for some time due to the latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>)—so too, even when all <s>karma</s> is destroyed, the continuance of the body is based on the persistence of the latent impression of the fruition being experienced. Like the rotation of a [potter's] wheel after the potter's effort has ceased.

[Objection]: In the first view, since the fall of the body occurs immediately after the knowledge of reality, the description of the characteristics of the <s>sthitaprajña</s> (one established in wisdom) would be untenable: '<s>sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā</s>' ('What is the description of one established in wisdom?') and so forth. The second [view] too is untenable, since if all [<s>karmas</s>] are destroyed, the delay (<s>ciratva</s>) is not possible, and the specification of a [particular] limit would be unfitting. It is replied: The <s>sthitaprajña</s> is not one for whom all <s>avidyā</s> has completely vanished; rather, he would be a <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner) who has attained a particular stage. And we do not say that the separation from the body occurs immediately after the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>. Rather, the exhaustion of <s>karma</s> whose effects have begun—

children.text:
nanvevaṃ brahmavido 'pi cedbhokrādivibhāgadarśanamanuvartate, dehapātāduttarakālamapyanuvarteta, tatra viduṣo 'pi nāvaśyaṃbhāvi kaivalyaṃ syāt /
tathā ca ‘tāvadeva ciram'; iti śrutyā virodhaḥ /
athocchedādavidyāyā nānuvṛttiḥ, kṣaṇamapi na syāditi sa eva virodhaḥ, saiṣobhayataḥpāśā rajjuḥ /
ucyate /
yathā bhayavigame labdhāśvāsasyāpi saṃskāramātrātkampādyanuvṛttiḥ, na ca bhayavigame 'pyanuvṛttirityetāvatā cirakālā bhavati /
na ca mūlakāraṇatulyaphalaḥ saṃskāraḥ /
na ca sthāyī /
anyathā kampādīnāṃ nivṛttireva na syāt /
na ca bhayavigamahetostattvadarśanāttannivṛttaye hetvantaramapekṣate /

tathā nivṛttāyāmavidyāyāṃ karmasu cāviśeṣeṇārabdhakāryeṣvanārabdhakāryeṣu ca nivṛtteṣvārabdhavipākasaṃskārāccharīriṇaṃ bhoktāramiva cāyamātmānaṃ pratyetyābhāsamātreṇa vidvānapi, na tvavidvānivārūḍhābhiniveśaḥ /
sa cāyamīdṛśaḥ sthitaprajño varṇitaḥ vītakāma ātmarūpasaṃtuṣṭo duḥkheṣu cchāyāmātrarūpeṣu tattvadarśanādabhiniveśātkṛtrimebhya iva vyāghrādibhyo 'nudvignamanāḥ sukheṣu ca kṛtrimaramaṇīyeṣviva vigataspṛhaḥ /
yathā khalvaviduṣo mṛddāruracite stryādau viṣaye chāyāmātradarśanamabhiniveśavikalam, tathā viduṣaḥ kṣīṇakarmāvidyasya

tatsaṃskāramātrāddarśanaṃ chāyāmātreṇaiva viṣayeṣu /
tathā ca ‘tadyathāhinirlvayanī valmīke mṛtā pratyastā śayīta evamevedaṃ śarīram'iti viduṣaḥ śarīre 'nāsthāṃ darśayati /

sā ceyamavasthā jīvanmuktiriti gīyate /
ārabdhakāryakarmasaṃskārakṣayaśca dehapātādeva gamyate /
