yena hi karmaṇā yaccharīramārabdhaṃ tatraiva tadvipākaśeṣābhāsaḥ /
anārabdhakāryāṇāṃ tvalabdhavṛttīnāmeva nivṛttatvānnāsti tatsaṃskāraḥ /
labdhavṛttikāraṇasaṃskārāddhi kāryaleśānuvṛttiḥ /
na khalu bhaye 'pratilabdhavṛttāvanupajanitakampādau tatsaṃskārāt kampādyanuvṛttiḥ /
tasmādanārabdhakāryāṇāmanālabdhavṛttitvādārabdhakāryasaṃskārakṣayasya ca dehapātādavagamādviduṣaḥ patite 'smin śarīre kaivalyamavaśyaṃbhāvi /
atra ca labdhavṛttikāraṇasaṃskārādvā kāryaśeṣaḥ, kāryasaṃskārādeva vā, tathobhayasaṃskārādeva vā kampādyanuvṛttiḥ /
bhayasaṃskārādvā bhayam, tataḥ kampādayaḥ /
kampādisaṃskārādvā kampādyanuvṛttiḥ /
sarvathā bhavati kāraṇavigame 'pi kāryaśeṣānuvṛttiḥ, saṃskārāt /
ato labdhavṛttikarmasaṃskārāttadvipākādvā viduṣo 'pi śarīrasthitiḥ /
taduktaṃ tantrāntare 'pi ---
‘tiṣṭhati saṃskāravaśāccakrabhramavaddhṛtaśarīraḥ'; iti /
children.translated_text: the perception of objects is merely from latent impression, as a mere shadow. And thus the <s>śruti</s> '<s>tadyathāhinirlvayanī valmīke mṛtā pratyastā śayīta evamevedaṃ śarīram</s>' ('Just as a [snake's] cast-off skin lies dead and discarded on an anthill, even so is this body') shows the wise person's indifference toward the body. Since the latent impression does not have the same effect as the root cause—just like trembling and the like. And the continuation is not long-lasting, because the latent impression is short-lived. And likewise, no other cause is required for its cessation, since from the vision of reality alone that [latent impression] too gradually ceases, or [ceases] of its own accord. And this state is celebrated as <s>jīvanmukti</s> (liberation while living). And the exhaustion of the latent impression of <s>karma</s> whose effects have begun is known [to occur] only from the fall of the body. Since if that [latent impression] continued, the fall of the body itself would not occur—therefore, after the fall of the body, even the shadow-like perception of that fruition is not possible. For it is only in the body that was initiated by a particular <s>karma</s> that the remnant-appearance of that fruition [manifests]. But for those [<s>karmas</s>] whose effects have not begun and which never attained operation, since they have already ceased, there is no latent impression of them. For it is from the latent impression of a cause that has attained operation that a remnant of the effect continues. Surely, when fear has not attained operation and trembling and the like have not been produced, there is no continuation of trembling from a latent impression of that [fear]. Therefore, since the [<s>karmas</s>] whose effects have not begun never attained operation, and since the exhaustion of the latent impression of those whose effects have begun is known from the fall of the body—for the wise person, when this body has fallen, <s>kaivalya</s> is inevitable. And here, the continuation of the effect-remnant is either from the latent impression of the cause that has attained operation, or from the latent impression of the effect itself, or from the latent impression of both. Likewise, the continuation of trembling is either from the latent impression of fear, whence fear [arises], and thence trembling; or from the latent impression of trembling itself. In every case, even when the cause has ceased, the continuation of the effect-remnant occurs, from latent impression. Therefore, from the latent impression of <s>karma</s> that has attained operation, or from its fruition, even the wise person's body persists. As stated also in another system: '<s>tiṣṭhati saṃskāravaśāccakrabhramavaddhṛtaśarīraḥ</s>' ('By the force of latent impression, like the rotation of a wheel, [the liberated one] maintains the body').

[Objection]: If even for the knower of <s>Brahman</s> the perception of the division into experiencer and so forth continues, it would continue even after the fall of the body; and then even for the wise person, <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation/liberation) would not necessarily occur. And thus there would be contradiction with the <s>śruti</s> '<s>tāvadeva ciram</s>' ('only so long is the delay'). [Reply]: But if, due to the destruction of <s>avidyā</s>, there is no continuance, then [there should be no continuance] even for a moment—and that is the very same contradiction; this is a rope that binds from both sides. It is replied: Just as for one who has regained composure upon the removal of fear, trembling and the like continue merely from latent impression—yet this continuation does not become long-lasting [merely] because [it exists even] after the removal of fear. And the latent impression does not have the same effect as the root cause. Nor is it permanent. Otherwise, trembling and the like would never cease at all. And no other cause is required for their cessation beyond the vision of reality that removed the fear. From that [vision] alone, [the trembling] gradually ceases, or [ceases] of its own accord, like the latent impression of a potter's wheel's rotation. Likewise, when <s>avidyā</s> has ceased and <s>karmas</s>—both those whose effects have begun and those whose effects have not begun—have [all] ceased indiscriminately, the wise person too, due to the latent impression of the commenced fruition, experiences the self as if it were an embodied experiencer—but only as a mere appearance, not with the firm conviction of an ignorant person. And such a <s>sthitaprajña</s> (one established in wisdom) has been described as one who is free from desire (<s>vītakāma</s>), content in the nature of the self, undisturbed in mind regarding sufferings that are mere shadows—like [being undisturbed by] artificial [images of] tigers and the like due to the vision of reality—and free from longing regarding pleasures that are like artificially charming [things]. Just as, for an ignorant person, the perception of objects such as women and the like [when they are] fashioned of clay and wood is a mere shadow-perception devoid of firm conviction—so too for the wise person whose <s>karma</s> and <s>avidyā</s> are exhausted,

children.text:
ye tu manyante ---

children.translated_text: For an arrow can be obstructed by walls and the like, and destroyed by cutting and the like. And pacificatory rites (<s>śāntika karmas</s>) are for the destruction of <s>karmas</s> that are to be experienced in the present body, whose fruition is indicated as imminent by dreams and the like. Therefore, the persistence [of the body] is from latent impression alone.

But those who think: For <s>karmas</s> whose experience has commenced, the obstruction of their ongoing momentum is not possible, like that of an arrow [already shot] or a wheel [already spinning]—hence [one] awaits their exhaustion through experience—that is wrong.

nanu saṃskārakāryaśeṣāvavidyaiva /

children.translated_text: [Objection]: But the residual effect of latent impression is <s>avidyā</s> itself. In that case, how is there the dissolution of all <s>avidyā</s>, and how is there nothing remaining to be cut off? It is replied: Seized by the antidote of the pure vision of oneness, those two [the remnant-appearance and the latent impression], though having arisen, are as good as dissolved, since they are inefficacious and non-binding, and since no other cause is required for their cessation. For one who directly experiences the pure self, the appearance of fruition, not touching [the self], is inefficacious and as good as dissolved in its character as bondage. Just as, for one who experiences the reality of a painting or the like, the appearance of women and so forth is not the cause of passion and the like—so too, for one who knows the self as pure, or conversely, the appearance of dark color and the like in swords and so forth, even though it arises, finds no scope due to the vision of reality and is as good as dissolved. And thus [the wise one] does not grieve for the self on account of defilement caused by that [appearance], nor does he exult on account of splendor. For even though those two appear in the self, their appearance is counteracted by the vision of reality. And thus, as for the [question]: 'Would the persistence of the body be from <s>karma</s> or from latent impression—what is the difference? And what is the destruction of <s>karma</s> when the effect continues? For the destruction of that [<s>karma</s>] is known from the cessation of that [effect].' Therefore, '<s>bhogena tvitare kṣapayitvā saṃpadyate</s>' ('But the others are exhausted through experience, and then [one] attains')—this alone is fitting. That too is refuted. For the fruition of <s>karma</s> touches the self and occasions grief and exultation for the ignorant, but for the wise, since it does not touch [the self], it is a mere appearance, like the specific basis of a gem, a sword, or a mirror. It is not [true] fruition, since it is neither welcomed nor detested. And thus it has been shown: '<s>tattatprāpya śubhāśubham / nābhinandati na dveṣṭi</s>' ('Attaining this or that, auspicious or inauspicious, he neither welcomes nor detests'). Likewise: '<s>yasyāṃ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ</s>' ('That in which beings are awake is night for the seeing sage'). For the seeing [sage], the manifold of body and so forth is night, since due to non-contact with it, it is as though unseen.

children.translated_text: Objection: If the appearance of the phenomenal world, even when arisen, is obstructed by the knowledge of reality and thus does not touch the Self, is of no effect, and is not bondage—since it arises from <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) alone—then what is the purpose of <s>upāsanā</s> (meditation) and the like? It is replied: Verbal knowledge (<s>śābdajñāna</s>) is of a mediate nature (<s>parokṣa</s>), while the appearance of the phenomenal world is of an immediate nature (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). Therefore, since there is no contradiction between the two, the appearance of the phenomenal world does indeed touch the Self, is not without effect, and is indeed bondage—just as in the case of a substance whose sweetness is ascertained through another means of knowledge, the appearance of bitterness arising through the sense organ, being of the nature of direct perception, does not remain as mere appearance without touching the substance, and thus that substance, as though truly bitter and as though its sweetness were unascertained, causes suffering. But for one who has directly realized the truth of the Self through <s>upāsanā</s> (meditation) and the like, the appearance of the phenomenal world, even though existing, does not touch the Self due to the contradiction [with direct realization]—just as the appearance of a lion [does not touch] <s>Devadatta</s>. In the superimposition 'This <s>Devadatta</s> is a lion,' even though appearing, [the lion-appearance] does not touch him, is of no effect, and is not a cause of fear. And the illumination of the truth of the Self is eternal; therein there is no room for subsequent error. But verbal knowledge is momentary, dependent on a means of knowledge; therein there is room for error again. For it is observed that when the means of knowledge is not attended to, there is again fear of the rope due to the delusion of a snake. Well then, one should continuously attend to the verbal knowledge here too. What is <s>upāsanā</s> (meditation) other than this? Therefore, the cutting off of the cause of bondage is itself <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge), not something to be accomplished by it. The same should be said regarding the non-attachment of subsequent [sins]: 'Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so sinful action does not cling to one who knows thus'—since the distinction between agent and action dissolves through <s>vidyā</s>. Thus there will be no need to postulate multiple results for <s>vidyā</s>, and the statements in the present tense will not be transformed into injunctions of results. As for what was said—that <s>Brahman</s> is not the object of verbal knowledge—to that it is replied:

children.translated_text: Indeed, it is not mere cognition that is enjoined, but a particular cognition with a [specific] object. And there can be no injunction regarding what is unknown and undetermined. For one cannot enjoin [someone] with respect to an unknown object. And the particularity of cognition is [determined] through its object. But an unknown object is not capable of determining that particularity. And the nature of the Self cannot be established from anything other than <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony). And if it is not established even from <s>śabda</s>, then since the particular cognition mediated by it is not established, the injunction is untenable due to the inapplicability of [its] object.

children.translated_text: Moreover, he shows that for those who maintain the view that a particular cognition is enjoined, the very authority [of scripture] regarding the truth of the Self is undermined:
The injunction is either aimed at establishing itself, or directed toward accomplishing an action;
The apprehension of the non-dual truth of <s>Brahman</s> is without cause [i.e., not produced by injunction]. MBs_2.110
If the cognition [of <s>Brahman</s>] has the purpose of being a subsidiary action [derived] from an injunctive connection,
then, not being directed toward that [reality], it is not a valid means of knowledge—like a cognition arising from an <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage). MBs_2.111
An injunction, being concerned with action, is not capable of operating with respect to an [already existing] substance;

children.translated_text: but if [one says] the substance is established through its connection with existence [implied in the injunction], that [position] is rather refuted. MBs_2.112

even a cognition qualified [by object-content], when arising from injunction, [pertains only to] the object [as subsidiary]. MBs_2.113
It does not establish existence at all, since it is possible through [mere] superimposition.

children.translated_text: If only the obligatoriness of the injunction itself were cognized, then it would terminate in its own accomplishment together with the verbal [expression]. If, on the other hand, through the injunctive connection there is apprehension of the obligatory nature regarding the object, even then [it terminates] in the establishment of the object. In either case, it does not touch the reality of the thing. In that case, the apprehension of the non-dual truth of the Self would be without valid authority. To this one might say: From [statements like] 'The Self that is free from evil, free from old age...'—through the co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) of the words, or through some other connection, there is apprehension of the reality of the thing. But that is not so, because [those statements] are subordinate to something else.

children.translated_text: For that [cognition] does not terminate in 'this is thus,' but rather in 'this is to be cognized thus'—it is directed toward obligatory action and is not a valid means of knowledge regarding the reality of the thing, just as a cognition arising from an <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage) [is not authoritative] regarding [actual] states of affairs, because it is subordinate to something else. Nor is the truth of the Self itself the object of the injunction, since [an injunction] has as its object what is to be performed, and since [the Self] is not of the nature of action; for when a substantive term [denoting something already established] is employed, there can be no operation with respect to a substance that is not to be performed. Rather, through its connection with existence in one of the three times—that which is not enjoinable—the establishment of the nature of the substance [follows]: 'Such a thing existed, exists, or will exist.' Therefore, [the position that injunction] establishes the nature [of the Self] is refuted. For there is no apprehension of the existence of what is to be enjoined in any of the three times. Indeed, when one says '<s>yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice), the existence of the sacrifice in the past, present, or future time is not cognized. Objection: The future time is cognized, since the injunction has the future as its domain. Reply: This is not so, for what is enjoined is not [certain to be] performed due to the injunctive obligation; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that there is no fault in not performing what is enjoined. Objection: It is accepted that a statement expressing a qualified action is a valid means of knowledge even regarding the qualifier—just as in '<s>somena yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with <s>Soma</s>); likewise in 'The son of <s>Devadatta</s>, wearing armlets and earrings, with a broad chest, is studying'—the entire cluster of qualifiers is cognized along with the action of studying. Reply: True, a [statement that is a] valid means of knowledge regarding a qualified action is indeed a valid means regarding the qualifier too, [but only] when there is no [independent] cognition [of the qualifier] from elsewhere. For a cognition that is being validated, qualified by a particular object, does not establish the existence of that particular object, since it is possible [for such cognition to occur] through superimposition upon what is otherwise—as in 'That world, O <s>Gautama</s>, is the [sacrificial] fire,' where fire is not perceived in heaven and the rest.
Here one objects:

children.translated_text: because it would not be a cognizer [of the object], even dependence on something else would not establish the object from it. What then is this [experience] when the eye is in contact with a nacre [shell] and one [cognizes] 'silver'? It is memory, due to the apprehension of a generic [feature]. Then how is there error? Due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between what is directly perceived and what is being remembered. This non-apprehension of difference amounts to a belief in non-difference for those lacking discrimination—just as from a distance, when the interval [between trees] is not apprehended, there is a belief in their being joined together. Therefore, this is a memory of silver devoid of discrimination [from the perceived], [experienced as] 'I am remembering.' To this it is replied:

Indeed it is not proper [to say] that one thing appears as another, because of the contradiction with experience. How can the object be different when something [else] is being experienced? And because of the lack of confidence [that would result]: in a cognition that deviates from the form of the [actual] object, there could be no certainty regarding that object from it. Moreover, a cognition that does not conform to the form of the object would have no object, no basis (<s>ālambana</s>), and would be utterly non-apprehending. For what is merely a cause of cognition without being its basis is not an <s>ālambana</s>—like the eye and so forth. Similarly,

children.translated_text: This is not so, for [if it were mere memory] one would not then proceed [to act] toward the piece of nacre. MBs_2.115

One proceeds to act precisely there [where something is perceived]—that is caused by the proximity of that [object];
the activity differs [from activity] elsewhere because of the apprehension of difference [there], and [proceeds here] because of the non-apprehension of distinction [here]. MBs_2.117

children.translated_text: If there is no cognition [of silver] there [in clods], then there should be none in the piece of nacre either;

The non-activity toward unseen [objects] and toward the piece of nacre is the same [on your view];

If [one says error arises] from the non-discrimination of what is perceived and what is remembered, let this be examined:
Does the cognition of silver [arise] from the awareness of reality, or from the non-awareness of non-reality? MBs_2.121
In the first case [awareness of reality], the activity is toward what is perceived—[this amounts to] the erroneous nature of cognition;
the difference between what is seen and what is unseen in the latter [case] is of no use. MBs_2.122

na kathañcidagṛhīte 'saṃprayukte vaindriyakaḥ samāropa upapadyate /
children.translated_text: would not be cognized by him—just like a clod of earth and the like. Nor is that activity directed toward the silver being remembered, because of its non-proximity to that location. For even when an object has come into cognition, one who desires it does not proceed to act where it is not present. One might say: The activity [occurs] there because of the cognition of silver and the non-cognition of [its] non-proximity. That is not so, because the activity is toward the piece of nacre itself. And the activity there is dependent on the proximity of that [nacre]. Since the cognition is of silver in general, and since the memory lacks discrimination, the activity should occur elsewhere too, as the non-apprehension of non-proximity is equally [present] there. Suppose one thinks: In the case of objects in other locations, since they are perceived with specific [distinguishing features] through direct perception, there is non-activity because of the apprehension of their difference from silver; but in the case of nacre, due to the perception of only the generic white, shining form common to silver, and due to the specific cognition [arising from] the memory that presents silver, there is activity because of the non-apprehension of difference from silver. Even so, in the case of unseen [places] like other worlds, there should be activity due to the non-ascertainment of their difference from that [silver]. And if there is no cognition of silver in those [cases], then there should be none in the other [nacre] case either. Or else, erroneous cognition with a contrary object would be admitted. And if [one says] there is no activity toward unseen things precisely because they are unseen, then there should be no activity toward nacre either. Objection: But it is not cognized by that silver-form [in unseen cases]. Reply: Just as there is no such cognition for what is not in contact with the eye, so too even for nacre that is in contact [with the eye, the silver-form is not truly cognized]. If one thinks: One proceeds to act only with respect to what is in contact with the eye, because of the discrimination born of the conjunction of what is seen and what is remembered, and not toward the other—then here too this should be examined: Since there is no discrimination when difference is not apprehended, does the activity [arise] from the cognition of proximity through the apprehension of non-difference, and from that [cognition] the activity? Or [does it arise] merely from the absence of the apprehension of difference? In the first case, there is error [i.e., a cognition of what is not the case]. In the latter, there is no distinction between what is seen and what is unseen, or between what is in contact and what is not in contact [with the sense organ], since the non-apprehension of difference is equal [in both cases]. For the non-apprehension of sense-contact or of perception is of no use [in explaining activity]; rather, it is relevant for unreal superimposition. And no sensory superimposition is possible with respect to what is in no way apprehended or not in contact [with the senses].

api cedaṃ tatra bhavān vyācaṣṭām ---
smaryamāṇaṃ dṛśyamānātsvajñānādeva vivicyate, na vā ---
smṛtijñānasya svarūpameva tādṛśaṃ yatpramātavyādbhedenāvabhāsayati, svarūpamātraniṣṭhaṃ vā /
tatra pūrvasmin smaraṇagocarayoravivekaḥ kutaḥ, svajñānādeva viviktatvāt? itarasminnapi sadā smṛtau viparyayaḥ syāt, sāmānyadarśane cānyasmṛtāvavivekāt /
na ca tattathā, saṃśayasyāpi darśanāt /
atha matam ---
ekasmṛtau viparyayaḥ, tato 'vivekāt /
anekasmṛtau tu saṃśayaḥ /
naikasmādavivekāt /
tadasat /
anekasmaraṇe 'pi hi dṛśyate viparyayaḥ /
yadi ca pratyakṣe 'rthe viśeṣajñānātsmaryamāṇaṃ vivicyate, na svajñānāt /
asati tatra viśeṣajñāne ca dvayoḥ smṛtau saṃśaya eva syāt, naikāvabhāso viparyayaḥ /
atha tu svajñānātsmṛtaṃ vivicyate, smṛtiviparyayabhedaścābhyupagamyate /
tadānekasmaraṇe 'pīndriyadoṣaviśeṣādyukto viparyayaḥ /
darśitaṃ cedam ---
sāmānyadarśane 'pi kadācidekāṃ koṭiṃ smarato na saṃśayo na viparyayaḥ, doṣāṇāmapuṣṭeḥ /
ataḥ svajñānādeva tadā smṛtaṃ vivicyate, na dṛśyaviśeṣaparicchedāt /
evaṃ cetkuto dṛśyamānasmaryamāṇāvivekaḥ?
children.translated_text: Now, let Your Honor explain this: Is what is remembered distinguished from what is perceived by its own cognition alone, or not? Is the very nature of memorial cognition such that it manifests [its object] as distinct from the object to be known, or is it grounded in its own nature alone? In the first case, whence comes the non-discrimination between [the object and] what falls within the scope of remembrance, since it is already distinguished by its own cognition? In the latter case too, there would always be error in memory, and in the perception of a generic feature, there would be non-discrimination with respect to another remembered [object]. But that is not so, since doubt is also observed. Now, if it is held: in a single memory, there is error due to non-discrimination; in multiple memories, there is doubt; not from a single [memory] is there non-discrimination—that is wrong. For error is observed even in multiple rememberings. Moreover, if what is remembered is distinguished from a perceived object through the cognition of a specific feature, and not from its own cognition, then in the absence of the cognition of that specific feature, when two [objects are] in memory, there would be only doubt, not error appearing as one. On the other hand, if what is remembered is distinguished by its own cognition, and the distinction between memory and error is accepted, then even in multiple rememberings, error is justified on account of a particular defect in the sense organ. And this has been shown: even in the perception of a generic feature, sometimes one remembers only one alternative, [and yet] there is neither doubt nor error, because the defects are not strengthened. Therefore, at that time, what is remembered is distinguished by its own cognition alone, not by the ascertainment of a specific feature in the perceived [object]. If so, whence comes the non-discrimination between what is perceived and what is remembered?

children.text:
api ca anyadeva smarataḥ pūrvarūpamekatvaṃ śaśini dvitvavibhramaḥ, na smaryamāṇāvivekajaḥ /
na ca jñānendriyavṛttibhedāvivekāt, tayorapratyakṣatvātsmaryamāṇatvācca /
śuktikāhitacetasaśca salilaṃ pipāsato na syādviparyayaḥ /
salilābhāso vā, smaryamāṇasya svajñānavivekāt /
children.translated_text: Moreover, the unity that one who remembers [perceives] with a prior form is itself something different—the illusion of duality in the moon is not born from non-discrimination of what is remembered. Nor is it from the non-discrimination of the distinction between the activities of the cognitive organ and the mind, since both of those are non-perceptible and are themselves remembered. And for one whose mind is fixed on a mother-of-pearl, [yet] who is thirsty for water, there would be no error; or [it would be] a mere appearance of water, since what is remembered is distinguished by its own cognition.

children.text: na ca sarvā niyogena bhrāntiḥ sādṛśyabandhanā // MBs_2.129 //
children.translated_text: And not every illusion is necessarily bound to similarity. (<s>MBs</s> 2.129)
The illusion of yellow is seen in what is white, the illusion of bitter in what is sweet;

children.text: kiñcitsādṛśyato hi syānna kaścittatra na bhramaḥ // MBs_2.130 //
children.translated_text: indeed, from some [degree of] similarity there would be [error], but there is no case where there is no illusion at all [even without similarity]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.130)
Therefore, according to the division of the power of the defects of the sense organs,

children.text: bhrameṣu niyamo doṣādagrahe na bhrame yamaḥ // MBs_2.131 //
children.translated_text: there is a fixed rule regarding illusions [arising] from defect, but no rule [restricting] illusion in [the case of mere] non-apprehension. (<s>MBs</s> 2.131)

children.text:
yadi ca sadṛśadarśanātsadṛśasmṛterbhramaḥ, kathaṃ śvete pītabhramaḥ madhure vā tiktabhrāntiḥ? āntarapittasaṃvedane 'vyāpārayato 'pi bahirindriyaṃ syāt, añjanavaccākṣigatasya tadgatakṛṣṇimādivaccādṛśyatvāt /
kiñcitsādṛśye sarvaprakārabhramaprasaṃgaḥ /
tasmādindriyadoṣasāmarthyabhedānniyatā viparyayotpattiḥ /
agrahamātre tu doṣavyāpāre kāmilādidoṣādbhrāntiniyamo na syāt /
na hi sādṛśyanimittaḥ, asadṛśe 'pi bhrāntidarśanāt /
children.translated_text: Moreover, if error arises from the perception of a similar [object] and the memory of a similar [object], how then is there the illusion of yellow in what is white, or the illusion of bitter in what is sweet? Even when the external sense organ is not engaged, [error] could arise from the perception of internal bile, and like collyrium applied to the eye, it is not visible because the darkening and so forth pertaining to the eye [are not visible]. If even a slight similarity [sufficed], there would be the absurd consequence of illusion of every kind. Therefore, the arising of error is determined by the differences in the power of the defects of the sense organs. But if the operation of the defect were restricted to mere non-apprehension, then there would be no rule restricting illusion to [cases like] jaundice and the like. For [error] is not caused by similarity, since illusion is observed even in what is dissimilar.
Nor, on account of the remembrance of specific features, is there non-apprehension of those [features] even in memory;
and what is remembered is not discriminated by virtue of the specific features of place and time. (<s>MBs</s> 2.132)
What has been apprehended in numerous places is not subsequently distinguished from those [places];
the cognition 'it is a memory' is itself stated to be something other than the memory [it qualifies]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.133)
And that [discrimination] is not established from [a result] different from the result of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), in the absence of [such a distinguishing] result;
and if there is discrimination of memory, [then] the illusion of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) [would also have to be explained]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.134)
Now, if [it is said that] the object that is not present is useless, [and error arises] through [appearing] as if present—
then from memory that is not discriminated, there would be erroneous content in this way. (<s>MBs</s> 2.135)
And because the mind is not impaired, there is no apprehension of non-presence;
for a defect is cited as the cause of non-apprehension [only] with respect to the sense organs. (<s>MBs</s> 2.136)
And it has been stated here that there would be no rule governing activity;

children.text: sarvajñānāni mithyā ca prasajyante 'tra kalpane // MBs_2.137 //
children.translated_text: and in this supposition, all cognitions would turn out to be false. (<s>MBs</s> 2.137)
For no cognition grasps an object in its entirety;
thus, from the error of the double moon and so forth, [arising] from the non-discrimination of what is [actually] known, (<s>MBs</s> 2.138)
who, seeing [the world] through the continued [appearance], could deny his own self?

children.text:
atha matam ---
svajñānādeva smṛtaṃ vivicyate /
kadācittu tatra pratyakṣa iva viśeṣāgrahastato 'vivekaḥ /
sato tu viśeṣagrahaṇa indriyasaṃyukte sāmānyadarśane 'pi nāvivekaḥ, tata ubhayakoṭismaraṇe na saṃśayaḥ, ekasmṛtau na saṃśayo na viparyayaḥ /
evamapi dvayoḥ smaraṇe na viparyayaḥ syāt /
na ca smṛtau viśeṣagrahaṇam, viśeṣasmaraṇāt /
atha deśakālaviśeṣātsmaryamāṇaṃ vivicyate, tatra deśakālabhedāgraha iti /
tanna, anantadeśakālabhedāvagataṃ taddeśāvagataṃ ca dṛśyātsmaryamāṇaṃ viviktaṃ gamyate /
na ca deśakālabhedagrahaṇāt, anantasmaraṇānupapatteḥ, taddeśāvagate ca deśabhedābhāvāt /
atha smaryamāṇatayā agrahaṇādavivekaḥ smaryamāṇatājñānācca vivekaḥ, tasmāt ‘smarāmi'; iti jñānaśūnyāni rajatādijñānāni bhrāntihetavaḥ /
paripūrṇaiva tarhi smṛtiḥ, na tayā svaviṣayasya kiñcinna gṛhītam /
children.translated_text: Now, if it is held: what is remembered is distinguished by its own cognition alone; but sometimes there is non-apprehension of specific features in it, as in the case of direct perception, and from that comes non-discrimination. But when there is apprehension of specific features in what is connected with the sense organ, then even in the perception of a generic feature, there is no non-discrimination; therefore, when both alternatives are remembered, there is no doubt; when there is a single memory, there is neither doubt nor error. Even so, when both are remembered, there would be no error. Nor is there apprehension of specific features in memory, since there is [merely] remembrance of specific features. Now, if what is remembered is discriminated by the specific features of place and time, [and the error arises] from the non-apprehension of the difference in place and time—that is not right, because what has been cognized across countless differences of place and time, and what has been cognized in that [particular] place, are understood as distinct from what is perceived and what is remembered. Nor is [discrimination] from the apprehension of differences in place and time, since the remembrance of countless [such differences] is not possible, and in what has been cognized in that [very] place, there is no difference of place. Now, if non-discrimination [arises] from non-apprehension [of the object] as being remembered, and discrimination [comes] from the cognition of its being remembered, then cognitions of silver and the like that are devoid of the cognition 'I remember' are causes of error. But then memory is fully complete—there is nothing of its own object that it has not grasped.

children.text:
svayameva sā svaviṣayaṃ dṛśyādvivinaktīti nāsti dṛśyamānasmaryamāṇayoravivekaḥ /
yataḥ smarāmi iti jñānamanyadeva darśanasmaraṇavivekakāri smṛteḥ /
tatredaṃ vicāryam ---
smṛtiḥ svaviṣayaṃ vivinakti vā na vā? yadi vivinakti, tadā viparyayābhāvaḥ /
atha na smṛtiḥ svaviṣayaṃ vivinakti, tadā sāmānyadarśane cānyasmṛtau viparyayaḥ syādityuktam /
na ‘smarāmi'iti vivekāccet, sa eva smṛteḥ svayamavivecakatvena syāt, kāryagamyasya hi jñānasya bhedaḥ kāryaviśeṣonneyaḥ /
na cetsmṛteḥ pramāṇakāryātkāryaṃ viviktaṃ syāt, kena sā viviktā gamyeta? satyapi smṛtiviveke dṛṣṭaḥ pratyabhijñābhramaḥ ‘sa eva'; iti na ca pratyakṣasyāvivekaḥ, ekavivekenobhayorvikārātsmṛtādavivekācca smṛtivibhramaḥ syāt, na pratyakṣabhramaḥ /
tasmānna ‘smarāmi'iti pramoṣādavivekaḥ /
athāsaṃnihitasya

saṃnihitātmanā pratītiravivekaḥ, smṛterviparītārthatvaprasaṃgaḥ /
athāsaṃnidhyagrahaṇāt, bhavatu sa svapnajñāne, natvindriyajāyāṃ bhrāntau /
manaso 'nupaghātādupaghātahetutvāccāgrahaṇasya /
na cetthaṃ pravṛttiniyamaḥ syādityuktam /
sati ca vastugrahe kasyacidaṃśasyāgrahādbhrāntau sarvajñānabhramatvam /
na hi kasyacijjñānasya sarvātmanā vastu viṣaya iti /
satyapi ca vivekajñāne pramāṇāntarād dvicandradiṅmohādyanugatirdṛṣṭeti nāgrahaṇamātraṃ viparyayaḥ /
children.translated_text: the cognition of it as having the nature of what is present is the non-discrimination, [then] there would be the absurd consequence that memory has erroneous content. Now, if [the error is] from non-apprehension of non-presence—let that be so in dream cognition, but not in illusion born of the sense organs. Because the mind is not impaired, and because non-apprehension is [held to be] the cause of impairment [only of the senses]. And if [it were from mere non-apprehension], there would be no rule governing activity, as has been stated. Moreover, if illusion [arises] from the non-apprehension of some aspect while the object is [otherwise] apprehended, then all cognitions would be erroneous. For no cognition has the object in its entirety as its content. And even when there is discriminative cognition, the continuation of [illusions like] the double moon and directional confusion is observed through another <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge)—therefore mere non-apprehension is not [the same as] error.

Memory itself discriminates its own object from what is perceived—thus there is no non-discrimination between what is perceived and what is remembered. For the cognition 'I remember' is itself something other [than memory], which produces the discrimination between perception and remembrance. Here the following should be examined: Does memory discriminate its own object or not? If it does discriminate, then there is the absence of error. But if memory does not discriminate its own object, then, as stated, there would be error even when seeing a generic feature and having another memory. If [it is said that] there is discrimination from [the cognition] 'I remember'—that itself would [show] that memory is by its nature non-discriminating. For the distinction of a cognition that is known through its effect must be inferred from a particular effect. And if the effect of memory were not distinct from the effect of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), by what would it be known as distinct? Even if there is discrimination of memory, the illusion of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>)—'it is the same one'—is observed. And it is not that perception lacks discrimination. From the alteration of both by a single discrimination, and from the non-discrimination of what is remembered, there would be memorial error, not perceptual error. Therefore, non-discrimination does not [arise] from the loss of [the cognition] 'I remember.' Now, if [it is said that error arises because] of a non-present [object]—
<s>Khyāti</s> (apprehension/manifestation), which is of the nature of the negation of what is [wrongly] attributed, is postulated [only] when there is [prior] attribution. (<s>MBs</s> 2.139)
Non-apprehension, being an absence, is not productive [of error]; [rather,] erroneous cognition is productive [of attribution].

children.text: ye ca khyātī tu rajataścakṣuḥsaṃyuktavastunoḥ // MBs_2.140 //
children.translated_text: And as for the two apprehensions—of silver and of the object connected with the eye— (<s>MBs</s> 2.140)
this negation of the object presented by them is not [merely] understood [as non-apprehension];
nor does this cognition sublate [error] through mere non-apprehension. (<s>MBs</s> 2.141)
For if all [error were] sublated by the sublation of non-apprehension, then no [error] of such a kind would arise.
This discriminative cognition is not a cognition that negates what is [merely] attributed. (<s>MBs</s> 2.142)
One who speaks thus, out of perversity, denies his own experience.

children.text: na krame yaugapadye vā vivekamatirīdṛśī // MBs_2.143 //
children.translated_text: Neither in sequence nor in simultaneity is discriminative cognition of this kind [possible]: (<s>MBs</s> 2.143)
it would be justified when there is the cognition of unity that has been [wrongly] attributed, not when the distinction has not been ascertained.
One who remembers silver and [perceives] the object connected with the eye, (<s>MBs</s> 2.144)
seeing [them] through their generic [similarity] and not having cognized the distinctness from silver,
subsequently discriminates [and] cognizes [the truth]—it is not so in [the case of merely] perceiving a generic feature. (<s>MBs</s> 2.145)
In the absence of the remembrance of both alternatives, doubt does not necessarily [arise];
due to the absence of the apprehension of distinction, [there is instead] the cognition of temporal presence. (<s>MBs</s> 2.146)
From appearing in that manner, [the error] that has been attributed would be an apprehension otherwise [than what is the case];
therein, non-apprehension may be the cause, or alternatively, the apprehension of presence. (<s>MBs</s> 2.147)
Devoid of the sublation of the apprehension of distinction, [it is] of the nature of a positive entity;
if error is not accepted [as positive], the illusion grounded in non-apprehension— (<s>MBs</s> 2.148)
is said to be known through words alone; non-apprehension would be grounded in [further] non-apprehension.

‘nedaṃ rajatam'iti prasaktapratiṣedharūpā pratītirnāgrahaṇe 'vakalpate, prasaṅgābhāvāt /

yuktā, viviktayorgrahaṇe 'vivekapratiṣedharūpatvāt /

api ca bhavati kadācit ---
yaḥ smarati ca rajatasya, cakṣuḥsaṃyuktasya vastunaḥ sāmānyamātradarśī, na rajatādvivekaṃ gṛhṇāti, punaścakṣuḥprasādātpratyeti /
na ca tadā tathā pratītiravivekagrahaṇābhāvāt /
nanu sāmānyadarśane na cedviparyayaḥ, saṃśayaḥ syāt /
tadapanodi ca nirṇayajñānamīdṛśameva /
naitatsāram /
na hyasati koṭidvayasmaraṇe sāmānyadarśane 'pi saṃśayaḥ, na ca viparyayaḥ /
bhavati hi puro 'vasthite bhāsvararūpamātrapratītiḥ, rajate ca smṛtiḥ /
na ca tayoranyatvaṃ pratipadyate, naikatvaṃ ca /
tatra na vivekajñānamevaṃrūpam, ekatvāpratipatteḥ /
atha matam ---
vivekāgrahaṇātkālasaṃnidhipratīteśca rajataṃ vā cakṣuḥsaṃprayuktavadavabhāsate, cakṣuḥsaṃyuktaṃ vā rajatavat /
ataḥ prāptiriti pratiṣedhopapattiḥ /
abhyupetā tarhi viparītakhyātiḥ /
na hyanyā sā, atadātmanastathāvabhāsanāt /
kāmaṃ

tattvājñānanimittā syāt /
na hi sā tattvajñāne satyudeti, virodhāditi /
tatrāpi saṃnidhikhyātireva nibandhanam /
tasyāstu vivekagraho 'pavādaḥ /
agrahaṇe nirapavādā saiva kāraṇam, nābhāvaḥ /
viparītakhyātyanabhyugame cāgrahaṇanibandhano bhrama ityagrahaṇamagrahaṇanibandhanamiti suvyāhṛtam /
svapne ca dvitīyābhāvātkuto 'vivekaḥ, smṛtatvenāviviktasya tathā viveke dharmiṇi pratipanne dharmāntarapratipanne dharmāntarapratipatterbādhakatvaṃ pūrvasyāśca bhrāntitvaṃ syātāmiti /
children.translated_text: let it be caused by ignorance of the true nature [of the object]. For it does not arise when there is knowledge of the true nature, on account of the contradiction. Even there, the apprehension of presence (<s>saṃnidhikhyāti</s>) is itself the basis. Let the apprehension of distinction be its sublator. In [the case of] non-apprehension, that [apprehension of presence] alone, being unsublated, is the cause—not [mere] absence. And if erroneous apprehension (<s>viparīta-khyāti</s>) is not accepted, [and] illusion is grounded in non-apprehension, then 'non-apprehension is grounded in non-apprehension'—how well-spoken [indeed]! And in dream, since there is no second [object present], whence comes non-discrimination? If [the object] that is not discriminated as being remembered is [regarded as] thus in discrimination, then when the substrate (<s>dharmin</s>) is cognized [as one thing] and a different property is cognized, there would be the sublation of the latter and the erroneousness of the former.

The cognition of the form 'this is not silver,' which is of the nature of the negation of what has been [wrongly] attributed, is not possible in [the case of mere] non-apprehension, because there is nothing [wrongly] attributed. For non-apprehension is not productive of any [wrong] attribution. For it is an absence. But erroneous apprehension (<s>viparītā khyāti</s>), showing the silver-nature of what is present, or the presence of [actual] silver, is what produces the [wrong] attribution. Now, it is objected: there are two apprehensions—of silver and of the object conjoined with the eye. Those very two are productive [of attribution]. True. But this cognition of negation does not pertain to those two as presented [by them]. For we do not apprehend that what is negated in 'this is not silver' is mere silver or mere object connected with the eye. Rather, [what is negated is] the silver-nature of what is connected with the eye, or the being-connected-with-the-eye of silver. And the non-apprehension of these two is not productive [of attribution], precisely because it is non-apprehension. Therefore, erroneous apprehension (<s>viparīta-khyāti</s>) must necessarily be resorted to for the [wrong] attribution that is to be negated. Nor is it the case that in 'this is not [silver],' mere non-apprehension is what is being negated, for then there would be the absurd consequence that the same [applies] to all cognitions. And if all cognitions were to arise from the sublation of non-apprehension, then this discriminative cognition would be merely [discrimination] and not of the form of negating what is [wrongly] attributed—this accords with one who follows experience. For when silver and a piece of mother-of-pearl are apprehended simultaneously as distinct, such a cognition [of negation] does not [arise], nor [does it arise] in sequence. If [it is said that] it would [arise] when they are apprehended as not distinct—[that is] fitting, since in the apprehension of [them as] distinct, it is of the form of negating non-distinction. In the apprehension of [them as] distinct, there is no [wrong] attribution to be negated, [so it is] fitting. Moreover, it sometimes happens: one who remembers silver and [yet] perceives only the generic feature of the object connected with the eye, [and] does not apprehend the distinction from silver, subsequently cognizes [the truth] through the clarity of the eye. But such a cognition [of negation] does not [arise] then, because there is no apprehension of non-distinction. Now, if there is no error in perceiving a generic feature, there should be doubt. And discriminative cognition of this kind is what removes that [doubt]. That is not sound. For in the absence of remembrance of both alternatives, even in the perception of a generic feature, there is neither doubt nor error. For there is merely the cognition of a shining form before one, and a memory of silver. And one neither cognizes their difference nor their identity. In that case, a discriminative cognition of this form [i.e., 'this is not silver'] does not [arise], because of the non-cognition of identity. Now, if it is held: from the non-apprehension of distinction and from the cognition of temporal presence, silver appears as if connected with the eye, or what is connected with the eye appears as if it were silver—therefore there is [wrong] attribution, and hence the negation is justified. Then erroneous apprehension (<s>viparīta-khyāti</s>) is [in fact] accepted. For it is nothing other than that—the appearing as such of what does not have that nature. Very well—

children.text: 'idaṃ śuklaṃ rajatam'iti sāmānādhikaraṇyena pratīterātmopālambhaḥ parasminnāsajyate pratītivirodhaḥ, jñānabhedakalpanāyāḥ pramāṇābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: The reproach of one's own self [theory] is cast upon another [theory on the basis of] the conflict with experience, [which arises] from the cognition [expressed] through co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) as in 'this white [thing is] silver,' because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) for the supposition of a distinction in cognitions.
The distrust in what is being known is sublated by cognition itself. (<s>MBs</s> 2.150)
Due to deviation, there is incapacity—not from the attainment of its effect.
When the object to be known [is established] from deviation, the effect itself is not obtained. (<s>MBs</s> 2.151)

children.text:
tatra vyabhicārādaprāmāṇyam, api tu paricchedakāryābhāvāt /
tadabhāvaśca hetvabhāvāt /
avyabhicārāddhi liṅgālliṅgiparicchedaḥ /

children.translated_text: there is invalidity due to deviation; rather, it is due to the absence of the effect of determination. And that absence is due to the absence of the cause. For the determination of what is signified comes from an invariable sign. But where invariability is not the cause, even when deviation is present, if there is determination, validity is undisputed. In the sense organs, knowledge too is the cause of determination in just the same way, not like an inferential mark. Nor does deviation damage validity by producing doubt, because in what is properly determined, the twofold nature is not a cause of doubt. One does not doubt about a post that has been ascertained as being upright. By its very arising, knowledge determines the object. What fails to determine is simply not under consideration here. And to say that there is non-determination from determination itself is self-contradictory. The very person who demands invariability of knowledge for the sake of confidence is the one who lacks confidence, because even regarding knowledge of invariability there is no confidence. For that — whose own deviation is unestablished — is not a cause of confidence in itself and in other cognitions. If established through another cognition, there is infinite regress. Moreover, if there is no confidence in the object from the nature of knowledge, in the absence of the establishment of the object, with what would the invariability of knowledge be ascertained? Furthermore, invariability too is stated only from the nature of knowledge, since in erroneous cognition there is a contradiction with it. That being so, knowledge itself is the establisher of the object — invariability is superfluous. And it has been said that deviation does not damage validity.

For one who, regarding the object being known, has the insecurity 'it might be otherwise' — the arising of a cognition that determines its being-such-and-such is blocked by that very knowledge. For to remove the insecurity, only such knowledge is required. And that indeed exists. Nor is it proper to say that knowledge is an incompetent means of knowledge due to the defect of deviation, since the effect of a valid means — determination — is established from the very nature of knowledge. For validity consists in determination. And deviation and non-deviation are irrelevant — because even without deviation, the non-deviating smoke and the like would not be valid means, and even the deviating eye regarding white and black and the like is a valid means when determination is present. Nor has deviation been observed anywhere as a cause of sublation, damaging validity like a defect, since the eye and the like are valid means despite deviating. Objection: Deviation has been observed as damaging validity, as in the case of being an object of knowledge, uprightness, and the like. This is not sound. Not
Moreover, what is desired in the case of non-apprehension, which is based on discrimination,
is not contradicted by rules in the case of seeing the opposite.
Defects are not causes that amplify and destroy the capacity of effects.
There would be a distinction between apprehension and non-apprehension from the existence and non-existence of that.
In the case of error, indeed, the damage is even greater,
through the obstruction of the desired effect and through the arising of the opposite.
Therefore, discrimination is conceived here too from the existence and non-existence of that.
And how does the apprehension of non-apprehension cease when there is no defect?
For even when the cause exists, the existence of the effect is not necessarily from an injunction.

children.text: pratyakṣaṃ kāryamevaṃ ca hetunānumitaṃ bhavet // MBs_2.156 //
children.translated_text: The effect is directly perceived, and thus it would be inferred from the cause.
In the case of the opposite, the absence of the fruit follows from the absence of the cause.

children.translated_text: And the means of discrimination is the presence and absence of defects for apprehension and non-apprehension — not something barred by rules. In the case of error, the causes of error are especially damaging, all the more so because of the obstruction of the desired effect and the arising of the opposite. And even in the sense organs that are free from defects, the apprehension of non-apprehension does not cease, because even when the cause exists, the effect does not necessarily follow by injunction, and there could be error. Non-perception by direct awareness would be inferred from the cause. But from the fruit, the existence of the cause is inferred. From the absence of defects, the non-existence of the effect of error is a valid inference, because the effect does not arise in the absence of the cause.
The consequence of being without a supporting object, and the attribution of another form —
these would apply even in the case of non-apprehension, since the non-attribution of one's own form is the same.

atha viparyaye cakṣuḥsaṃyuktasyālambanatvādanyatrāpyanālambanatāśaṅkā, agrahaṇe 'pi tulyā /
yathā khalu viparyayajñāne cakṣuḥsaṃprayuktavastusvabhāvanirapekṣatā dṛṣṭā samyagjñāne 'pi śaṅkyate jñānatvasāmānyāttathā cakṣuḥsaṃprayuktamapi vastu nāvikalarūpaṃ gṛhyate, tenānālambanaṃ bhavati, sadṛśasmṛtihetutāṃ ca pratipadyate ---

cakṣustvanyathāpi nālambyate /
ālambanārthaśca rajatavyavahārayogyatā śukteḥ, tathā hi rajatārthī tāmādatte /
ghaṭasyāpi hi naivānyatsvajñānālambanatvamanyatra vyavahārayogyatāyāḥ, yato na viṣayākāraṃ jñānam /
tatra śuktiḥ svarūpeṇa nālambitā rajatajñānena, tannibandhanavyavahārabhāvāt /
rajatarūpeṇa tu tannibandhanasyopādānavyavahārasya tatra bhāvāditi /
children.translated_text: If because of the supporting-object status of what is in contact with the eye in the case of error, there is apprehension of the absence of support elsewhere — the same applies to non-apprehension. Just as in erroneous cognition, the independence from the nature of the object in contact with the eye is observed, and is suspected in correct cognition too because of the common nature of being cognition — so too, even an object in contact with the eye is not apprehended in its complete form, and therefore is without a support, and one arrives at its being a cause of similar memory. Thus, the absence of support observed in non-apprehension — why should it not be suspected in apprehension too? If one says: because of the absence of defects — the same applies in error, and in the case of apprehending otherwise, there is not absence of a support. The eye, however, is not supported even otherwise. And the purpose of being a support is fitness for the practical activity of silver — for one who desires silver takes that. Even for a pot, there is no other supporting-object status for its own cognition than fitness for practical activity, since cognition does not have the form of the object. There, the mother-of-pearl is not supported in its own form by the cognition of silver, because of the absence of practical activity based on that. But in the form of silver, because of the presence of practical activity of taking based on that.
Even when the injunction has action as its culmination, someone says the following for establishing the nature of the thing:
Just as the purpose of substances is established for beating, sprinkling, and the like,
knowledge too by its nature has substances as its purpose, and because of the self being the object of action, likewise.
Let it be so; but even then, from where is the establishment of the desired form accepted?
The word is established as having the effectuality of that object of knowledge as its culmination.
What other purpose does knowledge have for the knowable than the manifestation of its own form?

children.text: adṛṣṭakalpanā yuktā na ca dṛṣṭasya saṃbhave /
children.translated_text: The postulation of something unseen is proper only when what is seen is not possible.
Therefore, just as from the injunction of sprinkling and the like regarding rice grains,
an unseen purificatory effect is understood, so too from the injunction of knowledge, the form of the self.

children.text:
yathā avaghātaprokṣaṇādayaḥ svarūpeṇaiva dravyārthāḥ, dvitīyayā ca dravyasya karmatvena nirdeśāt, tathā jñānamapi svarūpeṇa parārtham /
karmatvena cātmano nirdeśāttadartham /

bhavatu jñānasyātmārthatābhipretā /

‘evaṃvidhātmoddeśena jñānaṃ kuryāt'; na tu ‘evaṃvidha ātmā'; iti /
tatrocyate ---
na hi tatrākiñcitkarasya tādarthyena kartavyatā yujyate /
jñānasya ca karmaṇi nānyatphalaṃ tadrūpasaṃvitteḥ, na hi tasyāṃ dṛṣṭāyāmanyasyādṛṣṭasya kalpanā /
tatra yathā ‘vrīhīn prokṣati'iti prokṣaṇavidhereva vrīhiṣvadṛṣṭasaṃskārāvagamaḥ prokṣaṇaviṣayādapi /
nānyathā vrīhyarthe prokṣaṇe kartavyatā yujyate /

anupāye cenniyujyate, na svargakāmo niyukto bhavati /
anuṣṭhito 'pi na svargakāmenānuṣṭhito bhavatīti kriyāviṣayādapi vidheḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvāvagamaḥ śābdaḥ ---
tathā jñānaviṣayādapi vidherātmarūpabodhaḥ /
na hi tadvidhamātmānamuddiśyajñānaniyogo yujyate, atadvidhaścedātmā tena jñānena pratīyata iti /
children.translated_text: Just as beating, sprinkling, and the like serve the purpose of substances by their very nature — and by the instrumental case, the substance is indicated as the object of action — so too knowledge is for another's purpose by its nature. And by the instrumental case, the self is indicated as its purpose. Therefore, even an injunction that has knowledge as its object touches the form of the self; it does not culminate in knowledge alone, because from the understanding that knowledge is to be done for the purpose of the self's form, the self's form is implied by the very injunction of knowledge. One might say: Let the intended purpose of knowledge be the self. But a valid means must be stated for the cognition of the self as free from evil and the like. The word has culminated in the obligatoriness of such knowledge of the self — 'One should produce knowledge with reference to such a self' — not 'The self is of such a nature.' To this it is replied: It is not proper that what is ineffective should be made obligatory for that purpose. And knowledge has no other fruit in its action than the awareness of that form — for when that is seen, the postulation of another unseen thing is not proper. There, just as from the injunction of sprinkling 'one sprinkles the rice grains,' the understanding of an unseen purificatory effect in the rice grains comes from the injunction of sprinkling regarding its object — otherwise the obligatoriness of sprinkling for the purpose of the rice grains would not be proper. For if it does nothing there, sprinkling would not be done for that purpose — thus from the injunction alone comes the establishment of an unseen purificatory effect, just as 'one who desires heaven should sacrifice.' Otherwise, the cognition that sacrifice is obligatory for one who desires heaven would not be proper if sacrifice were not a means to heaven. And if one is enjoined regarding what is not a means, one who desires heaven would not be one who is enjoined. Even when performed, it would not be performed by one desiring heaven — thus even from the action-directed injunction, the understanding of the means-end relation is verbal. Similarly, from the knowledge-directed injunction too comes the understanding of the self's form. For the injunction of knowledge directed at such a self would not be proper unless the self were of that nature, since by that knowledge a self not of that nature would be cognized.
This has been answered, since knowledge has been shown to illuminate even what is not of its form.

children.text: jñānaṃ pradarśitaṃ na syādanyathā tadvidheḥ phalam /
children.translated_text: Otherwise there would be no fruit of that injunction of knowledge.

children.text: layo nivartyo na tathā vikṣepo hi yathāsukhaḥ // MBs_2.166 //
children.translated_text: Absorption (<s>laya</s>) is what should be removed, not distortion (<s>vikṣepa</s>); for distortion occurs easily.
And the distinction between absorption and distortion would not exist in mere non-apprehension.
Objection: In the manifestation of a non-real form, there would be the postulation of an unseen fruit.
But in the manifestation of the real form, the fruit is seen, characterized by the establishment of that.

children.text: na dṛṣṭamātrād dṛṣṭārthaṃ puruṣārthānugaṃ tu tat // MBs_2.168 //
children.translated_text: It is not merely from what is seen that the purpose is seen; rather, it follows the goal of human life.
And the nature of that does not differ between the manifestation of the real form and the non-real form.
Just as when reality is illuminated by knowledge as devoid of the elaboration of multiplicity,
the cessation of suffering, <s>karma</s>, and <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) would occur even when the non-real is manifested.
And this would be proper here, because of non-conflict with perception and the like,
and the ritual injunctions, which are non-figurative in meaning, would have their scope, since they pertain to action.

svapnajāgaritayorvikṣepikā, suṣupta ācchādikā layalakṣaṇā /
tatrācchādakāvidyānivṛttirjñānavidheḥ phalam /
taccāsat /
yato nācchādikāyā avidyāyā nivṛttiḥ puruṣeṇārthyate tathā yathā vikṣepasya /
sa hi vividhaduḥkhātmakaḥ /
layastu vividhaduḥkhanivṛtterasakṛdānandatvena śrutau gītaḥ pratyutārthanīyaḥ syāt /
api ca viparyāsamanicchato 'vidyābheda eva na syāt, avasthātraye 'pyagrahaṇamātratvāt /
tasmādagrahaṇaviparyayagrahaṇe dve avidye kāryakāraṇabhāvenāvasthite /

children.translated_text: Verse 150 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
svapnajāgaritayorubhe, kāraṇabhūtāgrahaṇalakṣaṇā suṣupta ityavidyāpravibhāga upapadyate /
taduktam ---
children.translated_text: Both are present in waking and dreaming; in deep sleep, only the causal form characterized by non-apprehension — thus the division of <s>avidyā</s> is explained. As it has been said:

From the injunction of knowledge directed at the self, this much is understood: Through knowledge, it is illuminated, is made the object of cognition, and attains fitness for practical activity. And that illumination is seen both in its own form and in another form — as when mother-of-pearl appears as silver. This has been established: This is not mere non-apprehension, but erroneous cognition (<s>anyathākhyāti</s>). Now when both are possible, from where does this follow: that the cognition of reality must be accepted, not the cognition of one thing as another? Otherwise, the injunction of self-knowledge would have no fruit. For that injunction is for the purpose of dissolving the non-self form. For it is seen that the understanding of a thing comes through the dissolution of its non-self form. And if there is no manifestation of the self in the form of the elaboration of name and form, what would be dissolved? If one thinks: This <s>avidyā</s> is of two kinds — concealing and projecting. In waking and dreaming, it is projecting; in deep sleep, it is concealing, characterized by absorption. The fruit of the injunction of knowledge is the removal of the concealing <s>avidyā</s>. But that is wrong. Because the removal of the concealing <s>avidyā</s> is not desired by a person in the way that the removal of distortion is. For distortion is of the nature of manifold suffering. But absorption, being repeatedly praised in scripture as the cessation of manifold suffering and as bliss, would rather be something to be desired. Moreover, for one who does not desire error, there would be no distinction of <s>avidyā</s>, since in all three states it would be mere non-apprehension. Therefore, non-apprehension and erroneous apprehension are two forms of <s>avidyā</s>, standing in a cause-effect relation.
'<s>Viśva</s> and <s>Taijasa</s> are bound by both cause and effect;

children.text: prājñaḥ kāraṇabaddhastu dvau tu turye na sidhyataḥ'; //
children.translated_text: <s>Prājña</s> is bound by the cause alone; but in <s>Turīya</s> (the fourth state), neither of the two is established.'

children.text:
nanvanyathāyaṃ bhedaḥ ---
agrahaṇasamyaggrahaṇābhyām /
agrahaṇalakṣaṇācchādikā suṣupte, asamyaggrahaṇamitarayoḥ /
tathā hi ---
abhinnasya vastuno 'pradeśasya grahaṇe tathābhāvasya cāgrahaṇātpṛthaktvena pratyavabhāsaḥ /
naitatsāram /
yadi tāvadasamyaggrahaṇamātraṃ tadapaṭutvaṃ vā jñānasya kenaciddrūpeṇa vā grahaṇam, na sarvātmanā /
tatra dūrasthe sūkṣme ca bhavatyapaṭu jñānaṃ sāmānyajñānam /
na ca tadavidyā /
na ca kiñcijjñānaṃ sarvātmanārthasya grāhakamiti sarvajñānamithyātvāpātaḥ /
abhedasyāgrahaṇe 'pi bhedasyāvartane 'pi bhedasyāsaṃvitterna nivartanīyamasti vidyayā /
na khalvabhedāgrahaṇaṃ nivartanīyam /
na hi tatkiñcidaparādhyati /
bhedastu vividhaduḥkhāyatanam /
athāsamyaggrahaṇaṃ pṛthakpratyavabhāso 'pṛthagātmanaḥ, abhyupetā tarhi viparyayakhyātiḥ ---
apṛthak pṛthak prakāśata iti /
children.translated_text: [Objection]: But the distinction [between deep sleep and waking/dreaming <s>avidyā</s>] is otherwise—through non-apprehension and erroneous apprehension. The concealment characterized by non-apprehension [obtains] in deep sleep; erroneous apprehension in the other two [states]. For thus: When an undivided, partless entity is apprehended, [but] its [undivided] nature is not apprehended, there is an appearance as separate. [Reply]: This is not sound. If erroneous apprehension is merely the dullness of cognition, or the apprehension through some [partial] form but not in its entirety—then in the case of a distant or subtle [object], the cognition is dull, [constituting] general knowledge. Yet that is not <s>avidyā</s>. And since no cognition whatsoever apprehends an object in its entirety, the absurd consequence would be that all cognition is false. Moreover, even if non-difference is not apprehended, and even if difference presents itself, since difference is not cognized [as real], there is nothing to be removed by knowledge. Surely, the non-apprehension of non-difference is not what needs to be removed. For it does not cause any harm. But difference is the source of manifold suffering. Now, if erroneous apprehension is the appearance as separate of what is not separate in its nature—then the doctrine of erroneous cognition (<s>viparyayakhyāti</s>) is [already] accepted: what is not separate appears as separate.

children.text:
athocyeta ---
na brūmaḥ pṛthak prakāśate, kiṃ tu pṛthagiva prakāśata iti /
ka ivārthaḥ? yadi yathā pṛthagbhūtamaprakāśamānaikatvaṃ prakāśate tathaikamapyātmatattvamagṛhyamāṇaikatvaṃ prakāśata iti /
kenacidaṃśena grahaṇaṃ sarvātmanā cāgrahaṇamuktaṃ bhavati, tatra coktam /
atha prakāśata iva, na tu prakāśate /
prakāśane ka upamārthaḥ? tannibandhanavyavahārapravṛttiḥ /
tannibandhanaścedvyavahāraḥ /
prāptaṃ prakāśanam ---
nāsati kāraṇe kāryaṃ bhavatīti /
athābhedāgraha eva pṛthaktvagrahābhimānaḥ /
tadasat, agrahaṇasyābhāvasya svarūpeṇa pararūpeṇa vā grahaṇānabhyupagamāt /
aprakāśamāne ca pṛthaktve kutastadavagrahaḥ? abhinne ca bhedābhimānaṃ parityajyābhedāgrahaṇe bhedagrahābhimānamūrīkurvatā kiṃ parihṛtaṃ syāt? tasmātsuṣṭhūcyate ---
‘layavikṣepabhedaśca na syādagrahamātrake'; iti /
children.translated_text: Now it might be replied: We do not say [that what is non-separate] appears as separate, but rather [it appears] as if separate. What is the meaning of 'as if'? If [it means that] just as [something] that has become separate appears while its oneness is not manifest—so too, even though one, the truth of the self appears while its oneness is not grasped—then the apprehension through some [partial] form while not [apprehending] in its entirety has already been stated, and [our reply] has been given regarding that. But if [it means]: it appears as if [separate], but does not [actually] appear [as separate]—what is the purpose of the comparison? [Answer]: The occurrence of transactions based on that [appearance]. If the transaction is based on that [appearance], then the [full] appearing is entailed—for an effect does not arise without a cause. But if [it is said that] the mere non-apprehension of non-difference is the conviction of separateness—that is wrong, since it is not accepted that absence, either in its own form or in the form of another, is apprehended. And when separateness is not manifest, whence would the [supposed] apprehension of it [come]? And by one who, having abandoned the conviction of difference regarding what is non-different, adopts the conviction of the apprehension of difference regarding the non-apprehension of non-difference—what would be avoided? Therefore it is well said: 'The distinction of dissolution, projection, and [their] difference would not obtain in mere non-apprehension.'

children.text:
nanvanātmarūpeṇa pratipatterna dṛśyate kiñcitphalam /
tatrādṛṣṭakalpanā syāt /
ātmarūpapratipattestu dṛṣṭaṃ phalaṃ tatsvarūpasiddhiḥ /
ucyate ---
na yasya kasyaciddarśanād dṛṣṭārthatā, kiṃ tu puruṣārthasaṃsparśinaḥ /
tena hi tadvidhirnirākāṅkṣā bhavati /
na ca puruṣārrhabhedastattvātattvapratipattyoḥ /
yathā hi viśuddhamadvaitamātmānaṃ pratipadyamānastathābhūto na śokena saṃspṛśyate, śocanīyābhāvāt /
na karmāśayamupacinoti, kartavyābhāvāt /
na kvaciddrajyati kiñcid dveṣṭi vā, viṣayābhāvāt /
‘evaṃ jīvanneva vidvānvimukto bhavati /
tathā atathābhūtamapi tathābhāvanāpuraḥsaraṃ sākṣādiva pratipadyamānaḥ /
abhūto 'pyarthaḥ paribhāvanātiśayādbhūtavyavahāraheturbhavati /
idameva cātra yujyate, pratyakṣādīnāmavirodhāt, karmavidhīnāṃ ca bhūtārthatvāt /
paramārthe hi prapañcaśūnyatve pratyakṣādīni pramāṇāni bādhyeran /
karmavidhayaścābhūtakalpanopādānavyavahārasiddhārthagocarāḥ syuḥ /
tasmādaparamārthenaivādvaitātmajñānavidhiryujyate /
children.translated_text: [Objection]: From the cognition in a form that is not the self's [own form], no fruit is observed. In that case there would have to be a postulation of an unseen [fruit]. But from the cognition of the self's [own] form, the observed fruit is the establishment of that nature. [Reply]: Not from the cognition of just anything is there observed purposefulness, but [only] from [cognition] that has contact with the human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>). For through that, the injunction [regarding knowledge] is free from expectation [of further fruit]. And there is no difference in human goal between the cognition of the truth and the cognition of what is not the truth. For just as one who cognizes the self as pure and non-dual is, in that state, not touched by sorrow—due to the absence of anything to grieve about; does not accumulate a store of <s>karma</s>—due to the absence of anything to be done; does not become attached to anything or detest anything—due to the absence of objects: 'Thus, even while living, the wise person becomes liberated.' So too, one who cognizes [the self] in a form that is not [its true form], preceded by meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) on that [form], cognizes [it] as if directly. An unreal object too, through the intensity of meditation, becomes a cause for real-world transactions. And this alone is fitting here, since it does not conflict with perception and the other [means of knowledge], and since the injunctions of ritual actions have existing facts [as their domain]. For if, in ultimate reality, [all] were void of the manifold, perception and the other means of knowledge would be sublated. And the injunctions of ritual actions would have as their domain [only] objects constituted by unreal conceptual construction. Therefore, the injunction of the knowledge of the non-dual self is fitting precisely as non-ultimate.
If [one says] 'he knows' refers to the knowledge of the truth, [it is replied:] not so, due to the qualifier of falsity and so forth. (<s>MBs</s> 2.171)
The self would not be known in that way, if [one objects:] not so, since that form is not enjoined.
If [the self's form] is established by another means of knowledge, all the less so otherwise. (<s>MBs</s> 2.172)
The knowledge of it is enjoined in the form presented by scripture.
Even in a form that is not [ultimately] real, the cognition of it is [still] possible. (<s>MBs</s> 2.173)

children.text:
yadi matam ---
‘sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ'; iti jānātistattvapariccheda eva vartate /
tena nābhūtasamāropeṇa jñānavidhiḥ syāditi /
tanna, mithyātvādibhirjñānaṃ viśeṣyate ---
mithyājñānaṃ samyagjñānaṃ saṃśayajñānamiti /
tadekaniyame nopapadyeta, paunaruktyādvirodhācca /
syādetat ---
asvarūpeṇa pratipattau na tadātmajñānam, anyajñānameva bhavati /
tattvajñānaṃ ca vidhīyate /
tasmāttattvasiddhiriti /
tacca na /
na khalvetāvadeva tat ---
‘ātmā jñātavyaḥ iti /

yadi syāttadrūpajñānavidhiḥ /
tacca na, ubhayathānupapatteḥ /
pramāṇāntarasiddhaṃ cedātmarūpaṃ na tajjñānaṃ vidheyam /
athāsiddham, aśakyameva tat /
syādetat ---
‘apahatapāpmā vijaro vimṛtyuḥ'; ‘idaṃ sarvaṃ yadayamātmā'iti śabdasamarpitarūpasya tasya jñānaṃ vidhīyate, tena ca tattvenāpi tatsaṃbhavati samāropitenāpi, tena na niyogatastathābhūtajñānavidhestathābhāvo 'sya pratīyate /
children.translated_text: if there were an injunction of knowledge of [the self's] true form. But that is not [tenable], since it is untenable in either way. If the self's form is established by another means of knowledge, that knowledge [of it] need not be enjoined. But if [its form is] not established, then that [knowledge] is simply impossible. [Objection]: The <s>śruti</s> '<s>apahatapāpmā vijaro vimṛtyuḥ</s>' ('Free from evil, ageless, deathless') and '<s>idaṃ sarvaṃ yadayamātmā</s>' ('All this is what this self is')—the knowledge of it in the form presented by scripture is enjoined; and through that [scriptural form], it is possible both as truth and as superimposition; hence it is not the case that by force of the injunction, the knowledge in its true form is [necessarily] understood.

If it is thought: '<s>sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ</s>' ('He is to be inquired into')—here the root <s>jñā</s> ('to know') functions in the sense of ascertaining the truth. Hence there would be no injunction of knowledge through unreal superimposition. [Reply]: That is not so, since knowledge is qualified by [the adjectives] 'false,' and so forth: false knowledge, correct knowledge, doubtful knowledge. If restricted to one [meaning alone], this would not be tenable, due to redundancy and contradiction. [Objection]: But cognition in a form that is not [the self's own] form is not knowledge of that self; it is simply knowledge of something else. And what is enjoined is knowledge of the truth. Therefore, the establishment of the truth [follows]. [Reply]: That too is not so. For surely this alone is not [the whole of it]: 'the self is to be known'—

children.text: jñānaṃ yadi ca dṛṣṭārthaṃ prāptaṃ dṛṣṭata eva tat /
children.translated_text: And if knowledge has an observed fruit, it is established from the observed [fruit] alone.
For one who desires to inquire about the self's form, [knowledge] of one who does not desire to inquire is pointless. (<s>MBs</s> 2.174)
And if the means to that [knowledge] is not known, let the injunction be regarding that [means] alone.
Injunctions such as threshing and the like are not devoid of contact with the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>). (<s>MBs</s> 2.175)
If this knowledge is enjoined because it is supramundane,

children.text: na rūpasiddhaye tāvadyataḥ kartavyatā vidheḥ // MBs_2.176 //
children.translated_text: [the injunction is] not for the establishment of the [self's] form, since the obligatory character [of an injunction is needed for that]. (<s>MBs</s> 2.176)
And the obligatory character regarding an observed object is established from the observed [fruit] alone.
Therefore, when the supramundane form of the object has been communicated by scripture, (<s>MBs</s> 2.177)
a person is spontaneously inclined toward the knowledge [of it], since [knowledge] is the means to the knowable.

children.text: tadupāye tvavijñāte vidhinā sa pravartyatām // MBs_2.178 //
children.translated_text: But when the means to that [knowledge] is unknown, let him be prompted by an injunction. (<s>MBs</s> 2.178)
The entry of injunction [into the knowledge of existing reality] thereby destroys [its] authoritativeness as a means of knowledge.
[<s>Brahman</s>] is an existing fact, and therefore should not be meditated upon by one who desires the understanding of existing fact. (<s>MBs</s> 2.179)

children.text:
yadi ca jñānasya dṛṣṭaṃ phalam, tata eva pravṛttisiddhe vyartho vidhiḥ /
yo hyātmarūpamanubhavitukāmaḥ, sa tasya jñāne svayameva yatate /
yastu na tathā, tasya tadvyarthamiti vidhiśatenāpi sa na pravartyate /
athopāyājñānāddṛṣṭaphale 'pi na pravartate svayam, ato vidhīyata iti /

eva /

advaitātmajñānamadṛṣṭapūrvamalaukikam /

kimarthaṃ vidhīyate /
pramāṇāntarāgocarasya svarūpapratipattyartham, āhosvidanuṣṭhānārtham? tatra na svarūpasiddhyartham, anuṣṭhānaphalo hi vidhirnānuṣṭhānāya, dṛṣṭārthatvādeva tatsiddheḥ /
tasmādalaukike 'pahatapāpmādirūpa ātmatattve śabdātpratipanne tasya sākṣājjñānaṃ prati tadanubhavopāyatvātsvayameva puruṣasyābhimukhyaṃ bhavatīti vyarthaṃ tadvidhānam, yathāścaryabhūte kasmiṃścidarthe āgamātpratipanne tasya sākṣātkaraṇe svayamevonmukhatvaṃ bhavati /
tadupāyeṣu tvajñāteṣūpāyatvajñāpanāya vidhānaṃ yujyate /
tadevaṃ jñāne niyogānupapatterniyoge ca vasturūpāvagame prāmāṇyāyogādvyavasthitātmatattvapratipattimicchatā śabdānna tasya niyogānupraveśo 'bhyupagantavya iti /
children.translated_text: of his own accord. [Objection]: But even in cases like threshing and the like, which have an observed fruit, an injunction is observed. [Reply]: True, but not one devoid of contact with the unseen. For even there, the fruit [that comes] from restriction—[namely,] the accomplishment of the principal [ritual], [whether the rice is obtained] from the [unhusked] grains or through a winnowing basket—is unseen indeed. Now it is thought: The knowledge of the non-dual self is unprecedented and supramundane. Hence, even though having an immediate fruit, it is enjoined. To this it is replied: For what purpose is it enjoined? For the establishment of the [self's] nature, which is not within the domain of another means of knowledge? Or for [prompting] performance? In that case, it is not for the establishment of [its] nature, since an injunction has performance as its fruit, not performance [as its means]; for the establishment of that [nature] is already [achieved] from the observed [fruit] alone. Therefore, when the supramundane reality of the self—characterized as free from evil and the like—has been communicated by scripture, a person spontaneously becomes inclined toward its direct realization, because of the means-character of [knowledge] for that experience—just as when some wondrous object, communicated through scripture, [is known], one spontaneously becomes inclined toward its direct realization. But regarding the means [to that realization] that are unknown, an injunction for making known their means-character is fitting. Thus, since an injunction is untenable regarding knowledge, and since in the case of an injunction, authoritativeness for the comprehension of the reality of [an existing] object would be unfitting—one who desires the comprehension of the established reality of the self from scripture should not accept the entry of injunction into it.

And if knowledge has an observed fruit, then since engagement [in knowledge] is established from that alone, an injunction is pointless. For one who desires to experience the self's nature strives of his own accord toward that knowledge. But one who does not [so desire]—for him it is useless, so even a hundred injunctions would not prompt him. [Objection]: But even regarding an observed fruit, [a person] does not engage spontaneously due to ignorance of the means; hence [the means] is enjoined. [Reply]: That is fine. Then let that very means be enjoined, regarding which he has not engaged due to ignorance. But regarding knowledge, since it has an observed fruit, he does engage
Now, for the refutation of the second [type of] injunction—[namely,] the injunction of the cognition-continuum (<s>vijñānasaṃtānavidhi</s>)—[the author] says:
For that very reason, there is no [need for] the culmination in an injunction of a cognition-continuum.
In that case too, as before, there would be no valid cognition of one's own nature. (<s>MBs</s> 2.180)
But from scripture, which terminates in [the self's] own nature, [the self] having been known, from another statement
the injunction of meditation (<s>upāsanā</s>) may be [derived]; or even that would be pointless, since [one is already] inclined. (<s>MBs</s> 2.181)
Since through repetition (<s>abhyāsa</s>), the intensification of the cognition is observed,
therefore, the authoritativeness of the <s>Vedānta</s> [texts] regarding an object that is not to be accomplished is established. (<s>MBs</s> 2.182)
