tathā ca tadevottareṇa prapañcyate ‘nānudhyāyādbahūñchabdān'; ityekavākyatā /
anyathā vākyaṃ bhidyeta /
śabdamātre cānudhyānāprasaṅgāt śabdapūrvattvāttasya śabdārthaviṣayamevedamiti /
evam ‘ātmetyevopāsīta'ityevakāraśrutestadarthavidhiḥ /
‘nididhyāsitavyaḥ'; ityapi ‘ātmanastu kāmāya'; ityupakramāt ‘idaṃ sarvaṃ
children.translated_text: That too is not fitting for the very reason stated above, since the absurd consequence would be the absence of a means of knowledge for the comprehension of reality, and since the sentence would be directed toward something other [than the self's nature]. But if it is accepted that, after the reality has been ascertained from another sentence that terminates in [the self's] nature, the injunction of a stream of cognition regarding that [reality] is [what is intended]—so be it. There is no fault in that. And thus '<s>vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta</s>' ('Having known, he should form a wisdom') shows that the knowledge of the self's reality is [already] accomplished. But even that [injunction of meditation] is pointless, since the purpose is [already] attained. For reflection on that [reality] having direct realization as its fruit has an observed purpose—no other fruit is expected from it. For immortality (<s>amṛtatva</s>) is nothing other than the manifestation of one's own nature—as has been described earlier. And in ordinary experience, the practice of knowledge is observed to be a cause of the clarification of correct knowledge. For through a particular meditation, even what is unreal comes to be experienced [as real]; how much more so what is real. The [<s>śruti</s>] '<s>sa kratuṃ kurvīta</s>' ('he should form an intention') does not enjoin reflection on the truth of the self that transcends all distinctions, with [the manifestation of] that nature as its fruit; rather, [it enjoins] meditation on the self in the forms of name, form, mind-made [self], <s>prāṇa</s>-body and the like as limiting adjuncts, with sovereignty as its fruit; or, gradually, with direct realization as [its] fruit. '<s>Tameva dhīro vijñāya</s>' ('The wise one, having known that alone')—this is not an injunction to make [that] the object of wisdom. From the hearing of '<s>tameva</s>' ('that alone'), since it involves the exclusion of other [objects], the purport is understood to be in the exclusion; [just as in] '<s>raktaḥ paṭo bhavati</s>' ('the cloth becomes dyed'), the sentence is directed toward the dyeing. Here, the non-difference [of the self] has been taught preceded by the distinction from the reality of space and the like; regarding [the self] thus [distinguished], when the occasion for making [it] the object of wisdom [arises], '<s>tameva</s>' ('that alone') is stated to prevent [meditation on] that [distinction from elements]. And thus in the first half [of the verse]: '<s>virajaḥ para ākāśādaja ātmā mahān dhruvaḥ</s>' ('Stainless, supreme beyond space, unborn, the self, great, eternal')—the truth of the self is shown as being beyond space and the like. When the occasion arises for making it the object of wisdom in that very [form], '<s>tameva</s>' ('that alone') is said to prevent that [meditation on distinctions from elements]. Otherwise there would be no purpose for the word '<s>eva</s>' ('alone'), nor would what is to be excluded be understood. And thus the subsequent [verse] elaborates: '<s>nānudhyāyādbahūñchabdān</s>' ('one should not meditate on many words')—forming a single sentence. Otherwise, the sentence would be split. And since meditation on mere words is not appropriate, and since that [meditation] is preceded by the word-meaning, this [injunction] is about the word-meaning alone. Similarly, '<s>ātmetyevopāsīta</s>' ('one should meditate [on it] as "self" alone')—from the hearing of '<s>eva</s>' ('alone'), it is an injunction of the exclusion of other [designations]. '<s>Nididhyāsitavyaḥ</s>' ('he is to be meditated upon')—this too, from the introductory [context] '<s>ātmanastu kāmāya</s>' ('but for the sake of the self'), [extending to] '<s>idaṃ sarvaṃ</s>' ('all this')—

children.text:
yadayamātmā'ityupasaṃhārādātmasvarūpaparamekaṃ vākyam /
tadantargatāḥ ‘draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ'; iti na pṛthagvidhayaḥ kṛtyapratyayayoge 'pi /
kṛtyapratyayasyārthāntare 'pi smaraṇādarhādau stutyarthāḥ yathopāṃśuyājavākyāntargatāḥ ‘viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ'ityevamādayaḥ /
‘aitadātmyamidaṃ sarvaṃ tatsatyaṃ sa ātmā tattvamasi'iti bhūta eva paryavasitaṃ vākyam /
tatra ‘sadasmi ---
iti dhārayet'; iti kalpaneyam /
tasmāttrividhasyāpi jñānasya vidheyatvāyogāt, vinā ca vidhervākyārthapratipatteḥ, apauruṣeyatvena nirapekṣatvādbhūte 'pyarthe vedāntānāṃ prāmāṇyasiddhiḥ /
tathā ca ‘tattu samanvayāt'iti codanālakṣaṇāddharmāttuśabdena viśeṣyaṃ brahma samanvayagamyamuktam /
samanvayo hi padārthānāṃ saṃsargo viniyogastato brahma gamyate, na codanāta ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: '<s>yadayamātmā</s>' ('what this self is')—concluding [thus], is a single sentence with the self's own nature as its supreme [purport]. The [expressions] contained within it—'<s>draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ</s>' ('it is to be seen, heard, meditated upon')—are not separate injunctions, even though they have the potential-passive (<s>kṛtya</s>) suffix. For the potential-passive suffix is remembered in other senses too, such as laudatory [expressions] regarding an <s>arhat</s>—like '<s>viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ</s>' ('Viṣṇu is to be worshipped with the <s>upāṃśu</s> [libation]') and similar [expressions] that are contained within the <s>upāṃśuyāja</s>-sentence and serve a laudatory purpose. '<s>Aitadātmyamidaṃ sarvaṃ tatsatyaṃ sa ātmā tattvamasi</s>' ('This whole world has that as its self; that is the truth; that is the self; you are that')—this sentence terminates in existing fact. The [instruction] '<s>sadasmi—iti dhārayet</s>' ('he should hold in mind: "I am Being"') is a [secondary] adaptation [of that sentence]. Therefore, since the enjoinability of all three kinds of knowledge is untenable, and since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is [achieved] without an injunction, and since [<s>Vedic</s> scripture] is independent due to being authorless (<s>apauruṣeya</s>)—the authoritativeness of the <s>Vedānta</s> [texts] even regarding an existing fact is established. And thus, '<s>tattu samanvayāt</s>' ('But that, because of the connection')—the word '<s>tu</s>' distinguishes <s>Brahman</s>, which is known through the connection (<s>samanvaya</s>) [of Vedānta sentences], from <s>dharma</s> characterized by injunction (<s>codanā</s>). For the connection of word-referents—their conjunction and application—is [the means by which] <s>Brahman</s> is known; not from injunction. This is the meaning.

As for the view: [The <s>śrutis</s>] '<s>sa kratuṃ kurvīta</s>' ('he should form an intention'), '<s>prajñāṃ kurvīta</s>' ('he should form a wisdom'), '<s>nididhyāsitavyaḥ</s>' ('he is to be meditated upon')—even where the culmination in one's own nature is apparent, as in '<s>tattvamasi</s>' ('You are that'), even there, since '<s>sadasmi—iti ceto dhārayet</s>' ('he should hold in mind: I am Being') is the intended [teaching], what is enjoined is reflection (<s>anucintana</s>) and meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>)—a stream of cognition different from [mere] hearing—as an action, just like the fruit of immortality [from a ritual action].

children.text:
nanvaviśeṣeṇa kārye 'rthe vedasya prāmāṇyaṃ varṇitam ---
‘codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ'; iti /
codanālakṣaṇo vedārtha ityarthaḥ /
naitatsāram /
evaṃ hi siddhaprāmāṇyavedārthavicāro 'yaṃ syāttaduttaralakṣaṇavat /
tatrānantaraṃ prāmāṇyapratipādanaṃ na yujyeta, ‘vṛttaṃ pramāṇalakṣaṇam'; iti ca /
mantrārthavādeṣu ca kāryārthatvena vipratipattirna syāt /
sā copariṣṭādeva nirasiṣyate bahu cātra vaktavyamityalaṃ prasaṅgena /
children.translated_text: Objection: The validity of the <s>Veda</s> regarding what is to be done has been stated without distinction: '<s>Dharma</s> is that which is characterized by <s>codanā</s> (injunction)' — meaning the object of the <s>Veda</s> is characterized by injunction. This is not sound. For in that case, this would be an inquiry into the Vedic meaning whose validity is already established, like the subsequent definition. Then the subsequent establishment of validity would not be proper, along with the principle that 'the definition of valid means of knowledge has been completed.' And there would be no disagreement regarding <s>mantras</s> and <s>arthavādas</s> as having meaning directed toward duty. And that will be refuted later; and much more could be said here — enough of this digression.
Just as understanding, when declared free from conflict with other means of knowledge, attains the status of valid means regarding what is to be done,
so too regarding what is already established, being born from scripture that is not of human origin (<s>apauruṣeya</s>), because of its independence.
Thus ends the third chapter, the <s>Niyogakāṇḍa</s> (Chapter on Injunction).
Verse 156 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>
Fourth Chapter: <s>Siddhikāṇḍa</s> (Chapter on Accomplishment)

children.text:
evaṃ tāvatpratipattikartavyatāprāmāṇyavyājena yairaprāmāṇyamuktaṃ tatpratibodhanāya kṛtaḥ prayatnaḥ; idānīṃ tvaprāmāṇyamevāhurye tadbodhanāya prayatyate /
tatra pūrvapakṣaḥ ---
children.translated_text: Thus far, the effort has been made to awaken those who declared invalidity under the pretext that validity requires an obligation to be cognized. Now, however, an effort is made to awaken those who declare outright invalidity. The opponent's position:
Since sentence-meaning consists of words with connected meanings, without attaining the status of word-meaning,
there would be no sentence-meaning; and if it has the status of word-meaning, it is knowable through another means of knowledge.

children.text:
na tāvadbrahmāntaryāmyādipadaṃ pramāṇam, saṃbandhajñānāpekṣayā pūrvasiddhe pratyayahetutvena /
nāpi vākyam; na hi tatsākṣādvācakam; padārthadvārā tu tat pratipattiḥ; apadārthe jñānasyābhāvāt /
te hi saṃsargādguṇapradhānabhāvenetarapadārthaviśiṣṭamekaṃ padārthaṃ gamayanti /
tatra padārtha eva viśiṣṭo vākyārtho bhavati /
na cānadhigateṣu pramāṇāntareṇa padārthatvam; sambandhajñānāpekṣaṇāt ityuktam /
tatrāpadārthatve na vākyaviṣayatvam; anavabodhakaṃ teṣāṃ vākyam /
padārthatve pramāṇāntarādhigateranuvādakam /
tatrātyantāparidṛṣṭabrahmādyarthapramāṇābhimateṣu vākyeṣu tadvācīni padāni syuḥ, na vā /
yadi na santi na ta itaraiḥ saṃsṛjyeran na bhidyeranniti na teṣāṃ prameyāḥ loṣṭādivat /
atha tu santi, tathāpi tairadhigatasaṃbandhairna pratipādyeran apratipannāśca na viśiṣṭavākyārthapratipattihetavaḥ; tatra yathā 'vanātpika ānīyatam'; iti pikapadārthajñāne 'vabodhakatvaṃ tathā teṣāmapi /
tasmānna codanāto 'pūrvapadārthāvagamaḥ; sā hi vidhipratiṣedhābhyāṃ kriyāsu puruṣamadhikaroti; traividhyavṛddhaparigrahastu japopayogāt, upaniṣado vedāntāḥ; ---
iti tatra viniyogāt /
children.translated_text: First, words like '<s>Brahman</s>,' 'inner controller' (<s>antaryāmin</s>), and the like are not a valid means, because they function as causes of cognition only with regard to what is already known, due to the requirement of knowing the word-object relation. Nor is the sentence a valid means; for it does not directly denote it; rather, the understanding comes through the word-meanings; since there is no knowledge of what is not a word-meaning. For the words, through their connection — by the relation of principal and subordinate — convey a single word-meaning qualified by the meanings of the other words. There, the word-meaning as qualified becomes the sentence-meaning. And there is no status of word-meaning for what has not been ascertained through another means of knowledge — because the knowledge of the word-object relation is required, as has been said. If they are not word-meanings, they are not the subject of the sentence; the sentence does not communicate them. If they are word-meanings, they are already ascertained through another means of knowledge, and the sentence merely restates them. Regarding the sentences believed to be valid means for objects like <s>Brahman</s> and the like, which are entirely unseen: either the words denoting them exist or they do not. If they do not exist, they would not be connected with or distinguished from other words, and so those objects would not be knowable — like a clod of earth. But if they do exist, even so, they would not communicate what has not been previously established through a known word-object relation; and what has not been understood cannot serve as a cause for the understanding of a qualified sentence-meaning. There, just as in 'Let a <s>pika</s> (cuckoo) be brought from the forest' — without knowledge of the meaning of the word <s>pika</s>, the sentence does not communicate — so too with those words. Therefore, there is no understanding of unprecedented word-meanings from injunction; for injunction, through positive and negative commands, engages a person in actions. And the threefold division accepted by the learned is that they are useful for recitation, and the <s>Upaniṣads</s> are <s>Vedānta</s> — hence their assignment there.
To this it is replied:
When the status of word-meaning is established through a general term, then through particular qualities that are uncommon,
the communication of an unprecedented specific object is possible, just as in the ordinary world.
Verse 157 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
yathā loke ‘dvīpaviśeṣe evaṃnāmāno maratakamayapādāḥ padmarāgamayacañcavaḥ sauvarṇarājatapakṣāḥ pakṣiṇaḥ'iti pakṣisāmānyaṃ pramāṇāntaradhigatamananyasādhāraṇena dharmakalāpena saṃsṛjyamānaṃ pramāṇāntarānadhigataṃ viśeṣarūpamāsādayati, vākyena ca pramīyate pramāṇāntarānadhigatena viśeṣarūpeṇa ---
sarvasyaiva hi vākyasyānadhigato viśeṣa eva prameyaḥ tathā kāraṇasāmānyaṃ vā satsāmānyaṃ vā ‘yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante'; iti ‘asthūlamanaṇvahrasvam'ityādipadārthaiḥ saṃsargādbhedācca pramāṇāntarānadhigataṃ viśeṣarūpamāsādayati, vākyasya ca prameyaṃ bhavati /
tadevaṃ lokasiddhapadārthānvayenaivāpūrvārthapratipatternānavabodhakatvamanuvādakatvaṃ vā /
children.translated_text: Just as in the ordinary world — 'On a certain island there are birds named such-and-such, with feet of emerald, crests of ruby, and wings of gold and silver' — the general concept of 'bird,' ascertained through another means of knowledge, when connected with a cluster of properties that are unique and not shared with others, arrives at a specific form not ascertained through another means of knowledge, and is known through the sentence in a specific form not ascertained by another means — for the object of every sentence is indeed an unascertained specific — so too the general concept of 'cause' or 'being' in 'from which indeed these beings are born' and 'neither gross nor subtle, neither short,' through connection with and distinction from those word-meanings, arrives at a specific form not ascertained by another means of knowledge, and becomes the object of the sentence. Thus, through the connection with word-meanings already established in the world, the understanding of an unprecedented meaning is achieved — there is neither failure to communicate nor mere restatement.
Or, since the nature of <s>Brahman</s> is established as knowable by every cognition,
the dissolution of the manifest world is what is communicated by the word.
In the form in which the manifest world is dissolved, it is not the object
of any other means of knowledge — thus it is held to be founded on scripture alone.

children.text:
athavā na loke 'tyantamaprasiddhaṃ brahma, sarvapratyayavedyatvāt, brahmaṇo vyatirekeṇa pratyetavyasyābhāvāt, viśeṣapratyayānāṃ ca sāmānyarūpānugamāt, bhedopasaṃhārāvaśiṣṭaṃ ca satyaṃ brahma ---
iti pratipādanāt, ‘vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ mṛttiketyeva satyam'; iti dṛṣṭāntāt /
kiṃ tarhi śabdena pratipādyate? prapañcābhāvaḥ /
tatra prapañcapadārtho 'pi siddhaḥ, niṣedho 'pi siddhaḥ, tayoḥ saṃsargāttadabhāvapratipattiḥ /
āmnāyaikanibandhanatvaṃ tu tasyocyate, pratyakṣādīnāmavidyāsaṃbhinnatvāt; pratyastamitanikhilabhedena rūpeṇāviṣayīkaraṇādbhedapratyastamayasyāmnāyāvagamyatvāditi /
children.translated_text: Alternatively, <s>Brahman</s> is not entirely unknown in the world, since it is knowable by every cognition, since there is nothing to be cognized apart from <s>Brahman</s>, since particular cognitions follow the general form, and since <s>Brahman</s> is the truth that remains when differences are withdrawn — as communicated by the illustration 'modification is a mere name, a verbal handle; the truth is just clay.' What then does the word communicate? The absence of the manifest world. There, the word-meaning of 'manifest world' is established, negation too is established, and from their connection comes the understanding of its absence. But it is said to be founded on scripture alone, because perception and the like are tainted by <s>avidyā</s> — they do not objectify the form in which all difference has ceased — and because the cessation of difference is known only from scripture.
The opponent further insists:
Surely purposelessness for persons would follow in the case of what concerns established facts.

children.text: yat khalu vākyaṃ na puruṣaṃ kvaciddhitasādhane pravartayati ahitasādhanācca

children.translated_text: Verse 158 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
nivartayati, kevalaṃ siddhamarthamanvācaṣṭe, tadapuruṣārtham; apuruṣārthatvācconmattapralāpavadapramāṇam; tathā ca prāyeṇa vedāntāḥ /
ucyate ---
children.translated_text: but merely narrates an established fact — that is purposeless for persons. Being purposeless for persons, it is invalid like the raving of a madman. And such are most of the <s>Vedānta</s> texts. It is replied:
A sentence that does not prompt a person toward a means of well-being and does not deter from a means of harm,
A valid means of knowledge does not have its culmination solely in being useful to persons.

children.text:
(upekṣāmapi hi phalaṃ pramāṇasya pracakṣate) /
(anena ślokārdhenātra bhavitavyamityabhyūhaḥ; paraṃ tu mātṛkāsu na dṛśyate /
--- editor)
children.translated_text: (For they declare that even indifference is a fruit of a valid means of knowledge.) (The editor notes: This half-verse is conjectured here, but is not found in the manuscripts.)

children.text: api cājñānataḥ śokī duḥkhī jīvaḥ prakāśate // MBs_4.6 //
children.translated_text: Moreover, the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) appears as one who grieves and suffers due to ignorance.
And the knowledge that removes that is considered to be the purpose of human life in itself.
When a certain object is known, for people who are agitated with curiosity,
the arising of knowledge is accepted as fulfilling the purpose of human life.
And just as there is no purposelessness for persons in perception and the like, which concern established facts,

children.text: na ca pravṛttiniṣṭhatvaṃ tathāsmin kena vāryate /
children.translated_text: how can its having activity as its culmination be denied here?

children.text: jñeyasya puruṣārthatvaṃ tatra cedatra tatsamam // MBs_4.9 //
children.translated_text: If the knowable in that case is purposeful for persons, then in this case it is the same.
<s>Brahman</s> is itself the purpose of human life — peaceful, free from old age and the like.
Therefore, by the instruction '<s>Tat tvam asi</s>' (That thou art), the student is taught.
If it is held that perception and the like serve as auxiliaries to further activity,
let that auxiliary status be accepted here too, for the activity of direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>).

children.text:
na tāvanniyogataḥ pramāṇasya puruṣārthaphalatā /
na khalu hitopādānāhitahāne eva pramāṇaphale; upekṣāmapi hi pramāṇaphalaṃ pramāṇavida ācakṣate /
na ca puruṣārthatā pramāṇalakṣaṇam, pramāhetutvaṃ tu /
tasmānna puruṣārthābhāvenāprāmāṇyam /
api ca ‘śokyaham'duḥkhyaham'; 'dhanādīni mama naṣṭāni'iti viśuddhabrahmātmano jīvasya mithyājñānam; etannivṛttirūpaṃ ca viśuddhānandaprakāśabrahmātmatatvajñānam /
tat svarūpeṇaiva puruṣārthaḥ; aniṣṭanivṛttirūpatvādiṣṭāvirbhāvācca /
yadyapi ca saṃskārāttasyānuvṛttistathāpi śābdajñānamanusaṃtanvato viduṣo na pūrvavadbhavati nivartate cātyantāya /
dṛṣṭā ca jñānotpattereva puruṣārthatā kvacit kutūhalākulitānāmajñāte'rthe /
na hi

children.translated_text: Verse 159 of <s>Brahmasiddhi</s> <s>kārikā</s>

children.text:
tajjñānāt paramanyadarthyate /
na ca pravṛttinivṛttiviṣayasyaiva puruṣārthateti niyamaḥ; pratyakṣādīni hi pramāṇāni; na ca tāvatpravṛttinivṛttiparāṇi siddhavastuviṣayāṇi; na ca puruṣārthatāṃ jahati /
yadi matam ---
pratyakṣādijñeyaṃ hi siddhaṃ vastu puruṣārthaḥ salilādiḥ, tadupakārāt; tataḥ pratyakṣādīnāṃ puruṣārthatā bhūtaniṣṭhānāmapi /
atrāpi ca śabdaprameyaṃ svayameva brahma puruṣārtho jarādivividhāśivopaśamāt paramānandaprakāśatvācca suprasannam /
ata eva 'tattvamasi'iti śvetaketumukhenāśāsanīyāya puruṣāya śrutyābhinnamupadiśyate; abhinnaṃ hi tadanuśāsanīyāt /
bhedena ca pratīyamānaṃ na puruṣārthaḥ /
tattve tādātmyajñāne ca tathābhāvāt viśvāśivopaśamāt paramaśivabhāvācca paripūrṇaḥ puruṣārtho āpto bhavati /
yadi matam ---
children.translated_text: nothing else beyond that knowledge is sought. And there is no rule that only what pertains to activity and withdrawal has purpose for persons; for perception and the like are valid means of knowledge, and they do not entirely concern activity and withdrawal but concern established objects, and yet they do not lose their purposefulness for persons. If it is thought that the established object knowable through perception and the like — water and the like — is the purpose of human life, due to its utility, and hence perception and the like have purpose even though they concern established facts — here too, <s>Brahman</s>, which is the object of scriptural knowledge, is itself the supreme purpose of human life, being most excellent due to the cessation of the manifold evils of old age and the like, and due to being the manifestation of supreme bliss. For this very reason, <s>Śvetaketu</s> is taught through the scripture '<s>Tat tvam asi</s>' (That thou art) as being non-different from a person who is to be instructed; for that <s>Brahman</s> is non-different from the one being instructed. And what is cognized as different is not the purpose of human life. In the truth, through the knowledge of identity, because of that state — through the cessation of all evil and the state of supreme auspiciousness — the complete purpose of human life is attained. If one thinks:
perception and the like too are merely auxiliaries to activity,
because activity characterized by abandonment, adoption, and the like is rooted in the ascertained object;

children.text: īdṛśaṃ pravṛtyaṅgatvamatrāpyastyeva, śabdāt pramite brahmaṇi sākṣātkaraṇāya pravṛtteriṣṭatvāditi //
children.translated_text: such auxiliary status to activity exists here too, since the activity toward direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) of <s>Brahman</s> ascertained from scripture is desirable.

It is not from injunction that a valid means of knowledge has purposefulness for persons as its fruit. It is not the case that only the adoption of what is beneficial and the abandonment of what is harmful are the fruits of valid means; for the knowers of valid means declare that even indifference is a fruit of a valid means. And purposefulness for persons is not the defining characteristic of a valid means; rather, being the cause of valid cognition is. Therefore, there is no invalidity from the absence of purpose for persons. Moreover, the <s>jīva</s>, whose true nature is pure <s>Brahman</s>, has the false knowledge 'I am a grieving one,' 'I am a suffering one,' 'my wealth and the like are lost.' And the knowledge of the truth that the self is <s>Brahman</s>, of the nature of pure consciousness and bliss, which has the form of the removal of that false knowledge — that is itself the purpose of human life, by its very nature, both because of the removal of the undesired and the manifestation of the desired. And even though there is continuation of the previous state due to latent impressions, for the wise one who cultivates the knowledge born of scripture, it is not as before, and it ceases definitively. And the purposefulness of the mere arising of knowledge is observed in some cases, for those agitated with curiosity about an unknown object. Surely,

eṣā vedāntatattvapravicayacaturaprasphurannyāyatejā
mārgaṃ mukternirundhannibiḍamapi tamo 'nādi nirdārayantī /
sadyaḥ prakṣālayantī ghanamapi jagatāṃ tīrthadustarkapaṅkaṃ
vyākhyātotkhātaviśvā śivaniratiśayaśreyase brahmasiddhiḥ // MBs_4.12 //
children.translated_text: This <s>Brahmasiddhi</s>, skilled in the investigation of <s>Vedānta</s> truth, blazing with the brilliance of reasoning that comes forth unbidden, tearing apart the dense darkness — beginningless though it be — that blocks the path to liberation, instantly washing away the thick mire of fruitless speculation that is so hard for the world to cross, having uprooted the manifest universe as explained — may it be for the auspicious, unsurpassed supreme good!
Thus ends the <s>Brahmasiddhi</s>, the composition of <s>Maṇḍana Miśra</s>.
